Without those specifics and supporting budget documents or reporting, the assertion that 'we had to cut $13 billion in state spending over two years' is unprovable and thus treated as false for lack of evidence.

claim: "Leonardo DiCaprio explains why he’s moving to Casselberry, Florida."
rationale: There are no credible news reports or statements from Leonardo DiCaprio indicating he is moving to Casselberry, Florida. Celebrity relocations are widely reported and DiCaprio’s known residences are elsewhere, so this claim appears to be rumor or satire rather than fact.

claim: Wisconsin has "the fastest-shrinking middle class in the country."
rationale: The statement is a definitive superlative without specifying a time period or income-definition. While Wisconsin has seen middle-class shrinkage in some analyses, reputable sources (Census, Pew, Brookings) do not consistently rank Wisconsin as having the single fastest-shrinking middle class across standard measures and time frames. The claim overstates the evidence as presented.

claim: "Just passed into law today: You cannot go 5 miles over speed limit" in North Carolina.
rationale: I am not aware of any North Carolina law, as of my latest knowledge cutoff, that was just passed banning driving 5 mph over the speed limit statewide. Changes to speed enforcement or statutory speed limits require passage by the North Carolina legislature and publication by state authorities; there were no widely reported emergency enactments of this rule. Social posts claiming immediate new statewide bans are often misunderstandings or refer to proposed bills, local ordinances, or enforcement practices rather than a new law.

claim: Says "Joe Biden is absolutely on board with defunding the police."
rationale: Joe Biden has publicly and repeatedly said he does not support "defunding the police." During his 2020 campaign and in office he has advocated policing reforms and targeted investments in community policing, mental health, and violence prevention rather than eliminating or wholesale defunding of police departments.

claim: Says Jacob Blake "declared he had a gun in the car and was going to go get it" and was "brandishing" a knife
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and released video/bodycam evidence do not support that Jacob Blake himself clearly declared he had a gun in the car and was going to retrieve it, nor that he was actively brandishing a knife at the time he was shot. Police and some officials suggested a knife was involved and later said a knife was found in Blake’s vehicle, but no gun was found and eyewitness/video evidence shows Blake leaning into his SUV rather than brandishing a weapon.

claim: Says of El Paso that some years, "in a city of almost 700,000, we had five murders the entire year. Our average over the last 10 years is 18 (murders per year). We exceeded that average just on one day" after a gunman opened fire at a Walmart in the city.
rationale: El Paso’s population is roughly 680,000–700,000 and the city is known for very low homicide counts; some reported years had single‑digit homicides (as low as five). A ten‑year average in the high teens is consistent with city homicide data, and the August 2019 Walmart shooter killed 22 people—exceeding a roughly 18‑per‑year average in one day.

claim: "More than 32,000 Americans lose their lives to gun violence each year."
rationale: U.S. official mortality data show annual firearm-related deaths well above 32,000 in recent years (for example, roughly 43–49 thousand in 2020–2021). Those totals include suicides, homicides, accidental shootings, and legal interventions, so the broad statement is accurate for overall gun-related fatalities.

claim: In Sauk City, Wisconsin, "the ID office" that provides identification for voting "is only open on the fifth Wednesday of every month" -- a total of four days in 2016.
rationale: I could not corroborate the assertion that any Sauk City office that issues voter IDs was restricted to opening only on 'the fifth Wednesday' and therefore only four days in 2016. Municipal and county offices that issue IDs (city clerk, county clerk or DMV) generally maintain regular schedules or offer alternative appointment times, and the claim provides no verifiable source or specific office. While 'fifth Wednesdays' do occur only a few times per year, the specific schedule stated is unsubstantiated.

claim: In the wake of the Republican-backed tax bill, "more than 100,000 American workers have already been laid off in 2018."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the 2017 Republican-backed tax law directly caused more than 100,000 U.S. layoffs in 2018. While many companies announced job cuts in 2018 (particularly in retail and other struggling sectors), fact-checks and news analyses found those losses were driven by business-specific factors (restructuring, automation, competition) and not the tax bill, and the number tied to the law is far lower.

claim: Says the USMCA is the "biggest trade deal ever made."
rationale: The USMCA is a major North American trade agreement replacing NAFTA among three countries, but it is not objectively the largest trade deal ever. Larger or more comprehensive arrangements exist (for example the EU single market and other multilateral pacts) depending on metrics like membership, GDP covered, or trade volume. The claim is an overstatement without a defined metric.

claim: "Military arrests former President George W. Bush."
rationale: There are no credible reports or evidence that the U.S. military has arrested former President George W. Bush. U.S. law heavily restricts domestic military law-enforcement actions and an arrest of a former president would be an extraordinary, widely reported event—which has not occurred.

claim: "Barack Obama had 150 days in the U.S. Senate where he was able to vote quite often 'present.' "
rationale: Official Senate roll-call records and independent fact-checkers do not support the assertion that Obama had 150 days in which he frequently voted 'present.' He cast only a small number of 'present' votes during his Senate tenure, and there is no evidence of 150 separate days characterized by frequent 'present' voting. The '150' figure appears to be a misstatement or misinterpretation of voting data.

claim: "Congress files charges against Nancy Pelosi."
rationale: There is no record that Congress has filed criminal charges or articles of impeachment against Nancy Pelosi. Criminal charges are brought by prosecutors in the executive branch, and while the House can impeach officials, Pelosi has not been impeached, expelled, or the subject of congressional criminal charges.

claim: "The soda tax can make a difference by reducing consumption of unhealthy soda pop and sugary beverages."
rationale: Economic theory and multiple empirical studies of real-world soda taxes show that raising the price of sugar-sweetened beverages reduces purchases and consumption; jurisdictions that implemented taxes (e.g., national or local SSB taxes) have reported measurable declines in sales. The magnitude of the effect varies by tax rate, how much of the tax is passed to consumers, and substitution or reformulation responses.

claim: Says Donald Trump "spent the least amount of money of any of the competitive primary contenders that he beat so badly."
rationale: Public campaign finance records and contemporaneous reporting show Donald Trump’s campaign did not universally spend the least money among the competitive Republican primary contenders he defeated. Several rivals (for example, Kasich and Cruz in some reporting) spent less than Trump on their campaigns, while others (including Jeb Bush and outside super PACs supporting candidates) spent more, so the blanket statement is inaccurate.

claim: The wife of the Ferguson, Mo., police chief said African-Americans in Ferguson "are feral and violent."
rationale: Multiple contemporary fact-checks and news reports found no credible evidence that the Ferguson police chief’s wife made the quoted statement; the social-media posts were misattributed and identification of the author was ambiguous. Investigations by journalists were unable to verify the claim and concluded it was false or unproven.

claim: "Pope Francis says covid vaccine will now be required to enter heaven."
rationale: Pope Francis has publicly encouraged COVID-19 vaccination as an act of love and social responsibility, but he has not said that vaccination is required to enter heaven. The claim contradicts both the Pope’s recorded statements and core Catholic teaching that entry to heaven is not conditioned on receiving a medical treatment.

claim: "An estimated 8 million children worldwide live in orphanages or residential institutions. Shockingly, 80 percent of these children are not orphans."
rationale: Multiple international agencies, NGO reviews and academic studies have estimated on the order of 8 million children living in residential institutions worldwide, and research summarized by UNICEF/advocacy groups has found that a large majority (commonly cited around 80%) of institutionalized children have at least one living parent and are not true orphans. The figures are widely cited in child welfare literature to highlight that institutionalization often reflects poverty, disability, or lack of family support rather than parental death.

claim: "There's only three countries in the entire world where there's no paid vacation by law, we happen to be one of them."
rationale: The claim that only three countries in the entire world have no legal paid vacation is not supported by available information and depends heavily on definitions and changing national laws. While the United States is one of the notable countries without a federal statutory requirement for paid annual leave, counting exactly three countries is inaccurate because whether a country guarantees paid vacation varies by how ‘paid vacation’ is defined (annual leave vs. paid public holidays), and some small states or territories have different legal arrangements.

claim: "Florida Governor Rick Scott now listed as ‘critical’ after bizarre hurricane cleanup accident."
rationale: There are no credible reports that Rick Scott (who is currently a U.S. senator, not the sitting Florida governor) was rendered 'critical' after any hurricane cleanup accident. Media coverage and official statements do not support this claim, which appears to be a rumor or misattributed social-media post.

claim: Says that guidance urging vaccinated people to avoid travel and continue wearing masks is "profoundly anti-science."
rationale: Labeling guidance that asks vaccinated people to avoid travel and continue masking as 'profoundly anti-science' is a value judgment rather than a factual statement. Public-health agencies issued such guidance based on evolving evidence about breakthrough infections, transmission risk, and new variants and used the precautionary principle to reduce spread, which is consistent with evidence-informed practice rather than being inherently anti-science.

claim: "We've seen 115,000 jobs created in the American auto industry since GM and Chrysler emerged from bankruptcy."
rationale: There is no authoritative, time‑invariant source that confirms exactly 115,000 American auto‑industry jobs were created specifically “since GM and Chrysler emerged from bankruptcy.” Reported job gains vary considerably depending on the exact start/end dates and which subset of the auto sector is counted (assembly, parts manufacturing, dealers, suppliers). Because the claim gives a precise number without specifying dates or the definition used, it is misleading as stated.

claim: "Sotomayor has had her rulings thrown out by the court a troubling four times."
rationale: The claim is misleading and likely incorrect as stated: it gives a precise count (“four times”) without specifying which court or timeframe. Publicly reported counts of Supreme Court reversals of Sotomayor’s Second Circuit opinions vary by how cases are counted and by cutoff date, and she has been reversed more than or fewer than four times depending on definitions, so the flat statement is not accurate.

claim: This is the first time since World War II that five nuclear-powered aircraft carriers were docked together.
rationale: The claim is unlikely: nuclear-powered aircraft carriers did not exist during World War II, and since the 1960s multiple U.S. nuclear carriers have at times been berthed in the same ports or shipyards. There is no authoritative historical record that five nuclear carriers have never been docked together before this recent event, and the phrasing is ambiguous and misleading.

claim: A video shows an animal chip scanner detecting a microchip where a woman was vaccinated.
rationale: A beeping animal microchip scanner in a video does not prove a vaccine implanted a microchip. RFID/ISO animal scanners can be triggered by nearby metal, labeled vials, phones, or tags and can be mistaken or staged; there is no credible evidence that vaccines contain trackable microchips and vaccine ingredient lists do not include such devices.

claim: "I'll tell you what I can tell this country: If they want a president who doesn't believe in God, there's probably plenty of choices."
rationale: This statement is an opinion and not a verifiable factual claim. Whether there are "plenty of choices" for a president who "doesn't believe in God" depends on the country, the election cycle, and how one defines disbelief; historically major-party presidential candidates explicitly identifying as nonbelievers have been rare. As phrased it is speculative and unsupported as an objective fact.

claim: Says President Donald Trump "put out a $297 million contract to a vendor to show him how to hire Border Patrol. So, the first payment they made was $14.8 million. You know how many Border Patrol they hired with $14.8 million? Two."
rationale: The specific claim—that President Trump issued a $297 million contract to a vendor to show him how to hire Border Patrol and that an initial $14.8 million payment resulted in only two hires—is not supported by verifiable public record and is implausible. Hiring Border Patrol agents is administered by CBP through federal hiring and academy processes, not by a single outside vendor in the manner described, and no credible reporting corroborates those exact figures or outcome.

claim: "Paul Ryan has blocked all action to strengthen our gun laws."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that Ryan "blocked all action," which is false. As Speaker he had substantial control over the House floor and opposed many gun-control proposals, but he did not singularly prevent every piece of gun-related legislation — some bipartisan measures were considered and in some cases passed by Congress during his tenure. The assertion overstates his individual power and ignores recorded legislative activity on firearms while he was Speaker.

claim: "I remember landing under sniper fire."
rationale: This is a first-person memory claim that cannot be independently verified from the provided statement. Without corroborating evidence (contemporaneous records, witnesses, or other documentation) a fact-checker cannot confirm its truth and must treat it as unverified rather than established fact.

claim: "24 of every 100 kids in school today speak Spanish."
rationale: The statement gives a precise 24% figure with no geography, time period, or definition of ‘speak Spanish.’ Language statistics vary widely by country, state, and measurement (e.g., speak at home vs. conversational fluency), and available U.S. data do not support a universal, exact 24% of all schoolchildren speaking Spanish nationwide today.

claim: North Carolina is home to "two rivers of the top five most polluted rivers" in the U.S.
rationale: There is no widely accepted, authoritative national ranking that identifies two of the top five 'most polluted' U.S. rivers as being in North Carolina. Claims like this depend entirely on the specific pollutant, metric, time period, and the source compiling the list, and commonly cited lists do not corroborate two NC rivers occupying two of the top five slots.

claim: "Marjorie Taylor Greene just scrubbed her Twitter feed of all things Gaetz."
rationale: I cannot verify real-time changes to social media and have no contemporaneous evidence that Marjorie Taylor Greene removed all posts referencing Matt Gaetz. The claim is time-sensitive and uncorroborated here, so it cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: "The only time government employment has gone down during a recession has been under me."
rationale: This claim is false. Government employment has fallen in other recessions — for example, state and local government payrolls declined markedly during the 2007–2009 Great Recession and again during the 2020 COVID-related downturn — so a decline is not unique to a single administration. Thus the statement that it only happened under the claimant is incorrect.

claim: "95 percent of the income gains in the last few years have gone to the top 1 percent."
rationale: The statement is too broad and lacks necessary context (time period, country, income measure). While some analyses for specific periods in the U.S. recovery have shown a very large share of income gains going to the top 1%, the exact figure of 95% is not a universal, time‑invariant fact and estimates vary widely by dataset and time window.

claim: Says he predicts the weather better than Punxsutawney Phil.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it gives no named subject, date, or source for who allegedly said they predict the weather better than Punxsutawney Phil. Without a specific person and verifiable quote or reporting, I cannot confirm the assertion. In absence of supporting evidence, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: "Black and Latino people in NYC are arrested at TEN times the rate of white people for virtually the same rate of marijuana usage."
rationale: Multiple analyses of New York City arrest data have shown that Black and Latino New Yorkers were arrested for marijuana possession at many times the rate of white New Yorkers (commonly reported in the roughly 8–10x range) while survey data show similar rates of marijuana use across racial groups. This disparity has been documented by civil-rights groups and researchers using NYPD arrest records and national usage surveys.

claim: "By any measure, New Jersey has one of the most segregated school systems in the country."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad generalization. New Jersey does rank among the most segregated states on several commonly used measures (for example racial isolation and concentrations of high‑poverty schools), but rankings vary by metric and year and other states rank higher on some measures. Saying "by any measure" is therefore inaccurate.

claim: Says Dr. Robert Gallo, the man who helped discover the HIV virus, confessed he was "forced" to "create the HIV virus as a secret weapon to wipe out the African race."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or record that Dr. Robert Gallo ever confessed to being forced to create HIV as a secret weapon to wipe out Africans. Mainstream scientific literature and public records show HIV arose via cross‑species transmission (SIV to humans) and Gallo’s public statements and testimony do not support this allegation. The claim matches a long-running racist conspiracy theory that has been debunked by scientists and journalists.

claim: "Gov. (Rick) Perry helped balance his budget with about $6 billion worth of federal help, which he happily took, and then started blaming the members of Congress who had offered that help."
rationale: The claim bundles precise figures and political motives that are not clearly supported by available public records. While Texas under Gov. Perry did accept federal funds (for Medicaid, stimulus-era programs and other reimbursements) governors commonly use such funds in budgets, there's no clear, documented instance that Perry used exactly $6 billion of federal money to 'balance his budget' and then publicly blamed the specific members of Congress who provided it in the manner asserted.

claim: "When President Obama landed in Cuba on Air Force One, no leader was there, nobody, to greet him -- perhaps an incident without precedent in the long and prestigious history of Air Force One."
rationale: When Air Force One landed in Havana in March 2016, Cuban President Raúl Castro did not meet Obama on the tarmac, but Cuban officials (including the foreign minister) did greet him; the claim that 'nobody' greeted him is inaccurate. The suggestion that this was without precedent is also false — heads of state or other senior officials do not always meet U.S. presidents at the runway, and arrivals have varied by country and protocol.

claim: "The difference between what I support and what you support, Vice President Biden, is that you require them to opt in (to a Medicare public option), and I would not require them to opt in. … They would automatically be enrolled. That’s a big difference. … Are you forgetting what you said two minutes ago?"
rationale: This accurately summarizes the policy distinction in the 2020 Democratic primary debate: Biden advocated a public Medicare option that people would need to choose or enroll in, whereas the speaker (advocating Medicare for All) described automatic enrollment of everyone into a public plan. That difference — opt-in public option versus universal automatic coverage — is real and frequently highlighted in their debate exchanges.

claim: The Affordable Care Act alters the "sensible doctor-patient-relationship-centered health care program ... we see today."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act implemented major changes — insurance rules, expanded coverage, payment and delivery reforms (e.g., ACOs, value-based payment, quality reporting) and new administrative requirements — that altered how care is organized and reimbursed and thus affected the traditional doctor–patient-centered model. Those systemic changes have shifted some decision-making toward team-based care, care coordination, and insurer-driven rules.

claim: "Of the top five cities for staged automobile accidents, three are in Florida. … We rank No. 1 in the country in staged auto accidents."
rationale: The claim presents a specific national ranking without citing a source or time period; there is no single authoritative, consistently updated national ranking that confirms three of the top five staged-accident cities are in Florida or that 'we' are #1. While some insurer or local law-enforcement reports have identified Florida hotspots for staged crashes in certain years, such lists vary by source and year and cannot be taken as a definitive national ranking as stated.

claim: Says Rick Scott "cut Medicaid" so people can't "get Obamacare."
rationale: The claim mixes facts and asserted motive. As Florida governor Rick Scott did sign budgets that reduced some Medicaid payments and he refused to adopt the ACA’s Medicaid expansion, which left many low‑income residents uncovered; however there is no clear evidence he specifically 'cut Medicaid' with the explicit stated goal of preventing people from getting coverage via the ACA. The statement also conflates Medicaid (a state/federal program) with marketplace/subsidy enrollment under Obamacare, which operate differently.

claim: Supported in-state tuition in Arkansas for illegal immigrants "if you'd sat in our schools from the time you're 5 or 6 years old and you had become an A-plus student," among other things.
rationale: I cannot verify the specific quoted statement or a clear policy in Arkansas matching that description. Arkansas has not been widely documented as enacting a broad in-state tuition policy for undocumented immigrants framed in those exact terms, and the claim appears to conflate anecdotal political rhetoric with a verified state policy or attribution.

claim: Says the FDA said that Pfizer "falsely misled" the agency about the safety of the COVID-19 vaccines and that the shots are killing more people than they save.
rationale: The FDA has not issued a statement saying Pfizer "falsely misled" the agency about COVID-19 vaccine safety, nor concluded that the vaccines are killing more people than they save. The FDA authorized and later approved Pfizer’s COVID-19 products based on clinical trial data and ongoing safety monitoring, and multiple studies and surveillance systems show the vaccines prevented substantial numbers of hospitalizations and deaths.

claim: "More than one in five of veterans aged 20 to 24 can’t find a job to support their family or to ease the transition to civilian life."
rationale: The claim asserts that over 20% of veterans aged 20–24 cannot find a job; routinely reported labor statistics and veteran employment surveys do not support such a high unemployment rate for that age cohort. Official sources (BLS veteran unemployment data and VA/DoD transition surveys) show younger veteran unemployment/underemployment can be elevated but is generally well below one-in-five, and phrasing in the claim mixes objective unemployment with subjective difficulty transitioning.

claim: "Only in the Third World do you see this habitual use of prosecutions of former leaders."
rationale: Prosecutions of former leaders are not limited to so-called 'Third World' countries; numerous developed democracies have investigated, charged, or convicted former heads of government (for example Italy's Silvio Berlusconi, South Korea's Park Geun‑hye, Israel's Ehud Olmert and recent indictments of other leaders). While frequency and motives vary by country, the practice occurs across both wealthy and developing states rather than exclusively in the 'Third World.'

claim: Under Gov. Tom Corbett, "Pennsylvania ranks 49th in job creation."
rationale: The statement is presented as an absolute fact but lacks a defined time period or metric; state job‑creation rankings change year to year and by how 'job creation' is measured. While Pennsylvania often trailed the national average during Tom Corbett’s 2011–2015 term, it was not uniformly ranked 49th across the entire tenure and rankings vary by source and timeframe, so the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: "Biden says he doesn’t need voters to get elected."
rationale: There is no credible record of President Biden openly stating he 'doesn’t need voters to get elected.' On the contrary, Biden has repeatedly campaigned for votes and urged turnout; viral clips misquoting or taking remarks out of context have circulated but do not substantiate the absolute claim.

claim: In President Barack Obama’s 2015 State of the Union address, "the words ‘al-Qaida’ were never used, the first time those words have not been used in a State of the Union address since February 2001."
rationale: The claim depends on an exact-word count and on which prior addresses are being compared. While Obama’s 2015 State of the Union emphasized ISIS/ISIL and avoided frequent use of the term, verifying the precise absence of the exact spelling 'al-Qaida' and the assertion about February 2001 requires checking official transcripts and accounting for spelling variants and phrasing. Because of that ambiguity the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: Says last year "13 million (health insurance) rebates went out, in all 50 states. Another 8.5 (million) rebates are being sent out this summer, averaging around 100 bucks each."
rationale: The claim gives precise counts and timing for unspecified “health insurance rebates” but provides no source or year and I cannot verify those exact figures against official rebate reports. While insurers do issue annual medical-loss-ratio (MLR) rebates and other consumer payments, the totals and timing vary by year, state, and program; the quoted 13 million and 8.5 million (averaging ~$100) are not confirmable as a general fact without a specific program and year and therefore are likely misleading or inaccurate as stated.

claim: Jim Renacci "voted repeatedly to end Medicare."
rationale: Jim Renacci did not cast votes to literally repeal or terminate the Medicare program; however, he voted for Republican budgets and measures (such as Paul Ryan-style budgets and ACA repeal efforts) that proposed converting Medicare to a premium‑support/voucher or block‑grant model. Opponents characterize those proposals as 'ending Medicare,' but that description is politically charged and not a precise account of the specific votes.

claim: "Statistics show one male cat can father 420,000 kittens in five years."
rationale: That figure is not supported by realistic cat biology. While a tom can sire kittens with many queens, limits such as average litter size (about 3–5), ~63-day gestation, age to maturity, roughly 50:50 sex ratio, mortality, and practical limits on how many females one male can mate make 420,000 kittens in five years virtually impossible; the number stems from unrealistic exponential assumptions (all offspring reproduce immediately, all are female, 100% survival).

claim: A photo shows ex-Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin wearing a "Make Whites Great Again Hat."
rationale: Independent fact-checkers determined the viral image was misattributed and/or digitally altered; there is no verifiable authenticated photograph showing Derek Chauvin wearing a hat labeled "Make Whites Great Again." Reliable image analysis and reporting traced the photo to manipulation or misidentification rather than an original unaltered photo of Chauvin.

claim: "Studies have shown that voter fraud is non-existent in Texas."
rationale: Research and official reports find voter fraud in Texas is very rare but not zero; there have been documented incidents and prosecutions. Saying studies show it is 'non-existent' overstates the evidence and ignores confirmed isolated cases.

claim: Says Democratic opponents Cal Cunningham and Erica Smith support sanctuary policies.
rationale: The blanket claim that both Cal Cunningham and Erica Smith support sanctuary policies is not supported by public records or their campaign statements. Available reporting and legislative records show nuanced or different positions on immigration and do not demonstrate clear, explicit endorsements of 'sanctuary city' policies by both individuals.

claim: In Afghanistan, "over 100 billion dollars spent on military contracts."
rationale: Multiple government and audit reports show that cumulative U.S. contract obligations to support military operations and reconstruction in Afghanistan over the course of the war exceeded $100 billion. Audits from bodies such as the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction and Department of Defense contracting summaries document tens of billions of dollars in wartime contracts that together surpass the $100 billion threshold.

claim: It’s warmer on Mars than it is in parts of the United States and Canada during the polar vortex.
rationale: Mars' surface temperatures commonly range from about -125°C at the coldest to up to ~20°C in warm equatorial daytime; many Martian locations are around -60°C on average. During strong polar vortex events, parts of the U.S. and Canada have recorded air temperatures (not including wind chill) below -50°C to -60°C, which means some Earth locations can indeed be colder than many places on Mars.

claim: "Under (Obamacare), you can’t reward a person for better behavior. You can’t have incentives to be healthier."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act bars insurers in the individual and small-group markets from charging different premiums based on health status, but it does not prohibit rewarding healthier behavior. The law and subsequent federal rules explicitly allow employer and plan wellness programs that provide financial incentives or rewards for healthy behaviors or meeting health outcomes, subject to statutory limits and nondiscrimination requirements.

claim: Brookhaven homeowners pay hundreds of dollars less in property taxes compared with owners of the same-value homes in unincorporated DeKalb County.
rationale: This claim is too general and not universally true. Property taxes are determined by combined millage rates for county, city, school and special districts and can vary by year and parcel; some Brookhaven homeowners may pay less than comparable unincorporated DeKalb homeowners in some years, but others may pay more depending on the applicable levies and exemptions.

claim: Say North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper was arrested for driving while intoxicated in Stanly County.
rationale: There are no credible reports or official records indicating that North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper was arrested for driving while intoxicated in Stanly County. An arrest of a sitting governor would be widely reported and documented, and no such coverage or public record exists through mid-2024.

claim: Says the state’s budget shortfall is "not that much different" than it was in 2003.
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely misleading because it names no state or metric; comparing a budget shortfall from 2003 to today requires specifying the state, whether amounts are adjusted for inflation, and whether the comparison is absolute dollars or share of the budget. Many states’ deficits have changed substantially since 2003 once adjusted for inflation and policy changes, so the blanket statement cannot be supported without more detail.

claim: "Workers in the United States are making less than they were almost 20 years ago, and yet they are working harder."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and misleading. While many U.S. workers have seen long-term real wage stagnation and compensation has not kept pace with productivity growth, median household income and some measures of real wages have risen over the past ~20 years, and average hours worked have not clearly increased nationwide—so it is not accurate to state categorically that workers are 'making less' and 'working harder' without specifying the metric and timeframe.

claim: "I cut spending while serving in the state Legislature"
rationale: The assertion gives no identifying details (who, which state, or when) and cannot be independently verified from the standalone sentence. In most legislatures individual members cannot unilaterally cut overall spending—budget changes require bills, votes, or appropriations actions—so verification would require legislative records showing votes, sponsored bills, or enacted measures that produced net spending reductions attributable to that person. Without that evidence the claim is unproven and treated as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "The Clintons' foundation took millions from foreign governments" including United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia.
rationale: Public tax filings and investigative reporting show the Clinton Foundation and affiliated entities received donations totaling millions of dollars from foreign governments and state-linked donors, and reporting has identified contributions tied to Saudi and UAE sources. The scale and exact channels vary by year and entity, but the basic claim that the foundation took millions from foreign government-linked donors is supported by documented records.

claim: Says the Obama administration purged "training courses and information about Islamism, jihad, Sharia, and the Muslim Brotherhood."
rationale: While the Obama administration had agencies review and in some cases remove or revise a small number of inaccurate or inflammatory training slides about Islam-related topics, investigations and contemporary fact-checking found no evidence of a broad, deliberate administration-wide purge of materials about Islamism, jihad, Sharia, or the Muslim Brotherhood. The claim conflates isolated reviews and corrections with a systematic policy of suppression.

claim: "President Obama has the most border patrols and border security deployed at the border of any previous president."
rationale: During the Obama administration Border Patrol staffing and border-security resources increased to record levels compared with prior administrations. DHS/CBP personnel data show hiring surges and the largest numbers of Border Patrol agents and expanded border-security deployments occurred during his presidency.

claim: "The Cleveland police has issued a stand down order to officers."
rationale: There are no widely reported or official statements indicating the Cleveland Division of Police issued a city-wide "stand down" order to officers. Without a specific date or a reliable source, the claim is unverified and contradicts typical practice that such significant operational orders would be publicly communicated. Treat the assertion as false until attributable evidence is provided.

claim: "Missouri has one of the highest rates of uninsured children in the country."
rationale: State-level data from sources like the U.S. Census and KFF show Missouri's uninsured child rate has generally been near or slightly above the national average but not among the very highest; states such as Texas, Oklahoma, Nevada, and Florida typically have higher child uninsured rates. Missouri's ranking has improved after Medicaid expansion in 2020, so the blanket claim that it 'has one of the highest' rates is misleading without a specific year.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to keep big government in charge" of federally-owned land.
rationale: Donald Trump and his administration generally pursued policies to reduce federal control over public lands—ordering reviews and rollbacks of national monument designations and promoting state or private management and expanded resource development—so the claim that he “wants to keep big government in charge” of federally owned land contradicts his documented positions and actions.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s "Make America Great Again" hats were made in China.
rationale: Multiple contemporaneous news reports and photographs from the 2015–2016 Trump campaign showed many 'Make America Great Again' caps bearing 'Made in China' labels, indicating a substantial portion were manufactured in China. While production later included U.S.-made versions, the claim that the hats were made in China is accurate for much of the early campaign merchandise.

claim: Says opponents of proposed Austin school district bonds say the district’s "debt load doubles with these new bonds."
rationale: The assertion that the district’s “debt load doubles” with the new bonds is misleading. While issuing new bonds increases the district’s outstanding obligations and future debt service, typical bond packages do not literally double total outstanding debt once existing schedules and different debt categories are accounted for. Whether debt rises dramatically depends on the exact amounts, timing, and which types of debt are being compared, so the blanket “doubles” claim is not supportable as stated.

claim: "ALERT: Massive Easter Egg Recall Leaves MILLIONS Of Children In Danger- THROW THEM AWAY- They WILL Kill Your Kids."
rationale: The claim is a sensational alarm with no supporting evidence; there is no widespread authoritative reporting of a simultaneous mass Easter-egg recall that is imminently lethal to millions of children. Product recalls are announced by agencies (CPSC, FDA) and retailers with specific brands and batch numbers; such a dramatic, unspecified warning would have been widely documented by major news outlets and regulators if true. While isolated recalls do occur, they rarely match the hyperbolic language here.

claim: Says Tennessee’s higher education funding model "is 100 percent outcomes-based" and "we are already seeing this model changing the way our postsecondary institutions do business."
rationale: Tennessee has moved to a performance- or outcomes-informed funding model, but core state appropriations and base funding elements remain and only a portion of funds are tied to outcome metrics. Describing the system as "100 percent outcomes-based" is inaccurate; however, institutions have reported adjusting programs and policies in response to the performance incentives.

claim: "The minimum number of infrastructure (needs) in Atlanta is $900 million."
rationale: The statement gives a precise minimum dollar amount without any timeframe, scope, or source. Estimates of Atlanta's infrastructure needs vary widely by sector (roads, water, transit, schools), jurisdiction (city vs. metro vs. state), and year, so a standalone claim that the minimum is $900 million is not supported.

claim: "Of all the 62 counties in New York state, all of them, unemployment is going up except for the five counties of New York City."
rationale: The claim asserts a uniform statewide trend (unemployment rising in all 57 non‑NYC counties and not rising in the five NYC counties), which is extremely unlikely and not supported by typical labor data. County unemployment rates vary over time and across counties; historical BLS and state labor reports show mixed increases and decreases by county rather than the single pattern claimed. Without a specific timeframe or data source the sweeping statement is not credible.

claim: "As compared to last year, Texas has about 15% more power generation capacity."
rationale: The claim gives no baseline year or definition of capacity and is implausible given typical annual changes; Texas’s total generation capacity is on the order of tens to low hundreds of gigawatts and year‑to‑year additions are normally a few gigawatts, not ~15% of the total. A 15% single‑year increase would be unusually large and would require specific, cited buildouts to verify, which are not provided.

claim: "The Railroad Commission of Texas has nothing to do with railroads."
rationale: Despite its name, the Railroad Commission of Texas no longer regulates railroads. It was created in the 19th century to oversee railroads, but its regulatory responsibilities shifted long ago and today it primarily oversees oil and gas, pipelines, gas utilities and certain mining matters.

claim: "Arizona audit" shows 86,391 voters "don’t appear to exist."
rationale: The widely circulated '86,391 voters don't appear to exist' number came from the Arizona audit's database-matching process and was a count of records that did not match other data sources, not verified evidence that those people are nonexistent. State election officials and independent fact-checkers found many mismatches were explained by duplicates, people who moved or re-registered, data-entry differences, or other routine record issues rather than proof of phantom voters.

claim: John McCain and George W. Bush want to spend "a trillion dollars in Iraq over the next 10 years."
rationale: There is no clear public record that John McCain or George W. Bush explicitly proposed or pledged to spend exactly “a trillion dollars in Iraq over the next 10 years.” While CBO and other analysts projected that long-term costs of the Iraq war (including operations, reconstruction, and veterans’ care) could approach or exceed a trillion dollars over extended periods, that is an external cost estimate rather than an expressed policy commitment by McCain or Bush to spend that specific amount over ten years.

claim: Barack Obama is the "first president to file lawsuits against the states he swore an oath to protect."
rationale: This is false. The federal government, acting through the Department of Justice under many presidents before Obama, has long brought lawsuits against states (including Reconstruction-era enforcement actions and numerous civil‑rights and regulatory suits in the 20th century). Also, presidents themselves rarely 'file' suits personally—the executive branch brings litigation on the United States' behalf.

claim: "There were slaves in 1845 who helped construct and build the Old Capitol."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify: 'the Old Capitol' can refer to multiple buildings in different places and I cannot confirm that enslaved people worked on a particular 'Old Capitol' in 1845 without a location or sources. While enslaved labor was used on some U.S. public-building projects in the 18th and 19th centuries, that general fact does not prove the specific, unspecified claim.

claim: "One would have to go back more than a century to find a scenario where a president’s nominee for the Supreme Court was confirmed by the opposition party in the Senate when the vacancy occurred during an election year."
rationale: The claim asserts a blanket historical gap of more than a century but that requires checking specific nomination and Senate-majority pairings; based on general knowledge of many election‑year confirmations and frequent shifts in Senate control, it is unlikely no such cross‑party confirmation occurred within the last 100 years. Establishing the claim as true would require checking detailed roll‑call and majority-party records for each election year, which is not reflected in reliable common summaries.

claim: "The first (state) budget that came out of our Republican leadership slashed funding to Planned Parenthood...It resulted in the reduction of hours, the elimination of days, elimination of access to women in my city and all over my state."
rationale: The claim cannot be confirmed as stated because it lacks a specific state and time period; some Republican-led state budgets have cut funding to Planned Parenthood and those cuts have in some cases contributed to reduced hours or clinic closures, but the broad, unqualified assertion that the 'first (state) budget' under Republican leadership produced those exact effects 'in my city and all over my state' is unverifiable without details. Because the statement is ambiguous and potentially true in some contexts but not universally, it cannot be treated as a factual, general claim.

claim: Says President Donald Trump's "effort to roll back regulations means that Big Ag now gets to inspect its own pork" and "they decided to stop testing for E. coli."
rationale: This claim exaggerates and misstates regulatory changes. The Trump-era USDA pursued inspection “modernization” that shifted some tasks to plant employees under USDA oversight (e.g., pilot programs increasing industry responsibilities), but regulators retained legal inspection and enforcement authority—industry did not simply "inspect its own pork." Likewise, USDA/FSIS adjusted some sampling and testing protocols, but it did not wholesale stop testing for pathogenic E. coli (such as E. coli O157:H7); assertions that testing was entirely halted are misleading.

claim: "We could cut unemployment in half simply by reclaiming the jobs taken by illegal workers."
rationale: The claim is overly simplistic and incorrect: unemployment is a rate based on people actively seeking work, and the number of jobs held by unauthorized workers is not remotely large enough relative to the unemployed to halve the unemployment rate. Economic research also shows immigration (including unauthorized) has only modest effects on native unemployment because labor markets adjust (different sectors, wages, and labor-force participation). Simply 'reclaiming' jobs would not automatically translate into half as many unemployed people.

claim: Says Virginia Republican "Scott Taylor has been convicted in at least four different courts across the country, at times failing to even appear, and having a warrant issued for his arrest."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or public court-record evidence that Virginia Republican Scott Taylor has been convicted in at least four different courts nationwide, repeatedly failed to appear, and had a warrant issued as described. Major news outlets and accessible court records document at most isolated legal matters involving him and do not support the broad, multi-jurisdiction conviction/warrant claim.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton sold 20 percent of America’s uranium to Russia and then "the Russian government gave $145 million to the Clinton Foundation." Former FBI Director and special counsel Robert Mueller "delivered it."
rationale: The claim conflates and misstates multiple events. The 2010 Uranium One transaction was approved by the multi-agency CFIUS committee (of which the State Department was one member), not sold personally by Hillary Clinton, and there is no credible evidence she or the Russian government paid or received $145 million to the Clinton Foundation as a quid pro quo. Robert Mueller had no role in approving the transaction and did not "deliver" it; later reporting and fact-checks found no proof of the alleged pay-for-play scheme.

claim: "The Red Cross sells your donated blood to hospitals for $150 and then that hospital charges you thousands for a blood transfusion."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Blood centers (including the Red Cross) charge hospitals fees to cover collection, testing, processing and distribution — fees vary by product and are often higher than $150 for some components — and hospitals in turn bill for the transfusion encounter (product plus administration, facility and related care), which can result in total charges of thousands. The claim’s specific fixed price ($150) and implication that donors’ blood is simply sold for a small flat fee while hospitals arbitrarily charge patients thousands is inaccurate.

claim: Says that in 41 states, government workers "are better paid than the taxpayers who support them."
rationale: The statement is vague and unsupported as written. While some analyses have found that public-sector employees in many states receive higher average total compensation than private-sector workers, results depend heavily on definitions (wages vs total compensation), controls for occupation, hours, education and age, and the specific year and data source; there is no authoritative, context-free finding that in exactly 41 states "government workers are better paid than the taxpayers who support them."

claim: Bull sharks were released in an Arkansas river.
rationale: There are no credible news reports or wildlife agency confirmations that bull sharks were intentionally released into an Arkansas river. While bull sharks can tolerate fresh water and have been found upriver in Gulf-connected systems, documented occurrences in Arkansas rivers or confirmed releases there are lacking.

claim: Says science shows the physiological effects of wearing masks include hypoxemia, hypercapnia, shortness of breath, toxicity and increased muscle tension.
rationale: High-quality studies and public health agencies show that ordinary cloth and surgical masks do not produce clinically significant hypoxemia or hypercapnia or systemic 'toxicity' in healthy people; objective measurements of oxygen and CO2 remain within normal ranges. Some users report subjective shortness of breath, discomfort, headaches, or increased breathing effort with tight-fitting respirators (e.g., prolonged N95 use), but these are not evidence of the broad physiological harms listed in the claim.

claim: "America owns 3 percent of the world’s oil but consumes 25 percent of its global reserves."
rationale: While the U.S. does hold only about 2–3% of proven global oil reserves, it does not consume 25% of the world’s reserves. Recent data show U.S. oil consumption is roughly 18–21% of global oil consumption (a flow), and the claim also mixes up 'reserves' (a stock) with consumption (a flow), making it misleading and inaccurate.

claim: "Two Iraqis came here to this country, were radicalized and they were the masterminds behind the Bowling Green massacre. … It didn't get covered"
rationale: There was no ‘Bowling Green massacre.’ In 2011 two Iraqi nationals were arrested in Bowling Green, Kentucky, for attempting to send weapons/IED components to al‑Qaeda in Iraq, but no mass‑casualty attack occurred. The claim that they were masterminds behind a massacre and that it “didn't get covered” is false; the arrests and prosecutions were reported and publicly documented.

claim: Says his Twitter account has 1.3 million followers.
rationale: The statement is unverified as presented because it omits who “his” refers to and gives no date; Twitter follower counts change frequently. Without a named account and timestamp, the assertion cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false in this fact-checking context.

claim: "Condemning violence against the police and urging support for the police" is "markedly absent" from President Barack Obama’s public remarks.
rationale: President Obama publicly condemned violence against police on multiple occasions and urged support for law enforcement (for example his statements after the July 2016 Dallas ambush where he said there is no justification for violence against police). While he also criticized policing practices and called for reform, that does not mean condemnations of violence or appeals to support police were "markedly absent."

claim: When Mitt Romney was governor, "the fact is that the average income for a family in Massachusetts went up by $5,500."
rationale: The $5,500 figure is misleading because it depends on which income measure and years are chosen and whether the dollars are adjusted for inflation. Independent fact-checkers and official data show that using median (not mean) family/household income or adjusting for inflation produces a much smaller gain or no real gain over Romney’s full term.

claim: "When did the decline of coal start? It started when natural gas took off … that started to begin in (President George W.) Bush’s administration."
rationale: In the United States, coal-fired electricity generation peaked in the mid-2000s (around 2007) and then began a sustained decline as shale gas production and associated price drops enabled widespread coal-to-gas switching. The commercial-scale boom in unconventional natural gas (fracking/shale) accelerated in the mid-2000s, which falls within President George W. Bush’s administration.

claim: "In Washington, Congressman Joe Heck supports privatizing (Social Security), turning our savings over to Wall Street and risking it on the stock market."
rationale: The claim asserts Joe Heck supports outright privatizing Social Security and handing benefits to Wall Street; public records and his statements show he has called for reforms to ensure solvency but do not clearly show he backed full privatization that would turn benefits over to the stock market. The statement is therefore misleading and presented as an absolute that is not supported by clear evidence.

claim: Says Obama opposes offshore drilling and a gas tax holiday.
rationale: The claim presents a blanket stance that Obama opposed both offshore drilling and a gas tax holiday. While he did oppose a temporary federal gas tax holiday, his record on offshore drilling is mixed—he supported limited expanded offshore drilling during his 2008 campaign and took varying positions as president (including restrictions after the 2010 spill). Therefore the combined assertion is inaccurate without temporal context.

claim: A record number of immigrants not from Mexico are "being apprehended at the border."
rationale: The statement lacks a timeframe and is therefore misleading: while U.S. Customs and Border Protection has reported record or near-record numbers of non‑Mexican nationals in specific months or fiscal years, that is not a universally true, always-current fact. CBP statistics vary by month, fiscal year, and by whether one counts 'apprehensions' versus 'encounters' or removals, so the claim as stated is unsupported without more context.

claim: Says a Twitter account for "Scarsdale NY Antifa" tweeted that "chapters of Antifa around Oregon have collaborated to ignite fires around the state."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that a Twitter account named 'Scarsdale NY Antifa' posted that 'chapters of Antifa around Oregon have collaborated to ignite fires around the state.' Claims like this have circulated before but have been unverified or traced to parody/misattributed accounts; without corroborating screenshots, archived posts, or reputable fact-checks, the assertion should be treated as false.

claim: Says Dick Cheney "supported gay marriage sooner" than Hillary Clinton.
rationale: This is incorrect as stated: Hillary Clinton publicly announced her support for same-sex marriage in 2013, whereas Dick Cheney's earlier public comments were generally about civil unions or were private/qualified and his clear public endorsement of marriage equality did not precede Clinton's. The claim conflates different kinds of statements and timelines.

claim: It’s "typical" for a presidential candidate to release 10 or 11 years of tax returns.
rationale: While many presidential candidates voluntarily disclose multiple years of tax returns, there is no uniform standard and the number released varies widely. Releasing 10–11 years is not uniformly typical—some candidates have released a decade or more, others have released far fewer years or none at all—so calling 10–11 years 'typical' is inaccurate.

claim: "In France, they have a (surveillance) program a thousandfold more invasive" than the United States.
rationale: The statement is a hyperbolic, quantitative comparison that lacks any defined metric or empirical basis. Both France and the United States operate extensive surveillance and intelligence programs with different legal frameworks and capabilities, but there is no credible evidence showing France’s programs are "a thousandfold" more invasive than U.S. programs.

claim: "1776 flag flying over White House!" in January 2021. "Revolution Signal."
rationale: Photographs and official images from January 6–7, 2021 and reporting from fact-checkers show the U.S. flag on the White House flagpole; there is no evidence a “1776” or similar revolutionary flag was flown from the White House itself. Social media images of 1776-style flags circulated, but they were on protesters, nearby lampposts or fences, not flying from the White House flagstaff as claimed.

claim: Texas has "the nation's highest rate and highest number of uninsured."
rationale: The statement is presented as an absolute but lacks a time frame or data source. While Texas has frequently had one of the highest uninsured rates and in some recent years the largest number of uninsured residents, these rankings change by year and by data source, so the claim is misleading without specifying when and according to which dataset.

claim: "Victory! Republicans by 2 to 1 vote to endorse Mark Neumann on first ballot at GOP convention."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific 2-to-1 first-ballot endorsement of Mark Neumann but provides no date or jurisdiction and I find no clear, corroborated record of such a dramatic, widely reported convention result. Mark Neumann’s campaigns (notably for U.S. Senate in Wisconsin) involved contested primaries and endorsements that are not documented as a 2-to-1 first-ballot sweep, so the specific assertion is unverified and likely false as stated.

claim: "The Lancet peer-reviewed study confirms vaccine efficacy, not as 95% stated by the vaccine companies, but as: AstraZeneca 1.3%; Moderna 1.2%; J&J 1.2%; Pfizer 0.84%."
rationale: The claim is false: no Lancet peer‑reviewed study reported vaccine efficacies as ~1% for those products. Phase 3 trial results and subsequent peer‑reviewed analyses reported relative risk reductions of roughly 94–95% for the mRNA vaccines and substantial (though lower) efficacy for AstraZeneca and J&J. The ~1% figures appear to be a misinterpretation or misuse of different metrics (such as short‑term absolute risk reduction or baseline incidence) and are not the published vaccine efficacy estimates.

claim: Statistically, law-enforcement officers die 10 years earlier than the general population.
rationale: This is an oversimplified and unsupported universal claim. While multiple studies report elevated risks of certain causes of death (cardiovascular disease, suicide, on-duty violence) among some groups of law-enforcement officers, estimates of overall life-expectancy reduction vary by country, cohort, time period and methods and do not consistently show a uniform 10-year shorter lifespan for officers compared with the general population.

claim: Attorney general candidate Brad Schimel "is in cahoots with Wisconsin Right to Life to make abortion a crime in Wisconsin."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Brad Schimel and Wisconsin Right to Life have a secret or formal conspiracy to "make abortion a crime" in Wisconsin. Schimel has been publicly anti‑abortion and has accepted support from pro‑life groups, and an attorney general can influence enforcement and defend laws, but criminalizing abortion requires legislative action and there is no proven coordinated plot tying the two to unilaterally change the law.

claim: A photo shows a helicopter rescue mission in Afghanistan where wounded men were loaded onboard.
rationale: I cannot verify the claim from the description alone and there is no independent corroboration provided. Images circulating online are frequently miscaptioned or taken in different places/times, so without the original photo, metadata, or reputable contemporaneous news reporting that identifies the location, date, and context, the claim that it shows a helicopter rescue in Afghanistan loading wounded men is unverified and therefore treated as false.

claim: Says when he was governor, "most of the Democrats" voted for his billion-dollar property-tax cuts, but U.S. Senate rival Tammy Baldwin "voted against it."
rationale: The claim conflates state legislation and a federal officeholder. State property-tax cuts are voted on by state legislators, not by U.S. senators; Tammy Baldwin served in the U.S. House and then the U.S. Senate during the relevant period and would not have cast votes in the Wisconsin Legislature. The assertion that "most of the Democrats" supported the cuts is unverified without specifying which chamber and which Democrats.

claim: "One out of every five people that the federal government charges with murder is an illegal alien."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that 20% of persons federally charged with murder are undocumented immigrants. Most homicide prosecutions occur in state courts, federal murder charges are relatively rare and specialized, and DOJ data do not support a consistent one-in-five share of federal murder defendants being "illegal aliens." The claim likely conflates immigration prosecutions with federal murder prosecutions or omits timeframe and definitions.

claim: "A strong bipartisan majority" in the House of Representatives "voted to defund Obamacare."
rationale: House votes to repeal or defund the Affordable Care Act have overwhelmingly been divided by party, with most such measures passing thanks to nearly unanimous Republican support and few Democrats joining. There is no record of a "strong bipartisan majority" in the House backing defunding; any Democratic support has been marginal, not enough to constitute a broad bipartisan majority.

claim: Says President Barack Obama has "been presiding over our jobs going overseas for seven years."
rationale: The statement implies President Obama was responsible for U.S. jobs moving overseas for seven years. While jobs did relocate abroad during his time in office, offshoring long predates his presidency and is driven by corporate decisions, trade dynamics and automation rather than direct presidential control; additionally Obama served eight years (2009–2017), so the phrasing is misleading.

claim: Says photo of beaten woman is Aracely Henriquez, a pregnant woman who George Floyd assaulted during an armed robbery.
rationale: Independent fact-checks and reporting found that the circulated photo was misattributed and there is no reliable evidence identifying the woman in the image as Aracely Henriquez or linking that specific photo to an assault by George Floyd. Court records and reputable news coverage do not corroborate the claim that the pictured woman was the pregnant victim from Floyd’s prior robbery case.

claim: Says that in three legislative sessions, his proposals opening pre-kindergarten to all Texas 4-year-olds never got heard or voted out of committee.
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it lacks identification of the speaker, the specific bills, and the legislative sessions in question. Committee actions on Texas prekindergarten proposals are matters of public record and would need bill numbers or session years to confirm whether they were heard or voted out of committee; without those details the assertion is unconfirmed and therefore treated as false. It is plausible such proposals could stall in committee, but the statement as presented is not verifiable.

claim: In the case of a catastrophic event, the Atlanta-area offices of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention will self-destruct.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official policy showing that the CDC’s Atlanta-area offices are equipped to physically “self‑destruct.” Federal agencies maintain continuity-of-operations, security, and hazardous-material containment protocols, but not explosive or automated demolition of their buildings in a catastrophic event. The claim appears to be an urban legend or misunderstanding of emergency containment procedures.

claim: Says Donald Trump offered his hotel "to our troops to sleep in after they were put in a car garage."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or documentation that Donald Trump offered his hotel "to our troops to sleep in after they were put in a car garage." The quoted wording does not match any verified public statement by Trump and major news outlets and fact-checkers have not substantiated such a claim.

claim: "Taking into account inflation, the federal minimum wage is actually worth less than what it was worth 50 years ago."
rationale: The federal statutory minimum wage has been $7.25 since 2009; when adjusted for inflation (using the CPI), that nominal amount buys substantially less than the federal minimum did about 50 years ago. Historical federal minimums in the mid-1970s convert to a considerably higher value in today’s dollars, so the real (inflation-adjusted) minimum wage is lower now than it was roughly 50 years ago.

claim: Says that PolitiFact Ohio confirms that Betty Sutton "maxed out federal debt"
rationale: There is no record that PolitiFact Ohio 'confirmed' a claim that Betty Sutton 'maxed out federal debt.' PolitiFact fact-checks specific statements and applies ratings (True, False, Mostly False, etc.); no such verification of that sweeping phrase appears in PolitiFact Ohio’s archives and the wording reads like a mischaracterization or fabrication of a checked claim.

claim: Democrats already agreed to "a deal that Republicans wanted, that Eric Cantor said would be a win."
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated because it names no specific agreement, time, or source for Cantor’s alleged remark; without identifying which deal and when, there is no evidence to confirm Democrats had already agreed to it or that Eric Cantor called it a "win." Historical records show Democrats and Republicans have reached various deals at different times and Cantor made many public comments while House GOP leader, but that does not validate this vague assertion.

claim: "John McCain said...in December he was surprised there was a subprime mortgage problem."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific December quote by John McCain admitting surprise at a subprime mortgage problem, but there is no well-documented public record of McCain making that exact statement in December. McCain did comment on the subprime and broader credit problems at various points during 2007–2008, but the precise quoted line and timing as presented are unverified and likely misattributed or taken out of context.

claim: During the past four years, "average wages have barely budged."
rationale: The blanket statement is misleading: U.S. average (mean) wages in nominal terms rose noticeably over the last four years and, after pandemic-related volatility, many measures of typical pay have recovered. While some workers or specific sectors have seen little real (inflation-adjusted) gain, overall average earnings increased, so saying they “barely budged” is inaccurate as a general claim.

claim: Sen. Mark Kelly voted "for benefits to illegals."
rationale: The statement is vague and misleading: Senate votes are on specific bills or amendments, and there is no single roll-call where Sen. Mark Kelly voted to grant blanket "benefits to illegals." Without identifying a particular bill, date, or benefit, the claim cannot be substantiated; some votes he has taken involved immigration-related provisions where eligibility and scope vary.

claim: "Foster children are disproportionately victims of identity theft."
rationale: Multiple government reports, advocacy organizations, and research indicate youth in foster care face elevated risk of identity theft compared with other children because their personally identifying information is exposed to many caregivers, placements, and agencies and is often not monitored. Studies and consumer-protection investigations have documented patterns of fraudulent use of Social Security numbers and other data belonging to foster children.

claim: "Hospitals, doctors, MRIs, surgeries and so forth are more extensively used and far more expensive in this country than they are in many other countries.''
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes. It is accurate that the United States (presumably the country referenced) has far higher health-care spending and higher prices for hospitals, doctors, imaging and procedures than most other high-income countries, but use is mixed: the U.S. has higher rates of some services (e.g., advanced imaging and certain surgeries) while having fewer hospital bed-days and fewer physician visits per capita than many peers. Saying all those services are 'more extensively used' everywhere is therefore incorrect.

claim: The administration has issued rules for "$1 abortions in ObamaCare" and "requires all persons enrolled in insurance plans that include elective abortion coverage to pay" an abortion premium.
rationale: The Affordable Care Act did not create a rule forcing “$1 abortions” nor require all enrollees to pay an “abortion premium.” Federal rules prohibit using premium tax credits to pay for elective abortions (except limited exceptions) and allow insurers in some markets to offer optional, separately billed abortion riders that only those who choose them pay for. Claims that the administration mandated a $1 abortion charge or forced all insured people to pay such a premium are inaccurate and misleading.

claim: Video shows Biden saying "salute the Marines" after hearing the words in an earpiece before his inauguration.
rationale: There is no verified footage showing Biden clearly say "salute the Marines" after hearing those words through an earpiece before his inauguration. The widely shared clip has ambiguous audio that appears to be off‑camera prompting and there is no confirmation he was wearing an earpiece; independent fact‑checks and full inauguration footage do not substantiate the claim.

claim: "Ninety six percent of employers in the Granite State are considered small businesses."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and does not match standard data sources. The U.S. Small Business Administration typically counts firms with fewer than 500 employees as small, and by that definition nearly all firms in New Hampshire qualify (well above 96%), so the specific figure of 96% is misleading without a definition. If a different employee threshold were intended the share could differ, but the claim as stated is not supported by standard SBA state profiles.

claim: "Nobody suffered any lasting injuries" from the CIA interrogation program.
rationale: Multiple official and independent investigations have documented that detainees subjected to the CIA interrogation program experienced enduring physical and psychological harm. The U.S. Senate Intelligence Committee report and medical and human-rights assessments describe chronic conditions such as PTSD, memory problems, chronic pain and other long-term impairments consistent with lasting injuries.

claim: George Allen voted for budgets that increased the national debt by $16,400 for every second he served in the U.S. Senate.
rationale: The per-second figure implies about $3.1 trillion of debt growth over Allen’s roughly six years in the Senate, but official U.S. debt totals for 2001–2007 show a smaller increase (roughly $2.5–3.0 trillion depending on measurement) and cannot be cleanly attributed to budgets he alone "voted for." The claim compresses collective Congressional actions, presidential policies, and other fiscal factors into a single per-second headline that overstates both the math and causal attribution.

claim: "More people now die in Wisconsin from drug overdoses than car crashes."
rationale: State and federal data in recent years show Wisconsin’s drug overdose deaths rose substantially and exceeded motor vehicle crash deaths. Reports from the Wisconsin Department of Health Services and CDC provisional mortality data indicate overdose fatalities have outnumbered traffic deaths in the most recent annual counts.

claim: The Obama administration is using as its "legal justification for these airstrikes (on the Islamic State), an authorization for military force that the president himself has called for repeal of."
rationale: The Obama administration mainly invoked the 2001 AUMF (and inherent self‑defense authorities) as the legal basis for strikes against ISIS; President Obama had publicly called for repeal of the 2002 Iraq AUMF, not the 2001 AUMF that was the administration’s primary cited authority. Thus the claim that the strikes rested on an authorization the president himself had called to repeal is misleading.

claim: Says U.S. House candidate Carlos Curbelo "supported raising flood insurance rates."
rationale: Carlos Curbelo publicly supported reforms to the National Flood Insurance Program that included moving toward risk-based premiums and phasing out some subsidized rates, which would result in higher flood insurance costs for some policyholders. He framed this as aligning rates with actual risk while advocating transitional or targeted assistance for low-income homeowners.

claim: "The media ... sort of made it sound like I had a feud with the intelligence community."
rationale: The statement is a broad, subjective claim about “the media” and cannot be verified as a universal fact. Coverage was mixed: some outlets framed public disputes between the speaker and parts of the intelligence community as a feud, while others reported more neutrally or highlighted different angles, so it’s inaccurate to say the media uniformly made it sound that way.

claim: Obama "suggested bombing Pakistan."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Barack Obama suggested bombing Pakistan as a country. While his administration authorized targeted counterterrorism strikes (including drone strikes) against militant groups operating inside Pakistan, that is not the same as proposing or endorsing bombing Pakistan itself, and public records and reporting do not support the blanket claim.

claim: Says it's not true that Florida black bears are an "apex predator."
rationale: Adult Florida black bears generally occupy the top tiers of their local food web and have few natural predators, so asserting that they are not an apex predator is incorrect. While humans are the primary threat and Florida panthers or alligators may occasionally kill cubs or rarely adults, those occasional predation events do not remove the bears' near‑apex ecological role.

claim: Republicans are "trying to create a fake unemployment insurance crisis."
rationale: The claim attributes a coordinated intent to an entire political party to fabricate a 'fake' unemployment insurance crisis, which is a broad and unproven assertion. While many Republican officials have highlighted alleged UI fraud and promoted reforms or spending reductions—sometimes using alarmist language—there is no clear evidence of a party‑wide, coordinated effort to create a wholly fabricated crisis; motivations and actions vary by individual and context.

claim: State Sen. Emmett Hanger "has voted for the three largest tax increases - proposed tax increases - in Virginia history."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific, historical ranking that requires precise definitions (which tax increases, by what metric, and over what period) and verifiable roll-call records. I cannot confirm that Emmett Hanger voted for the exact three largest tax increases in Virginia history; while he has supported some revenue measures, there is no clear, authoritative basis to label three particular bills he voted for as the three largest ever without detailed legislative and fiscal comparison.

claim: Says Miami Congressman Carlos "Curbelo supports drilling offshore" and "repeatedly voted against President Obama's ability to fight pollution and combat climate change."
rationale: The claim overstates and conflates mixed public positions and votes. Carlos Curbelo was a Republican known for acknowledging climate change and sponsoring market-oriented climate proposals while also voting with his party on some roll calls; there is not clear, consistent evidence that he broadly 'supports drilling offshore' for Florida waters or that he 'repeatedly voted against President Obama's ability to fight pollution and combat climate change' as a single, documented pattern.

claim: "Bloomberg says he wants to ban guns holding more than three rounds."
rationale: Michael Bloomberg has publicly advocated banning high-capacity magazines and certain assault-style weapons, but his stated proposals have typically targeted magazines holding substantially more rounds (commonly 10+), not a three-round limit. There is no reliable record of Bloomberg calling for a ban specifically on guns that hold more than three rounds.

claim: "The Defense Department received only one-half of 1 percent of the nearly trillion-dollar stimulus package funding."
rationale: The statement is not accurate: the nearly trillion-dollar 2009 Recovery Act (commonly cited) and later stimulus bills allocated more than a half-percent to defense-related spending. Official breakdowns and independent analyses show the Department of Defense and defense-related programs received multiple billions (well above the roughly $4–5 billion that 0.5% of a trillion would represent), so DoD’s share exceeded 0.5%.

claim: Says Barack Obama had "huge majorities" in Congress during his first two years in office and "did nothing with them to create jobs in America."
rationale: This is false. During Obama's first two years (2009–2010) Democrats held the majorities in both the House and the Senate, and Congress passed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 and other job-related measures intended to save and create jobs. Saying they did "nothing" ignores enacted stimulus spending, unemployment extensions, and hiring incentives, though debate exists over the size and effectiveness of those measures.

claim: Obama came into office "with a $1.3 trillion deficit before I had passed any law. ... We came in with $8 trillion worth of debt over the next decade."
