The FRC has been labeled a "hate group" by private organizations like the Southern Poverty Law Center, and it has been mentioned in government reports about threats or targets, but that is not the same as an official government terrorist designation.

claim: The new health care law "will cut $500 billion from Medicare. That will hurt the quality of our care."
rationale: While the law commonly called the Affordable Care Act was scored by the CBO as reducing projected Medicare spending by roughly $500 billion over about a decade, those were reductions in projected spending (largely via lower payments to plans and providers), not direct cuts to guaranteed Medicare benefits. Whether those payment reductions "will hurt the quality of our care" is speculative and not established; analysts and the CBO stated quality effects were uncertain and would depend on implementation.

claim: In head-to-head polls for the general election, "I beat Hillary Clinton by more than anybody, by 11 points."
rationale: There is no sustained national head-to-head polling showing the claimant beating Hillary Clinton by an 11-point margin or by more than every other Republican. During the 2016 campaign Trump sometimes led Clinton in specific polls or at particular moments, but typical national head-to-head margins were much smaller and many polls showed Clinton leading; the final November result also had Clinton winning the popular vote. The blanket claim of a consistent +11 advantage and "more than anybody" is not supported by the overall polling evidence.

claim: "There's one (study) that came out of Pew in 2008 that showed 14 percent of people who voted were noncitizens."
rationale: The 2008 Pew analysis does not show that 14% of people who voted were noncitizens. Independent fact-checks and re-analyses found the claim misreads or misstates survey results; Pew surveys at most identified a very small share of self-reported noncitizens saying they voted, and there is no credible evidence that 14% of voters were noncitizens.

claim: "Russ Feingold got a memo in 2009 that outlined veteran harm" at a Wisconsin VA facility "and nothing was done."
rationale: I found no verifiable public evidence that former Senator Russ Feingold received a specific 2009 memo detailing veteran harm at a Wisconsin VA facility and that no action was taken. Major reporting and timelines of Wisconsin VA scandals point to whistleblower complaints and investigations that surfaced in the mid-2010s and name different officials; the specific 2009 memo claim is unsubstantiated in available records.

claim: Potential Foxconn changes are due to "the wave of economic uncertainty" from Evers administration
rationale: There is no clear evidence that actions by the Evers administration created a distinct 'wave of economic uncertainty' that caused Foxconn to change plans. Public reporting and official statements have pointed to a mix of factors—global market conditions, shifts in corporate strategy, changes in demand, pandemic and supply-chain disruptions, and renegotiation of incentives—rather than a single state administration policy being the primary cause.

claim: Says federal regulations adopted in 2011 increased the cost of each vehicle for his business by $10,000.
rationale: There is no broad, verifiable evidence that federal regulations adopted in 2011 uniformly increased the cost of each vehicle for a business by $10,000. Regulatory cost impacts depend on the specific rule, vehicle type, and business practices, and published government and independent estimates for rules around that time generally show much smaller per-vehicle compliance costs than $10,000.

claim: "Pelosi’s $1.9 trillion bailout gives EVERY federal employee a $21,000 bonus check… they never lost their job!"
rationale: The American Rescue Plan (the $1.9 trillion bill) did not include a universal $21,000 bonus or check to every federal employee. The law provided $1,400 stimulus payments to eligible individuals, enhanced unemployment benefits, state and local aid, and targeted pandemic-related supports, but there was no blanket $21,000 payment for all federal workers. The claim that "they never lost their job" is also misleading and unrelated to any provision creating such a bonus.

claim: Says New Hampshire had the fourth-lowest unemployment rate in the country during Maggie Hassan’s time in the state Senate.
rationale: This claim is not verifiable as stated. Maggie Hassan served in the New Hampshire State Senate from 2004–2010, and although New Hampshire frequently had among the lower unemployment rates, Bureau of Labor Statistics state rankings changed year to year and I cannot confirm a consistent or clearly documented 'fourth-lowest' ranking for the state across her entire Senate tenure.

claim: Says North Carolina Republican Senate candidate Thom Tillis "called Obamacare ‘a great idea.’ "
rationale: There is no clear, well-documented instance in which Thom Tillis is on record plainly saying the entire Affordable Care Act was "a great idea." During his 2014 campaign he acknowledged that some provisions or ideas in health-care reform had merit, but he publicly opposed the law and fact-check summaries at the time noted he praised specific elements rather than endorsing Obamacare wholesale as a "great idea."

claim: "Over 73% of all donations raised (from the ALS Ice Bucket Challenge) are going to fundraising, overhead, executive salaries, and external donations."
rationale: Independent fact-checks and the ALS Association’s own financial statements show that the majority of Ice Bucket Challenge donations were directed to research, patient services, and grants; administrative, fundraising, and executive compensation made up a small fraction, not more than 73% of the funds. Claims that over 73% went to overhead and salaries misstate the reported allocations and ignore program spending and grant distributions.

claim: The GOP’s health bill will protect people with pre-existing conditions "every bit as well as Obamacare did."
rationale: Major GOP proposals (for example the 2017 AHCA and related bills) contained provisions — such as state waivers of community rating rules, different subsidy structures, and encouragement of high-risk pools — that experts and the CBO concluded would weaken protections for people with pre-existing conditions compared with the ACA. While some bills included language asserting protection, the policy mechanisms in those bills would likely allow higher premiums, narrower coverage, or greater financial barriers for many with prior conditions.

claim: "In seven years that (nuclear) deal will have expired, and Iran is free to go ahead and create nuclear weapons."
rationale: This is an oversimplification. The 2015 nuclear agreement (JCPOA) included time-limited restrictions on certain nuclear activities, but Iran would still be bound by the Non-Proliferation Treaty and subject to IAEA monitoring and verification; expiration of some limits would not automatically give Iran a legal or undetectable green light to build weapons and would likely trigger diplomatic, economic, and possibly other responses. Additionally, many limits expired on different schedules and key transparency measures remained.

claim: The presence of gorillas calls into question the concept of evolution.
rationale: The existence of gorillas does not undermine evolution; instead their anatomy, behavior, and genetics fit within the framework of common descent and divergence of species. Evolutionary theory predicts the existence of closely related species like gorillas and humans that share a common ancestor rather than one descending from the other. Genetic and fossil evidence supports gorillas as part of the great ape clade consistent with evolutionary relationships.

claim: Says "Nicolás Maduro is carrying out a genocide on his people."
rationale: Independent UN and regional human-rights investigations have documented widespread abuses by Venezuelan authorities — including extrajudicial killings, torture, and arbitrary detention — that amount to crimes against humanity, but they do not conclude there is legal evidence of a genocidal intent to destroy a protected group. The term "genocide" has a specific legal definition that generally covers intent to destroy a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, not political opponents, and public reporting has not established that element in Venezuela.

claim: "My mask will keep someone else safe and their mask will keep me safe."
rationale: The claim is too absolute. Masks do substantially reduce the risk of transmitting respiratory viruses (source control) and can also offer some protection to the wearer, but they do not guarantee that someone will be kept safe in all circumstances. Effectiveness depends on mask type, fit, correct use, and environmental factors like ventilation and exposure duration.

claim: Says Clint Eastwood is dead.
rationale: There were no credible reports or obituaries through my last reliable update (June 2024) indicating Clint Eastwood had died, so the assertion is likely false. However, I cannot verify events after that cutoff, so the claim should be confirmed with current sources before accepting as true.

claim: Newt Gingrich "was fined $300,000 for ethics violations."
rationale: In 1997 the House Ethics Committee found Newt Gingrich had violated House rules regarding the use of a tax‑exempt educational foundation and misleading the committee; the House voted to reprimand him and he agreed to a $300,000 payment as part of the sanctions. Sources commonly report this payment as a $300,000 fine or penalty related to the ethics ruling.

claim: Says U.S. Senate opponent Eric Hovde "supported billions in stimulus for high-speed rail"  and "billions more to bail out banks."
rationale: Eric Hovde has never served in the U.S. Congress and therefore did not cast votes to authorize 'billions' in high‑speed rail stimulus or bailouts. The claim presents voting support as if he were a legislator; there is no reliable record that Hovde enacted or voted for those federal spending measures.

claim: "In the last decade, the average income of the bottom 90 percent of all working Americans actually declined. The top 1 percent saw their income rise by an average of more than a quarter of a million dollars each."
rationale: The statement is misleading and not uniformly supported by publicly available data. Government and academic data (Census, IRS distributional statistics) show that median and many bottom-90 incomes generally recovered and in some measures modestly increased over the past decade rather than universally declining, while the top 1% did see large gains — but the precise claim that the top 1% rose by 'more than a quarter of a million dollars each' and the bottom 90% ‘‘actually declined’’ depends on the exact ten-year window, whether one measures mean vs median, pre-tax vs after-tax, and whether 'working Americans' means individuals or households.

claim: "President Obama pledged to go through the budget 'line by line,' but on his watch, non-defense spending has spiraled out of control, increasing by 67 percent in the last year alone."
rationale: While President Obama did say he would go through the budget 'line by line,' the claim that non-defense spending increased 67 percent in a single year on his watch is not supported by federal budget data. Year‑over‑year increases in non‑defense spending during the Obama years were much smaller; a 67% jump in one year would be unprecedented and contradicts OMB/CBO historical outlays.

claim: "Donald Trump praises Colonel Sanders for his service in the Civil War."
rationale: Harland 'Colonel' Sanders was born in 1890 and died in 1980, decades after the U.S. Civil War (1861–1865), so he could not have served in that conflict. While Donald Trump has at times praised Sanders as the KFC founder or referenced him by his honorary title, any claim that Trump praised Sanders for Civil War service is chronologically impossible and appears to be erroneous or satirical.

claim: There were no American flags at the first Democratic presidential debate.
rationale: The claim is underspecified and cannot be confirmed as stated — ‘the first Democratic presidential debate’ could refer to different years and events. In U.S. presidential debates it is common for American flags to be present on stage or in the venue, and many first Democratic debates historically have included at least some U.S. flags visible either on stage or in the audience. Without a specific date/contest to check, asserting there were none is not supportable.

claim: "More suicide deaths than coronavirus death past two months."
rationale: The claim is presented as a general statement but gives no timeframe, location, or data source, so it cannot be verified as a universal fact. In many countries and globally, COVID-19 caused more deaths than typical two‑month suicide totals during major pandemic waves; conversely, in some specific short periods or places suicide counts may exceed coronavirus deaths. Because the claim is ambiguous and stated without context, it is not reliably true as given.

claim: Says Texas routinely gets "a lot more federal spending" than it pays in taxes.
rationale: Most analyses of federal dollars by state (using Treasury/Census/Tax Foundation methods) show Texas has typically sent more in federal taxes than it has received in federal spending, so the statement that Texas routinely gets "a lot more" than it pays is incorrect. While certain years or categories (disaster relief, major military contracting, or temporary stimulus) can make Texas a net recipient in specific periods or localities, the routine, persistent pattern is that Texas is a net contributor overall.

claim: "Our (Texas) graduation rate ranks 43rd out of 50 states."
rationale: The claim gives no year or metric and is inconsistent with recent federal and Texas Education Agency data: Texas's four‑year high school graduation rate in recent years has been near or above the national average and has not consistently ranked as low as 43rd. Without a specific year or definition of 'graduation rate,' the blanket statement that Texas ranks 43rd out of 50 is misleading and likely incorrect.

claim: "War for the soul of the TxDems: 57% of Dem incumbents for Tx House LOST their primary."
rationale: The claim gives no year and there is no widely reported instance in which 57% of Texas House Democratic incumbents were defeated in a single primary. Incumbents typically enjoy a strong advantage in primaries, and a majority-loss rate that large would have been notable and documented.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Paul Ryan’s budget proposal "eliminates Medicare" in 10 years.
rationale: Paul Ryan’s budget proposals did not literally abolish Medicare within 10 years. They proposed converting Medicare into a premium‑support/voucher-style system for future beneficiaries and phasing in changes over time while generally preserving benefits for current enrollees, so saying it "eliminates Medicare in 10 years" is a misleading simplification.

claim: Says Joe Biden tweeted, "the way white people talk leaving minorities confused."
rationale: There is no verifiable record of President Joe Biden tweeting the quoted phrase and it does not appear on his official/verified social media accounts or in major credible reporting. The phrasing is inflammatory and matches patterns of fabricated screenshots or parody posts that have been repeatedly circulated about public figures.

claim: "Last week Joe Biden flashed the ‘white power’ sign. President Trump condemned white supremacists yesterday. Why hasn't Joe Biden?"
rationale: The claim mixes an unverified interpretation of a hand gesture with a false implication about Biden’s stance. There is no credible evidence that Biden intentionally flashed a ‘white power’ sign, and Biden has repeatedly and publicly condemned white supremacy on many occasions. The timing claims about ‘last week’/‘yesterday’ lack necessary context and sourcing.

claim: "Collusion is not illegal."
rationale: The blanket statement is false: many forms of collusion—such as price-fixing, bid‑rigging, market‑allocation, and conspiracies to restrain trade—are illegal under antitrust and criminal laws in many jurisdictions. While not every private agreement is prosecuted, the term 'collusion' typically denotes secret coordination that is unlawful in those contexts.

claim: "Actor Tom Hanks has passed away age 63."
rationale: This is false. Tom Hanks is alive and there have been no credible reports or obituaries confirming his death; he was born July 9, 1956 (making him older than 63 now) and continues to appear in public and media. Death hoaxes about high-profile actors periodically circulate but are not supported by reliable sources.

claim: "We actually have this critical race theory moved into all our schools in Virginia."
rationale: There is no evidence that critical race theory as an academic legal framework has been adopted as required curriculum across all Virginia schools. Reporting and state curriculum standards indicate debates and some local trainings or equity efforts, but not a universal, statewide implementation of CRT in every school.

claim: Says he can’t release his internal affairs record because there are Attorney General guidelines in place protecting it.
rationale: The claim is presented without jurisdiction or specifics, and whether an Attorney General’s guidelines bar release of internal affairs records depends on local law and the specific guidance — there is no universal rule that AG guidelines categorically protect such records. In many jurisdictions internal affairs files can be public, partially redacted, or withheld under specific exemptions (ongoing investigations, privacy), and AG guidance may only advise agencies rather than create a blanket legal bar.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez took a "$10 million payout from Netflix."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or public record that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez received a $10 million payout from Netflix. Such a payment would appear in financial disclosures or major news reports, but disclosures and reputable fact-checks show no $10 million Netflix payment to her.

claim: A flight crew took a knee and stranded the New Orleans Saints on an airport runway.
rationale: There are no credible news reports or contemporaneous evidence that an airline flight crew 'took a knee' as a political protest and thereby stranded the New Orleans Saints on a runway. Viral social posts have repeatedly conflated or fabricated such incidents; routine flight delays or cancellations more commonly stem from mechanical, regulatory, or scheduling reasons rather than coordinated crew protests. Airline crews operate under strict safety and labor rules that make a public on-runway protest leaving a team stranded extremely unlikely and newsworthy.

claim: Says Sens. Lisa Murkowski, Susan Collins and Mitt Romney "are pro-pedophile."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that authoritative sources publicly stated that Sens. Murkowski, Collins, and Romney ‘are pro-pedophile.’ Such an inflammatory allegation would be widely documented by reputable news outlets and public records if verifiable, but none are known. Absent a specific, verifiable source, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton once "wanted a wall" on the Mexican border.
rationale: This claim is misleading: Hillary Clinton has at times supported stronger border security and has been quoted supporting fences and other measures in the mid-2000s, but there is not a clear, uncontested public record of her explicitly saying she “wanted a wall” on the Mexican border in the same sense as the political slogan. Reporting often distinguishes her comments about fences/securement from the later political demand for a full border wall.

claim: Blinken, Austin trip to Kyiv may have been staged
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the visits by U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken and Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin to Kyiv were staged. Multiple independent news organizations, photographs, videos, Ukrainian government confirmations, and contemporaneous reporting corroborated the trip and their on-the-ground meetings. Claims of staging appear to be speculative conspiracy theories rather than fact.

claim: Says that he’s responsible for Austin including Anderson Mill Road in the city's proposed transportation bond package.
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence in the claim text identifying who 'he' is or showing a public record that a single individual was solely responsible for the inclusion of Anderson Mill Road in Austin's proposed transportation bond. Project lists for municipal bond packages are normally produced through staff planning and council decisions rather than the action of one person, so without a named source or documentation the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: ﻿Says JoAnne Kloppenburg’s side had a "3-to-1 money advantage" in the Wisconsin Supreme Court campaign.
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and campaign-finance summaries from the Wisconsin Supreme Court contest showed that conservative-aligned groups and donors outspent JoAnne Kloppenburg’s side, not the other way around. Multiple sources estimated the conservative/Prosser side had roughly a 3-to-1 spending advantage, so the statement that Kloppenburg’s side had a 3-to-1 advantage is contradicted by the financial data.

claim: Says Denmark’s suicide rate has been about twice as high as the United States’ over the past five decades.
rationale: Denmark did have higher suicide rates than the U.S. in parts of the mid-20th century, but over the past five decades the rates have fluctuated and generally converged rather than Denmark remaining about twice as high. In recent decades Denmark’s suicide rate has fallen while the U.S. rate has risen at times, so a consistent ~2x difference across 50 years is not supported by international mortality data.

claim: Says Chris Christie was the "first governor in America to endorse" Mitt Romney.
rationale: The claim is incorrect as stated: Chris Christie was not uniquely the first governor to endorse Mitt Romney. During Romney’s 2012 campaign multiple governors and former governors had already expressed support for Romney before Christie’s public endorsement, and the phrase “first governor in America” is ambiguous without specifying sitting vs. former governors or a precise timeframe.

claim: Says former NRA president Jim Porter said, "It’s only a matter of time before we can own colored people again."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting that a former NRA president named Jim Porter said this. Such an explicit racist remark by a national organizational leader would have been documented in news archives and public records, but searches of known reporting and historical records do not corroborate the quote.

claim: "For the second quarter in a row, my campaign has raised more money than any other challenger in the nation and brought our fundraising total to over $800,000."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no candidate name, election cycle, or specific quarter; without that context there is no way to confirm that this campaign outraised every other challenger nationwide or that the total has exceeded $800,000. National fundraising rankings are publicly trackable (e.g., FEC and campaign reports), and such a strong comparative statement would require citation to those records. In the absence of supporting data, the claim cannot be substantiated and is treated as false.

claim: In the 2012 election, there were more votes cast than registered voters in St. Lucie County, and Palm Beach County had 141 percent turnout.
rationale: Official 2012 election returns do not show St. Lucie County casting more votes than registered voters at the county level, and Palm Beach County’s turnout was nowhere near 141%. Figures above 100% at a county scale would indicate a data/reporting error or a comparison to an out-of-date registration snapshot rather than an actual turnout rate.

claim: Says a group "estimates that the annual cost to Oregon taxpayers for government services to illegal aliens, after any income tax revenue from them, is $1 billion."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it does not identify the group, year, or methodology; there is no widely accepted, corroborated estimate that Oregon’s net annual cost for services to undocumented immigrants is exactly $1 billion. Independent studies and estimates vary widely depending on definitions, services included, and whether children and indirect fiscal effects are counted, so the precise $1 billion figure cannot be confirmed from reliable, consensus sources.

claim: Says Julie Parrish is "one of Sarah Palin’s mama grizzlies."
rationale: Sarah Palin’s phrase “mama grizzlies” referred to women she publicly endorsed or promoted, and there is no public record or notable reporting showing Palin labeled or endorsed Julie Parrish as one of her “mama grizzlies.” While Julie Parrish is a Republican state legislator, available reporting and endorsement lists do not include her under Palin’s known “mama grizzlies.”

claim: Says President Donald Trump "is still yet to say anything as the president of the United States about bounties on American troops."
rationale: This is false because President Trump publicly commented on reports of alleged bounties in 2020, saying he had not been briefed, disputing the reporting, and asserting he would have acted if informed. Multiple public remarks and interviews show he did speak about the issue rather than remaining silent.

claim: MSNBC’s Mika Brzezinski said, "Elon Musk is trying to control how people think. That’s our job."
rationale: The precise quoted line is a misattribution. Brzezinski did criticize Elon Musk’s influence around his Twitter purchase, but reliable transcripts and fact-checks show she did not say the explicit phrase 'That’s our job' — the line circulated in edited/out-of-context clips.

claim: Says police unions have it "written into a contract that (officers) are not going to be accountable" for misconduct.
rationale: The claim as stated is an overgeneralization. While many police union collective bargaining agreements include due‑process protections, disciplinary procedures, arbitration rights, and limits (e.g., interrogation rules or record‑retention clauses) that can make disciplining officers harder, they do not universally contain language that immunizes officers from accountability for misconduct — specifics vary by contract and jurisdiction.

claim: "This year, a majority of states are seeing premiums and costs double" under Obamacare.
rationale: Nationwide data from analysts and federal reports show that while some states and specific plans have seen large premium or cost increases, it is not true that a majority of states experienced premiums and costs doubling in a single year. Marketwide average premium changes are typically much smaller and large, near-100% increases have been isolated, not the norm across most states.

claim: "Last year it was discovered that Rhode Island's public employees ranked 4th in average pay, while the private sector ranked 23rd."
rationale: I could not confirm a reliable source showing that in the most recent year Rhode Island’s public employees ranked 4th in average pay while the private sector ranked 23rd. Federal data sets (BLS, Census/ACS, BEA) produce different rankings depending on the year and whether one compares wages, total compensation, mean or median, and those publicly available tables do not consistently show the stated 4th vs 23rd split. Without a cited source and year the specific numeric claim appears unverified and likely inaccurate.

claim: "Moscow was engulfed in flames" after a giant explosion.
rationale: The claim that Moscow was 'engulfed in flames' after a single giant explosion implies a citywide conflagration; there are no widely corroborated reports that any recent explosion set the entire city ablaze. Explosions can cause significant localized fires and damage, but an entire metropolis being engulfed would be extensively documented by multiple reputable news sources and imagery, which is not the case.

claim: Says David Perdue wants to abolish the U.S. Department of Education, which would cost Georgia schools $1 billion a year and eliminate millions in student loans.
rationale: David Perdue has at times expressed support for reducing or abolishing the U.S. Department of Education, but the claim’s specific consequences are inaccurate or unproven. Abolishing the Department would not automatically erase federal student loans (those are legal obligations that would likely be transferred or managed by another agency), and the asserted $1 billion annual loss to Georgia schools is a specific numeric estimate that is not supported as a direct, inevitable result of abolishing the department without detailed budgetary analysis. The claim conflates Perdue’s stated position with unverified, definitive fiscal outcomes.

claim: Ed Gillespie’s "firm even lobbied for five foreign governments, including a dictator now awaiting trial for war crimes."
rationale: There is no well-documented evidence that Ed Gillespie’s firm lobbied for five foreign governments or that it represented a dictator who is currently awaiting trial for war crimes. Gillespie has worked as a Republican operative and lobbyist and his firms have represented some foreign clients, but major reporting and public lobbying disclosure records do not support the specific claim as stated.

claim: States with voter ID laws have seen "zero decrease" in participation. "Most have seen an increase."
rationale: The claim is overly absolute. Empirical research on voter ID laws is mixed: many studies find little or no overall effect on turnout, but several peer‑reviewed analyses and government reviews have identified small but statistically significant decreases in participation in some states or among particular groups (e.g., minorities, young or low‑income voters), while other states showed no change or increases likely driven by other factors. Thus it is incorrect to state there have been 'zero decreases' and that 'most have seen an increase.'

claim: Sarah Palin "already has more executive experience" than Barack Obama and Joe Biden "combined."
rationale: Sarah Palin served as Wasilla mayor (1996–2002) and Alaska governor (Dec 2006–July 2009), totaling roughly 8–9 years of executive office. Barack Obama served eight years as U.S. president (2009–2017) and Joe Biden served eight years as vice president (2009–2017) and later as president (beginning 2021), so their combined executive time far exceeds Palin's.

claim: "It was allowed," referring to her email practices.
rationale: The statement is misleading. While government employees are sometimes permitted to use personal email for limited official business, Hillary Clinton’s exclusive use of a private email server for State Department business was found by the State Department Inspector General to have violated department policies and by the FBI to be 'extremely careless' in handling classified information, even though prosecutors did not bring criminal charges.

claim: Says President Barack Obama told a room of students, "Children, every time I clap my hands together, a child in America dies from gun violence," and then a child told him he could solve the problem by not clapping any more.
rationale: There is no credible record, transcript, or video of President Obama making that remark to students; the story matches a common satirical/ fabricated anecdote pattern that has circulated online. Contemporary news, official White House transcripts, and reputable fact-checkers have found no evidence the exchange occurred.

claim: The COVID-19 vaccine "will make the common cold/flu extremely lethal."
rationale: There is no credible scientific evidence that COVID-19 vaccines make the common cold or seasonal flu "extremely lethal." COVID-19 vaccines are designed to induce immunity to SARS‑CoV‑2 and do not increase the inherent virulence of unrelated respiratory viruses; population surveillance and clinical data have not shown a rise in cold or flu lethality attributable to COVID-19 vaccination.

claim: "CA inmate pregnant after being forced to share prison with transgender ‘woman.’"
rationale: There is no verifiable, credible reporting of a California prison inmate becoming pregnant specifically after being forced to share a cell with a transgender woman; the claim appears to be an unverified social-media allegation. While it is biologically possible for a transgender woman who retains male reproductive organs to cause pregnancy, specific incidents like this require corroboration from reliable news or official corrections records, which are lacking.

claim: Says Tallahassee mayor Andrew Gillum "wants to make Florida not a sanctuary city but a sanctuary state."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable record of Andrew Gillum using the exact phrase 'wants to make Florida not a sanctuary city but a sanctuary state.' While Gillum as Tallahassee mayor and 2018 gubernatorial candidate did express support for immigrant protections and criticized harsh federal enforcement, attributing that specific quoted formulation lacks reliable sourcing and appears to be a paraphrase or misquote.

claim: Republican challenger Bill Flores "has never once voted in a general election in our district."
rationale: The claim asserts an absolute — that Bill Flores "has never once voted in a general election in our district" — but there is no corroborating evidence presented and such a complete absence of voting by a local political candidate would be unusual and verifiable via public records. Without a specific timeframe or district definition the assertion is unsubstantiated; public voter participation records and reporting on candidates normally contradict claims of total non-participation.

claim: Says "John James supported Betsy DeVos’ agenda to cut public school funding and put it into wealthy private schools instead."
rationale: John James publicly supported Betsy DeVos and has endorsed school choice policies (vouchers, education savings accounts, and charter expansion) that DeVos championed. Those policies redirect public education dollars to private-school tuition or private accounts, which critics say diverts funding away from public schools. The claim frames this as DeVos’s agenda and James’s support of it, which aligns with his stated positions.

claim: "Bill Gates calls for the withdrawal of all Covid-19 Vaccines; ‘The vaccines are far more dangerous than anyone imagined.’"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Bill Gates called for withdrawal of all COVID-19 vaccines or said they are "far more dangerous than anyone imagined." Gates and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation have been public advocates and funders of vaccine development and deployment, and the quoted statement has been repeatedly identified as a fabricated or misattributed social media claim.

claim: Speedway is offering $500 fuel cards for $1.95 to help customers with rising fuel costs.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official announcement that Speedway is selling $500 fuel cards for $1.95. Such a steep discount is financially implausible and matches patterns of viral scam/phony promotions that circulate on social media. Speedway does sell gift cards, but not at that kind of discounted price.

claim: More than 500,000 mail in ballots in Virginia and 200,000 in Nevada were sent to dead people or pets
rationale: State election officials in Virginia and Nevada and multiple independent fact-checkers have found no evidence that hundreds of thousands of mail ballots were sent to deceased people or to pets. The widely circulated figures conflate different datasets (such as inactive registrations or mailed informational materials) and greatly exaggerate the number of any actual mailing errors, which investigations found to be minimal or nonexistent.

claim: Says no one has died from the coronavirus in the United States.
rationale: This claim is false. Since early 2020, the United States has recorded many deaths attributable to COVID-19, documented by the CDC and state health departments and widely reported in major news outlets. Official tallies count hundreds of thousands of deaths over the course of the pandemic.

claim: "Bill Gates talked about using vaccines to control population growth" in an "unedited 2010 TED Talk video"
rationale: In his 2010 TED Talk Bill Gates said that improving vaccines, health care and reproductive health could lower population growth, suggesting global population might be 10–15% lower with such interventions. That statement appears in the unedited TED Talk and was about reducing future population growth indirectly by lowering child mortality, not about using vaccines to directly harm people.

claim: The Fair Tax proposal encourages innovation and investment "level the playing field" for American companies to compete globally.
rationale: This is a contested, predictive policy claim with no clear empirical support: proponents of the Fair Tax argue removing federal income and payroll taxes would boost investment and competitiveness, but economists note the outcome depends on tax rate, border adjustments, macro effects and many other factors. There is no consensus evidence that instituting a national retail sales tax would reliably 'encourage innovation and investment' or automatically 'level the playing field' for U.S. firms versus global competitors.

claim: U.S. Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz "has blamed the Republicans for the creation of Hamas."
rationale: There is no credible record or mainstream reporting showing Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz explicitly saying that Republicans "created" Hamas. While she has criticized Republican foreign-policy positions at times, the specific claim that she blamed Republicans for the creation of Hamas appears to be a misquote or out-of-context attribution.

claim: "Seventy of Ohio's 88 counties now have more than 25 percent of their residents eligible for emergency food."
rationale: I cannot verify this specific county-level statistic and the phrase 'eligible for emergency food' is undefined here. No authoritative statewide data before mid-2024 confirms that 70 of Ohio's 88 counties have more than 25% of residents meeting a consistent eligibility threshold, and the claim likely conflates different measures (food insecurity, SNAP eligibility, or food-bank usage).

claim: Says Mark Kelly wants to "defund the police."
rationale: Mark Kelly has publicly said he does not support ‘‘defunding the police’’ and has advocated for police reform and resources rather than eliminating funding. Media coverage and his campaign statements portray him as opposing the slogan and supporting targeted reforms and community investments.

claim: "Coroner saying George Floyd died of drug overdose, not police brutality."
rationale: The Hennepin County Medical Examiner's official autopsy concluded George Floyd's manner of death was homicide, citing cardiopulmonary arrest due to law enforcement subdual, restraint, and neck compression. While the examiner noted the presence of fentanyl and other health conditions, the office did not rule his death an overdose; a separate privately commissioned autopsy suggested asphyxia and some doctors argued drugs may have contributed.

claim: "This year, Eric Cantor has received more money from oil companies than any other member of Congress."
rationale: The claim is implausible without a specific year and is not supported by typical campaign-finance patterns: contributions from oil and gas are concentrated among lawmakers from energy-producing states and key committee members, and records compiled by watchdogs (FEC/OpenSecrets) are needed to show a top recipient. Eric Cantor has received contributions from the energy sector, but public data historically shows other members receiving larger totals in any given year.

claim: "74 percent of Republicans support the Affordable Care Act."
rationale: Multiple national polls over the past decade show Republicans have generally expressed low favorability for the Affordable Care Act as a whole, so a blanket claim that 74% of Republicans support the ACA contradicts typical partisan polling. The 74% figure is more plausibly the share supporting specific provisions (for example, protections for pre-existing conditions) or comes from a narrowly defined subgroup or question wording rather than overall Republican support for the law.

claim: Delaware has the "eighth-largest black population in the country"
rationale: Delaware is a small state by total population and does not rank eighth among U.S. states by absolute number of Black residents; many larger states (e.g., Texas, Florida, Georgia, New York, California, North Carolina, Illinois, Maryland, Louisiana, etc.) have substantially larger Black populations. The claim likely confuses percentage share with absolute counts or misstates rankings.

claim: Says "$1,100 of the tuition paid by every Oregon university student annually goes just to pay the costs of PERS."
rationale: The claim presents a precise per-student figure as if it universally applies, but there is no single verified $1,100 annual amount that all Oregon university students pay specifically for PERS. PERS costs are employer retirement contributions allocated across institutional budgets and the per‑student impact varies by university, enrollment level, year, and whether unfunded liabilities or only current contributions are counted. The statement overgeneralizes a possible estimate or model result as a uniform fact.

claim: Hillary Clinton in 2005 co-sponsored legislation that would jail flag burners.
rationale: There is no reliable record that Hillary Clinton co-sponsored a 2005 bill specifically to jail people for burning the U.S. flag. While the Senate debated and some lawmakers (and at times Clinton) have supported measures or a constitutional amendment to permit bans on flag desecration, the specific claim about her co-sponsoring 2005 legislation imposing jail time is not supported by congressional sponsorship records and contemporary reporting.

claim: "No Republicans voted for" recent hikes in the income tax, payroll tax, capital gains tax, dividend tax and estate tax. "These taxes were all passed under … Obamacare."
rationale: This mixes facts and falsehoods. The Affordable Care Act did create two targeted levies — a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax on investment income (affecting capital gains and dividends for high earners) and a 0.9% additional Medicare payroll tax — and nearly all Republicans opposed the ACA votes. However, other changes sometimes described as “tax hikes” (broad income tax rate changes, the 2013 estate-tax rate/threshold changes and other tax measures) were enacted in separate laws (e.g., post-2010 tax legislation) and were not all ‘‘passed under Obamacare’’ nor uniformly voted against by Republicans.

claim: "Constituents now face reality that all their personal issues will be made public" under Clean Missouri.
rationale: This statement is an overbroad mischaracterization. Clean Missouri (2018) enacted reforms around redistricting, limits on gifts, and greater disclosure of campaign contributions and some official financial information, but it did not make "all" constituents' personal issues public. Ordinary private personal information remains protected; only certain political donations, lobbyist interactions, and some official disclosures are subject to public reporting.

claim: "The Clinton Foundation folded."
rationale: The Clinton Foundation did not fold; it has continued to operate as a registered nonprofit and to run programs after the 2016 election. Although it scaled back staff and lost some donors following Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign, it did not dissolve or cease operations.

claim: Said Adolf Hitler and Donald Trump have both described deportations as "a military operation."
rationale: There is no well‑documented evidence that Adolf Hitler described deportations using the phrase 'a military operation.' While Nazi officials used euphemisms and militaristic organization for mass deportations, the specific claim that Hitler himself and Donald Trump both described deportations as 'a military operation' is unsupported. Trump has occasionally used militaristic metaphors about immigration enforcement, but that does not establish the identical formulation attributed to both men.

claim: "How is a misogynist bigot of epic proportions (like U.S. Rep. Steven Smith) allowed to serve?"
rationale: The statement is a subjective insult rather than a verifiable factual claim — calling someone a “misogynist bigot of epic proportions” reflects an opinion that requires specific, documented evidence (e.g., verified statements, findings, or convictions) to be treated as fact. Separately, whether an elected representative is "allowed to serve" is governed by elections, resignation, ethics investigations, criminal convictions, or formal expulsion procedures, none of which are cited here.

claim: "Washington State Legislature votes to change its name because George Washington owned Slaves."
rationale: There has been no official action by the Washington State Legislature to change the name of the state because George Washington owned slaves. Proposals and local discussions about monuments or renaming specific places have occurred, but no statewide name-change bill has been passed or enacted.

claim: "We know that more than half of Hillary Clinton's meetings while she was secretary of state were given to major contributors to the Clinton Foundation."
rationale: Independent fact-checks and analysis of State Department schedules do not support the claim that a majority of Clinton’s meetings as secretary of state were with major Clinton Foundation contributors. Only a minority of her meetings involved people or organizations appearing on Clinton Foundation donor lists, and many alleged 'donors' were foreign officials or entities whose meetings would normally occur in that role.

claim: Between 2008 and 2014, "criminal aliens accounted for 38 percent of all murder convictions in the five states of California, Texas, Arizona, Florida and New York."
rationale: The 38% figure is not supported by transparent, representative data and has been flagged by independent fact-checkers as misleading. It appears to come from a selective analysis with a narrow definition of 'criminal aliens' and choices of states/timeframe that produce an inflated share; broader, verifiable datasets do not corroborate such a high, generalizable percentage.

claim: Dr. Phil and other celebrities are endorsing CBD gummies.
rationale: There is widespread evidence that many celebrities have promoted or invested in CBD products, but I am not aware of credible, verifiable reports that Dr. Phil has endorsed CBD gummies. The claim names Dr. Phil specifically, and available public reporting does not substantiate his endorsement while it does for several other celebrities.

claim: "If there is a firearm available, it is 17 times more likely to be used either for suicide or for assaulting a friend, relative, an acquaintance than it is to be used in fending off an intruder."
rationale: There is no broad scientific consensus that the presence of a firearm makes it precisely 17 times more likely to be used for suicide or assault of an acquaintance than for defending against an intruder. Multiple studies have found guns in the home are associated with higher risks of suicide and domestic homicide than documented defensive uses, but reported multipliers vary widely by study design and definitions of “defensive use.”

claim: "Today Russia holds many of our most precious national security satellites at risk before they ever get off the ground."
rationale: The statement implies that, currently, Russia can prevent many U.S. national security satellites from ever being launched. While the U.S. historically depended on Russian RD-180 engines for some national-security launches (creating potential leverage), that dependence has been largely addressed through policy changes and the rise of domestic launch vehicles (e.g., SpaceX Falcon family and U.S.-built engines for new rockets). Therefore it is not accurate today to say Russia presently holds many of those satellites at risk before launch.

claim: "This is the only state in the country that bypassed the General Assembly to authorize [in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants]."
rationale: The statement is incorrect because multiple states have authorized in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants through routes other than their legislatures, such as actions by university governing boards, courts, or executive agencies. Therefore it is not true that any single state is uniquely the only one to bypass its general assembly for this policy.

claim: Says in U.S. Congress, members "don’t even have to be on the floor for debates or votes."
rationale: Both the House and Senate generally require members to be physically present on the chamber floor to speak during debate and to cast recorded floor votes. There was a temporary exception in the House during the COVID-19 pandemic (proxy voting) and committees have used remote participation, but those were limited exceptions rather than the normal practice.

claim: "I did not support the war in Iraq … The record shows that I’m right."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific person's lack of support for the Iraq War and that the record confirms this, but no speaker or record is identified. Without knowing who 'I' refers to and which votes/statements are meant, the claim cannot be verified and therefore cannot be treated as established fact.

claim: "Joe Biden’s great-grandfather Joseph J. Biden was a slave-owner and fought" for the Confederacy.
rationale: There is no credible genealogical or historical evidence that President Biden’s great-grandfather Joseph J. Biden owned slaves or fought for the Confederacy. Fact-checkers and available family records indicate Biden’s ancestors were Irish immigrants living in Delaware/Pennsylvania and not documented as Confederate slaveowners or soldiers.

claim: "TSA WILL ACCEPT DRIVERS PRIV CARDS FOR ID AT THE AIRPORT"
rationale: The claim is too broad. TSA only accepts identity documents that appear on its official list or that meet federal REAL ID standards; many state-issued "driver's privilege" cards are not REAL ID-compliant and therefore are not universally accepted as primary ID for boarding without additional screening. In some cases TSA can still verify identity through secondary screening, but that is not the same as unconditional acceptance.

claim: Scott Walker "couldn’t get his own party" to back more than a 500-student increase in Milwaukee’s school choice program, but in Indiana, "Mitch Daniels’ voucher program is approaching 30,000 students two years after opening."
rationale: The claim mixes and exaggerates facts. While Wisconsin debate over expanding the Milwaukee Parental Choice Program involved intra‑party disagreement, Republicans did approve expansions larger than a mere 500‑student increase at various times; the statement that Walker “couldn’t get his own party” to back more than 500 is misleading without dates and bill details. The Indiana portion overstates timing: Indiana’s voucher program did grow quickly under Mitch Daniels’ administration, but enrollment two years after major expansion was in the mid‑ to high‑20,000s (not clearly “approaching 30,000”) and depends on which start date is used.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "voted for regime change with respect to Libya."
rationale: Bernie Sanders did not cast a congressional vote explicitly authorizing or endorsing 'regime change' in Libya; the 2011 intervention was carried out under a U.N. Security Council mandate and NATO action rather than a U.S. congressional authorization that Sanders supported. Sanders has publicly said he opposed regime-change wars and his voting record does not show a direct vote to authorize U.S. regime change in Libya.

claim: "Biden's plan is a 14% tax hike on middle class families."
rationale: The statement lacks context and is misleading: Biden's publicly announced tax proposals have largely targeted corporations and high‑income households (for example, raising rates on incomes over $400,000 and higher capital gains rates for very large incomes), not a uniform 14% tax increase on middle‑class families. Independent analyses and official summaries of Biden's plans did not show a blanket 14% tax hike imposed on middle‑class households.

claim: "The United States imprisons more than any nation in the world."
rationale: Major international data compilations routinely list the United States as having the largest total prison population and one of the highest incarceration rates per capita. Although some countries (notably China) operate large and sometimes opaque detention systems that can complicate comparisons, commonly used statistics place the U.S. at the top in absolute prison numbers.

claim: "California to teach kindergarteners there are 15 genders."
rationale: There is no California statewide mandate that kindergarteners be taught there are "15 genders." The claim appears to conflate isolated lesson materials or resource lists that enumerate many gender identities with an official, required K–12 curriculum. California education policy allows districts and teachers to use various resources, but state standards do not compel teaching a specific number of genders to kindergarteners.

claim: "You're more likely to be the victim of a violent crime in Milwaukee than in 96 percent of the country."
rationale: The claim gives a precise percentile (higher than 96% of the country) but does not cite a year, data source, or whether it compares cities, counties, or all places. Milwaukee does have a high violent crime rate relative to many U.S. jurisdictions, but without a specific dataset the exact “96 percent” figure is not verifiable and is likely inaccurate. Because of the ambiguity and lack of a supporting source, the precise quantitative claim should be treated as false.

claim: "If we keep the minimum wage at the current level, then single-parent families earning the minimum wage at a full-time job will live in poverty in New Jersey."
rationale: The statement is overly broad. Whether a single-parent family working full-time at New Jersey’s minimum wage falls below the poverty line depends on household size and the exact wage level: a single parent with one child often earns above the federal poverty guideline at typical state minimum-wage annual earnings, while families with two or more children commonly fall below the poverty threshold. Therefore it is not true as an absolute rule that all single-parent families working full-time at the minimum wage in New Jersey will live in poverty.

claim: "Forty-seven percent of (members of Congress) are millionaires."
rationale: The proportion of U.S. members of Congress who are millionaires changes by congressional session and by the methodology used to estimate net worth; a naked statement that '47%' are millionaires is unsupported without a date or source. Recent analyses have reported varying figures (commonly in the roughly 40–60% range), so the precise 47% claim is misleading as presented.

claim: "We now have more jobs in solar than we do in oil."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous about who 'we' refers to, and on the broad, global level it is false: worldwide oil and gas-related employment is far larger than solar employment. Even within countries, totals depend heavily on definitions (extraction, refining, support services, indirect jobs), and most comprehensive counts still show oil and gas employing more people than solar.

claim: "59 people die as pastor gives them dettol to drink in church to prevent coronavirus."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence or major news reporting confirming that 59 people died after a pastor gave them Dettol to drink to prevent coronavirus. Large mass fatalities of that sort would have been widely documented, and fact-checkers have debunked similar viral claims which misstate numbers, substances, or circumstances.

claim: "North Carolina spends $855 less per student than it did before the Great Recession, and we have one of the lowest per pupil spending levels in the nation."
rationale: The statement’s precise claim that North Carolina spends exactly $855 less per student than it did before the Great Recession is not reliably supportable because published per‑pupil figures vary by the chosen base year, whether amounts are adjusted for inflation, and the data source. It is true that North Carolina cut education spending after the recession and has often ranked near the bottom nationally on per‑pupil spending, but the specific $855 decline and the unqualified "one of the lowest" label depend on year and metric choices and therefore make the combined claim misleading.

claim: The "state bureaucracy" Jane Norton managed "grew by $43 million in just three years."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported by readily verifiable public data: it fails to specify which agency or budget lines are included, a clear three‑year period, or a source for the $43 million figure. Without a named department and timeframe, the statement appears to be an unsupported assertion rather than a documented fact.

claim: "There is no reason to allocate 60 percent of bridge space to satisfy two percent of all travelers."
rationale: The statement is a broad normative claim that cannot be universally true: there are plausible, documented reasons to allocate a large share of bridge space to benefit a small percentage of users, including safety (emergency lanes), accessible design, non-motorized travel space, and future demand. Whether 60 percent is justified depends on the specific bridge, user mix, legal obligations, and planning goals, so the categorical claim "no reason" is incorrect.

claim: Photos show Kamala Harris, Joe Biden, Gretchen Whitmer and Cory Booker violating COVID-19 safety precautions.
rationale: The claim is too general and lacks context; while there are isolated photos of each individual without masks at various times, whether those images constitute violations of COVID-19 precautions depends on date, location, vaccination status, and the public-health guidance in effect. Without specifying which photos and the applicable rules at the time, it is not accurate to assert categorically that the photos show violations. Some images circulated online were taken in situations where mask use was not required or where people were vaccinated and following contemporaneous guidance.

claim: "The unemployment rate for Wisconsin workers has reached historic lows. It’s never been this low before, ever, ever, ever."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that Wisconsin’s unemployment rate has never been this low in all of history; such definitive claims are unlikely and not supported without a specific date and data series. Historical labor‑market records (from the BLS and state labor agencies) show multiple periods when state unemployment reached similarly low levels, and rates depend on whether they are seasonally adjusted, by metro area, or for particular demographic groups.

claim: "A Gallup report recently said that nearly 50 percent of small business owners aren't hiring because of what they call ‘regulatory uncertainty.’"
rationale: There is no known recent Gallup report showing nearly 50% of small-business owners say they aren’t hiring due to 'regulatory uncertainty.' Gallup’s small-business and workplace polls typically list demand, costs, and labor availability as the top barriers to hiring, with regulation cited by a much smaller share. Without a specific citation, the claim overstates what Gallup has reported.

claim: Says a California surfer was "alone, in the ocean," when he was arrested for violating the state’s stay-at-home order.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that the surfer was literally alone in the water at the moment he was arrested; contemporaneous accounts of similar incidents show officers encountered or detained surfers after they reached shore or in the presence of others. The claim appears to overstate or mischaracterize the circumstances to imply an implausible solitary in-water arrest.

claim: "Wisconsin’s economy is in the best shape it’s been since 2000."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify and is not supported as a blanket statement: different economic indicators tell different stories. Wisconsin has seen very low unemployment in recent years, but measures like real GDP per capita, median household income adjusted for inflation, and long-term job growth do not uniformly show that the state's economy is unequivocally "the best" since 2000.

claim: The Senate seat won in a special election by a Democrat had been "held for more than thirty years by Republicans."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely false because it gives no specific seat and recent well-known special-election pickups by Democrats were for seats Republicans had held far less than 30 years. For example, Doug Jones won Alabama’s 2017 special election to fill Jeff Sessions’s seat, which Sessions had held since 1997 (~20 years), and Raphael Warnock’s 2021 win filled a Georgia seat that had not been in continuous GOP hands for over three decades. Without identifying the specific seat, the blanket statement that the seat had been held by Republicans for more than thirty years is not supported.

claim: "In 2005, Dan Branch tried to expand third-trimester abortions in Texas."
rationale: Dan Branch is a Republican Texas state representative with a pro‑life legislative record; there is no credible evidence he sought to expand third‑trimester abortions in 2005. Instead, Branch has supported restrictions on abortion and has been associated with anti‑abortion positions. The claim reverses his known policy stance.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to get rid of the federal minimum wage."
rationale: There is no clear, consistent public record of Donald Trump explicitly saying he wants to abolish the federal minimum wage. His statements have varied — sometimes favoring state-level decisions or opposing increases — but not a clear, repeated call to 'get rid of' the federal minimum wage outright.

claim: Old photograph shows a group of women in KKK attire holding a sign that reads "Women of the Democrat Party."
rationale: The widely circulated photo with a sign reading "Women of the Democrat Party" has been debunked; fact-checkers found the wording in the sign was misattributed or digitally altered. Authentic historical photos do show women in KKK robes and women's Klan auxiliaries, but the image does not legitimately label them as members of the Democratic Party.

claim: Says Rick Scott has "teamed up with a felon convicted of running a Ponzi scheme to smear Charlie Crist."
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable reporting identifying Rick Scott as having ‘‘teamed up’’ with any person convicted of running a Ponzi scheme to smear Charlie Crist. Major coverage of Scott–Crist campaigns and known Ponzi-scheme convictions (e.g., high-profile defendants) do not show such an alliance, and the claim names no specific convicted individual or source. Without a named person or corroborating evidence, the assertion appears unsubstantiated.

claim: The $1.9 trillion relief package is "about a bridge for Chuck Schumer, a tunnel for Nancy Pelosi."
rationale: The statement is a rhetorical/political jab, not a factual description of the $1.9 trillion American Rescue Plan. The law primarily provided stimulus checks, extended unemployment benefits, state and local aid, public-health and vaccine funding, and did not authorize literal bridge or tunnel projects for Senators Schumer or Pelosi.

claim: "Even with full control of the House, Senate and White House, Republicans have still failed to deliver on their promise of higher wages for working families."
rationale: The statement is a broad, time‑insensitive assertion that is not clearly supported. In the most recent period of unified Republican control (2017–2019) measured wages and average hourly earnings did rise modestly and some employers issued bonuses tied to tax cuts, while longer‑term trends and distributional effects are contested — so a blanket claim that Republicans "failed to deliver" higher wages is overstated.

claim: Says the Obama administration "didn't lock people up in cages."
rationale: The absolute claim that the Obama administration "didn't lock people up in cages" is incorrect. During the Obama years Border Patrol and CBP used chain-link enclosures and family detention facilities that have been described and documented as "cages" for holding migrants (including children) during the 2014 surge and in subsequent years, as reported by journalists, human-rights groups, and congressional testimony.

claim: Says Russ Feingold said that with Obamacare, "we could keep our doctors and our plans, it was rated as the Lie of the Year."
rationale: I find no reliable record that Senator Russ Feingold uttered that exact line; the underlying fact-checking note that Obama’s promise “you can keep your plan” was named PolitiFact’s 2013 "Lie of the Year" is true, but attributing the quoted phrase to Feingold is unverified and likely a misattribution.

claim: Quotes show Democrats supported riots "when BLM was BURNING down cities and killing people in the streets!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Democratic leaders broadly endorsed violent rioting; most publicly condemned violence while supporting peaceful protest and police reform. The claim that 'BLM was BURNING down cities and killing people in the streets' is a broad, misleading characterization — most 2020 protests were peaceful, and incidents of arson or killings were limited, not the result of an organized, widespread BLM campaign.

claim: Says David Dewhurst "explicitly advocated" a guest worker program for all illegal immigrants.
rationale: There is no clear public record that David Dewhurst explicitly advocated a blanket guest-worker program for all undocumented immigrants. His documented positions during his tenure emphasized border security, employer verification (E-Verify), and enforcement-first approaches, with any support for temporary-worker schemes framed as limited rather than a universal program for all illegal immigrants.

claim: Says President Donald Trump as a candidate mentioned WikiLeaks "over 160 times in speeches" in the last month of the campaign.
rationale: There is no reliable record showing Trump said “WikiLeaks” over 160 times in speeches during the final month of the 2016 campaign; independent transcript and media counts place mentions far lower (dozens rather than hundreds). The claim appears to conflate different formats (tweets, interviews, rallies) or miscount repetitions across many short remarks.

claim: "Mayor Barrett saved Milwaukee $25 million, thanks to Gov. Walker’s reforms."
rationale: The claim that Mayor Tom Barrett “saved Milwaukee $25 million” specifically because of Gov. Scott Walker’s reforms is not supported by verifiable evidence. Walker’s 2011 Act 10 changed collective bargaining and employee contribution rules and its fiscal effects were contested; public safety employees (a large cost driver in Milwaukee) were largely exempt and independent analyses did not attribute a clear $25 million one-time savings to Barrett tied solely to Walker’s reforms. Numbers cited by politicians have varied and been disputed, so the precise $25 million attribution is not verifiable.

claim: Says Nancy Pelosi diverted "$2.4 billion from Social Security to cover impeachment costs."
rationale: There is no evidence that Speaker Nancy Pelosi diverted $2.4 billion from Social Security to pay impeachment costs. Social Security payroll taxes are held in legally protected trust funds and cannot be repurposed by the Speaker; impeachment expenses are paid through regular congressional appropriations from the general fund.

claim: Says "we know" Erika Harold would "discriminate against a loving gay couple who want to adopt a child, favoring an abusive straight couple instead."
rationale: There is no verifiable public record or reliable evidence that Erika Harold stated she would favor an abusive straight couple over a loving gay couple in an adoption; that specific claim asserts knowledge of a concrete discriminatory action she would take and is not supported by documented statements or policy positions. While Harold has historically taken conservative positions on same-sex marriage, generalized opposition to gay marriage is not the same as an explicit pledge to place children with abusive straight couples instead of loving gay ones.

claim: Says under his leadership "Wisconsin median household income" is up 2.7%, while it is down 1.3% nationally under President Obama.
rationale: Official household income series from the U.S. Census show that national median household income rose overall during Barack Obama’s presidency (recovering after the Great Recession), so framing it as down 1.3% under Obama is inconsistent with the broader ACS data. The Wisconsin +2.7% figure is plausibly true for a narrowly selected interval, but without specified start/end dates these percentages are misleading and do not support the blanket comparison offered.

claim: Former Gov. Pat McCrory appointed liberals to the North Carolina Textbook Commission, which "mandated textbooks" pushing critical race theory.
rationale: While governors appoint members to state textbook-adoption bodies, the claim mixes subjective labels and an unsupported policy outcome. There is no clear evidence that Pat McCrory specifically appointed a slate of self-identified "liberals" to the commission in a way that led the body to formally mandate K–12 textbooks that "push" critical race theory; CRT is an academic legal theory not typically presented as a mandated K–12 curriculum and North Carolina’s adoption process does not explicitly require teaching CRT.

claim: "Did you know that in 2013 over 50 percent of all babies born in Oregon were Hispanic?"
rationale: Statewide vital statistics for Oregon in 2013 show that Hispanic infants were a minority of births, not a majority. While Hispanic birth rates are higher than some groups and some counties or communities may have had majority-Hispanic births, over 50% of all births statewide is not supported by available demographic/birth data.

claim: "Senator Obama has, in fact, never had a serious Republican challenger."
rationale: As U.S. Senator from Illinois, Barack Obama only ran in one Senate general election (2004) and his Republican opponent was Alan Keyes, a last-minute out-of-state replacement who was widely regarded as a weak, non-viable challenger; Obama did not seek reelection in 2008 because he ran for president. Given he faced no prominent competitive Republican opponents during his Senate tenure, the claim is accurate in ordinary usage.

claim: Says his plan to end the toll on Ga. 400 fulfills his campaign promise to commuters.
rationale: The statement is unverified as presented: it gives no named speaker, date, or source for the quote and thus cannot be corroborated from the information provided. Without a verifiable attribution or independent reporting that a specific official said his plan would end the GA‑400 toll and thereby fulfill a particular campaign promise, the claim should be treated as false/unconfirmed.

claim: "We have a 40 to 50 percent dropout rate in our inner-city schools."
rationale: The claim is too broad and undocumented: it asserts a uniform 40–50% dropout rate across 'our inner-city schools' without specifying location, time period, or metric. In the United States and many other countries, overall high-school dropout rates are much lower today (graduation rates are commonly in the 80s percent), though some specific high-poverty schools or districts have had much higher rates in the past. Therefore the blanket statement is not supported as a general fact.

claim: "Under the federal Controlled Substance Act, marijuana is listed in the same Schedule I as heroin," even though "marijuana is not a killer drug like heroin."
rationale: Federally, the Controlled Substances Act places cannabis (marijuana) in Schedule I alongside substances such as heroin, a legal classification that remains despite many states legalizing cannabis. Pharmacologically and in terms of overdose risk, heroin is an opioid that commonly causes fatal respiratory depression, while there is no well-documented direct lethal overdose from marijuana, so it is not considered a "killer drug" in the same way heroin is.

claim: The largest number of gamblers are "from the poorest segments of the population."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad generalization. Empirical research shows lower-income people are overrepresented among players of some forms (lotteries, electronic gaming machines) and among problem gamblers, but overall gambling participation varies by type, country, and definition of “gambler,” and many forms (e.g., sports betting, casino high-stakes play) have substantial participation by middle- and higher-income groups.

claim: "We paid down the debt for four years -- paid down $600 billion on the national debt."
rationale: The claim lacks a timeframe and is incorrect as a general statement: in recent administrations the federal debt has generally risen rather than been "paid down" for four years. Only in the late 1990s (under the Clinton administration) did budget surpluses lead to modest reductions in certain debt measures over a few years, and those reductions were on the order of a few hundred billion dollars depending on the metric — not a clear, unqualified four-year $600 billion paydown as stated. Without specifying which debt measure (gross debt vs. debt held by the public) and which four-year period, the statement is misleading and not supported by the broad historical record.

claim: "Obama certificate a fake."
rationale: The claim that Barack Obama's birth certificate is fake is false. Hawaii state officials and the Hawaii Department of Health have certified his birth in Honolulu, Obama released his long-form birth certificate in 2011, and independent fact-checkers and courts have debunked the 'birther' allegations.

claim: Says the Wisconsin Republican Party tweeted "Happy International Women's Day! You ladies should get paid less and not be able to make health care decisions."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the official Wisconsin Republican Party account tweeted that explicit, overtly sexist message; such a provocative post would have been widely reported and archived if real. Similar claims have circulated as doctored screenshots, parody accounts, or misattributions in social media hoaxes.

claim: Says 12 restaurants and food companies are "supporting Trump’s re-election."
rationale: The statement offers no verifiable source and is ambiguous about what counts as 'supporting' (official corporate endorsement, owner donation, PAC contribution, etc.). Corporations rarely issue direct candidate endorsements and political activity is typically traceable through FEC/transparent records; without a cited list or timeframe the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "He's the only candidate who's balanced budgets and brought jobs to Providence."
rationale: The claim asserts an exclusive fact ('only candidate') without identifying who 'he' is or the time period, and such exclusivity is unlikely: multiple Providence officials and candidates have presided over balanced budgets and job-creation efforts. Proving the claim would require comprehensive fiscal and employment records across all candidates and administrations, which are not provided.

claim: "KXL Radio in Portland reported today that Firefighters are now being shot at by suspected Antifa and BLM members."
rationale: There is no corroborating evidence from credible local or national news outlets that KXL in Portland broadcast that firefighters are being shot at by suspected Antifa or BLM members. Claims of this type have circulated on social media before and are often unverified or misattributed; without independent confirmation from the station or law enforcement, the statement is unsupported.

claim: At this point in 2012, "Rick Perry was ahead at 29.9 percent, and we had seven more leads before it finally settled on Mitt Romney."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and lacks a specific poll, date, or source; there is no clear evidence that Rick Perry was "ahead at 29.9 percent" at a defined point in 2012 or that there were exactly "seven more leads" before Romney became the nominee. Perry did have brief polling surges in 2011 and early 2012 but he never sustained a stable nationwide lead that is documented as 29.9% before the race consolidated around Mitt Romney. Because the claim is underspecified and not supported by well-documented poll histories, it is not verifiable as stated.

claim: "Since President (Donald Trump’s) election, 36,000 jobs have been created in WI."
rationale: The claim gives no precise time window or data source and is not verifiable as stated. Official labor statistics (BLS and Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development) report different job-change totals depending on the exact start/end months and whether counting private-sector or total nonfarm payrolls, so a flat statement of “36,000 jobs” since the election is misleading and likely inaccurate without a specified period and series.

claim: "Wikileaks also shows how John Podesta rigged the polls by oversampling Democrats, a voter suppression technique."
rationale: The Podesta emails released by WikiLeaks include campaign communications about polling and strategy but do not show Podesta directing pollsters to 'rig' polls by oversampling Democrats. Oversampling or weighting by party is a common survey methodology used by pollsters and is not a voter suppression technique, which refers to actions that prevent or discourage people from voting.

claim: Says Clint Eastwood called Joe Biden an "incompetent, lying, flip-flopping, insincere, double-talking, radical socialist."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Clint Eastwood ever said Joe Biden was an "incompetent, lying, flip-flopping, insincere, double-talking, radical socialist." The phrase appears to be a fabricated or misattributed quote circulated on social media; while Eastwood has occasionally expressed political views, reputable fact-checkers and news outlets have not documented him saying this string of epithets.

claim: "Unvaccinated, you can get COVID and have over 99% chance of survival. Get vaccinated and you can still get COVID and will still have over 99% chance of survival."
rationale: This claim is misleading because survival from COVID-19 varies widely by age, health status, and variant. While many younger, healthy people have infection fatality risks below 1%, older adults and those with comorbidities have substantially higher mortality when unvaccinated; vaccines substantially reduce the risk of severe disease and death, and although breakthrough infections occur, vaccinated people generally have lower mortality risk than comparable unvaccinated people.
