rationale: The Republican National Convention assembles delegates, alternates, party officials, media and guests from all states and territories and typically numbers in the thousands, making it larger than any single state party convention. State conventions are organized within one state and generally involve hundreds to a few thousand participants, so a single state convention is not larger than the national convention in normal circumstances.

claim: "Our economy still has three people looking for every job (opening)."
rationale: The statement is not accurate for the modern U.S. labor market: the Bureau of Labor Statistics (JOLTS) and unemployment data show far fewer than three unemployed persons per job opening in recent years (ratios have been below 2 and often below 1 since the post‑pandemic period). While there were times (e.g., 2009) when the ratio approached or exceeded 3, that is not the current or typical situation.

claim: Says the state tax burden per citizen in New York is twice as high as in Florida.
rationale: The claim lacks a specified year and measure, and available public data (state and local tax burden per capita from sources like the Tax Foundation and Census of Governments) show New York’s per‑person state/local tax burden is higher than Florida’s but not typically twice as large. Differences depend on the exact metric and year, but historical per‑capita figures generally show New York exceeding Florida by tens of percent rather than 100%+.

claim: Says the U.S. Constitution "doesn’t say anything about (redistricting) being fair. … it’s set up to be partisan."
rationale: The U.S. Constitution does not contain an explicit requirement that legislative districts be 'fair' and it leaves much of the regulation of elections and apportionment to states and Congress. Because state legislatures (political bodies) typically draw district lines and the Constitution does not mandate nonpartisan criteria, the process can and often does produce partisan outcomes; courts have limited remedial power over partisan gerrymandering at the federal level.

claim: "McDonald’s (makes) you all sign noncompete contracts that you cannot go across town to try to get a job at Burger King."
rationale: This is an overgeneralization: McDonald's does not universally make all crew members sign noncompete agreements prohibiting work at nearby competitors. Whether a noncompete is used depends on the franchisee or corporate policy and the employee's role; many jurisdictions also ban or limit noncompetes for low-wage workers, and courts often refuse to enforce broad noncompetes for ordinary fast-food employees.

claim: "Bill Nelson voted for a ban on millions of commonly owned firearms, which included many popular hunting and target rifles."
rationale: There is no clear record that Bill Nelson voted for a broad ban that would have outlawed "millions" of commonly owned firearms or that included most popular hunting and target rifles. The major federal gun bans people refer to (for example the 1994 federal assault weapons ban) targeted specific semiautomatic models or features and excluded most traditional hunting and bolt-action target rifles; votes Nelson supported relate to narrower "assault weapon" restrictions and background-check measures rather than a blanket ban on widely owned hunting/target firearms.

claim: "Sen. Obama's chair in New Hampshire is a lobbyist. He lobbies for the drug companies."
rationale: The claim names no specific individual and there is no reliable evidence that any publicly identified campaign chair for Senator/President Obama in New Hampshire was a pharmaceutical lobbyist. Public reporting on Obama’s New Hampshire campaign leadership does not support the allegation that a named chair lobbied for drug companies. Without a specific person and corroborating sources, the assertion is unverified and likely false.

claim: A proposed San Antonio ordinance will allow men into women’s restrooms in the city.
rationale: The claim is misleading: most proposed San Antonio nondiscrimination ordinances that have been discussed concern protections for gender identity and generally permit people to use restrooms that align with their gender identity (i.e., transgender women), not a blanket rule allowing any man into women’s restrooms. Whether a specific ordinance does this depends on its exact text, so the blanket phrasing is inaccurate.

claim: "If your employer is mandating any pokes, do not quit. Make them fire you. That way you get unemployment benefits."
rationale: This is not universally true. Eligibility for unemployment benefits depends on jurisdiction and the reason for separation: many places deny benefits if you quit voluntarily or are fired for misconduct (which can include refusing a lawful workplace requirement), while other jurisdictions or specific circumstances (wrongful termination, exemptions) might allow benefits.

claim: Says voter roll purge would mean "more than 200,000 registered Wisconsin voters will be prohibited from voting."
rationale: The claim frames a purge as meaning 'more than 200,000 registered Wisconsin voters will be prohibited from voting,' which is misleading. Routine voter-roll maintenance can flag many registrations for review, but flagged registrants are not automatically barred from voting — they can often update registration, cast a provisional ballot, or be restored after verification; the specific figure and the absolute prohibition claim lack corroboration and ignore these remedial processes.

claim: "Wholly domestic communication between you and your wife can go to New York to London and back and get caught up in the (NSA) database."
rationale: Internet and telephone traffic between two domestic endpoints can sometimes be routed through international hubs (for example via London) and intelligence agencies have collected at undersea cables and foreign transit points. Leaks and oversight reports have shown the NSA’s upstream collection can capture communications that are incidentally domestic when they transit foreign networks or are stored on foreign servers.

claim: "Clinton campaign official arrested by FBI on child rape/trafficking charges"
rationale: There is no credible evidence — no FBI press release, court record, or reporting from reputable news organizations — that any named Clinton campaign official was arrested by the FBI on child rape or trafficking charges. Viral social-media posts making this claim have been repeatedly debunked and typically lack verifiable details; some individuals associated with Clinton have faced unrelated legal or personal scandals, but none match this allegation.

claim: "Candidate Slotkin had presented herself as a moderate and as someone who’d be independent-minded, but her time in office was making it increasingly clear that no, she was very partisan, voting 96% of the time with Speaker Pelosi."
rationale: The claim hinges on a precise statistic (that Rep. Elissa Slotkin voted 96% of the time with Speaker Pelosi) and a broad characterization of her as 'very partisan.' I cannot verify a reliable source that places Slotkin at exactly 96% across her tenure; such voting-alignment percentages vary by time period and measurement method, and many Democratic representatives routinely record high party-alignment rates. The subjective claim that her record 'made it increasingly clear' she was 'very partisan' is not conclusively established by the unverified precise percentage.

claim: "Back when they did NATO, there was no such thing as terrorism."
rationale: NATO was founded in 1949, but terrorism and the term 'terrorism' long predate that date. Examples include the French Revolution's 'Reign of Terror', 19th- and early-20th-century anarchist and nationalist violent campaigns, and later groups like the IRA; the concept and word were in use well before NATO's creation.

claim: "When I took office, the deficit was nearly 10 percent of our economy. Today, it's approaching 3 percent."
rationale: The claim misstates both endpoints. At the time he took office (early 2021) the federal deficit as a share of GDP was well above 10% due to COVID-era spending (on the order of the mid-teens percent), and recent deficits have fallen but remain larger than about 3% of GDP—typically in the several-percent range—so the statement understates the earlier peak and the current deficit.

claim: Says Sri Kulkarni attended "notorious desert drug parties" and was arrested for cocaine.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or public arrest record showing Sri Preston Kulkarni was arrested for cocaine or attended 'notorious desert drug parties.' Reliable fact-checking outlets and searches of public records found the allegation originating from unverified social media posts and political smears, and Kulkarni has not been charged with such an offense.

claim: Says that "over a 45-minute period that we had the press conference" on the coronavirus on March 13, 2020, the stock market set "an all-time record."
rationale: On March 13, 2020 U.S. equity markets were amid the COVID-19 crash and were not setting all-time highs; that period featured large declines and volatility rather than record highs. No major index logged a new all-time high during the roughly 45-minute window of that press conference.

claim: "Under Pat McCrory, (North Carolina) has fallen to 41st in teacher pay."
rationale: This specific claim cannot be reliably confirmed. State teacher-pay rankings fluctuate year-to-year and by measure (average vs. starting pay), and while North Carolina dropped in national rankings during Pat McCrory’s term, available public data show varying ranks across different years and reports rather than a clear, consistently documented fall to exactly 41st tied to his tenure.

claim: If Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers "had passed his (gas) tax increases ... fuel prices would be at least a dime higher.
rationale: The statement is a categorical counterfactual that depends on the size of the proposed tax increase and on how much of any tax would be passed through to retail prices. Evers' proposals have varied and were not universally a 10¢/gal increase, and even a proposed tax doesn't guarantee a full or predictable one-for-one change in pump prices because of wholesale market movements and retailer margins.

claim: Hillary Clinton "agreed with (John McCain) on voting for the war in Iraq."
rationale: Both Hillary Clinton and John McCain, serving in the U.S. Senate in 2002, voted in favor of the congressional authorization to use force in Iraq (the 2002 AUMF). Thus Clinton did agree with McCain in casting a vote that enabled the Iraq War, though they later framed and defended their votes differently.

claim: Royalties for oil and other energy sources are the "second-largest revenue source to the federal government after the IRS."
rationale: Federal receipts from oil and other energy royalties are a relatively small line item (typically billions annually), whereas the largest federal revenues are individual income taxes and the second-largest category is payroll (Social Insurance) taxes. Payroll taxes, not energy royalties, are consistently the second-largest source of federal revenue.

claim: "The spillover violence (from Mexico) in Texas is real and it is escalating."
rationale: There is documented cross-border violence and occasional cartel-related incidents affecting parts of Texas, so the spillover is real; however, the assertion that it is broadly "escalating" across Texas is not consistently supported. Crime and enforcement data show localized, episodic outbreaks and vary by county and time period rather than demonstrating a clear statewide upward trend.

claim: "Corona is so bad, this guy died twice!"
rationale: The claim is a hyperbolic statement with no corroborating evidence that any person literally died twice from COVID-19. Medical definitions distinguish between clinical/biological death and being pronounced dead (which can on rare occasions be followed by successful resuscitation), but that is not the same as dying twice. There are no credible reports of someone experiencing two separate bona fide deaths due to coronavirus.

claim: "Obama’s Clean Power Plan ... eliminates coal-fired power plants."
rationale: The Clean Power Plan (CPP) set nationwide CO2 reduction goals for states and encouraged shifts from coal to lower‑carbon generation, but it did not mandate the outright elimination of coal-fired power plants. It gave states flexibility in how to meet targets and allowed existing plants to continue operating; some coal retirements occurred due to market and regulatory pressures, not because the CPP directly ordered plant closures.

claim: "Across the country, more than half of the U.S. attorney seats remain without a prosecutor chosen by Obama."
rationale: The claim lacks a timeframe and therefore cannot be asserted as a current fact; the number of U.S. attorneys serving who were or were not chosen by Obama changed over the course of his administration as nominees were submitted and confirmed by the Senate. At the start of a presidential transition many offices are held by holdovers or acting prosecutors, so the statement may have been true briefly early in his term but is not verifiably true as a general, time‑independent fact. Without a specific date this blanket claim is unreliable.

claim: Says Ronald Reagan "was behind in the polls in 1980 going into the debate with Jimmy Carter and then turned around 10 days later and won 40 states."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. Reagan did not win 40 states in 1980 — he carried 44 states — and the only Reagan–Carter debate was on October 28, 1980 with the election on November 4 (7 days later), not 10. While some polls earlier in 1980 showed Carter ahead, late-October polls were mixed or showed Reagan close or leading, so the "behind going into the debate then 10 days later won 40 states" framing is incorrect.

claim: "Covid-19 means ‘certificate of identification of vaccination with artificial intelligence.’"
rationale: COVID-19 is an abbreviation for 'coronavirus disease 2019', a name given by the World Health Organization to the disease caused by SARS-CoV-2. The suggested expansion 'certificate of identification of vaccination with artificial intelligence' is fabricated and unrelated to the official name.

claim: Says he can be on the ballot for Congress while serving time in jail.
rationale: Under the U.S. Constitution, the only qualifications for serving in Congress are age, citizenship duration, and residency; states may not add additional qualifications for federal office. Therefore being jailed or a convicted felon does not automatically prevent someone from appearing on a congressional ballot, though narrow exceptions (e.g., 14th Amendment insurrection disqualification) and practical filing hurdles can apply.

claim: "Before 1973 it was illegal in the U.S. to profit off of health care."
rationale: This is false. For-profit hospitals, private physician practices, and for-profit health insurance companies existed and operated in the U.S. long before 1973, and no nationwide law made earning profit from healthcare illegal. While specific statutes (e.g., the Anti-Kickback law of 1972) and some state rules on corporate practice of medicine regulated certain payments and ownership models, they did not create a blanket ban on profiting from health care.

claim: "CDC confesses: Vaccines are failing, and the vaxxed can be superspreaders."
rationale: The CDC has not 'confessed' that vaccines are failing. Public-health data and CDC guidance show COVID-19 vaccines remain effective at preventing severe illness, hospitalization, and death; while breakthrough infections can occur and vaccinated people can sometimes transmit the virus, vaccines overall reduce infection and transmission risk rather than creating 'superspreaders.' The claim misrepresents and exaggerates CDC statements.

claim: "There isn’t a single (Texas) legislator under the age of 30, even though millennials make up 25 percent of the electorate in Texas."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: recent Texas legislative sessions have included at least some members in their 20s, so it is not true that there are no legislators under 30. The related statement that millennials make up about 25% of the Texas electorate is plausible, but it does not make the absolute claim about legislators accurate.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "was against the auto bailout" and "voted against the money that ended up saving the auto industry."
rationale: Bernie Sanders opposed the 2008-2009 bailout measures for banks and automakers and voted against key legislative measures tied to that rescue. He voted against the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP) in 2008 and opposed subsequent emergency auto loan measures; portions of TARP and related emergency authority were later used to provide the financing that helped save GM and Chrysler.

claim: Say Ohio Reps. Marcia Fudge, Marcy Kaptur and Dennis Kucinich are "socialists who are openly serving in the U.S. Congress."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate on both counts: Marcia Fudge and Dennis Kucinich are not currently serving in Congress (Fudge left in 2021 to join the Biden administration; Kucinich left in 2013), and none of the three are widely known to self-identify as "socialists." Marcy Kaptur is a long-serving Ohio Democrat (and currently in Congress) but is generally described as a liberal/progressive Democrat, not an openly socialist member of Congress.

claim: Obama served on a board with former Weather Underground member William Ayers and "that relationship with Mr. Ayers on this board continued after 9/11."
rationale: Barack Obama did serve with William Ayers on the board of the Chicago Annenberg Challenge in the mid-1990s, but their joint board service did not continue after the September 11, 2001 attacks. Public records and contemporary fact-checks show their overlap was during the 1990s and the Chicago Annenberg Challenge concluded in 2001, with no evidence they served together on that board after 9/11.

claim: "Paul Broun Jr. sides with sexual deviants to support sale of 'crush videos.' "
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Paul Broun publicly supported the sale of 'crush videos.' Broun is known for socially conservative positions and there are no records or reputable news reports showing he advocated for permitting or siding with producers/consumers of such fetish content. The claim appears to be a defamatory smear lacking corroboration.

claim: Says scientists are "in dispute" over whether being gay is a choice.
rationale: Major medical and scientific organizations and the bulk of peer-reviewed research conclude sexual orientation is not a voluntary choice; while scientists study biological, developmental, and environmental influences, there is not a mainstream scientific dispute that being gay is a choice. Claims of a significant scientific dispute are driven mainly by ideological or non‑expert sources rather than current scientific consensus.

claim: "Trudeau's foundation owns 40% of Acuitas Therapeutics which makes mechanic lipids for Pfizer."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation or any 'Trudeau' charitable foundation owns 40% of Acuitas Therapeutics. The Trudeau Foundation is a registered charity and does not hold disclosed majority equity in for‑profit biotech firms; Acuitas is a privately held company whose ownership is among founders and investors. While Acuitas has worked on lipid‑nanoparticle technology and collaborated with vaccine developers, the specific ownership claim is unsupported.

claim: "When my grandfather came to this country back in 1925, there were no government benefits."
rationale: The blanket claim is incorrect: by 1925 many governments already provided forms of public assistance. Examples include veterans’ pensions and benefits (from Civil War and WWI), municipal and state poor relief and 'mothers' pensions,' and workers' compensation laws in several jurisdictions; while national programs like U.S. Social Security began later (1935), that does not mean there were no government benefits at all in 1925.

claim: Says "Every time the Legislature 'suspended' the kicker, most recently the corporate kicker in 2007, Salem spent every penny and failed to stabilize the state's revenues."
rationale: The claim is an absolute blanket statement that whenever the legislature suspended a 'kicker' (citing a 2007 corporate kicker) Salem "spent every penny and failed to stabilize revenues." That is incorrect: suspensions or redirections of kicker rebates have varied by year and have been applied to different uses (reserves, schools, one-time budget fixes) rather than uniformly "spent every penny," and their effects on revenue stability have differed. The specific reference to a 2007 corporate-kicker suspension and a consistent pattern of failure is misleading.

claim: Says of MS-13 gang members, "We are getting them out of our country by the thousands."
rationale: Public records and contemporary fact-checking do not support the specific claim that MS-13 gang members are being removed 'by the thousands' in a short timeframe. Reporting and government data typically document arrests, prosecutions, and some deportations in the scores or low hundreds in given enforcement efforts, and officials’ statements using imprecise language have overstated the scale.

claim: Olive Garden employees are allowed to wear Black Lives Matter masks "but NOT the American flag."
rationale: This claim is misleading and lacks context. Fact-checkers and company statements showed Olive Garden’s parent (Darden) issued mask/uniform guidance about neutral or company-provided face coverings and sought to limit overt political messaging; reports that framed this as officially allowing Black Lives Matter masks while banning American-flag masks mischaracterized the policy, which varied by time and location.

claim: Under a public health care option, 120 million Americans will "lose what they now get from private companies and be forced onto the government-run rolls as businesses decide it is more cost-effective for them to drop coverage."
rationale: There is no authoritative evidence that a public option would categorically force 120 million Americans off private plans. Most public-option proposals are voluntary and empirical and CBO-style modeling of proposals anticipates at most modest crowd-out that varies with design and premiums, not a guaranteed transfer of that magnitude.

claim: Says the U.S. is developing an "antivirus" that includes a chip to track your movement.
rationale: There is no credible evidence the U.S. is developing an “antivirus” (or vaccine) that contains a covert tracking chip. Vaccine contents are publicly documented and independently tested, and the physical, power and size requirements for a GPS-style tracking chip make covert implantation in a vaccine infeasible. Public health agencies and independent fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked similar microchip vaccine claims.

claim: "Special education categorical aid" from the state "hasn’t been raised in over a decade."
rationale: The statement provides no specific state and presents a blanket claim. In the U.S., special education categorical aid policies and amounts vary by state and many states have changed or increased special education funding within the past decade, so the universal assertion that it 'hasn’t been raised in over a decade' is not verifiable and likely false as stated.

claim: "The richest 1 percent have more financial wealth than the bottom 95 percent combined."
rationale: Major global wealth reports show the top 1% own a very large share of wealth but not universally more than the combined bottom 95%—results vary by year, country, and whether one counts total net wealth or only financial assets. Broadly, the top 1% typically control tens of percent of global wealth, while the remaining 95% together still hold a substantial share, so the blanket claim is not generally supported.

claim: "Masks will kill quite a few people, it’s well known that they reduce blood oxygen levels and those with respiratory and cardiac disorders will die."
rationale: This claim is false: multiple clinical studies and guidance from major health agencies show that commonly used masks (cloth, surgical) do not meaningfully reduce blood oxygen saturation or raise CO2 to harmful levels in the general population. While masks can cause discomfort or breathlessness in some people, there is no evidence they are causing deaths among people with cardiac or respiratory disease; those with severe respiratory failure may need individualized medical advice.

claim: Says the House Rules Committee is the only panel, other than the Intelligence and Ethics committees, not able to telecast proceedings in its main hearing room.
rationale: This claim is incorrect because the Rules Committee is not uniquely restricted; while Intelligence and Ethics have well-known broadcasting limits (classified sessions and confidentiality rules), other House committee rooms historically have lacked permanent camera feeds or have had temporary restrictions. House broadcasting arrangements vary by room, equipment, and changing House rules, so it’s inaccurate to state only those three panels are unable to telecast in their main hearing rooms.

claim: Says over 1,000 mail in ballots were found in a dumpster in California.
rationale: There is no credible, verified evidence that more than 1,000 valid mail-in ballots were found in a dumpster in California. Fact-checkers and local election officials have investigated similar viral posts and found numbers were exaggerated or the items were undeliverable, duplicate, already-processed, or otherwise mischaracterized; only isolated, much smaller incidents have been documented.

claim: "(Mexican immigrants) are more law-abiding than U.S. citizens and that is a statistic."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed studies and U.S. government data have consistently found that immigrants, including many studies specifically of Mexican-origin immigrants, have lower crime and incarceration rates than native-born Americans. That pattern is supported by statistical analyses, though magnitudes and significance vary by offense type, time period, and adjustments for age and other demographics.

claim: Scientists are "questioning the original idea that man-made global warming is what is causing the climate to change. … (It is) more and more being put into question."
rationale: The overwhelming consensus in peer-reviewed literature and major scientific bodies is that recent global warming is primarily caused by human activities, and this conclusion has been reinforced by successive IPCC reports. Although individual scientists may debate details (climate sensitivity, regional impacts, feedbacks), the claim that scientists are increasingly questioning whether man-made greenhouse gases are driving climate change is inaccurate.

claim: Says Mitch McConnell voted "two times against the Violence Against Women Act."
rationale: While McConnell has opposed or blocked particular versions or procedural motions related to the Violence Against Women Act at times, Senate roll-call records and contemporary fact-checks do not support the simple claim that he voted against the Act on two separate final-passage votes. The statement conflates different years and procedural votes (e.g., cloture or amendments) with votes on final passage.

claim: "Rep. Paul Gosar asks Capitol Police to arrest illegal immigrants attending State of the Union."
rationale: There is no clear, reliable evidence that Rep. Paul Gosar formally asked the U.S. Capitol Police to arrest undocumented people attending a State of the Union; such an explicit, documented request has not been reported by credible outlets. The claim may conflate or exaggerate a rhetorical social-media comment or tweet with an official directive to law enforcement.

claim: Women pay 48 percent more for health insurance.
rationale: The statement is misleading as written. Certain U.S. studies of the pre-Affordable Care Act individual insurance market found women paid roughly 40–48% more than men for comparable individual policies, but that was specific to that market and time; employer-sponsored plans and post-ACA markets (where gender rating is banned) do not support a blanket 48% claim.

claim: "The platform of the Republican Party says deport everybody and to hell with it."
rationale: The exact phrase appears nowhere in any official Republican Party platform. Official platforms call for stronger border security, enforcement of immigration laws, and removal of unlawfully present immigrants, but do not include a blanket slogan like 'deport everybody and to hell with it.' The claim is a rhetorical mischaracterization rather than a factual quotation.

claim: Blames Mike McIntyre and Nancy Pelosi for the second straight year of no cost-of-living increases for Social Security beneficiaries.
rationale: Cost-of-living adjustments for Social Security are set automatically based on the CPI-W calculated by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, not directly decided by individual members of Congress; attributing a consecutive year of no COLA to Mike McIntyre and Nancy Pelosi misstates the mechanism. Also, Mike McIntyre left Congress in 2015, and the Speaker does not unilaterally set the automatic COLA calculation.

claim: "In Wisconsin, only half of all the adults with serious psychological distress received mental health treatment or medication."
rationale: I cannot find evidence that a definitive figure of 'only half' of Wisconsin adults with serious psychological distress received treatment; federal/state survey data (e.g., NSDUH and state health reports) typically report state-level treatment rates for serious mental illness or distress that vary by year and often exceed 50%. The claim is also ambiguous about the year and the exact measure (any mental health service vs. medication), so it cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: The Obama White House recognizes a "baby that has not been born" for security purposes.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that the Obama White House formally recognized an "unborn" baby as a security-protected person. Secret Service protection is provided to the president, vice president, their immediate families (including children), and others as statutorily or administratively designated, but standard policy and public records do not list fetuses or unborn children as protected persons. Media reports that suggest otherwise appear to be misinterpretations or lack supporting documentation.

claim: "Bernie Sanders voted in favor of every war during his tenure."
rationale: Bernie Sanders has a documented history of opposing major U.S. military interventions and notably voted against the 2002 congressional authorization for the Iraq War. Because he did not vote in favor of every war or authorization during his decades in Congress, the absolute claim is false.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ilhan Omar vowed "to remove senior’s ‘entitlements,’ Social Security/Medicare."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez or Ilhan Omar vowed to eliminate Social Security or Medicare; both lawmakers have publicly supported protecting and in some cases expanding programs for seniors and broad healthcare coverage. The claim appears to be a misattribution or distortion of their policy positions.

claim: "‘TrumpCare’ would allow insurance execs to personally make millions off your health care."
rationale: The claim is vague and asserts a direct causal effect that a particular "TrumpCare" law would let insurance executives personally pocket millions; no single provision in proposed GOP health bills explicitly hands executives personal payouts. While some repeal or replacement proposals could indirectly increase insurer revenues or reduce regulatory constraints (which might affect executive compensation), that is speculative and not the same as a law authorizing personal windfalls to named individuals.

claim: Says House Republicans "tried to change the definition of rape."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify as stated: without a specific bill, timeframe, or which members are meant, it cannot be confirmed that 'House Republicans' broadly attempted to change the definition of rape. While individual Republican lawmakers have at times proposed or supported legislative language affecting sexual-crime or sex‑trafficking definitions, there is no singular, universally documented act by all House Republicans that matches this blanket statement.

claim: Says that in fiscal year 2010, "nearly 80 percent of women served" in the Texas Women’s Health Program received services from a provider other than a Planned Parenthood clinic.
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim that 'nearly 80 percent' of women in FY2010 received care from non–Planned Parenthood providers; official state and independent analyses from that era reported different figures and noted that percentages vary widely depending on whether one counts unique clients, visits, or provider sites. Because the claim presents a single precise figure without specifying the counting method, it is misleading and not reliably supported by available summaries.

claim: The United States spent "2 trillion dollars to train and equip the Afghan military over the past 20 years. They fell in a week."
rationale: The claim conflates total U.S. spending on the Afghanistan war (which is on the order of $1.5–2+ trillion when all war-related costs are included) with the much smaller amount spent specifically to train and equip the Afghan security forces. Independent analyses put training/equipment for Afghan forces in the roughly $80–90 billion range, not $2 trillion. While Afghan forces did collapse rapidly during the Taliban’s August 2021 offensive (many provinces fell in days and Kabul in mid‑August), saying they “fell in a week” is an oversimplification of a complex, multi‑day collapse.

claim: "Ohio has lost more population than every other state in the country except for two."
rationale: The claim is vague about the timeframe and metric, and it is not consistently true. Ohio has seen population declines in recent years but is not reliably the third-largest numeric loser—states such as New York, California, Illinois (and at times Pennsylvania or Michigan) have shown larger losses depending on the year and whether you measure percent change, net domestic migration, or total population change.

claim: "There are still tens of thousands of missing service members from previous and current conflicts that our nation is working to find and repatriate."
rationale: U.S. government accounting agencies report on the order of tens of thousands of U.S. service members still unaccounted for from World War II, the Korean War, the Vietnam War, and other conflicts, and federal programs actively pursue recovery and repatriation. The scale and ongoing search-and-identification efforts make the statement accurate in general terms.

claim: Says Oregon’s highest income tax bracket included anyone making more than $250,000 in 2012 before the state expanded its upper bracket to include "anyone making more than $125,000."
rationale: The claim misstates Oregon’s bracket history and is ambiguous about filing status and income definition. Oregon’s top tax bracket thresholds and rates have varied by filing status (single vs. joint) and were changed through legislation at different times; it is not correct to say the top bracket uniformly covered “anyone making more than $250,000 in 2012” then was simply expanded to include “anyone making more than $125,000.”

claim: "The recidivism rate is nearly 29 percent and has been climbing steadily since detainees began being released from Guantanamo."
rationale: The statement is misleading: reported post-release "re-engagement" rates for Guantánamo detainees vary by definition ("confirmed" vs "suspected") and by time period, and there is no clear, consistently measured long-term trend showing a steady climb to about 29%. Some combined metrics in certain reports have at times approached the high teens or low-to-mid twenties, but official figures and independent analyses disagree on the rate and do not support a simple claim of a near-29% rate steadily rising since releases began.

claim: North Carolina Republican Senate candidate Thom Tillis would let insurance companies "deny coverage for pre-existing conditions."
rationale: Thom Tillis has repeatedly backed repeal and replacement plans for the Affordable Care Act and supported state waiver approaches (and votes tied to repeal efforts) that would have allowed states and insurers to opt out of ACA protections such as guaranteed issue and community rating. Those policy changes would permit insurers to deny coverage or charge much higher premiums to people with pre-existing conditions.

claim: "The Democrat(ic) position on abortion is now so extreme that they don’t mind executing babies AFTER birth."
rationale: No mainstream Democratic platform, elected Democratic official, or major advocacy group endorses killing infants after they are born. The party’s positions support legal access to abortion before birth under varying restrictions, but U.S. law and medical ethics criminalize homicide of newborns and Democratic leaders have not advocated for post-birth execution. Assertions to the contrary are based on mischaracterizations or fringe academic rhetoric that was widely condemned.

claim: Because of union rules, cooks helpers moved into DMV jobs they were not trained for
rationale: There is no broad evidence that union rules routinely place untrained cook helpers into DMV positions. DMV jobs typically require specific hiring procedures, certifications, or civil-service exams, and union contracts usually protect job classifications and require training rather than enable indiscriminate reassignment into specialized roles. Absent specific documentation from a particular jurisdiction or case, the claim appears unfounded.

claim: Says Sen. Rand Paul’s 2011 budget "included a big cut in the CDC."
rationale: Sen. Rand Paul’s 2011 Senate budget blueprint proposed substantial reductions across federal agencies and specifically trimmed funding for public health programs, including the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Contemporary reporting and his own budget outline described significant cuts to CDC funding as part of broader spending reductions.

claim: "The U.S. spends more money on its military than the 16 biggest military budgets in the world" combined.
rationale: Authoritative aggregates of national military expenditures (e.g., SIPRI and national budget tallies) show the U.S. is the largest single military spender but does not exceed the combined spending of the next 16 largest countries; it typically exceeds the combined total of a smaller number of top spenders (commonly cited as around the next 8–12) depending on year and method.

claim: "Some of the things that (Megyn Kelly) said, I didn’t say."
rationale: The claim is a short, context-free quote and cannot be verified as true or false without knowing who is speaking, when it was said, or what specific statements are at issue. There is no supporting transcript, recording, or corroborating source provided here. Because of that missing context and evidence, the statement cannot be reliably confirmed.

claim: Siemens has been unable to fill approximately 200 skilled trade positions in metro Atlanta.
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim that Siemens has been unable to fill approximately 200 skilled trade positions in metro Atlanta. Publicly available, well-documented sources through mid-2024 do not corroborate that exact figure or an official Siemens statement making that claim; Siemens comprises multiple subsidiaries and local hiring situations can vary, so an unqualified, precise number is not supported by verifiable evidence I can confirm.

claim: In-N-Out cups say "Let’s go Brandon."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that In-N-Out officially printed "Let’s go Brandon" on its cups; viral images appear to be altered or user-modified and no reputable news reports document a company-issued cup with that slogan. In-N-Out has generally avoided overt political messaging on its packaging, making an official print unlikely.

claim: Says Marco Rubio took "three quarters of a million dollars from fossil fuel executives" during the 2016 Senate election.
rationale: Marco Rubio did not run a 2016 Senate campaign (he was running for the Republican presidential nomination that year), and there is no clear evidence that he personally took $750,000 from 'fossil fuel executives' tied to a 2016 Senate race. Public campaign finance records and contemporaneous reporting do not support the specific figure or the claim as stated.

claim: "Iraq is costing each household about $100 a month."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and not verifiable as stated because it doesn’t specify which country’s households or what time period and costing method are meant. Estimates of the financial impact of Iraq (for example the Iraq War) vary widely depending on whether one counts direct military spending, veterans’ care, reconstruction, or long-term interest, and different calculations yield very different per-household figures. There is no single, universally accepted number that supports the blanket statement that "Iraq is costing each household about $100 a month."

claim: Abigail Spanberger "wants a tax increase of $32 trillion - that’s with a `T,’ to pay for her socialist health care plan."
rationale: Abigail Spanberger has not proposed a $32 trillion tax increase to pay for a "socialist" health care plan. The $32 trillion figure is commonly cited as a multi‑year cost estimate for broad Medicare‑for‑All style proposals (or projections of federal health spending) and has been misattributed to many Democrats, but Spanberger is a moderate who has not advocated a $32 trillion tax hike.

claim: Says "Bruce Starr voted to throw 6,000 Oregonians off unemployment."
rationale: This statement is misleading: while Bruce Starr voted for legislation that affected unemployment policy, there is no clear evidence that a single vote by him directly "threw 6,000 Oregonians off unemployment." Specific casualty counts like 6,000 are typically estimates tied to policy implementation and administrative decisions rather than a one-to-one result of a single legislator's vote.

claim: Patrick Rose "voted to explore a state income tax."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable record showing Patrick Rose voted for a measure specifically described as "to explore a state income tax." Public legislative records and contemporaneous news accounts of his tenure do not identify a particular vote where he supported formally exploring a state income tax, so the claim is unverified and likely false as stated.

claim: "The nine-day deer hunt contributes more than $1.3 billion in revenue to the state of Wisconsin."
rationale: Reports commonly state that Wisconsin’s nine-day gun deer season generates roughly $1.3 billion in economic activity statewide, but that is not the same as ‘revenue to the state’ (i.e., money paid into the state treasury). Direct tax or fee revenues accruing to the state government from the hunt are substantially smaller, so the claim as worded is misleading and incorrect.

claim: Says Nikita Khrushchev brought an extra shoe to a United Nations session in 1960, which he banged on the desk in protest.
rationale: The famous story that Khrushchev intentionally brought an extra shoe and banged it on the United Nations desk in 1960 is disputed. Contemporary film and archival footage do not conclusively show him pounding a shoe, and accounts vary (some witnesses say he waved or banged a shoe, others say he merely waved it); there is no reliable evidence he had brought an extra shoe for the purpose.

claim: "Measles is one of the most common causes of child blindness worldwide."
rationale: Measles can cause keratitis and corneal scarring, particularly where vitamin A deficiency and limited access to care exist, and historically (and still in many low-resource settings) has been a major preventable cause of childhood blindness. Vaccination and vitamin A supplementation have substantially reduced its contribution in high-income and well-immunized populations, but it remains among the common causes globally.

claim: "Today, the United States has, sadly, one of the lowest voter turnouts of any major country on earth."
rationale: The United States is not uniformly among the very lowest turnout countries; recent presidential elections have seen moderate-to-high turnout (for example, about 66.8% of the voting-eligible population in 2020) and the U.S. typically ranks around the middle among advanced democracies. Turnout varies by election type (presidential vs. midterm) and by metric (voting-age vs. voting-eligible population), so the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: "Every poll you see, the overwhelming majority of people want [E-Verify]."
rationale: While many polls have shown pluralities or majorities supporting E‑Verify, not every poll finds an "overwhelming majority," and results vary substantially with question wording, sample, and timing. The categorical statement that "every poll" shows overwhelming support is demonstrably false and overstates the consistency and magnitude of public opinion.

claim: "I remember one of [Curt Schilling's] teammates said he painted his sock, the bloody sock."
rationale: There is no credible record that any of Curt Schilling’s Red Sox teammates publicly said he "painted" the bloody sock; teammates, medical staff, and Schilling himself consistently treated the injury and the sock as authentic. Claims that the sock was painted come from conspiracy speculation and unverified anecdotes rather than documented teammate admissions.

claim: "Bill Gates says you don't have a choice to be vaccinated or not."
rationale: This exact categorical statement is not supported by available public records. Bill Gates has repeatedly advocated for broad vaccination programs and spoken about public-health measures and the role of governments and institutions (e.g., travel rules or mandates) in increasing vaccine uptake, but he has not been documented as saying people categorically “don’t have a choice” to be vaccinated. Many online claims are misquotes or taken out of context from discussions about policy and public-health tradeoffs.

claim: Seniors and the disabled "will have to stand in front of Obama's 'death panel' so his bureaucrats can decide, based on a subjective judgment of their 'level of productivity in society,' whether they are worthy of health care."
rationale: The "death panel" claim is false and repeatedly debunked: the Affordable Care Act did not create panels to deny care or to judge seniors and disabled people by their "productivity in society." The law only included modest provisions such as reimbursing voluntary advance-care planning discussions and created an advisory board (IPAB) with limited, indirect cost-containment roles—not authority to withhold individualized care or make subjective worthiness determinations.

claim: "Justin Amash is rated Michigan’s No. 1 conservative" by National Right to Life.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that National Right to Life explicitly labeled Justin Amash as "Michigan’s No. 1 conservative." NRL issues pro‑life scorecards and percentages, and several Michigan Republicans have historically received top pro‑life scores; NRL does not commonly publish a statewide single "No. 1 conservative" ranking tied to Amash.

claim: "The State Department asked all secretaries of state to send their emails over." Hillary Clinton's "the only one who’s done it."
rationale: The State Department did ask former secretaries to search for and provide work-related emails, but the claim that Hillary Clinton was “the only one who’s done it” is misleading. Other former secretaries were contacted and some indicated they had no relevant records or had already produced records; compliance and the records produced varied. Saying she was the sole person to comply oversimplifies and misstates the situation.

claim: "92 million Americans aren't working."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and therefore misleading. A figure near 92 million has sometimes been reported for people aged 16+ who are 'not in the labor force' (i.e., not working and not looking for work) in particular months, but it is not the count of unemployed Americans — the official unemployed total is much smaller. Without a defined timeframe and definition of 'aren't working' the claim is not accurate as presented.

claim: "We have one of the most expensive General Assemblies, per capita, in the entire country."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify which state’s General Assembly, the year, or which cost components are being counted; per-capita legislative costs vary widely by state and by the methodology used. Without specific comparative data showing this legislature ranks among the highest per capita nationally, the statement cannot be confirmed.

claim: The media has "a lower approval rate than Congress."
rationale: The claim is overly general and depends entirely on the poll source and timing. Public approval ratings for "the media" and for Congress fluctuate across polls and years; sometimes media ratings are lower, sometimes Congress's are lower. Without a specific survey, date, and methodology the comparative statement cannot reliably be judged true.

claim: Says Tom Hanks was photographed wearing a T-shirt with progressive slogans on it.
rationale: There is no well-documented, verifiable instance widely reported by reputable sources or fact-checkers showing Tom Hanks photographed wearing a T‑shirt emblazoned with explicit progressive slogans. Viral images of celebrities are often miscaptioned or taken out of context, and no authoritative media coverage confirms this specific claim about Hanks. Given the lack of verifiable evidence, the claim is likely false.

claim: Photos show Ukrainian citizens destroying two Russian tanks with Molotov cocktails in Kyiv.
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that the photos in question show Ukrainian citizens destroying two Russian tanks with Molotov cocktails specifically in Kyiv. Independent verification and open-source investigators have repeatedly found that images and videos of burning Russian vehicles during the invasion were frequently misattributed or lacked provenance; while civilians did sometimes use improvised incendiaries in some clashes, these particular photos are not reliably tied to Kyiv or proven to show tanks destroyed by Molotovs.

claim: "President Barack Obama (is) the first president in history to cut Medicare by $700 billion."
rationale: The statement is misleading: the Affordable Care Act contained provisions that the Congressional Budget Office and Joint Committee estimated would reduce projected Medicare spending by roughly $700 billion over a decade, but these were reductions in projected spending (largely via lower payments to providers and Medicare Advantage plans), not one-time benefit cuts to beneficiaries. It is also inaccurate to say Obama was the "first president in history" to cut Medicare, since prior administrations and Congress have enacted laws that slowed or reduced Medicare spending growth.

claim: Photo shows a trashed venue in Glastonbury after climate activist Greta Thunberg spoke there.
rationale: The photo has been widely misattributed online; independent fact-checkers found the image was not verifiably taken immediately after Greta Thunberg spoke at Glastonbury and was used out of context to blame her. Glastonbury is a large festival site where litter can appear in many places and times, so a single photo does not demonstrate it was the aftermath of her speech.

claim: A campaign poster for New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern with the slogan, "No jab. No job, no refunds."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Jacinda Ardern or her campaign produced an official poster reading "No jab. No job, no refunds." The phrase appears to be a fabricated or satirical image circulated online, not a documented piece of official campaign material.

claim: Wisconsin's $3 billion incentive offer to Foxconn is "the largest gift ever by a state to a foreign company."
rationale: The $3 billion Wisconsin package for Foxconn was widely described as among the largest state incentive deals, but it is not clearly the single largest "gift" ever to a foreign company. Many other large state packages (especially to foreign automakers and manufacturers) and varying accounting methods (including local and federal incentives, grants vs tax credits, and present-value calculations) produce larger or comparable totals. The Foxconn deal was also mostly conditional tax credits rather than an upfront cash "gift."

claim: "Most of Ted Cruz’s money comes from Washington, from outside the state of Texas."
rationale: The claim is too broad and unsupported as stated. ‘‘Most of Ted Cruz’s money’’ and ‘‘from Washington’’ are ambiguous: Cruz has raised substantial out-of-state and national support (especially during presidential bids), but campaign finance records do not uniformly show a majority of his total funds coming specifically from Washington, D.C. rather than Texas; the pattern varies by election cycle and by whether one counts individual donors, PACs, or total receipts.

claim: ‘The Simpsons’ predicted Canada’s trucker convoy protest.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that The Simpsons specifically predicted the 2022 Canadian trucker 'Freedom Convoy.' The show has depicted protests, roadblocks, and truck convoys in various episodes over decades, and viral posts have pointed to superficial similarities, but those are coincidences or misattributions rather than a direct prediction.

claim: Obama "voted for and even sponsored amendments that were intended to kill the (immigration overhaul) legislation."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate or misleading: as President Obama he could not vote for or sponsor congressional amendments, and there is no clear evidence that then-Senator Obama sponsored or voted for amendments specifically designed to 'kill' a major immigration overhaul. Legislative records for the 2007 Senate immigration debate and later proposals do not show Obama sponsoring 'killer' amendments intended to defeat the bills.

claim: "When I go on Letterman" the "ratings go up."
rationale: The claim is a blanket, unverified assertion without specifying who or which episodes; TV ratings fluctuate due to many factors. While some celebrities have produced measurable spikes on talk shows, saying ratings categorically 'go up' whenever a particular person appears on Letterman cannot be confirmed without episode-level Nielsen data and context.

claim: "Now remember, property taxes went up 70 percent in the 10 years before I became governor."
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated because it does not identify which governor, which jurisdiction, or the exact 10-year period; without that context the assertion cannot be confirmed. Property-tax changes vary by state/locality and can be measured in different ways (rates, assessments, or total levies), so the blanket 70% figure cannot be treated as fact without specific data.

claim: "Jackie Evancho’s album sales have skyrocketed after announcing her inauguration performance."
rationale: Contemporary reporting after Jackie Evancho’s announced and then-performed inauguration appearance described short-lived, modest spikes in chart position and small sales increases on platforms like iTunes and Amazon, not a sustained or massive 'skyrocketing' of album sales. There is no evidence of a lasting, dramatic sales surge across major retail metrics attributable to the announcement/performance.

claim: In nine Democratic debates, "We've not had one question about a woman's right to make her own decisions about reproductive health care, not one question."
rationale: Major Democratic primary debates included multiple questions about abortion and reproductive rights; moderators and audience members asked about Roe v. Wade, access to contraception, and protections for reproductive healthcare in several debates. Therefore the assertion that there were no questions across nine debates is incorrect.

claim: Facebook is changing its hate speech policy to ban "Let’s go Brandon."
rationale: There is no public evidence that Meta/Facebook announced a blanket change to its hate speech policy specifically banning the phrase "Let’s go Brandon." Facebook’s hate speech rules target slurs and content attacking protected classes; the slogan is a political insult aimed at an individual (President Biden), so it does not fit the standard definition of protected-class hate speech. Platforms may still remove posts using the phrase when paired with threats, harassment, or policy violations, but that is not the same as a categorical ban of the phrase.

claim: When McCain was questioned about hiring lobbyists to his campaign staff, "his top lobbyist actually had the nerve to say, 'The American people won't care about this.' "
rationale: There is no well-documented, contemporaneous attribution of that exact quote to any 'top lobbyist' for John McCain when his campaign's hiring of lobbyists was questioned; the line appears to be a critical paraphrase or misattribution rather than a verifiable direct quotation. Major media coverage of the controversy did not report a lobbyist saying 'The American people won't care about this.'

claim: Ethylene oxide used in COVID-19 testing swabs "literally changes the structure of the building blocks of your own body."
rationale: While ethylene oxide is an alkylating chemical that can modify DNA and proteins at sufficiently high exposures, properly sterilized and aerated COVID-19 swabs contain only trace residual amounts far too low to "literally change the structure" of a person's biomolecules. There is no credible evidence that routine use of EtO‑sterilized diagnostic swabs chemically alters the building blocks of users' bodies.

claim: Says up to a quarter of African Americans don’t have government photo ID.
rationale: Research by reputable groups has found that roughly one in four African American adults lacked a government-issued photo ID in some studies. For example, a 2012 Brennan Center report estimated about 25% of black adults lacked such ID, though later studies and different definitions yield lower or varying estimates.

claim: "Ron Johnson is trying to let insurance companies deny coverage to people with pre-existing conditions like cancer, depression, pregnancy, diabetes—or even COVID."
rationale: Senator Ron Johnson has supported efforts that would remove or weaken Affordable Care Act protections—such as backing repeal efforts, state waiver approaches, expansion of short-term plans, and supporting the court challenge to the ACA—actions that would permit insurers to sell plans that exclude or charge more for pre-existing conditions. Those policy positions and votes would, if enacted, allow insurers in many cases to deny coverage or make it unaffordable for people with conditions like cancer, depression, pregnancy, diabetes, or COVID-related claims.

claim: The "top ten most unhealthy U.S. cities" are San Francisco; Seattle; Portland, Oregon; San Diego; Honolulu; Washington; Austin, Texas; Irving, Texas; Portland, Maine; and Denver.
rationale: The list is implausible and inconsistent with widely used city health rankings: many of the named places (San Francisco, Seattle, Portland OR/ME, San Diego, Honolulu, Denver, Austin, Washington) are typically ranked among the healthier U.S. cities. Without a cited source, the claim contradicts established indices of chronic disease, obesity, and health behaviors that usually place poorer-health cities in other regions.

claim: A mansion in photo is Joe Biden’s house.
rationale: No photo or trustworthy provenance was provided, so the claim cannot be verified. Images of mansions are frequently misattributed online to politicians; without independent confirmation (property records, reputable news, or official statement) the assertion is unsupported.

claim: U.S. debt is "now equal to 100 percent of the GDP."
rationale: The statement is misleading: U.S. federal debt is not precisely “equal to 100% of GDP” right now. Depending on the measure, gross federal debt has been slightly above 100% of GDP in recent years while debt held by the public is lower, so the exact ratio differs by definition and date.

claim: A video clip from the Notre Dame cathedral fire shows a man walking alone in a tower of the church "dressed in Muslim garb."
rationale: The clip was widely circulated but independent fact-checkers determined the footage is low-resolution and ambiguous; there is no reliable evidence identifying the person as Muslim or confirming the clothing is 'Muslim garb.' The image and context do not support the specific claim that a lone man in Muslim attire was depicted.

claim: When it comes to income taxes, Wisconsin is "one of the best places in the country to be poor" but "top 4 or 5 worst" for middle-income earners.
rationale: The broad direction of the claim has some basis—Wisconsin’s tax code (progressive income tax plus credits) can yield relatively low effective tax rates for the poorest households—but the assertion of a precise ranking (‘one of the best’ for the poor and ‘top 4 or 5 worst’ for middle-income earners) is not reliably supported. Different reputable analyses use varying definitions (state income tax only versus combined state and local taxes, different income brackets and years) and produce inconsistent rankings, so the specific categorical ranking is misleading.

claim: Says only seven percent of 2009’s stimulus bill went toward transportation projects, yet they created over one-third of the bill’s total jobs.
rationale: This claim is misleading. While a relatively small share of ARRA dollars was devoted to transportation and infrastructure depending on classification (often cited near single-digit percentages), independent analyses and official OMB/CBO reporting do not support the specific assertion that transportation projects produced over one-third of all jobs from the 2009 stimulus; job estimates vary by model and attribution method and generally show a much smaller share. The headline percentages conflate different accounting methods and timeframes.

claim: Allen West called Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" and said "this country's got to get on sound footing by destroying it."
rationale: Allen West has publicly referred to Social Security as a 'Ponzi scheme' and advocated major changes, but there is no reliable record of him using the exact line 'this country's got to get on sound footing by destroying it.' The phrasing appears to be a misleading or amplified paraphrase of his calls for overhaul or repeal rather than a verbatim quote.

claim: "The current (agriculture) commissioner allowed tainted beef to be sent to school cafeterias."
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated: it lacks any jurisdiction, timeframe, or definition of “tainted,” and there is no clear, widely reported evidence that a named current agriculture commissioner knowingly authorized sending contaminated beef to school cafeterias. Food safety recalls and inspections are typically handled by food safety agencies and produce public records; accusations of this magnitude normally require specific, corroborated reporting. Without those specifics, the assertion cannot be confirmed and is more reasonably treated as false.

claim: "American Hustle shows the FBI making real-life bribes to Washington politicians. I know, because as your U.S. senator, I turned them down."
rationale: American Hustle is a fictionalized film loosely inspired by the FBI Abscam sting in which undercover agents posed as wealthy investors and offered money to several public officials, and some politicians were recorded accepting payments. However, the specific first‑person claim that a named U.S. senator personally 'turned them down' is not supported by public records and cannot be verified; there is no documented, verifiable case of a sitting senator publicly stating they were offered and declined an Abscam bribe in the way claimed.

claim: "Biden’s Air Force One is not the same as Trump’s Air Force One," which indicates Biden is not the real president.
rationale: The statement is a non sequitur: 'Air Force One' is the radio call sign for any U.S. Air Force aircraft while the president is aboard, and administrations may use different physical planes or the same ones over time. A change or difference in the specific aircraft used does not bear on whether someone is the legitimately elected president, which is determined by constitutional and electoral processes.

claim: In 2000, "I wrote about Osama bin Laden, ‘We’ve got to take him out.’"
rationale: The claim is unverified as presented because it omits who supposedly wrote the line and there is no well-documented public record showing that someone authored the exact phrase 'We’ve got to take him out.' about Osama bin Laden in 2000. While officials and commentators did call for action against bin Laden before 9/11, I cannot confirm this precise quoted sentence attributable to a specific, verifiable 2000 source.

claim: Says Nancy Pelosi "made millions in coronavirus insider trading."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Nancy Pelosi personally 'made millions' from coronavirus-related insider trading. Public disclosures and multiple fact-checking organizations found the claims unsubstantiated; trades linked by some to Pelosi involved her husband and were not shown to be based on nonpublic information or to have generated millions attributable to insider knowledge. No formal findings of illegal insider trading against Pelosi exist.

claim: President Joe Biden was confused, "turned around and shook hands with thin air" after a speech.
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable evidence that President Biden was demonstrably confused and literally 'turned around and shook hands with thin air' after a specific speech. Multiple viral clips making this claim have been cropped or taken out of context and independent fact-checkers have found they more plausibly show him gesturing toward people or aides off-camera rather than deliberately shaking an empty space.

claim: "Torture is illegal by our laws. It's illegal by international laws."
rationale: While international law broadly prohibits torture (through instruments like the UN Convention Against Torture, the Geneva Conventions, and customary international law), the phrase "our laws" is ambiguous and cannot be assumed to prohibit torture in every domestic jurisdiction. Domestic statutes, exceptions, and enforcement vary by country, so the blanket domestic claim is not universally true.

claim: "Colorado raked in $60 million in marijuana taxes and licensing fees in the past year."
rationale: State revenue reports show Colorado collects several hundred million dollars per year from marijuana taxes alone, and adding licensing and regulatory fees pushes the total well above $60 million. The claim therefore materially understates statewide annual marijuana-related revenue.

claim: Elena Kagan "has published five scholarly review articles, mostly on administrative law and the First Amendment. These articles were mostly on technical and procedural issues."
rationale: Elena Kagan has a relatively small body of academic scholarship focused in areas like administrative law and constitutional issues, but the specific claim that she "has published five scholarly review articles" and that they were "mostly on administrative law and the First Amendment" is imprecise. Public records show a handful of law-review pieces and essays, but counts vary depending on which writings are counted and the characterization of their topics and tone is debatable.

claim: Says Mitt Romney did not pay taxes for 10 years.
rationale: Romney released multiple years of tax returns and independent fact-checkers reviewed them; they show he paid federal income taxes in most years and did not go ten consecutive years without paying taxes. While some years showed low reported liability due to deductions and charitable giving, the claim that he paid no taxes for 10 years is contradicted by his filings and reporting.

claim: Says Michele Bachmann said on Fox News, "This country could use a president like Benjamin Franklin again."
rationale: I could not find a reliable record or widely reported transcript of Michele Bachmann saying on Fox News the exact line "This country could use a president like Benjamin Franklin again." While Bachmann has invoked founding-era figures in speeches, this precise quote appears unverified and likely misattributed or paraphrased.

claim: Once people become citizens under the DREAM Act "and turn 21, they can sponsor their illegal immigrant parents for legalization."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The federal DREAM Act has not enacted a current blanket path to citizenship (DACA is not a path to citizenship), and while a U.S. citizen aged 21 or older can petition for parents, that petition does not automatically legalize parents who entered unlawfully because adjustment of status often requires lawful entry or waivers and other bars may apply.

claim: "President Trump has lifted the prospect of voters across Vermont, overseeing a 11,742 decline of Vermont residents on food stamps."
rationale: The claim is unclear and unsupported: there is no evidence that President Trump personally “lifted the prospect of voters across Vermont” or that he directly ‘oversaw’ a specific decline of exactly 11,742 Vermont residents on food stamps. SNAP enrollment can change for many reasons (economy, state administration, policy changes) and I find no authoritative data attributing that precise drop to an action by Trump. Without a clear time period, source, or causal link, the statement is not verifiable as presented.

claim: "Sixteen [federal] programs exist to fight homelessness" and some of them are duplicative.
rationale: Multiple government reviews and watchdog reports have identified on the order of a dozen to two dozen federal programs specifically aimed at homelessness, with a commonly cited count of 16 programs. Those same reviews (e.g., GAO and interagency summaries) have noted overlap, fragmentation, and potential duplication among programs and agencies.

claim: "Colorado school forces students to wear hijabs."
rationale: There is no evidence of a Colorado public-school policy forcing students to wear hijabs, and public schools in the U.S. cannot mandate religious dress under the First Amendment. While some private religious schools may require head coverings as part of their own dress codes, that does not make the broad claim about Colorado schools true.

claim: Six states "decided to stop counting" votes as Donald Trump was "headed for a win" on election night.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that six states collectively 'decided to stop counting' votes to preserve a Trump lead on election night. Local jurisdictions often stop reporting for the night for routine reasons and resume counting the next day, and election officials and multiple independent fact‑checks confirmed that states continued counting legally cast ballots until completion. The claim conflates normal reporting pauses with an intentional halt to the count to produce a false result.

claim: Says Mitt Romney’s tax plans would "give an additional $250,000 tax cut to millionaires and billionaires" while raising taxes on the middle class.
rationale: The claim is misleading. Analyses of Mitt Romney’s tax proposals showed that higher‑income households would receive much larger dollar tax cuts than lower‑income households, but the exact $250,000 figure and the assertion that the plan would categorically raise middle‑class taxes depend on which version of the plan, which baseline year, and which deductions are counted. Nonpartisan analysts produced a range of estimates rather than a single definitive $250,000 “additional” cut and found mixed effects on middle‑income taxpayers depending on modeling assumptions.

claim: Says Chuck Todd said the Roy Moore story "felt completely orchestrated."
rationale: I find no reliable transcript or contemporaneous citation showing Chuck Todd explicitly saying the Roy Moore story "felt completely orchestrated." While Todd discussed the allegations and media coverage, the exact quoted phrasing appears to be a misquote or paraphrase attributed elsewhere, not a documented Todd quote.

claim: "The VA negotiates prescription drug prices. Medicare doesn't do that."
rationale: The VA does have statutory authority to obtain negotiated prices and typically secures lower drug prices. However, saying Medicare "doesn't" negotiate is misleading: private Medicare Part D plans already negotiate prices with manufacturers and, after the Inflation Reduction Act, Medicare itself gained limited authority to directly negotiate prices for selected high-cost drugs starting in the mid-2020s. Thus the absolute statement is incorrect.

claim: "The committee that advises @GovEvers and his department tasked with leading during this pandemic is recommending allowing prisoners to receive the vaccine before 65 year old grandma?"
rationale: There is no clear evidence that the Wisconsin advisory committee to Gov. Evers recommended vaccinating incarcerated people ahead of all people aged 65+. Wisconsin and federal vaccine-priority frameworks prioritized health-care workers, long-term care residents, and older adults (65+) in the earliest phases; some guidance included congregate settings for early consideration but did not broadly place prisoners before the 65+ age cohort.

claim: "China owns about 29% of (the U.S.) debt."
rationale: China does not own about 29% of U.S. debt. China’s holdings of U.S. Treasury securities are on the order of roughly $1–1.3 trillion while total U.S. federal debt is in the tens of trillions, so China’s share of total U.S. debt is only around 3–5% (and about 10–15% of foreign-held Treasuries), not 29%.

claim: The Tampa Bay Rays' "prices have been judged the most affordable in all of professional sports."
rationale: While the Tampa Bay Rays have frequently ranked among the more affordable Major League Baseball teams for tickets and in-stadium costs, the broader claim that their "prices have been judged the most affordable in all of professional sports" is unsubstantiated. Pricing rankings vary by year and by methodology, and other teams and leagues (including many minor-league clubs) are often cheaper on various measures. No consistent, authoritative consensus declares the Rays the single most affordable across all professional sports.

claim: Obama's budget plan would "take national debt up to about 80 percent of gross national product. ... Historically, it's been about 40 percent."
rationale: The claim is misleading because whether debt reaches ~80% depends on the time horizon and which debt measure is used (gross federal debt vs. debt held by the public) and Obama’s budgets and CBO projections do not uniformly state '80% of GNP'. Historically the commonly-cited ~40% figure more closely matches debt held by the public in some post‑war decades or earlier periods, not gross federal debt, and 'GNP' is the wrong metric in most modern analyses which use GDP. Some projections under certain assumptions did show debt rising toward roughly 70–80% of GDP, but the statement as phrased is imprecise and therefore misleading.

claim: Rubio's "got more experience than Obama had."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and not clearly true: measured in total years of elected office both men have roughly similar legislative experience (about 12 years), and Obama had U.S. Senate service and a national profile before becoming president. Whether Rubio “got more experience” depends on what kind of experience is counted (state vs. federal, executive vs. legislative), so the blanket assertion is misleading.

claim: "A year ago we had the lowest unemployment in history without using taxpayers money."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify and likely false: it asserts a historic low unemployment 'a year ago' and that this occurred 'without using taxpayers money.' Unemployment records depend on the country and specific month, and many low-unemployment periods have coincided with government-funded measures (stimulus, tax policy, benefits) that are financed by taxpayers.

claim: In Texas, "the No. 1 name for new male babies — many of whom will vote one day — is Jose."
rationale: Recent state-level birth name data (e.g., Social Security and Texas vital statistics) show names like Liam, Noah, and Mateo among the top male newborn names in Texas; Jose is not the overall #1 for recent years. The claim omits a year or subgroup and appears to conflate statewide rankings with specific communities or past decades.

claim: While in Congress, Nathan Deal was a leader when it came to protecting our borders.
rationale: The statement is a value judgment that overstates his role. While Nathan Deal voted for and supported some immigration and enforcement measures in the House, there is little objective evidence he was a national leader on border security (he was not widely recognized as the principal sponsor or committee chair driving major border-security legislation).

claim: Says Marco Rubio "voted to deport" young people known as Dreamers.
rationale: There is no clear roll-call vote in which Marco Rubio literally cast a vote “to deport” DACA recipients; deportation is not typically enacted by a single yes/no vote labeled that way. Rubio has repeatedly opposed DACA protections and supported stronger immigration-enforcement measures, and critics sometimes summarize those positions as having “voted to deport” Dreamers, but that phrasing is rhetorical rather than a precise description of a specific roll-call vote.

claim:
Says U.S. Sen Sherrod Brown "promised that the first stimulus bill would fund the
Brent Spence Bridge."
rationale: There is no clear record that Sen. Sherrod Brown promised the "first stimulus bill" would fund the Brent Spence Bridge. Brown has repeatedly advocated for federal investment in the bridge, but the 2009 stimulus (and other early stimulus packages) did not specifically pledge or earmark funding for that project; funding efforts occurred later through other federal programs and appropriations.

claim: The U.S. government spends less on energy innovation "than the pet food industry invests in its own products."
rationale: Available budget figures and typical industry R&D levels make this claim implausible: U.S. federal spending on energy research and innovation (across DOE offices, ARPA‑E, and related programs) runs into multiple billions annually, while the pet food industry’s spending on product R&D and similar investments is typically much smaller (hundreds of millions). The statement appears to conflate total industry sales or marketing with R&D/investment and thus overstates pet food industry investment relative to federal energy innovation spending.

claim: "NFL attendance and ratings are WAY DOWN. Boring games yes, but many stay away because they love our country."
