Any binding changes from a trade agreement typically require implementing legislation or are enforced through dispute mechanisms (including state‑to‑state or investor‑state panels) that can lead to penalties or pressure to change laws, not an immediate executive override.

claim: "Here, we have Thanksgiving, we have Christmas, we have the 4th of July. Every year in Iran, they celebrate Death to America day."
rationale: Iran holds annual state-organized commemorations—most notably the Nov 4 anniversary of the 1979 U.S. embassy takeover—during which crowds and officials commonly chant 'Death to America.' While the wording 'celebrate' may imply a civic holiday like Thanksgiving or the Fourth of July, the underlying claim that such annual events occur is correct.

claim: "House Speaker Nancy Pelosi said this week that the Democrats have to pass their terrible health care bill so that the American people can actually find out what's in it."
rationale: This exact claim is misleading. Nancy Pelosi did say in March 2010, regarding the Affordable Care Act, words to the effect of "we have to pass the bill so that you can find out what's in it," but she did not describe it as a "terrible" bill and the remark was made in 2010, not "this week."

claim: "Mitt Romney: ‘Trump has some very serious emotional problems, he must resign before we…’"
rationale: There is no reliable record of Mitt Romney saying the exact quoted line. While Romney has publicly criticized Donald Trump’s temperament and character on multiple occasions, this specific phrasing—especially the ‘he must resign before we…’ segment—appears to be a misquote or fabricated and is not supported by verifiable sources.

claim: In the weekend after the terrorist attacks in Paris, the White House said "this couldn't happen in the United States. ISIS couldn't reach us here."
rationale: There is no record of the White House issuing that exact categorical statement. After the November 2015 Paris attacks, White House officials emphasized vigilance and that there was no specific, credible threat to the United States at that time, but they did not say flatly "this couldn't happen in the United States. ISIS couldn't reach us here." The quoted wording appears to be a misstatement or misattribution of officials' more cautious public comments.

claim: Says NASCAR "bans the confederate flag but FORCES all their drivers to do Muslim prayer."
rationale: While NASCAR did announce a ban on the public display of the Confederate flag at its events in June 2020, there is no evidence that NASCAR forces drivers to perform Muslim prayer. Forcing religious practice would be unlawful and would have been widely reported; reports instead show individual drivers may pray on their own, but no organizational mandate exists.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that public school in the United States "will not teach the tenets of Islam or Sharia Law."
rationale: There is no Supreme Court decision that states the quoted sentence as a holding. The Court has ruled that public schools may not endorse or promote religious doctrine under the Establishment Clause (e.g., Engel v. Vitale, Abington v. Schempp), but it has also allowed the secular, objective teaching about religions in an academic context. The claim misrepresents and overstates what the Court has expressly ruled.

claim: "Nearly 180,000 illegal immigrants with criminal records, ordered deported from our country, are tonight roaming free to threaten peaceful citizens."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that nearly 180,000 deportable immigrants with criminal records are currently 'roaming free.' Publicly cited figures have repeatedly been shown to conflate different categories (encounters, arrests, convictions, removal orders, and past removals) and do not support the claim that that many people with criminal records are presently at large threatening citizens.

claim: Says Emma Gonzalez, a survivor of the Parkland school shooting, ripped up a copy of the U.S. Constitution
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Emma Gonzalez ripped up a copy of the U.S. Constitution. Contemporary news reports and independent fact-checks traced the claim to miscaptioned photos and viral posts; no verified video or trustworthy source shows her tearing the Constitution.

claim: Teachers "are working their third consecutive year -- some longer than that -- without salary increases."
rationale: The statement is too broad and cannot be affirmed as a universal fact because teacher pay changes differ widely by country, state, and school district. While some teachers have indeed gone multiple years without raises in certain districts, many other districts and states provided raises, step increases, or one-time supplements in recent years through negotiated contracts, state budget changes, or federal relief funds.

claim: Sen. Jim Webb "persists on negating" Sen. Mark Warner’s votes
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: Sen. Jim Webb and Sen. Mark Warner are both Virginia Democrats who overlapped in the Senate (2009–2013) and while they sometimes voted differently, Webb did not consistently or persistently vote to negate Warner on a clear pattern. Roll‑call records show mixed agreement and occasional divergence rather than systematic negation.

claim: "Obama said he would unilaterally renegotiate the North American Free Trade Agreement."
rationale: Barack Obama did not say he would unilaterally renegotiate the North American Free Trade Agreement. Renegotiation of NAFTA, a trilateral agreement, requires agreement from Canada and Mexico and cannot be imposed unilaterally by a U.S. president; Obama’s public statements generally supported multilateral trade frameworks rather than claiming unilateral rewrite authority.

claim: "Six people in Florida die as a result of (not expanding Medicaid) every day."
rationale: The specific claim that exactly six people in Florida die every day as a direct result of not expanding Medicaid is not a verifiable fact but a model-based estimate. Analyses that try to quantify deaths attributable to a state’s failure to expand Medicaid produce varying results depending on methods and assumptions; some advocacy calculations have produced similar daily estimates for Florida, but there is no consensus or direct causal count supporting the precise claim.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Perry is "by far and away the highest-paid state employee on an hourly basis."
rationale: The claim is unsupported: a governor’s annual salary is public and in most states (including Texas under Gov. Rick Perry) it is not the highest state employee pay. Many state employees — for example university system chancellors, hospital executives, and some agency heads — receive higher annual compensation than the governor, and the claim’s ‘hourly basis’ comparison is unverifiable because it depends on assumed hours worked. Without concrete hourly calculations or a defined comparison group, the assertion that Perry was "by far and away" the highest-paid is not substantiated.

claim: Claims Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg said "she prefers the South African Constitution over the United States Constitution."
rationale: Ruth Bader Ginsburg publicly praised aspects of the South African Constitution—calling it a model in some respects and noting its explicit equality provisions—but she did not state a blanket preference for it over the U.S. Constitution. Her remarks were about admiring particular provisions and approaches, not an assertion that she preferred the South African Constitution overall.

claim: Says Gerald Daugherty is endorsed by the Austin American-Statesman.
rationale: There is no public record up to mid-2024 that the Austin American-Statesman formally endorsed a candidate named Gerald Daugherty. Major newspaper endorsements are published and archived by the paper; none match that name in known endorsement lists. Without a specific race or date the claim appears unverified and is likely false.

claim: "$53 million a week is coming across the border in drugs."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and lacks critical context (which border, timeframe, and whether wholesale or retail value). Publicly available law-enforcement and border-seizure reports do not support a specific, consistent figure of $53 million per week and estimates of illicit drug flows vary widely by drug type and methodology. Seizure data are incomplete and converting quantities to dollar values depends on uncertain purity and pricing assumptions, so a precise $53M/week claim is not verifiable.

claim: "Obama's Environmental Protection Agency sent emails for Hispanic Heritage Month with a photo of Che Guevara."
rationale: Contemporary news reports and fact-checkers documented that an EPA communication tied to Hispanic Heritage Month included an image of Che Guevara; the appearance prompted criticism and an EPA response. The agency said the material came from staff/partner contributions and was not an official endorsement of Guevara.

claim: "The only people in this town that have voted to cut Medicare spending are the people who voted in favor of Obamacare. That’s a fact."
rationale: The claim is an absolute local statement but provides no identification of who 'this town' refers to or which specific votes count as 'voting to cut Medicare spending.' While the Affordable Care Act included some Medicare payment reductions as cost offsets, many different votes and legislators at multiple levels have supported measures affecting Medicare. Without roll-call evidence tying every single person in the town who voted to cut Medicare to only those who supported the ACA, the blanket claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Wayfair CEO steps down."
rationale: The claim is too vague (no date or named CEO) and I am not aware of verified, widely reported news that Wayfair’s CEO resigned through mid-2024. Without a specific timeframe or named executive, the statement cannot be confirmed as a factual, current event. If a recent resignation occurred after my last knowledge update it could be true, but as stated it is unverified.

claim: Paul Ryan would "outlaw in vitro fertilization."
rationale: There is no clear evidence Paul Ryan has called for or introduced a federal ban on in vitro fertilization. During the 2012 campaign he stated he would not criminalize IVF and suggested regulation should be handled at the state level, though he has a long anti‑abortion record and has supported positions (like fetal personhood language) that critics say could indirectly restrict IVF. The claim that he "would outlaw" IVF as a direct, explicit policy is unsupported.

claim: "We have one of the lowest mortality rates in the world" from COVID-19.
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because 'we' and the time period/metric are unspecified; global COVID-19 mortality rankings depend on whether one uses case-fatality rate, deaths per 100,000 population, or excess mortality. Reported low mortality can reflect limited testing, age structure, reporting practices, or timing of waves rather than genuinely being among the world’s lowest.

claim: "We enacted the biggest tax cuts and reforms in American history."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act was a major overhaul and among the largest recent changes, but it is not clearly the biggest in American history when measured by standard metrics (percent of GDP, long‑term revenue loss, or rate reductions). Earlier reforms—most notably the 1981 Reagan tax cuts—produced larger cuts relative to the size of the economy and bigger top‑rate reductions, and other historical tax reforms also compare depending on how “biggest” is defined.

claim: Says that except for Donald Trump, "every other major party nominee" for the past 40 years has released their tax returns.
rationale: Modern fact-checking and historical records show that major-party presidential nominees dating back roughly 40 years before Donald Trump (e.g., Reagan, Mondale, Bush Sr., Dukakis, Clinton, Dole, Gore, Bush Jr., Kerry, McCain, Obama, Romney, Clinton) publicly released tax returns, whereas Trump declined to release his. Therefore the statement that, except for Trump, other major-party nominees in that period released their tax returns is accurate.

claim: "Jurisdictions representing about 80% of WI residents have passed referendums or resolutions in favor of fair maps."
rationale: While many Wisconsin cities and counties have passed advisory referendums or resolutions in favor of 'fair maps,' available compilations and reporting do not support the specific claim that jurisdictions representing about 80% of Wisconsin residents have done so. The claim appears to overstate the population coverage because numerous suburbs and rural counties (which together hold a substantial share of the state population) have not passed such measures or are not included in public tallies.

claim: "It’s estimated that in 2018 alone, dead people received $1 billion in benefits from Medicare, Medicaid, social security payments, and federal pensions."
rationale: I found no authoritative source confirming a single combined estimate of $1 billion paid in 2018 to deceased beneficiaries across Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security and federal pensions. Audits and agency reports do document overpayments to deceased beneficiaries in various programs, but amounts are reported separately, for different periods, and do not clearly add up to the stated $1 billion for 2018 alone.

claim: "Amazon accepts Dogecoin."
rationale: Amazon does not natively accept Dogecoin as a direct payment method. While third-party services and gift-card resellers can convert Dogecoin into Amazon gift cards or fiat for purchases, that is not the same as Amazon directly accepting Dogecoin payments.

claim: "Inequality in Texas is steadily getting worse, with very few rich people, a great many poor people, and fewer and fewer in the middle."
rationale: Multiple data sources show income inequality in Texas has increased over recent decades: the Gini coefficient and top-income shares have risen while the share of households in the middle-income band has fallen and poverty rates remain above the national average. That matches the claim’s broad pattern of greater concentration of income at the top, more people at lower incomes, and a shrinking middle. However, year-to-year trends are not perfectly monotonic and exact counts depend on how “rich/poor/middle” are defined.

claim: When it comes to urgency on passing a budget repair bill, "there’s no rush on this thing" because the fiscal year doesn’t end until June 30, 2011.
rationale: The statement is misleading. Fiscal-year end dates depend on the jurisdiction — the U.S. federal fiscal year ends September 30 (not June 30) — and even where the fiscal year ends June 30 (many states), that date alone does not eliminate urgency because budget repair bills affect cash flow, obligations, and legal timelines well before the fiscal year end.

claim: Says the NBA is asking Donald Trump to "resign or we’ll never play again."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the NBA as an organization issued an ultimatum demanding Donald Trump resign or threatening to stop playing. While individual players and teams have publicly criticized Trump or refused White House visits, those actions are not the same as an NBA-wide demand to resign.

claim: "Because of my policies, Black Unemployment has just been reported to be at the LOWEST RATE EVER RECORDED!"
rationale: The statement combines two claims — that Black unemployment is at the lowest rate ever recorded and that this is due to 'my policies.' While BLS data show Black unemployment hit historically low levels around 2019–2020, confidently attributing that decline solely to one person's policies is unsupported. Labor market outcomes reflect many factors including long-term recovery trends, monetary policy, and broader economic conditions.

claim: While the smoking rate nationally has fallen, more than 18 percent of Georgians still light up.
rationale: While adult smoking prevalence has fallen nationally, recent state-level estimates for Georgia place adult cigarette smoking in the mid-teens rather than above 18%. Therefore the specific claim that more than 18% of Georgians still smoke is inconsistent with recent CDC/Georgia Department of Public Health data.

claim: "Right to Work states have: faster private sector employment growth"
rationale: The empirical literature is mixed: while some studies find modest associations between right-to-work laws and higher private-sector employment growth, many well-controlled analyses find little or no robust causal effect. Results depend heavily on time period, econometric method, and other state policies, so the blanket claim is not generally supported as a fact.

claim: The federal government "reviewed and verified" his administration’s numbers showing Wisconsin added 23,608 jobs in 2011.
rationale: Federal statistical agencies do not simply "review and verify" a state's administration’s claimed job-add total; the BLS and other federal programs produce their own employment estimates and state preliminary counts are subject to revision. Contemporary fact-checks found no evidence that a federal agency officially reviewed and authenticated the Walker administration’s 23,608 jobs-for-2011 claim.

claim: Says Paul Workman "voted in the Democrat primary, supporting Democrats with his vote."
rationale: I find no verifiable public statement or reliable reporting showing a person named Paul Workman explicitly said he "voted in the Democrat primary, supporting Democrats with his vote." Without a cited source or direct quote, the assertion cannot be confirmed and should be treated as false.

claim: "The average cost of child care in this country is more than what it costs to send a child to college for one year."
rationale: The statement is too general and lacks a specified country, time period and definitions of “child care” and “college” costs; costs vary widely by country, region, type of childcare (infant vs. preschool, home vs. center) and type of college (public in-state, private). In many countries and jurisdictions one-year college costs (especially private or out-of-state tuition) exceed average childcare costs, while in some high-cost childcare markets the reverse can be true, so the blanket claim is not generally true.

claim: "Texas legislators have filed voucher proposals in every legislative session since 1995, but all of them have failed to become law."
rationale: While Texas lawmakers have repeatedly filed school voucher and school-choice proposals over many sessions, the blanket claim that proposals were filed in every single legislative session since 1995 and that all of them have failed is incorrect. Texas has enacted limited school-choice measures (for example tax-credit scholarship programs and targeted scholarship/ESA-like provisions for certain populations) and the term “voucher” has been applied inconsistently, so some voucher-like programs have become law. Because of these enacted, targeted programs and the ambiguity around definitions, the absolute statement is false.

claim: "Three years ago, a newly elected President Obama told America that if Congress approved his plan to borrow nearly a trillion dollars, he would hold unemployment below 8 percent."
rationale: There is no clear contemporaneous record of President Obama, as the newly elected president, explicitly promising that congressional approval of a nearly trillion-dollar plan would hold unemployment below 8 percent. Obama did urge passage of the roughly $787 billion stimulus in early 2009 and argued it would create/save jobs and reduce unemployment, but he framed benefits in probabilistic terms and did not make a categorical guarantee tied to an "under 8%" threshold. The "nearly a trillion dollars" phrasing also conflates different cost estimates.

claim: "The House has never failed to pass a budget in the modern era."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. In the United States, the House (and Congress overall) has at times failed to enact a budget or the required appropriations, producing government shutdowns (notably 1995–1996 and 2013) and multiple years where a final budget resolution was not adopted. The House has also relied on continuing resolutions when regular appropriations were not passed.

claim: The Milwaukee County Board’s staff grew from four workers to 38 over four decades and now costs taxpayers "a lot more," while the total county workforce was more than cut in half in the same period.
rationale: I could not verify the precise figures in the claim: public records and reporting do show the Milwaukee County Board’s professional staff has grown compared with several decades ago, but independent sources do not confirm a clean rise from exactly 4 to 38 over four decades, nor a concurrent more-than-50% drop in the county’s total workforce for the same period. The claim mixes a subjective phrase (“a lot more”) and specific numeric assertions that depend on definitions and time windows that aren’t specified.

claim: Says President Barack Obama "spent nearly a trillion dollars on make-work government jobs."
rationale: The statement mischaracterizes what was spent. The major 2009 stimulus (ARRA) totaled about $787 billion, and only a fraction funded direct public-sector job creation; much of the package was tax relief, transfers to states, and infrastructure/other spending. Independent analyses (CBO, economists) found the stimulus supported or saved jobs but did not consist of nearly $1 trillion of "make-work" government jobs.

claim: "Wages adjusted for inflation haven’t risen since the turn of the last century."
rationale: The claim as stated is too broad and incorrect for the typical interpretation (since the turn of the last century ~1900): long-run, inflation‑adjusted (real) wages in most industrialized countries have risen substantially over the 20th and 21st centuries due to productivity and economic growth. If the speaker instead meant ‘since ~2000’ or meant a particular country or median vs mean wages, there are cases of stagnation or slow growth, but that narrower claim is not equivalent to the blanket statement offered.

claim: Clips of Dr. Anthony Fauci show he "flip-flopped" on guidance for wearing masks, whether kids should be in school and whether people should change how they interact.
rationale: Short clips can show Fauci saying different things at different times, but that does not prove he simply 'flip-flopped.' His public guidance changed as scientific understanding and circumstances (supply of PPE, evidence about asymptomatic spread, schools' risk assessments, and vaccine availability) evolved. Many fact-checks found such clips are often cherry-picked or lack context showing evidence-based updates.

claim: North Carolina has "the strictest anti-gerrymandering standards in the entire country."
rationale: North Carolina has enacted and been subject to multiple anti‑gerrymandering measures and litigation, but it is not demonstrably the strictest state. Several other states (for example Iowa, California, and Arizona) use independent or nonpartisan redistricting processes or constitutional provisions that are widely regarded as stronger limits on partisan gerrymandering, and NC maps have been repeatedly struck down by courts.

claim: NBC News "covered up Hunter Biden laptop story."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that NBC News intentionally 'covered up' the Hunter Biden laptop story. In 2020 many mainstream outlets—including NBC—declined to amplify the original unverified Post report or exercised caution because provenance could not be independently confirmed and U.S. intelligence warned about possible disinformation; cautious reporting and delay are not proof of a deliberate cover-up. Subsequent public reporting and fact-checks have not produced evidence of a coordinated NBC suppression.

claim: Says a video shows Iranian rockets being launched toward U.S. airbases in Iraq.
rationale: I cannot verify that the referenced video shows Iranian rockets launched toward U.S. airbases in Iraq without the original footage, metadata, geolocation, or independent confirmation. Videos from conflict zones are frequently misattributed, reused, or lack clear evidence tying them to a particular actor or target, so the claim is not substantiated as presented.

claim: "Vice President Kamala Harris laughs at the plight of Ukraine; at idea of America offering assistance"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Vice President Kamala Harris laughed at the plight of Ukraine or at the idea of U.S. assistance; on the contrary, she and the Biden administration have publicly supported aid to Ukraine. Viral clips claiming otherwise have been debunked or shown to be taken out of context rather than documenting a deliberate dismissal of Ukrainian suffering.

claim: Says extras are needed to portray aliens in a Star Wars movie being shot near Rosenberg, Texas.
rationale: There are no credible reports or official announcements that a Lucasfilm/Star Wars feature is filming near Rosenberg, Texas, and casting notices claiming "extras needed to portray aliens" for a Star Wars movie are commonly misleading or fraudulent. Major Star Wars productions and official casting calls are publicly announced by Lucasfilm and reputable casting agencies, and none list Rosenberg as a location.

claim: "The U.S. Constitution owes its notion of democracy to the Iroquois Tribes."
rationale: While some Founding-era Americans admired the Iroquois Confederacy and cited it as an example of a federal union, the U.S. Constitution’s ideas primarily derive from Enlightenment political theory, British legal traditions, colonial charters, and debates among the states. Scholarship finds any Iroquois influence was at most indirect and limited, so claiming the Constitution 'owes' its notion of democracy to the Iroquois overstates the case.

claim: "We are in the sixth year of recovery, and median income is below what it was at the start of the recovery."
rationale: The statement is underspecified — it does not say which country, which recovery start date, or whether 'median income' is inflation-adjusted household or individual income. Depending on those choices (for example U.S. post-2009 recovery and whether one uses Census real median household income or nominal personal income), trends differ and the blanket claim cannot be confirmed. Because the claim is ambiguous and can be false for many plausible definitions, I judge it false without further context.

claim: "In six years, (U.S. Rep. Gary) Peters introduced zero bills that became law."
rationale: The claim is false. Legislative records (Congress.gov and other roll-call/legislation trackers) indicate that Gary Peters sponsored or was the lead sponsor of at least one bill that was enacted, so it is not correct to say he introduced zero bills that became law over a six-year span. The statement also lacks a clear timeframe and does not specify whether 'introduced' excludes cosponsorship, which affects counts.

claim: The Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine contains an "undisclosed ingredient. … How is informed consent possible?"
rationale: The Pfizer–BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine’s active and inactive ingredients are publicly disclosed in regulatory filings, EUA fact sheets, and the manufacturer’s product information (e.g., mRNA, specific lipid components, cholesterol, salts and sucrose). There is no credible evidence that the authorized formulation contains a separate 'undisclosed ingredient'; regulators review ingredient lists and independent analyses have not substantiated such a claim. Therefore informed consent can be based on the published ingredient lists and safety data.

claim: "South Florida ranks No. 1 in the gap between wages and housing."
rationale: The statement is too broad and no single, widely-accepted source identifies “South Florida” as universally No.1 for the gap between wages and housing. Rankings depend on the exact metric, geographic boundaries and timeframe, and many affordability studies typically place Bay Area, New York or Los Angeles metros at the top on measures like rent burden or housing-cost-to-income ratios. Without a specific study cited, the claim cannot be verified and is likely misleading.

claim: "We jumped 11 places since beginning this year in terms of being job-friendly."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify who "we" refers to, which job‑friendliness ranking or index is being used, or the precise timeframe. Without a named dataset and baseline ranking, the statement cannot be confirmed and therefore is treated as false in this fact-check context.

claim: Wisconsin is "clearly seeing a decline in COVID infections"
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no timeframe or data source; COVID-19 case trends fluctuate and require recent surveillance data to establish a clear decline. Without current case counts, 7–14‑day moving averages, or hospitalization data from Wisconsin health authorities, one cannot confirm a statewide, sustained decline, and trends often vary by county and metric.

claim: Giant companies like Toyota will not locate in a state that has not passed a right-to-work law
rationale: The claim is an absolute generalization and is not true: firms do not categorically refuse to locate in states without right-to-work laws. Corporate location decisions are driven by many factors (workforce, supply chain, tax incentives, logistics), and major manufacturers and corporations have located in both right-to-work and non-right-to-work jurisdictions. There is no evidence of a universal rule that companies like Toyota will only locate in right-to-work states.

claim: The expanded child tax credit in the Build Back Better Act has "no means testing," so people making $200,000 and $400,000 would get "the same as someone making" $70,000.
rationale: The expanded child tax credit proposals (and the 2021 expansion under the American Rescue Plan that Build Back Better sought to extend) were not completely without means testing: benefits were phased down or limited once household income exceeded specified thresholds. Households with very high incomes (for example, married filers above roughly $150,000) would not receive the same full per-child amount as lower‑income households, so $200,000 or $400,000 earners would not necessarily get the same credit as someone earning $70,000.

claim: "No city in the state can quarantine itself without state approval."
rationale: The claim presents a universal rule but authority to impose quarantines is governed by state law and often delegated to local health departments or city health officers. In many jurisdictions cities or local public health agencies can impose quarantines without separate state approval, though the exact rules vary by state.

claim: "Many Nevadans relied on Uber for work, but after accepting $70,000 from taxi companies, Catherine Cortez Masto went after Uber ... (driving) them out of town."
rationale: The statement combines a general truth (rideshare created work for many Nevadans) with a specific, unverified allegation that Cortez Masto took money and then personally drove Uber out of town. Public reporting and campaign finance records do not support a $70,000 payment to Cortez Masto from taxi interests nor show she enacted a policy that banished Uber; Nevada moved toward regulation of rideshares rather than an outright expulsion. The claimed quid pro quo and causal sequence are unsupported by available evidence.

claim: "Dolphins are rapists. Look it up."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization and anthropomorphizes animal behavior. Scientific studies document sexually coercive behavior and forced copulations by some male bottlenose dolphins and male alliances that coerce females, but this does not mean all dolphins behave this way nor that animal actions are identical to the human legal concept of rape.

claim: Says a photo shows President Ronald Reagan meeting with Taliban leaders in the White House.
rationale: Ronald Reagan left office in January 1989, while the Taliban did not emerge as a distinct organization until the early-to-mid 1990s and only seized Kabul in 1996. Therefore Reagan could not have met 'Taliban leaders' in the White House; photographs from the 1980s of Reagan with Afghan figures are sometimes miscaptioned and show mujahideen or other regional leaders, not the Taliban.

claim: Says the majority of candidates in Texas’ 25th Congressional District live outside the district.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no election cycle or date; whether a majority of candidates lived outside TX-25 depends on the specific race and filing period. U.S. House candidates are only required to reside in the same state, not necessarily the district, so occasional out-of-district candidates are common, but asserting a majority requires checking that cycle’s official candidate filings and residency records. Without that specific evidence, the blanket statement cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false.

claim: Says health insurance premiums will rise under Obamacare.
rationale: The statement as a blanket prediction is misleading — the Affordable Care Act changed market rules so premiums rose for some groups (for example younger/healthier individuals in some markets) but fell or were offset for others (sicker enrollees, many low- and moderate-income consumers received subsidies). Empirical evidence shows mixed results that vary by year, state, and whether coverage is individual-market versus employer-sponsored.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Trey Gowdy’s 8-year-old son found dead "in a dumpster in D.C."
rationale: No credible news outlets or official sources reported that Representative Trey Gowdy’s 8-year-old son was found dead in a dumpster in Washington, D.C., and Gowdy’s office and fact-checking organizations have debunked the claim. The story appears to be a viral piece of misinformation with no supporting evidence.

claim: Louisiana is turning down $100 million "that would require us to change our unemployment law, that would have actually raised taxes on Louisiana businesses."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim as stated: it bundles three factual assertions (Louisiana declined $100 million, the money required changing the state unemployment law, and that change would have raised business taxes). My training data contains no definitive, corroborated record that all three are true together; such funding disputes vary by program and often involve political framing. Without a named program, time, or official source, the composite claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "The president early on called on NATO member countries to step up their contributions ... and as a result of that countries have stepped up contributions toward their own defense."
rationale: While a U.S. president did publicly urge NATO allies early in his term to increase defense spending, the claim that countries stepped up spending solely 'as a result of that' overstates the causal link. NATO defense spending has risen since 2014 and especially after Russia's actions, driven by multiple factors (Russian aggression, NATO commitments, domestic politics) not only presidential pressure. Thus the causal claim is not supported.

claim: "Republicans in Congress are plotting to take away Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security."
rationale: The claim overstates and universalizes disparate policy positions: while many Republican lawmakers have advocated major reforms, spending cuts, block grants for Medicaid, or changes to Medicare financing, there is no evidence of a unified congressional plan or covert plot to completely abolish Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security. Proposals vary by legislator and party faction and typically frame changes as reforming or restraining growth rather than outright elimination.

claim: "We have cut taxes more than 40 times in four years."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits the jurisdiction, the exact four-year period, and what is meant by a 'tax cut' (rate cuts, credits, deductions, or administrative changes). Claims about counts of tax reductions require detailed legislative and administrative records; absent those specifics, the assertion cannot be confirmed and is misleading.

claim: "Maybe (the COVID-19 vaccine) doesn't work, and they're simply not telling you that."
rationale: Extensive randomized trials and large real-world studies have shown COVID-19 vaccines substantially reduce symptomatic infection, severe disease, hospitalization, and death. Regulatory agencies and independent researchers have published effectiveness and safety data publicly, and there is no credible evidence of a coordinated concealment that vaccines 'don't work.'

claim: The government pays out "$2,125/month in refugee benefits to refugees resettled in the United States," while Social Security recipients "who have paid into the system their whole lives receive $1,400/month on average."
rationale: The claim misstates both figures. Refugee resettlement provides a limited, typically short-term package (one-time reception payments and up to months of cash assistance in amounts similar to TANF and often well under $2,125/month); most refugees enter the workforce and do not receive that ongoing monthly cash. The average Social Security retirement benefit paid to retired workers in recent years is substantially higher than $1,400/month (roughly around $1,700–1,900 depending on year), and actual benefits vary by earnings history.

claim: "8 Syrians caught at Texas border in Laredo."
rationale: I cannot find verifiable, corroborated evidence in my training data or authoritative sources confirming the specific claim that exactly "8 Syrians" were caught at the Texas border in Laredo. Border apprehension reports are typically published by U.S. Customs and Border Protection or local law enforcement and specific counts and nationalities should be confirmed from those official statements or reputable news outlets. Without such sources this precise numeric-and-nationality claim is unverified and should be treated as likely false until proven.

claim: "Some neighborhood schools are closing."
rationale: The claim provides no time period or location, so it cannot be verified as universally true. While individual neighborhood schools do sometimes close in various districts for budget, enrollment, or policy reasons, the statement is too vague to confirm as a factual assertion.

claim: Says "roughly two-thirds of (state) corporations didn’t pay any income tax in Virginia."
rationale: I cannot verify the claim as stated because no specific year or source is given, and publicly available patterns vary by year and by how "corporations" are counted. While many corporate tax filers in states can show zero net liability in a given year (due to losses, credits, or pass‑through treatment), the precise fraction for Virginia is not established here and is unlikely to be reliably summarized as "roughly two‑thirds" without a cited dataset.

claim: "Woman set to testify against Clintons blown up in home explosion."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a woman ‘set to testify against the Clintons’ was killed by a home explosion. Major news outlets, local authorities, and independent fact-checkers have found no verification of such a claim and similar viral posts have been previously debunked as unfounded conspiracy-mongering.

claim: A video shows Joe Biden making a racist comment.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because no specific video, time, or source is provided. Many viral clips are edited, taken out of context, or manipulated, and while President Biden has made verbal gaffes, there is no identified, widely corroborated video showing him making an explicitly racist comment in the absence of supporting evidence. Without a precise source it cannot be confirmed as true.

claim: Says in 2000, Fox News broke the story of George W. Bush’s drunk driving arrest. "Who broke it? Fox News."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Fox News was the original breaker of a 2000 story alleging George W. Bush had a drunk-driving arrest; that rumor circulated via the Drudge Report, tabloids and other outlets and was repeatedly reported and debated but not first exposed by Fox News. Contemporary media analyses and later fact-checks do not identify Fox as the source that 'broke' the allegation.

claim: Millennials are "more pro-life than baby boomers and older Americans."
rationale: Multiple national polls over recent decades consistently show Millennials are, on average, more likely to identify as pro-choice and to support legal access to abortion than Baby Boomers and older cohorts. While opinions can vary by question wording, political ideology, religion, and time (notably after major events like the Dobbs decision), the general pattern contradicts the claim that Millennials are more pro-life than older Americans.

claim: "Hillary Clinton is in jail at Gitmo at the moment."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hillary Clinton is detained at Guantanamo Bay; she is a private citizen who has made public appearances since leaving office and no reputable news outlets or official agencies have reported such an arrest. Claims that she is 'in jail at Gitmo' are a baseless conspiracy theory contradicted by public records and reporting.

claim: AIDS was transmitted to humans because "one guy" had sex with "a monkey" and then started "having sex with men."
rationale: The scientific consensus is that HIV arose from multiple cross-species transmissions of simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIV) into humans—most plausibly via hunting/butchering and blood exposure—followed by onward spread through human sexual networks, medical procedures, and migration. There is no credible evidence that the pandemic began when a single man had sex with a monkey and then infected others; the origin involves multiple spillover events and complex social and epidemiological factors.

claim: Wrote that in 2006, Nancy Pelosi said she didn’t think capturing Osama bin Laden "makes us any safer," but in 2011 called his killing "historic."
rationale: Contemporaneous news reports and Pelosi's own statements show that in 2006 she questioned whether capturing Osama bin Laden would "make us any safer," and following the 2011 raid she called bin Laden's killing a "historic" moment. Both quotes were widely reported at the time and reflect her earlier caution about single-person solutions and later praise for the operation's significance.

claim: The state’s overall revenues only returned this year to 2007 levels.
rationale: The claim as written is unverifiable and therefore false because it does not specify which state or which year is meant by “this year,” nor whether revenues are nominal or inflation-adjusted. Comparing revenues from 2007 to a later year requires adjusting for inflation, population and revenue sources, and many jurisdictions show different nominal and real trajectories. Without those specifics the statement cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Kelly Ayotte voted to give big oil more than $20 billion in tax breaks."
rationale: The claim overstates and misattributes. While Ayotte did vote for some tax bills and procedural measures that included provisions or extensions which benefited energy companies, there is no simple, documented single vote in which she directly 'gave big oil more than $20 billion' as claimed; the $20 billion figure is an aggregate or estimate that campaign messages have used misleadingly. The vote record shows she supported broader tax-package or procedural measures, not a discrete, explicit $20+ billion oil subsidy bill.

claim: Says YouTube removed Tucker Carlson’s interview with Tony Bobulinski.
rationale: I am not aware of any reliable reporting up to mid‑2024 that YouTube removed a Tucker Carlson interview with Tony Bobulinski. Major platform removals of high‑profile interviews are typically reported, and I found no documented evidence that YouTube took down that specific interview.

claim: Says Beto O'Rourke's "father-in-law, a billionaire real estate developer who bankrolled a Super PAC to buy Beto a congressional seat…"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Beto O'Rourke's father-in-law is a billionaire real estate developer who single-handedly 'bankrolled a Super PAC' to buy O'Rourke a congressional seat. Public reporting and campaign finance records do not identify a wealthy father-in-law funding a Super PAC specifically to secure his congressional election; O'Rourke's campaigns and associated outside spending were supported by many donors and groups.

claim: "In 1972, we had a 179,000 human beings in jail in this country. Today, it's 2.3-million, and 70 percent of them are black, African-American."
rationale: The claim mixes inaccurate and exaggerated figures. While the U.S. incarcerated population did grow from the early 1970s to a peak around 2.1–2.3 million, the 1972 count cited (179,000) understates 1970s totals depending on whether prisons and jails are combined, and Black people do not make up 70% of today’s incarcerated population — recent data show roughly one-third of prisoners are Black. Therefore the overall statement is false.

claim: "Seventy percent of the people in the state of New Jersey want marriage equality."
rationale: The claim asserts a precise 70% support level for marriage equality in New Jersey but offers no time frame or source. Public-opinion polling on marriage equality varies by pollster, question wording, and date; while many polls show majority support in New Jersey and nationwide, a specific, consistently replicated 70% figure for New Jersey cannot be confirmed without a cited poll.

claim: "Trump just cut the scheduled federal pay raise, stating that he can’t do it now because of ‘serious economic conditions’ in America."
rationale: There is no credible, recent reporting showing that former President Trump 'just cut' a scheduled federal pay raise or issued a statement saying he could not do it now because of 'serious economic conditions.' Federal pay adjustments for civilian employees are set through a process involving the president's budget proposals and Congress or formal executive actions; a unilateral, immediate cut described in the claim would have generated widely reported documentation which is absent.

claim: A photo shows "the Lincoln Memorial. His head damaged and defaced."
rationale: There are no credible reports or official notices of the Lincoln Memorial’s seated Abraham Lincoln statue being decapitated or similarly 'damaged and defaced'; such major vandalism would be widely covered and promptly addressed by the National Park Service. Viral images alleging that the statue's head is damaged have typically been found to be edited, miscaptioned, or showing replicas/props rather than the real monument.

claim: Senate Democrats who left the state for weeks to delay a vote on union bargaining power exercised a "Wisconsin filibuster" provided by the state’s constitution.
rationale: In 2011 Wisconsin Democrats fled the state for weeks to prevent a quorum and thereby block a vote on legislation limiting collective bargaining; this delay tactic relied on the state’s constitutional quorum requirements. Calling it a "Wisconsin filibuster" is a common descriptive label for that quorum-denial strategy, which effectively prevented the legislature from taking action until the senators returned or rules changed.

claim: "They're saying that 40 percent of the traffic that goes over [the Sakonnet River Bridge is from] out of state."
rationale: I could find no authoritative evidence that 40% of Sakonnet River Bridge traffic is from out of state. Typical bridge counts in Rhode Island show most daily traffic is local or regional commuters, and a 40% out-of-state share would be unusually high without a clear seasonal or event-based explanation. Absent a specific source, the claim appears to be an unsupported assertion.

claim: Dr. Anthony Fauci has not spoken or appeared publicly for several weeks.
rationale: The claim is time-specific but gives no date and cannot be confirmed without up-to-date sources. Public-figure appearances can change quickly, and absent contemporaneous evidence this assertion is unverified and therefore assessed as false.

claim: Says the federal government is "the largest energy user in the country."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and generally incorrect as stated: across most countries (including the United States) entire economic sectors like industry, transportation, and residential consume far more energy than the federal government as a whole. While the federal government is a large energy consumer among single organizations and there are occasional claims that it is the largest single institutional energy user, it is not the largest overall energy user in the country.

claim: Dan Patrick "changed his name from Danny Goeb to hide from" his "debts."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Dan Patrick legally changed his name from Danny/Dannie Goeb to hide from debts. Public biographical information indicates he adopted the name 'Dan Patrick' as a professional/stage name during his broadcasting career, not as a documented scheme to avoid creditors.

claim: "Kasich’s budget raised taxes by billions, hitting businesses hard and the middle class even harder."
rationale: The claim is an oversimplification and not supported as stated. Kasich-era budgets included both revenue increases (through things like broadening the sales-tax base and closing loopholes) and tax cuts or business tax reforms, so net effects varied by year and by taxpayer; independent analyses found mixed distributional impacts rather than a clear result that businesses were hit hard and the middle class hit even harder. Without specifying which budget year, which taxes, and providing quantified distributional analysis, the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: Medicaid "is contributing to 70 percent of our budget deficit right now. It’s the one that is in our lap because of Obamacare."
rationale: Medicaid is not responsible for 70% of the U.S. budget deficit. Federal deficits are driven by a mix of factors (tax receipts, entitlement spending including Social Security and Medicare, discretionary spending, and interest), and Medicaid accounts for a substantial but far smaller share of federal and state spending. The Affordable Care Act expanded Medicaid eligibility but CBO analyses found the ACA did not create an overwhelming deficit driver and, on net over long windows, reduced federal deficits in many estimates.

claim: Democratic Party candidates for the state Assembly "actually received 200,000 more votes statewide" than their Republican counterparts in the 2012 election
rationale: The claim omits which state and gives a precise margin that cannot be verified without consulting that state's official 2012 Assembly vote totals. Aggregate vote counts and margins vary by state and by counting conventions (e.g., uncontested seats, third-party votes), so the blanket assertion of a 200,000-vote Democratic advantage is unsubstantiated as written.

claim: "Who’s really behind Jeanne Ives’ campaign for governor? Mike Madigan’s corrupt insider machine. They’ve bankrolled her campaign with thousands in shady labor union cash, turning Ives into another Madigan lackey."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Mike Madigan’s organization directly bankrolled Jeanne Ives’ gubernatorial campaign or that she was funded by “shady” labor-union cash. Public campaign finance records and contemporary news coverage show Ives’ funding came largely from conservative donors, small contributors, and Republican-aligned groups; allegations of Madigan backing her are unsupported. While parties sometimes engage in strategic spending in primaries, the specific claim as stated is not substantiated.

claim: The health care law could cost up to $2 trillion, "double what we were promised."
rationale: The statement is misleading: official budget estimates around the time the Affordable Care Act passed did not show a $2 trillion net federal cost nor a figure that was simply "double" a promised amount. CBO and other official estimates reported the law would reduce the federal deficit over the first decade or have net federal costs well below $2 trillion, while some opponents cited larger gross or multi-source spending tallies — a mix of incompatible measures rather than a single doubled promise.

claim: Says Joe Biden called ANTIFA "courageous Americans."
rationale: There is no credible record or primary-source transcript showing Joe Biden called ANTIFA 'courageous Americans.' Fact-checkers examined the alleged quote and found it to be a misattribution or distortion of his comments about protesters and violence. The available public remarks show he condemned violent actions rather than praising ANTIFA with that phrase.

claim: A U-Haul operated by antifa activists distributed "shields, weapons & black bloc" to protesters in Louisville, Ky., and is linked to "a George Soros-funded initiative."
rationale: Independent fact-checking reporting found no verifiable evidence that a U-Haul in Louisville was operated by 'antifa' activists to distribute weapons or that it was tied to a George Soros-funded initiative. Video and social posts showed people unloading items, but investigators found no proof the materials were weapons or that the vehicle was part of an organized, Soros-funded plot.

claim: "COVID cases in India plummet after government promotes ivermectin and hydroxychloroquine use."
rationale: Although some Indian states and advisors promoted ivermectin and hydroxychloroquine, high-quality clinical trials and WHO guidance found no clear benefit for these drugs in treating or preventing COVID-19. The post-peak decline in cases is better explained by factors such as rising population immunity, vaccination rollout, behavioral changes and public-health measures, and reporting artifacts, so attributing the plummet to those drugs is not supported by evidence.

claim: Says the unemployment rate for African-American youths is 59 percent.
rationale: Nationally representative labor-force data do not show a 59% unemployment rate for African‑American youths. While unemployment for Black teens and young adults is substantially higher than for other groups and can spike in recessions, BLS age-and-race series typically report rates far below 59%; the 59% figure likely stems from a narrowly defined subgroup, a particular city, or a different measure (e.g., 'disconnected' youth) and is misleading when stated without context.

claim: "We've seen six months of positive job growth by the private sector."
rationale: The statement is unverified as given because it does not specify a country or a six-month period; without a defined timeframe and jurisdiction it cannot be confirmed. Whether private-sector jobs grew for six consecutive months is an empirical question that requires checking official monthly payroll/employment reports.

claim: "In West Virginia alone, overdoses have increased by 50% during the #COVID-19 pandemic."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported as a clear statewide fact. Data from CDC and West Virginia reporting show overdose-related harms rose during the COVID-19 pandemic, but percentage changes vary by metric (fatal overdoses, ED visits, EMS calls) and by time period and county; there is no single authoritative statewide figure confirming a uniform 50% increase for all overdoses.

claim: "Our minority graduation rate went from levels below Milwaukee and Madison, to above 80%" when I was Beloit school superintendent.
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because no dates, superintendent name, or source data were provided; official graduation-rate comparisons require specific years and definitions. Without corroborating state or district reports showing Beloit's minority graduation rate rising from below Milwaukee and Madison to over 80% during that superintendent's tenure, the assertion is not confirmable.

claim: "When you sanction the Iranian central bank, that will shut down (Iran's) economy."
rationale: Sanctioning a country's central bank can severely restrict its ability to use the international financial system, reduce imports and oil revenues, and trigger sharp economic contraction, but it does not automatically 'shut down' the entire domestic economy. Iran has historically adapted through domestic measures, alternative payment channels, barter and trade with friendly states, and informal networks that allow economic activity to continue, albeit at reduced scale and with high economic pain.

claim: "I negotiated open borders to let fleeing refugees into safety from Kosovo."
rationale: The statement is unverified and implausible as presented because it does not identify who “I” refers to nor provide dates or corroborating evidence. Historical evacuations of refugees from Kosovo (notably 1998–99) were organized through government decisions, NATO/UN agencies and neighboring states rather than a single private negotiator, so the claim cannot be confirmed without specific, documentable proof.

claim: Police are "20.8 times more likely to kill than be killed by a criminal."
rationale: The statement is presented without any timeframe or jurisdiction and thus is not a verifiable universal fact. Annual counts of civilians killed by police versus officers killed by criminals do sometimes yield ratios in the high teens or low twenties for specific U.S. years and data sources, but the precise figure 20.8 is not a stable, universally supported statistic without specifying year and dataset.

claim: "A new poll shows 62 percent support the president's plan to reform health care. That means ... letting you choose between keeping the private insurance you have and a public health insurance plan."
rationale: The claim bundles an uncited poll result with a specific policy interpretation without providing the poll source or which president/plan is meant. Poll support figures depend heavily on question wording and timing, and proposed reforms differ — some proposals include a public option, others do not, and none universally guarantee a simple choice for every insured person. Without a specific, verifiable poll and text of the plan, the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Spanish was the first European language spoken in this country."
rationale: The statement omits which country is meant; whether Spanish was the first European language depends on that country's specific colonial/contact history. Many countries were first contacted by other Europeans (English, Portuguese, French, Dutch), so the claim cannot be verified as true without additional context and is therefore treated as false.

claim: Says Jim Renacci ran against the Washington establishment in the election, but is now "hypocritically embracing it with big money, special interest fundraisers."
rationale: The claim mixes a plausible campaign framing (Renacci ran as an outsider) with an unverified allegation that he is now 'hypocritically embracing' the Washington establishment via big‑money, special‑interest fundraisers. I have no definitive evidence in my available knowledge that he has specifically switched to hosting such fundraisers or that fundraising patterns changed as alleged, and the word 'hypocritically' is a value judgment rather than a factual statement.

claim: "BREAKING: Pennsylvania initiated a FULL audit of the RIGGED ELECTION"
rationale: There is no evidence that Pennsylvania initiated a statewide "full audit" that substantiated claims of a "rigged" election. Pennsylvania certified its results, state election officials and courts rejected widespread fraud claims, and while a few counties conducted limited post-election reviews, the state did not authorize a forensic statewide audit proving the election was rigged.

claim: Says Paul Ryan's budget relies on the same $700 billion in savings from Medicare that Mitt Romney and other Republicans have been attacking Democrats about.
rationale: Paul Ryan’s budget did propose roughly $700–716 billion in reduced Medicare spending over a decade, but those cuts were from Ryan’s own proposals (changes to payment rates and benefit structure) and are not the identical $700 billion in Medicare savings tied to the Affordable Care Act that Romney and other Republicans were attacking Democrats over. Saying Ryan’s budget "relies on the same $700 billion" falsely equates the source and nature of the savings.

claim: "$700 billion was robbed (from Medicare) to pay for Obamacare."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act was scored by the Congressional Budget Office as reducing Medicare spending by roughly $700–716 billion over a multi‑year window, but those were budgetary savings achieved mainly by lowering future payments to providers and reducing overpayments to Medicare Advantage plans—not a literal theft of beneficiary benefits. Saying $700 billion was "robbed (from Medicare)" mischaracterizes the nature of the savings and implies unlawful or direct seizure of beneficiary funds, which is unsupported by the budgetary record.

claim: "Part of the increase in the cost (of higher education) has been because state support has dropped. We now spend, under Governor Walker, more on corrections than we do on higher education."
rationale: It is correct that reduced state support under Governor Scott Walker contributed to rising higher-education costs, but the claim that the state spent more on corrections than on higher education is misleading. In Wisconsin, total higher-education spending (including tuition and institutional revenues) generally exceeded corrections spending in most budget years, although comparisons of just the state general fund or particular line items can show different results.

claim: "Connecticut's take on slot machines is 25 cents on the dollar. And the state's take on table games:  zero."
rationale: Connecticut's tribal gaming payments are governed by negotiated compacts and are not a simple flat '25 cents on the dollar' for all slot revenue, nor is the state's take universally zero for table games. The 2009/2012 agreements and later amendments include tiered revenue-sharing formulas, thresholds, and exclusivity payments, and table games are treated differently than slots depending on the specific contract and time period.

claim: Says there's a "100-year-old international norm not to use chemical weapons."
rationale: There has been an international prohibition on the use of chemical weapons for about a century: the 1925 Geneva Protocol outlawed use of chemical (and biological) weapons and the 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention later codified and strengthened the ban. Earlier Hague declarations also restricted poison gas, so describing a roughly 100-year-old international norm against use of chemical weapons is accurate, though the norm has been violated at times.

claim: "If we ban the practice of earmarks, we could save the American taxpayer anywhere between $15 (billion) to $20 billion dollars a year in pork-barrel spending."
rationale: The claim is misleading and unproven. While aggregate earmark totals have sometimes been in the low tens of billions in particular years, eliminating earmarks does not automatically translate to $15–20 billion in annual net 'savings' because funds can be reallocated, overall federal spending is much larger, and past earmark moratoria reduced earmarks without producing equivalent reductions in total outlays.

claim: Says that shutdowns are "ineffective" and that we now know that COVID-19 is not commonly spread "by someone going to work."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed studies and public-health analyses found that shutdowns and other non-pharmaceutical interventions (stay-at-home orders, business/school closures, gathering limits) reduced SARS-CoV-2 transmission and deaths, so calling them uniformly “ineffective” is incorrect. Workplace transmission was a documented and important source of spread in many settings (especially indoor, crowded workplaces and among essential workers), so the broad claim that COVID-19 is not commonly spread by someone going to work is also misleading.

claim: Says his office "has already recovered over $2 billion from Wall Street for the workers, retirees, and investors who were harmed."
rationale: The claim, as presented, lacks any identifying office, person, time period, or source and therefore cannot be verified. Recovery claims of 'over $2 billion from Wall Street' are specific factual assertions that require documentary evidence (official press releases, settlements, or accounting); without those details this statement should not be accepted as true.

claim: "The Earth is not warming."
rationale: Multiple independent observations show the Earth is warming: global surface temperatures have risen, ocean heat content has increased, glaciers and ice sheets are losing mass, and global sea level has risen. Major scientific assessments attribute the recent warming primarily to human-emitted greenhouse gases, so the claim that the Earth is not warming contradicts the broad body of evidence.

claim: "When I became president and CEO of Godfather’s Pizza, it was supposed to go bankrupt . . . We turned it around with common-sense business principles."
rationale: The claim overstates the situation. Herman Cain did serve as president/CEO of Godfather’s Pizza and led a period of improved operations and expansion, but contemporary records and fact-checkers show the company was not literally on the verge of immediate bankruptcy at his appointment and later ownership and financial problems complicate the simple "we turned it around" narrative. The statement compresses complex corporate history into a tidy, exaggerated claim.

claim: Says Russian President Vladimir Putin "calls me brilliant."
rationale: The claim as stated is unverifiable: it omits who 'me' refers to and provides no source or context. There are no reliable public reports or transcripts confirming that Vladimir Putin publicly said the unnamed person 'calls me brilliant,' so the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Wages are on the rise — in fact we were the top small-business wage growth state in the nation."
rationale: The claim is too vague and lacks a named state, time period, and data source, so it cannot be verified as stated. Wage-growth rankings depend on the metric and timeframe (quarterly vs annual, percent vs nominal), and while a state might have led small‑business wage growth in a specific dataset and period, the blanket assertion is unsupported without citation.

claim: "Our larger domestic threat is from racial supremacist groups."
rationale: Recent U.S. federal law-enforcement and homeland-security assessments have identified racially or ethnically motivated violent extremists (including white supremacist groups) as the most persistent and lethal domestic terrorism threat in the United States. Therefore, the general claim that our larger domestic threat comes from racial supremacist groups is supported for the recent U.S. context, though it simplifies a complex threat environment.

claim: In 2011, "the average annual compensation for a teacher in the Milwaukee Public Schools system will exceed $100,000."
rationale: Available data and typical pay levels show that in 2011 Milwaukee Public Schools teachers had average base salaries in the roughly $50k–$60k range; even after adding employer-paid benefits and retirement contributions, average total compensation was well below $100,000. Therefore the claim that average annual teacher compensation in MPS exceeded $100,000 in 2011 is incorrect.

claim: Says Gov. Tony Evers "tried to make us pay even more at the pump by hiking the gas tax."
rationale: The claim implies Gov. Tony Evers raised the gas tax or successfully made people pay more at the pump. While Evers has proposed transportation funding plans that included options such as higher fuel taxes or fees, those proposals were not enacted as a gas-tax hike by the Wisconsin legislature. The statement therefore misstates or overstates the outcome.

claim: "If Biden wins the election, there are people out there planning on mass murdering poc and lbgtq+ people. Please stay inside during the election and a few days after."
rationale: The claim asserts widespread, organized plans to carry out mass murder of POC and LGBTQ+ people if Biden wins; there is no credible public evidence supporting such a broad, coordinated conspiracy tied to that election outcome. While isolated threats and extremist plots have been documented around U.S. elections, those are case-by-case incidents and do not validate the sweeping, unverified assertion in the claim.

claim: "832,000 people lost their job while (Charlie Crist was) governor."
rationale: The statement gives a precise number without specifying the data source or exact start/end dates. Employment statistics for Florida during Charlie Crist’s term (Jan 2007–Jan 2011) did show very large losses during the Great Recession — on the order of several hundred thousand — but different measures (nonfarm payrolls vs. private jobs) and different month ranges produce varying totals, so the unqualified claim of exactly 832,000 lost jobs is not verifiable as stated.

claim: "[O]ver 200,000 ordinary citizens were given the opportunity to identify projects they preferred."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it provides no timeframe, location, or program details to check; without that context there is no evidence to confirm that over 200,000 ordinary citizens were given that opportunity. While large-scale participatory budgeting or consultation exercises can reach such numbers, the statement is unsubstantiated as written.

claim: "About 95 percent of (Ohio’s) electricity comes from burning coal."
rationale: Ohio has historically relied on coal but never to the extent of 95% of its electricity. Federal energy data show coal has supplied a substantial share in some years (often a plurality or majority in earlier decades) but in recent years coal's share is far lower due to natural gas, nuclear, and growing renewables.

claim: "Chinese lunar rover finds no evidence of American moon landings."
rationale: The claim is false because Chinese lunar rovers did not visit Apollo landing sites and thus could not meaningfully 'find' or disprove Apollo artifacts. Multiple independent lines of evidence confirm the U.S. moon landings, including retroreflectors left on the surface, lunar rock samples returned to Earth, and high-resolution orbital imagery that shows Apollo descent stages and rover tracks.

claim: Says "FBI and Texas State Police are both confirming that Raymond Peter Littleberry, the man accused of shooting up a Texas church, was an avid atheist on the payroll of the Democrat National Committee."
rationale: Major news organizations and official agencies have not published any FBI or Texas Department of Public Safety confirmation that a shooter named Raymond Peter Littleberry was an "avid atheist" or on the Democratic National Committee payroll. The claim appears to come from unverified social-media posts; employment on a party payroll would be a verifiable personnel matter but no credible sources corroborate it.

claim: "More than a million Californians" do not have "clean water to bathe in or drink."
rationale: Reports document significant problems with contaminated or intermittent water in some California communities, but official estimates and independent studies vary and do not clearly support a definitive, current figure that more than one million Californians lack clean water for bathing or drinking. Many estimates cite hundreds of thousands affected or approach one million depending on definitions (e.g., contaminated systems, private wells, intermittent access), so the blanket claim is unverified and likely misleading without more context or a specific timeframe.

claim: Fundamental changes made to the language describing the Wisconsin Idea in the University of Wisconsin System's mission statement were the result of a "drafting error."
rationale: Although UW System officials characterized the removal of traditional Wisconsin Idea language as a "drafting error," contemporaneous reporting and document comparisons showed the wording changes were made in administrative edits and were contested as deliberate policy edits rather than a simple clerical mistake. The university later restored much of the original language only after public and regent pushback, which undermines the claim that the substantive changes were merely an accidental drafting error.

claim: Ted Cruz is "unknown to the vast majority of Texans."
rationale: Ted Cruz is a prominent Texas politician who has served as a U.S. senator since 2013, won statewide elections, and was a high-profile 2016 presidential candidate, so he is widely known in Texas. The claim that he is "unknown to the vast majority of Texans" contradicts his statewide electoral success and extensive media presence.

claim: "The labor participation rate is at an all-time low."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and, as stated, is not generally true: labor force participation rates vary by country and over time. For example, in the U.S. the rate plunged in April 2020 during the COVID shock (one of the lowest points in recent decades) but has since partially recovered and is not at an all-time low; other countries show different trends. Without a specific country and date the blanket statement is unsupported.

claim: "Some of the men serving in the (Afghan) armed forces have never driven a vehicle before."
rationale: Many Afghan recruits have historically come from rural areas with low vehicle ownership and limited access to driving instruction; training programs and field reports during the past two decades repeatedly noted that some soldiers had never driven before and required basic vehicle-operation training. The claim is modest (saying "some") and consistent with those observations.

claim: During his time as House speaker, "unemployment came down from 5.6 percent to under 4 (percent)."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about which House speaker and does not match U.S. unemployment and speaker timelines. No recent Speaker's full tenure saw unemployment fall exactly from 5.6% to under 4%—for example, under Boehner unemployment fell from much higher (~9%) to around 5.6%, and under Paul Ryan it fell from about 5.0% to around 4.0%, but not from 5.6% to below 4% during a single speakership.

claim: Despite attention on global warming, "fewer Americans carpool today to work than carpooled in 1980" and "SUVs have never been a larger proportion of the vehicles being sold in this country."
rationale: U.S. commuting data show the share of workers who carpool has declined since 1980, and contemporary auto-industry sales data show SUVs/light trucks make up a record-high proportion of new-vehicle sales, larger than in past decades. Both trends are well-documented in Census commuting statistics and industry sales reports.

claim: Wagon arriving at Detroit counting center after deadline "may have been a ballot box."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the wagon arriving at the Detroit counting center contained ballots; available video does not clearly show ballots being unloaded and officials and independent fact-checkers reported the claim as unsubstantiated. Statements and reporting after the incident indicated the vehicle did not produce secret ballots and that chain-of-custody procedures were followed, contradicting the suggestion it 'may have been a ballot box.'

claim: "We raised the minimum wage to $15 first in city government. Now, working together with people in Albany, it's the law of the state."
rationale: New York City government enacted a $15 minimum for city workers/contractors in 2015 before the state acted, and the New York State legislature passed a 2016 wage‑increase law that phased in a $15 minimum for New York City. Thus the statement that the city raised $15 first in city government and then worked with Albany to make it law at the state level is substantially accurate.

claim: David Dewhurst "has never once cut one penny from the state budget."
rationale: David Dewhurst served as Texas lieutenant governor during legislative sessions (including the post‑2008 recession 2011 session) that enacted reductions and adjustments to the state budget. An absolute statement that he "has never once cut one penny" is contradicted by the reality that budgets were amended and funding was cut while he presided over and influenced budget legislation.

claim: "Four balanced budgets in a row, with no new taxes for anyone. The best job growth in 12 years. Nearly 130,000 new private-sector jobs. Merit pay to reward New Jersey’s best teachers, and the most education funding ever."
rationale: This is a bundle of claims mixing true, misleading, and unproven assertions. New Jersey did post several consecutive balanced budgets and saw notable private-sector job gains in certain multi-year windows, but the absolute claim of "no new taxes for anyone" is misleading (targeted tax/fee increases and revenue changes occurred) and statewide merit pay for teachers was proposed but not broadly implemented as described. Because at least one central claim is false or misleading, the overall statement is not accurate.

claim: A typical married couple "will contribute $119,000" into Medicare but will "receive $357,000 in Medicare benefits over their lifetimes."
rationale: Those precise dollar figures are drawn from specific projections and assumptions (age cohort, income, and present-value accounting) and are not a general fact about a “typical married couple.” Medicare contributions and lifetime benefits vary widely by earnings history, lifespan, and whether values are reported gross or net in present dollars, so presenting a single pair of numbers as typical is misleading.

claim: Medicare insurance premiums will be rising to "$120.20 per month in 2013 and $247.00 per month in 2014."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. The standard Medicare Part B monthly premium was about $104.90 in 2013 and remained around $105 in 2014; it did not rise to $120.20 or $247.00 for standard enrollees. While higher-income beneficiaries may pay larger income-related surcharges (IRMAA), the broad premium figures given are not accurate for the standard Medicare premium.

claim: Canadian-born Ted Cruz "has had a double passport."
rationale: Ted Cruz was born in Calgary to a U.S. citizen mother, giving him Canadian citizenship by birth while he was also a U.S. citizen; he therefore held dual nationality and had Canadian citizenship (and has been reported to have held a Canadian passport) until he formally renounced Canadian citizenship in 2014.

claim: Says Rick Scott "cut $700 million from water management."
rationale: There is no clear, authoritative record that Rick Scott personally cut exactly $700 million from 'water management' as a single, identifiable action. Budget changes during his governorship involved many line-item adjustments, vetoes, and federal/state program shifts, and public claims about a $700 million cut aggregate different programs and timeframes in a misleading way.

claim: Dan McCready backed state legislation that raised consumers "$149 million a year in higher energy costs."
