rationale: Investigations, statements from the Suez Canal Authority and the salvage teams, and maritime experts concluded the Ever Given grounded due to high winds, navigational/human error and channel conditions. No credible evidence has been produced that the blockage was planned or staged.

claim: Says he is the "ranking member" of the House select committee investigating the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol.
rationale: There was no official "ranking member" of the House January 6th select committee. The House minority leader nominated members (including Jim Jordan) but Speaker Pelosi rejected McCarthy's slate and instead appointed two Republicans (Liz Cheney and Adam Kinzinger) to the panel; neither was formally designated as a ranking member, so a claim that someone is the committee's "ranking member" is inaccurate.

claim: Says of Gov. Tony Evers and 2020 violence in Kenosha after the police shooting of Jacob Blake: "It took the loss of lives before help finally came."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and official timelines show that larger state assistance (including a substantial National Guard mobilization) was authorized after the Aug. 25 shootings in Kenosha that left two people dead. Critics noted that broader state deployment did not occur during the earlier nights of unrest, so the statement that help arrived only after lives were lost accurately reflects the sequence of major state action.

claim: "The CDC director just said that 75% of ‘Covid deaths’ occurred in people with at least four comorbidities."
rationale: There is no public record of the CDC director making that statement, and CDC data do not support a blanket claim that 75% of COVID-19 deaths had four or more comorbidities. CDC death-certificate summaries show many decedents had contributing conditions, but the distribution does not match the quoted 75% figure and such percentages have been widely misreported or taken out of context.

claim: "Tens and tens of thousands of bridges are in disrepair, some on the verge of collapse."
rationale: The claim is vague and appears exaggerated. While many countries (for example the United States) do report tens of thousands of bridges in poor or structurally deficient condition, the phrase “tens and tens of thousands” and the assertion that some are “on the verge of collapse” overstates available evidence: routine inspections and inventory programs identify bridges needing repair, and outright imminent collapse is rare and typically addressed urgently.

claim: "We’ve been down this road before—blanket protectionism is a big part of why America had a Great Depression."
rationale: Protectionist measures—most famously the 1930 Smoot–Hawley Tariff—raised U.S. tariffs, provoked retaliatory tariffs, and contributed to a severe collapse in international trade that deepened and prolonged the U.S. downturn. While other factors (bank failures, the stock market crash, and contractionary monetary policy) were central drivers, historians and economists widely view blanket protectionism as a significant worsening factor in the Great Depression.

claim: Democratic lawmakers who voted in favor of short-term spending bills "just voted to deport Dreamers."
rationale: The statement is misleading: voting for a short-term spending bill (a continuing resolution) does not itself enact a law ordering the deportation of DACA recipients. Most CRs simply extend funding levels and generally do not directly change immigration status or compel removals; deportation decisions are carried out by executive agencies and courts. Saying lawmakers "just voted to deport Dreamers" falsely equates a funding vote with a direct authorization of deportations.

claim: Says a photo shows a man wearing a "government issue Saint Laurent hazardous materials suit."
rationale: It is highly unlikely a government would 'issue' a luxury-brand (Saint Laurent) hazardous‑materials suit; governments procure certified protective gear from industrial suppliers, not fashion houses. Claims that a photo shows a government‑issued Saint Laurent hazmat suit are therefore almost certainly a miscaption or satire rather than a factual description.

claim: If Florida expanded Medicaid, "some studies indicate it would create about 120,000 jobs."
rationale: Multiple state-level economic impact analyses and advocacy reports have projected that expanding Medicaid in Florida would generate on the order of 100,000–130,000 jobs, so the statement that "some studies indicate about 120,000 jobs" accurately reflects those estimates. Estimates vary by model and assumptions, but the existence of studies showing roughly 120,000 jobs is supported.

claim: A photo shows Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson on Epstein Island.
rationale: No credible evidence supports that the photo shows Dwayne Johnson on Jeffrey Epstein’s private island. Multiple reputable fact-checks and media investigations have found the image to be misattributed or manipulated, and Johnson is not listed among verified associates or visitors to Epstein’s island in reporting.

claim: Says "Bill Pascrell voted to eliminate all estate taxes for billionaires, and I voted no."
rationale: There is no clear record that Rep. Bill Pascrell voted to "eliminate all estate taxes for billionaires." Pascrell, a Democrat, has generally opposed estate-tax repeal and is not known to have supported legislation that fully eliminated the estate tax. The portion claiming "I voted no" is unverifiable without identifying the speaker and the specific bill.

claim: Atlanta Tea Party co-founder Debbie Dooley "wants gas taxes raised."
rationale: Debbie Dooley is known as a Tea Party co-founder and founder of Conservatives for Energy Freedom who has publicly opposed tax increases and regulatory interventions; there is no clear, corroborated public record that she advocates raising gas taxes. Reports and her statements emphasize deregulation and market-based energy policies rather than wanting higher gas taxes, so the claim is not supported by the general record.

claim: It was President Obama's "inaction that caused over three weeks to go by before he even approved the governor's plan to protect our marsh."
rationale: The claim attributes a specific three-week delay directly to President Obama's personal inaction, but approvals for state marsh-protection plans are typically handled through federal agencies (e.g., FEMA, the Army Corps) and involve interagency and state processes. Public records and reporting do not show clear evidence that the President personally caused a three-week hold; delays are more plausibly explained by administrative review, state submission timing, or agency-level decisions.

claim: "That’s 5,615 projected coal-powered plants in just 8 countries. The USA has 15 - building 0 more."
rationale: There is no credible, current dataset showing exactly 5,615 projected coal-fired power plants concentrated in eight countries while the U.S. has only 15 and is building none. Global trackers (e.g., Global Energy Monitor) report a few thousand proposed/planned units worldwide but not that specific breakdown; moreover the U.S. has very few new coal proposals and effectively no large new coal plants under construction in recent years. The claim appears to conflate different metrics or misstate counts without necessary context (units vs. projects vs. capacity).

claim: Says Mitt Romney "runs away from Ronald Reagan."
rationale: The claim as written is ambiguous and provides no source, time, or speaker attribution, so it cannot be verified. Mitt Romney has at times invoked and praised Ronald Reagan but opponents have also accused him of distancing himself from Reagan’s positions; there is no clear, universally documented statement that he categorically 'runs away from Ronald Reagan.'

claim: Small businesses "create 70 percent of the jobs in America."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate as written: small businesses do not account for 70% of all jobs in the U.S. While small businesses (commonly defined as firms with fewer than 500 employees) employ roughly half of the private-sector workforce, some studies have found they account for a large share—around two-thirds—of net new jobs over particular periods, not 70% of total jobs. The claim conflates total employment with periodic job creation and overstates the share.

claim: This is the 911 call placed by the migrants trapped in the truck found in San Antonio, Texas.
rationale: There is no verified evidence or official confirmation that a 911 call from migrants trapped in the San Antonio truck exists or that a widely circulated audio clip is that call. Major local authorities and credible news fact-checks did not authenticate such a recording and several postings were identified as unverified or misattributed.

claim: State pension fund staffers "lost billions. Then Sink gave them bonuses."
rationale: The claim is vague and lacks key context (which state, which pension fund, what time period and which “Sink” is meant). There is no clear, verifiable record that a person named Sink personally approved discretionary bonuses for pension-staff immediately after causing or overseeing losses of “billions”; public pension investment losses during market downturns are typically market-driven and compensation decisions are set by boards, statutes, or pre-existing pay plans. Given the ambiguity and absence of specific corroborating evidence, the broad allegation as stated is not supported.

claim: "The son-in-law of the president met with Russian officials at the Trump Tower after having them come in the back door."
rationale: It is true Jared Kushner (the president’s son-in-law) attended meetings at Trump Tower that included Russian-linked individuals, but there is no credible evidence that he 'had them come in the back door' as claimed. Reporting documents the June 2016 meeting (and later contacts) but not that Kushner arranged a secret back-entrance entry; that additional allegation appears unsubstantiated or fabricated.

claim: Says Rep. Pramila Jayapal was not wearing a mask in Congress during the U.S. Capitol mob.
rationale: Contemporaneous photos and video from the January 6 Capitol attack show Rep. Pramila Jayapal wearing a mask while in the Capitol, and multiple news fact-checks debunked claims that she was unmasked. The assertion appears to rely on selective or out-of-context images rather than the full visual record.

claim: Says Anthony Bourdain tweeted, "This might be the best bat soup I ever had in my life. Someday everyone’s gonna be talking about Wuhan."
rationale: There is no record of Anthony Bourdain posting that tweet and major fact-checkers have debunked the attribution. Bourdain died in 2018, well before COVID-19 and the Wuhan news cycle, making it implausible he authored a tweet referencing Wuhan in that context.

claim: "Most of these killers tend to be 18, 19 years old."
rationale: The statement is vague and unsupported: it gives no definition of "these killers" or a place/timeframe. Broad crime statistics and studies of homicide and mass-shooter demographics show a wide age distribution rather than a majority concentrated at ages 18–19. Without specific context or data, the claim cannot be substantiated and is misleading.

claim: "Barbara Buono by the numbers: As a Trenton politician, she voted to raise taxes 154 times. Under her, property taxes up 70 percent. Backed a 16 percent sales tax increase. Utilities, nursing homes, cell phones, parking lots, lottery wins, gyms – She taxed them all. Architect of Corzine’s budget, she drove New Jersey $2 billion into debt. Barbara Buono by the numbers: taking New Jersey backwards."
rationale: The ad mixes accurate facts, misleading counts, and unsupported causal claims. Buono did serve in Trenton and was involved in budget votes as a Senate budget committee member, but the “154 votes to raise taxes,” “property taxes up 70% under her,” and the claim she alone “drove New Jersey $2 billion into debt” are exaggerations or lack context: roll‑call tallies include many different types of votes, tax changes were enacted by multiple actors and over many years, and state budget shortfalls cannot be attributed solely to one legislator. The “16 percent sales tax increase” appears to conflate a relative percent change with percentage points and omits broader context.

claim: Abraham Lincoln "visited and some say even danced in (the Ohio Senate) chamber."
rationale: Although Abraham Lincoln did visit Ohio on multiple occasions, there is no credible contemporaneous documentation that he 'danced in' the Ohio Senate chamber. The story appears in local lore and secondary anecdotes but is not supported by primary sources or mainstream Lincoln biographies.

claim: "Terry (McAuliffe) calls in his friend Joe Biden to actually put the DOJ on Virginia parents."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Terry McAuliffe personally called President Joe Biden to direct the Department of Justice to target Virginia parents. Reporting from the 2021 Virginia campaign and subsequent fact-checks do not document such a call or any direct, documented order from the White House to the DOJ at McAuliffe's request. The claim appears to be a politicized allegation without substantiating public records or reputable news sources.

claim: "David Dewhurst currently owes more than $1 million to vendors for services provided to his 2012 U.S. Senate campaign."
rationale: I am not aware of reliable, up-to-date public records or reputable news reports confirming that David Dewhurst 'currently' owes more than $1 million to vendors for his 2012 Senate campaign. While his 2012 campaign carried some post-election liabilities, available summaries and campaign-finance filings do not definitively show an outstanding vendor debt above $1 million, and debts may have been reduced or resolved since then. Because the claim uses a vague "currently," it is unverified as stated.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders marched with Fidel Castro and Che Guevara in Cuba.
rationale: This claim is false. Che Guevara was killed in 1967, long before Bernie Sanders’ documented visit to Cuba in 1985, and there is no credible evidence Sanders ever marched with or alongside Fidel Castro. Contemporary fact-checking and historical records show Sanders visited Cuba as part of a small group but did not participate in any march with Castro or Che.

claim: "Taxpayers are paying a fortune for the use of Air Force One on the campaign trail" by President Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton.
rationale: The claim as phrased is inaccurate: Hillary Clinton has never been president and therefore never used 'Air Force One' (the designation for the sitting president’s aircraft). While President Obama — like other sitting presidents — did use Air Force One for trips that included campaign events, presidential travel is funded by the government when it is official, and campaigns are generally only required to reimburse specific incremental or partisan expenses. Calling it a categorical statement that 'taxpayers are paying a fortune' for Air Force One on the campaign trail is a misleading generalization and the attribution to both Obama and Clinton is incorrect.

claim: Image of expansive pit shows a lithium mine.
rationale: Without the image file, geolocation, or sourcing/metadata it is not possible to verify that an unspecified photo of an expansive pit depicts a lithium mine. Many kinds of open-pit mines, quarries, evaporation ponds, or tailings impoundments can look similar in photos and are frequently misattributed online.

claim: Says that Biden’s ban on new federal leases will kill 120,000 Texas jobs.
rationale: The claim is a specific, causal forecast that lacks robust, consensus evidence. Estimates of 120,000 lost Texas jobs come from advocacy or single-model projections that use strong assumptions (no offsetting production or leasing, fixed demand), while independent analyses and historical experience show federal leases are only part of Texas oil/gas activity and losses would be smaller or partially offset over time. Because the outcome depends on policy scope, duration, market responses, and substitution to state/private leases, the precise figure is unsupported.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court is "five guys who start determining what contraceptions are legal."
rationale: The U.S. Supreme Court has nine justices, not literally 'five guys'; while a five-justice majority can decide cases, characterizing the Court that way is inaccurate and ignores female justices. The Court can rule on the constitutionality of laws affecting contraception, but longstanding precedents (e.g., Griswold and Eisenstadt) protect contraceptive rights and were not explicitly overturned by Dobbs.

claim: A photo shows three men on crosses who "feel like they’re being crucified by being required to stay at home."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a genuine photograph shows three men physically crucified who said they “feel like they’re being crucified” by stay-at-home orders. Viral images like this have been repeatedly miscaptioned or originate from staged performances, protests, or art rather than literal crucifixions tied to lockdown mandates.

claim: There are cities and counties in Georgia that don’t have websites, and where elected officials don’t have email addresses.
rationale: Many small, rural municipalities and some county governments lack the staff or budgets to maintain individual websites, and it is common for local elected officials at that level to not have public email addresses, relying instead on phone, mail, or shared office contacts. Reports and surveys of local government digital presence consistently show uneven online availability across jurisdictions, including in Georgia (U.S. state).

claim: "FOX Network Picks Up ‘Roseanne,’ Saying It Has No Problem With Occasional Racism"
rationale: This headline is false. ABC canceled Roseanne in 2018 after Roseanne Barr posted a racist tweet, and there are no credible reports that Fox picked up the show or issued a statement endorsing "occasional racism." The phrasing matches known satirical/hoax headlines rather than any verified network action or statement.

claim: "Prescription drug companies are charging Americans prices that are on average 4x higher than what's charged in other countries."
rationale: U.S. prescription drug prices are widely documented to be substantially higher than in many other countries, but the typical average multiple is lower than 4x and varies by study, drug set, and whether list or net prices are used. Some individual brand-name or specialty drugs are priced at 4x or more compared with particular countries, but claiming a blanket 4x average over all prescriptions and comparators overstates the consensus.

claim: "25,000 businesses have been created since (Scott) Walker took office."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and misleading: business-creation totals depend heavily on definitions (new firms vs. establishments, net vs. gross) and on the exact time window after Walker took office in January 2011. Independent data sources and prior fact-checks did not corroborate a clear, attributable increase of 25,000 new businesses tied to his tenure and the figure appears to overstate what reliable statistics support.

claim: A 50-50 public-private split for paying for a new Milwaukee Bucks arena would "be much better -- in terms of the portion of the public financing -- than most of the other arena projects done around the country."
rationale: Public shares of arena and stadium projects vary widely by sport, city and time period; while some projects have been heavily subsidized, many recent arena deals (particularly NBA/NHL arenas) have had public contributions at or below 50%. Therefore a 50-50 split would not clearly be "much better than most" other projects nationwide.

claim: Says "the mandate is 71 times that a child’s body will be injected with a disease" for immunizations.
rationale: The claim is a misleading characterization: immunization mandates do not mean a child is 'injected with a disease' 71 times. Vaccines deliver antigens or inactivated/attenuated organisms (or components) to stimulate immunity, not to cause the natural disease, and claims using a single large number (e.g., 71) usually mix cumulative doses, antigens, and combination vaccines in a confusing way. While very rare vaccine-derived infections can occur with some live vaccines historically, that is not equivalent to being repeatedly injected with the disease as the claim asserts.

claim: Says a poll showed Democrat Beto O’Rourke within 2 percentage points of Republican Sen. Ted Cruz.
rationale: The claim is too vague and unverified as stated because it provides no poll name, date, or sample; without that specificity there is no reliable way to confirm it. While some individual 2018 polls sometimes showed very close margins, most reputable polls and aggregate averages during the Cruz–O'Rourke race showed Cruz leading by more than two points, so the blanket statement that “a poll showed” within 2 points cannot be confirmed from the claim alone.

claim: The STAR Ohio fund "just received the highest possible credit rating one of these funds can receive."
rationale: The claim is unsourced and ambiguous about timing and which rating agency is meant. While STAR Ohio has often carried top short-term or long-term ratings from particular agencies, I cannot verify the assertion that it "just received the highest possible credit rating one of these funds can receive" without a date and agency; therefore the specific claim as stated is not verifiable and judged false.

claim: Rhode Island voters are moving away from the Democratic party to non-affiliation
rationale: State voter registration data over recent years show a modest decline in registered Democrats in Rhode Island alongside a growing share of voters registered as unaffiliated/independent, indicating movement away from the Democratic Party toward non‑affiliation. The trend is observable in official registration tallies though the shift is gradual rather than a sudden exodus.

claim: Austin was the "site of the first mass shooting in the country."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. While Austin is known for the 1966 University of Texas tower shooting (often called a landmark or 'first' modern mass-shooting episode), there were multiple mass killings in the United States before 1966 (for example the 1927 Bath School disaster and various 19th- and early-20th-century mass attacks). Therefore Austin was not the site of the country's first mass shooting.

claim: Colorado saw "increased incidents of emergency room visits by young people" and "increased incidents of driving while under the influence of marijuana" following the legalization of recreational pot.
rationale: Multiple Colorado and national public-health and traffic-safety analyses reported increases after legalization: emergency department visits and hospitalizations for cannabis exposures (including among children and adolescents) rose, and the proportion/number of drivers testing positive for THC in crashes and DUI-related incidents increased. However, presence of THC in drivers does not by itself prove acute impairment and causation is complex.

claim: "However, it took $19.5 million in Oregon Lottery funds for the Port of Newport to eventually land the new NOAA Marine Operations Center-Pacific."
rationale: I find no clear evidence that a single $19.5 million payment from Oregon Lottery funds was the decisive funding that ‘landed’ NOAA’s Marine Operations Center–Pacific for the Port of Newport. Public reporting and project summaries indicate the center’s establishment involved NOAA/federal funding plus local port investment and state/local grants, but not a confirmed $19.5M lottery transfer as described.

claim: Says, "Carl proposed a 'windfall' tax on real estate development when he was a Metro Councilor."
rationale: The claim is too vague and I cannot confirm a Metro Councilor named simply 'Carl' proposed a 'windfall' tax on real estate development; no specific city, time, or full name is provided and there is no clear, widely reported record matching that description. Without identifying which 'Carl' and which Metro council (and lacking supporting public-source evidence), the claim cannot be verified as stated.

claim: "Instagram has been limiting our posts so that no more than 7% of our friends see our posts."
rationale: There is no evidence Instagram enforces a universal hard cap that limits posts to being seen by no more than 7% of friends/followers. Instagram uses an algorithmic feed that prioritizes content based on factors like engagement, recency, and user behavior, so organic reach varies widely by account, post type, and timing rather than being fixed at 7%.

claim: Carbon dioxide is not "a primary contributor to the global warming that we see."
rationale: Extensive climate science shows CO2 is a primary driver of recent global warming: increased atmospheric CO2 from fossil fuel burning raises radiative forcing and traps heat. Multiple lines of evidence, including observations and climate model attribution studies summarized by the IPCC, attribute most post‑mid‑20th century warming to human greenhouse gas emissions with CO2 the largest single contributor.

claim: "I never had a filibuster-proof Senate."
rationale: The claim is unverified because the speaker is not identified; whether someone "never had a filibuster-proof Senate" depends entirely on their identity and the exact time period. Without that context the assertion cannot be established as true and is therefore treated as false for lack of evidence.

claim: "The government will be infiltrating" personal text messages.
rationale: The claim is a broad, unsubstantiated assertion about future government action and cannot be verified as a general fact. While some governments have legal powers or technical capabilities to access private messages in specific cases (e.g., with warrants, court orders, or exploitation of devices), there is no universal proof that "the government will be infiltrating" all personal text messages. Whether infiltration occurs depends on the country, legal framework, and the specific circumstances or targets involved.

claim: "We borrow $4 billion every single day, much of it from China."
rationale: The U.S. government’s net borrowing averaged in the low billions per day in some years, so an average near $4 billion/day can be a rough ballpark for certain periods but is not a fixed "every single day" amount. Moreover, the claim that "much of it" comes from China is false: the majority of U.S. debt is held domestically (by the Fed, trust funds, institutions and investors) and China holds only a few hundred billion to around a trillion dollars of Treasuries—a relatively small share of total U.S. debt.

claim: The last private rocket launch "cost $80 million. If the government did it, the same thing would have cost probably 40 or 50 times that amount of money. I mean, literally."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and implausible as stated. While some government-designed programs (e.g., NASA’s SLS) have multi‑billion dollar per‑launch averages, typical government-contracted launch vehicles (Atlas V, Delta IV Heavy, etc.) have per‑launch costs in the hundreds of millions — not 40–50 times an $80M private launch. Without specifying which launch, payload and which government program, the blanket 40–50x multiplier is misleading.

claim: " ‘Obamacare’ puts the federal government between you and your doctor."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act (Obamacare) expanded insurance coverage, created marketplaces, and regulated insurers, but it generally preserved private delivery of care and did not place a federal official or agency between individual patients and their doctors. The law increases federal oversight, funding (subsidies, Medicaid expansion) and rules that influence care, but does not replace the doctor–patient relationship with a federal intermediary.

claim: "I never called for a partition" of Iraq.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it omits who 'I' refers to and when the statement would have been made. Without identifying the speaker and context, one cannot confirm the absence of any past statements advocating partition; numerous politicians, analysts, and Iraqi actors have at various times proposed partition, federalization, or territorial rearrangements for Iraq. Because of that ambiguity, the blanket denial cannot be treated as established fact here.

claim: Amazon will ship baby formula to U.S. addresses if you change your preferred country on its website from the U.S. to Canada.
rationale: Changing the displayed country on Amazon's website does not override seller and shipping-address restrictions; Amazon and third‑party sellers generally determine fulfillment by the actual delivery address and may block cross‑border shipments of regulated goods like infant formula. While some individual sellers or freight‑forwarding services might send formula from Canada to the U.S., it is not a universal capability simply gained by switching your preferred country.

claim: "In ‘Resident Evil’ the Umbrella Corporation releases a virus that infects the people of Raccoon City. A biological research lab with the exact same logo as the Umbrella Corporation can be found in the city where the coronavirus outbreak originated."
rationale: The first part is correct in fiction: Resident Evil’s Umbrella Corporation is depicted as releasing the T-virus in Raccoon City. The second part is false — there is no credible evidence that a real-world research lab in the city where the COVID-19 outbreak began uses the exact Umbrella Corporation logo; images and claims linking a matching logo to Wuhan-area labs were debunked and appear to be manipulated or misattributed.

claim: The majority of revenue generated by a proposed Kenosha casino would be sent to the Seminole tribe in Florida.
rationale: While the Seminole Tribe owns Hard Rock International and could receive management or branding fees if involved, typical management/branding agreements and Indian Gaming compacts do not send a majority of a casino’s revenue to an outside tribe. The casino operator and the owning tribal government in Wisconsin would retain most revenue under normal contracts and regulatory rules, and there is no public evidence that a proposed Kenosha deal would divert the majority of proceeds to the Florida Seminoles.

claim: Says John F. Kennedy said, "If a Supreme Court Justice died one day before the election, it would be more Constitutional to indefinitely postpone the election than postpone the confirmation a single day."
rationale: There is no reliable historical record or authoritative JFK archive that attributes this quote to John F. Kennedy, and the claim is inconsistent with constitutional practice and JFK's documented rhetoric. The wording and substance match patterns of modern misattributed political memes rather than verified speeches or writings from Kennedy.

claim: Says Gov. Scott Walker’s proposed budget "would sell off Wisconsin’s state parks."
rationale: Media and opponents characterized Walker-era budget proposals as “selling off” public lands, but the budget language did not authorize blanket sales of Wisconsin’s state parks. It allowed sale or exchange of certain Department of Natural Resources properties acquired with specific funding since a given date, and many protected categories (including state parks and state forests) were excluded or treated differently in the actual statutory language.

claim: Says Donald Trump indicted Amy Coney Barrett.
rationale: There is no credible report or public record that Amy Coney Barrett has been criminally indicted, and U.S. presidents do not issue indictments. Indictments are brought by prosecutors or grand juries, and neither Donald Trump nor anyone else has indicted her.

claim: The WIC program "is an incredibly cost effective program, serving nearly 10 million Americans each year and costing less than $100 per person. In my district, more than 18 percent of residents suffer from food insecurity and depend on WIC to make ends meet."
rationale: The national arithmetic in the claim is misleading: WIC typically serves roughly 6 million people per month, and the program’s annual budget is on the order of multiple billions of dollars, which implies an annual cost per participant well above $100 rather than under $100. The district-specific statement about more than 18% of residents being food insecure and dependent on WIC cannot be verified without the district name and is presented as a local fact without supporting evidence.

claim: "Mayor Bloomberg was busy blaming African Americans and Latinos for the housing crisis in 2008."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Mayor Michael Bloomberg publicly blamed African Americans and Latinos for the 2008 housing crisis. His public commentary and news coverage at the time focused on lenders, mortgage brokers, predatory lending practices, risky financial products and regulatory failures, not wholesale blame of minority borrowers.

claim: "We proudly handed the Biden administration the most secure border in history. All they had to do was keep this smooth-running system on autopilot."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate as a factual claim: objective indicators such as U.S. Customs and Border Protection encounter statistics and numerous policy analyses show that border crossings and enforcement challenges increased after January 2021 rather than that a uniquely "most secure" system was simply maintained. Border security has long been measured by multiple metrics (encounters, unlawful entries, staffing, removals) and requires active policy and operational management, so it was not a "smooth-running" system that could be left on autopilot.

claim: "While all COVID-19 news has been going on, the U.S. Government has been sneakily trying to remove end-to-end encryption" which means "the government will be able to see all of your messages and listen to all of your calls."
rationale: While U.S. law enforcement and some politicians have publicly pushed for ways to access encrypted communications and lawmakers have introduced bills that could weaken end-to-end encryption, there is no evidence of a secret successful effort that has 'removed' E2E encryption across the board. The claim also overstates certainty: proposals exist and are contested, but they have not resulted in universal government ability to read all messages or listen to all calls.

claim: "More than half of women under 30 who give birth do so outside of marriage..."
rationale: The claim lacks a country and timeframe and therefore is misleading. While nonmarital birth rates are high among teenagers and some women in their early 20s in many countries, including the U.S., births to women aged 25–29 (who account for a large share of births) are still often more likely to be within marriage, so the combined category 'under 30' does not uniformly exceed 50%. National statistics and OECD data show large variation by country and cohort, so the blanket statement is not generally true.

claim: Spending increases, not tax cuts, are the major cause of the federal budget deficit.
rationale: This claim is overly categorical. Historical and official budget analyses show that both rising mandatory spending (Social Security, Medicare/Medicaid), interest costs, and episodic tax cuts (e.g., 1980s, early 2000s, 2017) have been major contributors to federal deficits; which factor dominates depends on the time period and policy choices.

claim: Photo shows Kim Jong Un’s weight loss
rationale: There is insufficient evidence to conclude a single photo "shows" Kim Jong Un’s weight loss. Verifying weight change requires authenticated, dated comparative images or reliable medical/official confirmation; a standalone image can be affected by angle, lighting, clothing, or manipulation. Without provenance and comparison, the claim is not supported.

claim: "We have counties where there have been one arrest under the SAFE Act. It indicates there's not a whole lot of interest in enforcing this in our upstate counties."
rationale: The statement mixes an unsupported factual assertion (that some counties have had only one SAFE Act arrest) with a speculative inference that this proves lack of interest in enforcement. Without specific, time‑bound arrest data for the counties referenced and context about prosecutions, charging decisions, or incidence of violations, the claim cannot be substantiated. Arrest counts alone do not reliably indicate enforcement priority because they can reflect low violation rates, different charging practices, or resource constraints.

claim: President Obama’s health care law says "when you sell your house now you have to pay a 3.8 percent tax."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act created a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) on certain investment income for higher-income taxpayers, but it is not a blanket tax on all home sales. Gains from the sale of a primary residence are often excluded (up to $250,000 single / $500,000 married) and the NIIT only applies if the gain is taxable investment income and the taxpayer’s modified adjusted gross income exceeds statutory thresholds.

claim: There are 86 languages spoken at Miami Dade College.
rationale: I cannot verify the exact claim and such counts vary over time; while Miami Dade College is known for a very linguistically diverse student body, asserting a precise figure of 86 languages without a cited source is likely inaccurate or outdated. Institutions often publish different totals for specific years or campuses, so the number is not reliably fixed at 86.

claim: "When Marcy Kaptur brought home $42 million for new manufacturing jobs, Dennis Kucinich voted 'no'."
rationale: This claim is unsubstantiated as stated. While Rep. Marcy Kaptur has secured federal funds for her district and Rep. Dennis Kucinich has voted against some larger spending bills, there is no clear, corroborated record that Kucinich specifically voted 'no' on a discrete $42 million measure labeled 'for new manufacturing jobs' brought home by Kaptur; such funding is typically embedded in larger omnibus bills, making the claim misleading without precise bill and vote identification.

claim: "Seventy four percent of Californians are absolutely against sanctuary state" policies.
rationale: There is no well-documented, reputable statewide poll showing that 74% of Californians are "absolutely against" sanctuary-state policies. Public opinion in California on sanctuary policies has varied by question wording and timing, and many polls show plurality or majority support or mixed results rather than such a high, unambiguous opposition rate. The claim provides no source or date and uses vague language ("absolutely against").

claim: "Americans not vaccinated before 2022 will be put in camps"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or government policy that the U.S. will imprison or place unvaccinated Americans in 'camps' for failing to be vaccinated before 2022. Vaccine requirements in the U.S. have been limited to certain workplaces, schools, and travel contexts, and mass detention would violate constitutional protections and require legal processes not present in law or announced policy.

claim: There are fewer wars, there are fewer people dying in wars "now than there have been in quite some time."
rationale: The claim is too broad and depends on the timeframe: while interstate wars and average battle deaths declined after World War II and especially since the 1990s, violent spikes (e.g., Rwanda 1994, Syria, Yemen, and the 2022 Russia–Ukraine war) mean deaths and active conflicts have not monotonically decreased and have recently risen. Empirical datasets show a long-term downward trend in some categories but substantial variation year-to-year and by conflict type, so the blanket statement that there are fewer wars and fewer people dying now than 'in quite some time' is misleading.

claim: "Every day over 450,000 Americans sit in jail not because they've been convicted of anything, but because they are too poor to pay bail & don't have high powered attorneys."
rationale: The headline number (roughly 450,000 people) matches widely cited estimates of the U.S. pretrial jail population in recent years, but the claim overstates causation and universality. Not all of those people are held solely because they cannot pay bail or lack “high-powered” attorneys—many are held for public-safety reasons, on no‑bail charges, awaiting transfer, or have court-appointed counsel; inability to pay bail is a major but not exclusive driver of pretrial detention.

claim: Says the Georgia Dome would need up to $350 million in work over the next five to seven years.
rationale: I cannot verify the statement as presented because it lacks a source, date, or attribution and I find no clear, widely reported authoritative estimate that the Georgia Dome specifically required up to $350 million of work over the next five to seven years. Without a contemporaneous official engineering report or credible news citation, the claim is unverified. It may reflect an anecdotal or outdated estimate but cannot be confirmed as fact.

claim: Annual precipitation "has increased in Rhode Island by over 12 inches in the last century."
rationale: While Rhode Island and the broader northeastern U.S. have experienced increases in annual and heavy precipitation over the 20th century, the measured century-scale rise for the region and for Rhode Island stations is much smaller than 12 inches. Typical long-term datasets and regional climate assessments show increases of a few inches to perhaps under ten inches, not a >12-inch statewide rise.

claim: North Korea’s missiles are "not going to have a capability to reach the United States anytime real soon."
rationale: North Korea has tested intercontinental-range missiles (e.g., Hwasong-14/15) and intelligence analysts have judged that Pyongyang either already possesses or is close to possessing a missile capability that can reach parts of the United States. While uncertainties remain about reliable reentry, warhead miniaturization, and operational deployment, the categorical claim that it is "not going to have" that capability in the near term is contradicted by observed tests and expert assessments.

claim: The state and local tax deduction is a major benefit for moderate-income households because "50% of households that claim State & Local Tax deduction make under $100K."
rationale: The claim is misleading: even if roughly half of filers who itemize SALT in some years may have incomes under $100K, the dollar value of the SALT tax benefit is heavily concentrated among higher‑income taxpayers. Analyses from IRS and tax policy researchers show the largest share of SALT deductions and tax savings accrue to upper‑income households, so it is not accurate to present the deduction as primarily a major benefit for moderate‑income households.

claim: Says John Cornyn dodged the draft during the Vietnam War.
rationale: There is no well-documented, credible evidence that Senator John Cornyn actively dodged the Vietnam draft; public biographical records and mainstream reporting do not substantiate a proven case of draft evasion. Allegations about draft status often hinge on interpretations of student deferments, timing, or administrative matters, but those do not equal documented draft-dodging.

claim: Quotes Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as saying "I’m speaking with myself, number one, because I have a very good brain and I’ve said lots of things."
rationale: The quoted line is a verbatim remark Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made in a widely circulated 2019 interview/video clip in which she said she speaks with herself because she has "a very good brain" and has "said lots of things." Multiple news outlets and the video/audio record reproduced the quote accurately.

claim: "As soon as Chris Christie was governor, he gave tax cuts to millionaires."
rationale: Chris Christie did not immediately enact explicit tax cuts for millionaires upon taking office; his early governorship was characterized by spending reductions and budget battles rather than an immediate targeted cut for high-income individuals. While some tax and business tax changes during his tenure later had benefits for higher earners, those were enacted over time and not 'as soon as' he became governor.

claim: Bernie Sanders has "never taken corporate lobbyist money in his *entire political career.*"
rationale: Sanders has long refused contributions from corporate PACs and prominent corporate interests, but the absolute claim that he has "never taken corporate lobbyist money" is false. Fact-checkers and campaign finance records show his campaigns have accepted individual donations from people who are lobbyists or corporate employees at times. The distinction between rejecting corporate PACs and accepting individual donations creates the discrepancy.

claim: Says "85 percent (of immigrants) don’t show up for a scheduled court hearing or call to schedule a court hearing."
rationale: The 85% figure is not supported by available government and court-record data and has been repeatedly flagged by fact-checkers. Immigration court appearance rates vary by program, jurisdiction, and supervision level, but nowhere do reliable nationwide records show that 85% of immigrants fail to appear or even call to schedule hearings.

claim: "Bill Nelson actually voted in favor of higher taxes 272 times."
rationale: The “272” number comes from a partisan tally that grouped many different kinds of votes (procedural votes, budget or revenue-related measures, and other contexts) as votes “for higher taxes.” Independent fact-checkers concluded the claim is misleading because those items do not represent clear, direct votes to raise taxes and the methodology inflates the count.

claim: "Under President Obama, U.S. security funding for Israel is at an all-time high."
rationale: In 2016 the Obama administration negotiated a 10-year Memorandum of Understanding pledging $38 billion in U.S. security assistance to Israel (about $3.8 billion per year), which was the largest such bilateral U.S. military aid commitment to Israel to date. That pledge made U.S. security funding levels for Israel an all-time high in terms of committed assistance.

claim: "We’ve still had more deaths to the flu this year than we've had COVID-19."
rationale: The statement provides no location or time frame and is therefore misleading; based on available data during the COVID-19 pandemic, COVID-19 has caused far more deaths than seasonal influenza both globally and in the United States. Although influenza activity was unusually low in some seasons because of public-health measures, overall COVID-19 mortality has exceeded typical and recent flu mortality by a large margin.

claim: Says "46 percent of people believe major national news organizations fabricate stories about me."
rationale: The claim gives a precise 46% figure but cites no source and is ambiguous about who “me” refers to. Public opinion surveys do show varying levels of distrust in major news outlets, but reputable polls use different question wording and there is no widely reported, verifiable poll that exactly finds 46% believe national news organizations “fabricate stories about” a specific individual.

claim: "The United States is the No. 1 country in the world for energy resources. … We are the king daddy dogs when it comes to energy."
rationale: The United States is a top global producer of oil, natural gas, and total energy (especially after the shale boom), but it does not unambiguously rank No.1 on all measures of 'energy resources.' Several countries (e.g., Venezuela, Saudi Arabia, Russia) have larger proven oil or gas reserves, so the broad claim that the U.S. is the single No.1 country for energy resources is misleading and exaggerated.

claim: Says Rep. Kyrsten Sinema supported a bill that is "essentially encouraging child trafficking."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Kyrsten Sinema sponsored or supported legislation whose purpose was to 'encourage child trafficking.' Such an extreme characterization is not supported by public legislative records or mainstream reporting and appears to be an inflammatory mischaracterization of a vote or policy position without a named bill or source.

claim: "Same little boy died of COVID-19 in three different countries. Still don’t believe the media is #fakenews?"
rationale: A single child cannot literally die in three different countries; the claim conflates or misrepresents reporting. Such viral stories usually stem from reused or miscaptioned photos, syndicated articles, or different children being presented as the same individual rather than multiple deaths of one boy.

claim: "Rosalyn Dance voted against President Obama’s Medicaid expansion."
rationale: Rosalyn Dance is a Democratic member of the Virginia legislature and voted in favor of Virginia’s Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act when the General Assembly approved expansion measures in 2018. Public roll calls and news coverage list her among legislators supporting expansion, so the assertion that she voted against Obama’s Medicaid expansion is incorrect.

claim: Says recent studies indicate that nationally, only 8 percent of white voting-age citizens but 25 percent of African-American voting-age citizens lack government-issued photo IDs.
rationale: Major national surveys and analyses do find racial gaps in possession of government-issued photo ID, but they do not support the specific claim that only 8% of white voting-age citizens and 25% of African-American voting-age citizens lack such IDs nationwide. Reported figures vary by study, definition (voting-age vs registered voters), and which IDs count, and most reputable sources produce different percentage estimates and smaller or differently measured gaps than the exact 8%/25% pair stated. The claim appears to be an oversimplification or misstatement of heterogeneous study results.

claim: "Replacing marriage licenses with domestic union contracts does not alter state or federal benefits."
rationale: Many state and federal benefits and obligations are explicitly tied to the legal status of 'marriage' in statutes, regulations, and benefit rules. Simply replacing marriage licenses with 'domestic union contracts' would not automatically preserve those benefits unless every relevant state and federal law and agency were amended or interpreted to treat the new contract as legally equivalent to marriage.

claim: "In my attorney general's office, we've cut the budget 18 percent."
rationale: The statement lacks identifying details (which attorney general, which office, and what time period) and I have no independent budget records to confirm an 18% cut. Without named jurisdiction and supporting public budget documents, the claim cannot be verified and therefore should be treated as unproven.

claim: "Switzerland (where the government) issues every household a gun . . . has the lowest gun related crime rate of any civilized country in the world!!!"
rationale: The claim is inaccurate on both counts: Switzerland does not ‘issue every household a gun’—it has a militia system where conscripts historically kept service weapons at home but not every household receives a government gun and regulations have changed—and while Switzerland has relatively low gun homicide rates compared with some countries, it is not demonstrably the lowest of all developed nations (countries like Japan, Singapore and others have lower gun-related crime rates). The phrase 'civilized country' is vague and the claim’s absolute superlative is not supported by international crime statistics.

claim: "My plan offers three times as much tax relief to the middle class as Senator McCain's."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it gives no specifics about which proposal, which time period, how "middle class" is defined, or what metric of "tax relief" is used. Comparative statements about tax cuts require concrete legislative text and third-party scoring to support a precise multiple like "three times." Without those details or independent analysis, the assertion cannot be substantiated and is therefore judged false.

claim: "We have more coal reserves in the United States than they have oil reserves in Saudi Arabia."
rationale: Measured in energy-equivalent terms, U.S. recoverable coal contains substantially more energy than Saudi Arabia’s proven oil reserves. U.S. coal reserves are on the order of a few hundred billion short tons while Saudi proven oil is ~250–270 billion barrels; because a short ton of coal contains roughly 3–5 times the energy of a barrel of oil, the coal energy exceeds the oil energy.

claim: Josh Mandel doctored an image in a campaign ad but "forgot to Photoshop the hands that clearly show he put his face on the body of a Black soldier."
rationale: I am not aware of credible, fact-checked evidence that Josh Mandel literally pasted his face onto the body of a Black soldier and left darker hands visible in a campaign ad. Major fact-checkers and news reports do not corroborate the specific claim as stated; it appears to be an unverified social-media allegation or mischaracterization of a composite/stock-image ad.

claim: Says photos show the Trump-Ukraine whistleblower with Chuck Schumer, Elizabeth Warren, Nancy Pelosi and Hillary Clinton.
rationale: Independent fact-checks and major news organizations found that the circulated photos were miscaptioned or manipulated and do not reliably show the Trump–Ukraine whistleblower posing with Chuck Schumer, Elizabeth Warren, Nancy Pelosi or Hillary Clinton. The whistleblower’s identity was not officially confirmed at the time and the images were traced to other people or altered, so the specific claim is unsupported.

claim: A recent on-air protest can’t be real because "there are no live on air television broadcasts in Russia. None. Ever."
rationale: The absolute statement is incorrect: Russia does broadcast live television, including live news programs, talk shows, sports events and live feeds. While the media environment is tightly controlled, and some politically sensitive material is often pre-recorded or censored, that does not amount to a blanket absence of live broadcasts.

claim: House Republican plan would increase costs for Oregon seniors by $6,000 with health care vouchers instead of Medicare
rationale: The claim is too specific to be verified without identifying which House Republican plan and what time period or metric is meant. Republican proposals have varied (some proposing premium-support/voucher models), and independent analyses (CBO and others) show differing impacts by age, income, and state; no single, widely accepted estimate confirms a $6,000 increase specifically for Oregon seniors. Because estimates depend on plan design and assumptions, the blanket statement is not supported as presented.

claim: Says Dan Feehan "would vote with Pelosi for open borders and amnesty, putting Minnesota families at risk."
rationale: The statement is a partisan characterization rather than a documented fact. Public information shows Dan Feehan has expressed support for comprehensive immigration reform and pathways to citizenship rather than endorsing ‘open borders’ or an unconditional amnesty, and there is no clear evidence he has pledged to vote identically with Nancy Pelosi on such extreme-sounding measures. Because the claim uses vague, charged terms and predicts how he 'would vote' without specific bills or votes cited, it overstates and misrepresents his known positions.

claim: "Eight in 10 people this year can find plans for $75 a month or less."
rationale: The claim is vague and not verifiable as stated because it does not specify the country, type of plan, or whether it assumes subsidy eligibility. Availability and monthly premiums vary widely by location, age, income, and plan type, so a blanket "8 in 10 people" figure is unsupported without those details. Because of that missing context and variability, the broad assertion cannot be treated as factual.

claim: Says there are thousands of registered voters over 110 years old in North Carolina, including one who is 219 years old.
rationale: The claim is not credible: there are not thousands of living people over 110 in a single U.S. state, and a reported 219‑year‑old is biologically impossible and would be a globally documented anomaly. Such assertions typically arise from data-entry errors, transposed birth years, or failure to remove deceased registrants from voter rolls rather than actual supercentenarians.

claim: Says two-thirds of groups targeted for IRS scrutiny were not conservative.
rationale: Official reviews (notably the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration) found that the IRS used inappropriate criteria that included both conservative and liberal keywords, but the underlying data do not cleanly support a claim that two-thirds of groups targeted were not conservative. Early scrutiny disproportionately flagged conservative terms like 'Tea Party,' and later analyses found a mix of organizations affected; no authoritative report concluded that two-thirds were non-conservative.

claim: Says "Snoop Dogg arrested for conspiracy after talking about his ‘murder Trump’ video."
rationale: Snoop Dogg was not arrested or charged with conspiracy over any ‘murder Trump’ video. He released a controversial 2017 music video (often described as depicting a clown resembling Donald Trump) that prompted criticism and calls for legal action, but no arrest or conspiracy charge resulted.

claim: The Senate GOP plan does not raise taxes for Americans earning less than $70,000.
rationale: The statement is overly broad and not supported by independent analyses of recent Senate Republican tax proposals (notably the 2017 tax overhaul). Nonpartisan reviewers (Tax Policy Center, CBO/JCT) found that while many lower- and middle-income households saw initial cuts, a substantial share of Americans earning below roughly $70k would face tax increases in later years or under specific family/deduction scenarios because many individual tax provisions expire or because deductions/credits were changed.

claim: "Space X’s Starlink internet constellation has angered Russia as it was reported that the Starlink satellite constellation was used to guide the fire" on the Russian ship Moskva.
rationale: Although Russian officials and state media publicly complained about SpaceX/Starlink and Russia was displeased with Starlink support to Ukraine, there is no publicly verified evidence that the Starlink satellite constellation was used to guide the fire or strike on the Russian ship Moskva. Independent reporting and statements from Western officials indicate the ship was likely struck by Ukrainian Neptune missiles and do not corroborate claims that Starlink provided targeting guidance.

claim: "Here in Florida, despite 14 school shootings in eight years, we still have some of the weakest gun laws in the nation."
rationale: The claim mixes an unclear count and a subjective ranking. The number of "14 school shootings in eight years" depends on the time window and how "school shooting" is defined, and Florida’s gun-law strength is mixed: the state enacted several post-Parkland reforms (age limits, waiting period, red‑flag-related measures) but also retains permissive policies like preemption and broad self‑defense laws, so it is not universally classified as among the very weakest by major scorecards.

claim: "Two out of our last three governors in Virginia were investigated by the FBI. One went to jail and one is running for office again in this election."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate as stated. Among recent Virginia governors, Bob McDonnell was federally prosecuted but his convictions were unanimously overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court and he did not ultimately serve prison time; there is not credible evidence that two of the most recent three governors were the subjects of FBI criminal investigations that resulted in one going to jail and one now running again. The claim also mixes timelines and lacks clear reference to which three governors or which election.

claim: Australia is microchipping its public.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Australian government is implanting microchips in the general population or running a mass human microchipping program. Reports that do exist concern voluntary implants (e.g., some individuals or workplaces) or pet microchipping, and fact-checkers have debunked claims linking COVID-19 vaccines or government programs to mass microchipping.

claim: "Given the results of the primary, the vote of one New Hampshire superdelegate is equal to the votes of about 10,000 grassroots activists."
rationale: The statement presents a precise equivalence without specifying the year, party, turnout, or how votes are being converted into delegates. A New Hampshire superdelegate casts one convention vote (or one unit of delegate power), and the number of primary voters represented per delegate varies by election, allocation rules, and turnout — it is not a fixed ~10,000-to-1 ratio. Without a specific calculation tying total primary votes and the exact number of delegates/superdelegates in that contest, the claim is misleading and unsupported.

claim: "Every day, a black name resume is 50 percent less likely to get responded to than a white name resume."
rationale: This claim overstates and universalizes a finding. Well-known audit studies (notably Bertrand & Mullainathan 2004) found that resumes with white‑sounding names received about 50% more callbacks than otherwise-identical resumes with Black‑sounding names in specific U.S. settings, but that is a study result, not a literal daily law applying everywhere and across all sectors, times, and methods.

claim: "Already, the Affordable Care Act is helping to slow the growth of (Medicare’s) health care costs."
rationale: Multiple government analyses and independent studies found Medicare spending growth slowed in the years after the ACA’s enactment, and the law included explicit Medicare payment reductions and delivery/payment reforms that contributed to that slowdown. However, other factors (economic downturn, low price inflation, sequestration and broader health-care trends) also played roles, so the ACA is a significant contributor rather than the sole cause.

claim: When the United States "first created the federal income tax, frankly, nobody below a million dollars a year paid anything."
rationale: The modern federal income tax enacted after the 1913 16th Amendment taxed incomes starting well below $1,000,000: the Revenue Act of 1913 imposed a 1% tax on net personal incomes above $3,000 ( $4,000 for married couples) with surtaxes applying at much lower thresholds (starting at $20,000). Thus it is false that only people with incomes of a million dollars or more paid anything when the federal income tax was first created.

claim: "In Florida felonies can be things like buying weed, tampering with an odometer or disturbing a lobster trap. So basically spring break."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate and misleading elements. Odometer tampering in Florida is commonly charged as a felony, and certain forms of interfering with protected fishing gear can be criminal, but simple purchase/possession of small amounts of marijuana is typically a misdemeanor in Florida unless amounts or conduct (sale/distribution) elevate it to a felony. The blanket suggestion that those everyday spring-break behaviors are felonies is therefore inaccurate and omits important thresholds and intent requirements.

claim: "In 2011, texting surpassed alcohol as the leading contributing factor in teen driving deaths."
rationale: National crash statistics do not support a clear finding that texting overtook alcohol as the leading contributing factor in teen driving deaths in 2011. Alcohol remained a major documented factor in teen fatal crashes, and ‘‘texting’’ is poorly and inconsistently recorded in crash reports, so claims that texting surpassed alcohol that year are unsupported by reliable federal data.

claim: Says series of 11 photos are "from the 1918 flu pandemic."
rationale: There is no way to confirm that an unlabeled set of 11 photos are from the 1918 influenza pandemic without provenance, metadata, or reliable archival sourcing. Many viral photo collections online are misattributed or combine images from different eras and events (including other epidemics or later periods).

claim: "When Abraham Lincoln made the Gettysburg Address speech, the great speech, do you know he was ridiculed? He was ridiculed."
rationale: Contemporary accounts show that Lincoln's short Gettysburg Address received ridicule and criticism from some newspapers and commentators at the time for its brevity and style. However, reactions were mixed and the speech's reputation improved rapidly in later years.

claim: Claims that Obama said, "For those who oppose our policies, you should just shut up and go away."
rationale: There is no credible record, transcript, or reputable news/fact-check source documenting Barack Obama saying, 'For those who oppose our policies, you should just shut up and go away.' The phrase has circulated on social media as a misattributed quote and is inconsistent with his publicly documented remarks.

claim: Say Portland Public Schools' central administration makes up less than 4 percent of the staff.
rationale: I could not verify that Portland Public Schools' central administration makes up less than 4% because I did not find authoritative, current staffing counts or a clear definition of 'central administration' for PPS. School-district central-office proportions vary and without a cited year or source the claim is unverified; under uncertainty I mark it false.

claim: "Workers have begun removing spires of Cinderella Castle at Magic Kingdom ahead of Hurricane Dorian."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and fact-checkers found no evidence that Disney removed Cinderella Castle spires at Magic Kingdom specifically in advance of Hurricane Dorian; viral photos were misattributed and originated from prior maintenance/refurbishment or other contexts. While Disney does secure parks and may remove loose decorations before storms, the specific claim that workers had begun removing Cinderella Castle spires ahead of Dorian is not supported by reliable sources.

claim: Says the United States is "the Saudi Arabia of coal."
rationale: The United States has large coal reserves and historically was a major producer, but it does not have the kind of dominant, market-controlling share of global coal reserves or exports that Saudi Arabia holds for oil. Coal reserves and production are more widely distributed (notably Russia, Australia, China, Indonesia), and U.S. coal production and export role have declined in recent years, so the comparison is an exaggeration.

claim: "I’m proud to say that under my administration, as you just heard, we will be building the first new heavy icebreakers the United States has seen in over 40 years."
rationale: The United States has not built a new heavy polar-class icebreaker since the 1970s (e.g., USCGC Polar Star and Polar Sea were commissioned in the mid‑ to late‑1970s). Subsequent U.S. icebreaker construction (for example USCGC Healy) produced medium-class cutters, so commissioning new heavy icebreakers after that gap would indeed be the first in over 40 years.

claim: "Registered Republican not allowed to vote."
rationale: As a general statement this is false: being registered with a political party (e.g., Republican) does not prevent a citizen from voting. Voter eligibility is determined by citizenship, age, residency and legal status, and registered Republicans routinely vote in general elections and in primaries (subject to each state's primary rules).

claim: Says Texas GOP platform calls for end to teaching "critical thinking" in public schools.
rationale: The statewide Texas GOP platform has contained language opposing critical race theory and so-called 'divisive' teachings and calling for more 'patriotic' education, but it does not explicitly call for ending the teaching of 'critical thinking' as a general skill in public schools. Claims that the platform bans 'critical thinking' are mischaracterizations or confusions with opposition to specific theories or curricular content.

claim: The Obama administration "spent more money on the Cash for Clunkers program than the space program."
rationale: The Car Allowance Rebate System ('Cash for Clunkers') was funded at about $3 billion in 2009. NASA’s annual budgets during the Obama years were roughly $17–19 billion per year, so cumulative U.S. civilian space spending under that administration far exceeded the CARS outlay. Therefore the claim that Cash for Clunkers spent more than the space program is incorrect.

claim: "I certainly supported Barack Obama and Joe Biden. ... I was there both times for them."
rationale: This is a first‑person claim about personal support and attendance but provides no identifying information, dates, or corroborating evidence. Such claims about an individual’s actions are not verifiable from the text alone, so I must classify it as false under the requirement to prefer false when uncertain.

claim: A photo shows Democratic U.S. Rep. Maxine Waters and House Speaker Nancy Pelosi posing and smiling in front of a Trump 2020 sign.
rationale: The image circulating that shows Rep. Maxine Waters and Speaker Nancy Pelosi smiling in front of a 'Trump 2020' sign has been shown to be digitally manipulated; original event photos and provenance checks do not show them posing with such a sign. Independent fact-checkers analyzed the image and found editing artifacts and inconsistencies in lighting and perspective indicating the sign was added.

claim: "No state generates as much solar power as California, or has as many people whose jobs depend on it."
rationale: California has long been the U.S. leader in installed solar capacity and annual solar electricity generation and also consistently reports the largest number of solar-related jobs of any state. Industry and government data (state generation and solar job censuses) show no other state matches California’s totals.

claim: Says Daniel Radcliffe has the coronavirus.
rationale: Daniel Radcliffe publicly confirmed a positive COVID-19 test in March 2020 and reported mild symptoms and self-isolation, and he later recovered. There is no evidence he currently has the coronavirus, and the claim gives no timeframe.

claim: Says Florida Agriculture Commissioner Nikki Fried "spent millions of dollars to put her face on every gas pump across this state."
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that Nikki Fried personally spent millions to place her face on every gas pump in Florida. Reporting around her office's consumer-outreach and advertising efforts shows some paid advertising and outreach about gas prices, but not a statewide, multimillion-dollar program that put her photo on every pump.

claim: "You had (4,925) out-of-state voters… in Georgia."
rationale: The claim gives a precise figure but provides no election year, data source, or definition of 'out-of-state voters,' so it cannot be verified. Official counts of voters in Georgia are reported by the Secretary of State and vary by election and category (registered elsewhere, absentee, etc.), and there is no universally recognized figure of exactly 4,925 without additional context.

claim: Says a Congressional Budget Office report found low-income seniors in Florida will face "800 percent premium increases" under the American Health Care Act.
rationale: The Congressional Budget Office's official analysis of the American Health Care Act did not report that low-income seniors in Florida would face 800% premium increases. CBO produced national-level estimates showing some older or low-income people could face substantially higher costs, but the specific 800% Florida figure appears to be a misinterpretation or originates from a different state-level or third-party analysis, not the CBO report.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "voted against the bipartisan Violence Against Women Act."
rationale: Marco Rubio was among the senators who voted against the 2013 bipartisan reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act, which the Senate passed with broad bipartisan support. His 'no' vote on that roll call is part of the public Senate voting record.

claim: Says Joe Biden said, "the Germans bombed Pearl Harbor."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Joe Biden ever said the exact line 'the Germans bombed Pearl Harbor.' Viral claims repeat a misattribution or edited clip; while Biden has made verbal slips and historical gaffes, fact-checkers have not found a verifiable instance of him saying that specific statement about Germans bombing Pearl Harbor.

claim: Says that except for foreign policy, Ron Paul’s voting record and his voting record are virtually identical.
rationale: The claim compares Ron Paul’s voting record to Ron Paul’s voting record and asserts a difference limited to foreign policy; any individual’s voting record is identical to itself across all issue areas, so the statement is false and appears to be a mistaken self-comparison. If the intent was to compare Ron Paul to a different person, the claim as written is invalid.

claim: In the United Kingdom, "81% of COVID-19 deaths are among the vaccinated."
rationale: The blanket claim is misleading and cannot be taken as a general fact: percentages of COVID-19 deaths occurring in vaccinated people have varied over time, by age group, variant and by the definition of 'vaccinated' (one dose, two doses, boosted). At times when most elderly were vaccinated, a large share of deaths occurred among vaccinated people simply because vaccination coverage was very high, but age-adjusted death rates and vaccine effectiveness data show vaccines substantially reduce risk of death. Without a specific date range, age breakdown, and vaccination-status definition the assertion '81% of deaths are among the vaccinated' is unsupported.

claim: "Tonight in Ohio, more people came out to vote for Barack Obama in an unopposed race than voted for (Mitt) Romney and (Rick) Santorum combined."
rationale: Contemporaneous Ohio primary vote totals do not support this claim: the contested Republican primary garnered more combined votes than the unopposed Democratic tally for Obama. Contested races typically drive higher turnout than an uncontested incumbent primary, so it is unlikely more people voted for Obama than for Romney and Santorum combined.

claim: "Last week Senator Obama's running mate said, get this, 'Raising taxes is patriotic.' "
rationale: The claim asserts a specific recent quote but there are no widespread or credible reports that Senator Obama's running mate uttered the exact line 'Raising taxes is patriotic' last week. Such a notable, provocative quote would have been widely reported and documented; absence of corroborating sources and the vague timing make the claim unreliable and likely a misquote or fabrication.

claim: U.S. Rep. Connie Mack "voted to raise his own pay several times."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous (doesn't specify Connie Mack III or IV) and I find no clear, documented record that a Representative named Connie Mack voted to raise his own pay "several times." While Congress has occasionally approved pay adjustments, asserting that a specific Rep. Mack repeatedly voted for raises is unsupported without specific roll-call evidence.

claim: The Redskins Training Camp deal "generated $40 million in new private investment in the city."
rationale: There is no clear, independently verified evidence that the Redskins training-camp deal directly produced $40 million in new private investment in any specific city; reported figures have varied and often mix pledged or projected investment with actual private spending. Claims of an exact $40 million impact appear to be unsupported or overstated in publicly available municipal and news accounts.

claim: Anthony Fauci was on the Clinton Foundation board for 20 years and "currently serves on Gates Foundation."
rationale: Both parts are incorrect: Anthony Fauci has not served on the Clinton Foundation board for 20 years and is not a current board member of the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. Public biographies and official board/trustee listings do not show him as a board member of either foundation.

claim: Says "56 percent of (the U.S.-Mexico) border is not under our control."
rationale: The claim is vague and lacks a time frame or definition of what “not under our control” means; there is no authoritative, widely accepted source showing that 56% of the U.S.–Mexico border is outside U.S. control. The United States retains sovereignty and law-enforcement responsibility along the entire border, though degrees of physical barrier or continuous operational control vary and are measured differently by agencies. Without a precise metric or source, the 56% figure cannot be verified and is misleading.

claim: Keystone Pipeline was blocked by Obama on Warren Buffett’s behalf.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Obama blocked the Keystone XL pipeline on Warren Buffett’s behalf. The Obama administration publicly rejected the project in 2015 citing climate impacts and insufficient long-term economic benefits; although Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway owned BNSF (which could benefit from oil-by-rail), reporting and investigations have not produced proof of a quid pro quo or that the decision was made to favor Buffett.

claim: Says New Jersey Rep. Leonard Lance voted repeatedly "to let insurance companies charge more to people aged 50 and over."
rationale: Representative Leonard Lance voted for Republican health-care bills (including the 2017 House AHCA and related repeal/replacement measures) that would have allowed states or insurers to widen age-rating so older enrollees could be charged substantially higher premiums. Those measures explicitly permitted higher age-rating ratios (up to five-to-one in the AHCA debate), which would disproportionately raise costs for people in older age groups such as those 50 and over.

claim: Says that under the law, New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio "can’t open" the city’s schools.
rationale: It is not legally correct in general to say the New York City mayor “can’t open” the city’s schools. The mayor has substantial control over the NYC Department of Education and school operations, but reopening can be constrained by state education authority, public-health emergency orders, and collective-bargaining obligations, so the statement is an overbroad claim rather than an absolute legal prohibition.

claim: Says Joe Biden repeatedly told Americans he's going to raise their taxes.
rationale: Joe Biden has not repeatedly told Americans that he personally will raise their taxes; instead he repeatedly stated during the campaign and as president that he would not raise taxes on households earning under $400,000 and that tax increases would target corporations and high-income earners. Opponents sometimes paraphrase or claim he will raise 'your taxes' broadly, but Biden’s public statements are more limited and targeted.

claim: Says Texas is "last in mental health expenditures."
