rationale: The statement as presented is too absolute and not supported without a specified year or spending metric. Texas has frequently ranked near the bottom of states on per‑capita mental‑health spending in several reports, but rankings vary by year and by whether you measure per‑capita spending, percentage of the behavioral‑health budget, Medicaid mental‑health spending, or total dollars — and Texas is not universally the last state across all these measures.

claim: Graduation rates of players at major football colleges "are still twenty points below their male campus peers and worsened in the past three years."
rationale: The claim presents a blanket statement that is not supported by available national data: differences between football-player graduation rates and their male campus peers vary widely by institution and by which metric is used (NCAA GSR vs federal rate), and aggregate athlete graduation rates have generally been stable or improving rather than uniformly falling over the past few years. While some individual programs may still show large gaps, a uniform “twenty points below” gap that worsened over the last three years is not accurate as a general claim.

claim: "We [the city of Atlanta] are overbuilt on housing."
rationale: This is a subjective, broad claim about Atlanta’s housing supply that can’t be verified without specific data. Atlanta has seen heavy recent construction in some neighborhoods alongside strong demand and affordability pressures in others, so you cannot conclude it is objectively 'overbuilt' without vacancy rates, permitting and absorption data, price/rent trends, and a defined timeframe and geography. Lacking that evidence, the claim is not supported.

claim: Says his administration has made "progress" on border enforcement by "putting more boots on the southern border than at any time in our history and reducing illegal crossings to their lowest levels in 40 years."
rationale: The statement bundles two claims that are not supported by available data. Official CBP staffing and historical records do not clearly show an unprecedented peak of 'more boots on the southern border than at any time in our history,' and encounters/apprehensions in recent years have been among the highest in decades rather than at their lowest levels in 40 years. Therefore the combined assertion is inaccurate.

claim: "Crime has been getting worse since Jerry Brown was elected governor."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad generalization. Empirical crime data during Jerry Brown’s most recent governorship (2011–2019) show mixed trends: some overall crime rates declined in several years and many categories, while certain crimes or localities experienced increases at times. Thus it is inaccurate to state unqualifiedly that "crime has been getting worse" since he was elected.

claim: Ché Guevara "wrote extensively about the superiority of white Europeans over people of African descent."
rationale: Ernesto "Ché" Guevara did not produce a body of work arguing that white Europeans were superior to people of African descent. His major writings are Marxist, anti-imperialist, and focused on guerrilla struggle and socialism; while some of his private diaries and reports (notably from the Congo mission) include derogatory or stereotypical descriptions of African fighters that critics call racist, they do not constitute an extensive ideological advocacy of white supremacy. The claim overstates and mischaracterizes the overall content and aims of his published corpus.

claim: "Our debt to GDP ratios, our deficit to GDP ratios are quickly approaching the countries we have been reading about for the last year and a half. We are not far behind Ireland, Greece, Portugal and Spain and all these countries we have been reading about."
rationale: The claim overstates similarities: while some countries’ deficits and debts rose at various times, Greece’s debt-to-GDP was far higher than typical U.S. levels and Ireland’s GDP figures are distorted by multinational accounting, so direct comparison is misleading. The U.S. has had large deficits at times, but it was not uniformly “not far behind” all of Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain across standard measures and typical recent years.

claim: "Principal bans candy canes."
rationale: The statement provides no context (which principal, which school, when) and cannot be verified as a general claim. While a specific school principal might have banned candy canes, there is no evidence to support the unqualified assertion as stated.

claim: Shirley Sherrod "was forced to resign before anybody on Fox said a word about this."
rationale: This is false. The edited video Andrew Breitbart posted that prompted Shirley Sherrod’s resignation was publicized on July 19, 2010 and was discussed by multiple outlets, including Fox, the same day; Sherrod resigned that day but Fox had already covered the story. Her resignation was later withdrawn after the full video emerged, but the claim that Fox said nothing before she was forced out is inaccurate.

claim: On Sandra Day O'Connor: "I think one reason she was a good judge is she had no judicial experience" before she joined the Supreme Court.
rationale: Sandra Day O'Connor served as a judge on the Arizona Court of Appeals from 1979 until her 1981 appointment to the U.S. Supreme Court, so it is incorrect to say she had no judicial experience before joining the Court. She also held prior legal and legislative roles, but she did have state appellate judicial experience immediately before her Supreme Court nomination.

claim: Regarding the surgery that saved Jimmy Kimmel's son, "Medicaid has stopped providing this kind of service."
rationale: Medicaid has not categorically stopped providing the type of life‑saving pediatric heart surgery Jimmy Kimmel's son received. Federal Medicaid rules (EPSDT) require coverage of medically necessary diagnostic and treatment services for children, and many states cover pediatric cardiac surgery for eligible beneficiaries.

claim: "Drone technology now allows an individual to be recorded in their homes by drones as small as birds and immediately uploaded to the internet."
rationale: Modern micro-drones and insect-scale aerial vehicles exist with integrated cameras and wireless transmitters; many consumer and research models are comparable in size to small birds. Such devices can stream or upload video in real time over Wi-Fi or cellular links, so technologically it is possible for an individual to be recorded inside a home and the footage immediately uploaded. Practical factors like physical entry, battery life, signal availability, and legality vary by situation.

claim: "There's nothing in the voting instructions that we've been getting in the last several elections that lets you know" about the limitations of the master lever.
rationale: The claim is a broad universal statement about 'the voting instructions ... in the last several elections' and is not verifiable as written. Election instructions and voter guides vary by state and locality, and many jurisdictions do include warnings or explanations about straight‑ticket or master lever behavior on their ballots or polling place instructions. Because practices differ widely, it is unlikely that there is universally 'nothing' in all recent instructions informing voters about such limitations.

claim: "Big pharmaceuticals pay off — they literally pay off — generics to keep the prices and the competition off the market."
rationale: There is documented evidence that brand-name drug makers have paid generic manufacturers in so-called 'pay-for-delay' (reverse‑payment) settlements to postpone generic entry, delaying competition and keeping prices higher. These practices have been the subject of FTC investigations, antitrust lawsuits, and a Supreme Court decision, although not every company or settlement involves such payments.

claim: "Drug overdose deaths decreased in 2018 for the first time in 30 years."
rationale: The claim is misleading. U.S. provisional CDC data showed a small drop in drug overdose deaths from 2017 to 2018, but that change was modest and the statement that it was the "first time in 30 years" is incorrect and lacks context. National overdose deaths did not follow a simple 30-year uninterrupted rise that makes 2018 uniquely the first decrease over three decades.

claim: The U.S. "only ranks 25th worldwide on defense spending as a percentage of GDP."
rationale: Recent international data sources (SIPRI, World Bank) show U.S. military spending at roughly 3.5–4% of GDP, which typically places the United States well above 25th worldwide—more often in the top 10–15 by percent of GDP. Although several small or oil-rich states have higher ratios, there are not enough such countries to push the U.S. as low as 25th in standard datasets.

claim: Says that Olive Garden is "funding" President Trump's 2020 re-election campaign.
rationale: There is no evidence that the Olive Garden restaurant brand directly funded Donald Trump’s 2020 re-election. U.S. federal law prohibits corporations from making direct contributions to federal candidates; reported donations come from individuals, Political Action Committees, or company-affiliated PACs rather than a corporate brand itself.

claim: Says Kelly Loeffler supports "raising taxes on Georgia's middle class."
rationale: Kelly Loeffler, a Republican who campaigned as a fiscal conservative, has publicly supported tax cuts (including backing the 2017 tax law) and opposed tax increases; there is no clear evidence she explicitly advocated raising taxes on Georgia’s middle class. Opponent ads may have distorted votes or policy nuances, but the straightforward claim is not supported by her public record.

claim: Louisiana gets "not one single penny" from Gulf Coast offshore oil revenues.
rationale: Louisiana does receive money from Gulf offshore oil revenues: the state collects mineral royalties and severance taxes on production in state waters and from state leases, and it also receives a share of federal Outer Continental Shelf receipts under revenue‑sharing laws such as the Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act (GOMESA). Parishes on the coast also receive direct payments. Therefore the statement that Louisiana gets “not one single penny” is incorrect.

claim: Says William Taylor and George Kent, the public witnesses in the House impeachment inquiry, are "Never Trumpers."
rationale: Labeling William B. Taylor and George P. Kent as 'Never Trumpers' is inaccurate: both are career State Department officials and diplomats who testified in their professional capacities, not known leaders of the 'Never Trumper' movement. There is no clear evidence they publicly identified as members of an anti‑Trump activist faction; their records show long service across administrations rather than partisan activism.

claim: "I'm the only candidate in the Democratic primary, or actually on either side, who Wall Street financiers and hedge fund managers are actually running ads against."
rationale: This is incorrect — multiple candidates in recent Democratic primaries (and candidates on the GOP side) have been targeted by ads funded by Wall Street financiers and hedge-fund–linked donors. For example, independent expenditures and ad buys from financial-industry interests have run ads against Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren, among others, so the speaker is not uniquely targeted.

claim: Says when New Jersey adopted guaranteed coverage and cost provisions without a mandate individual health insurance market rates "doubled or tripled" and enrollment dropped from 180,000 people to 80,000 people.
rationale: The specific assertion that New Jersey’s move to guaranteed-coverage and cost rules (without a mandate) caused individual market premiums to "double or triple" and enrollment to fall exactly from 180,000 to 80,000 is not supported by a clear, uncontested body of evidence. Analyses of New Jersey’s 1990s reforms are mixed and attribute premium and enrollment changes to multiple factors (policy design, risk pools, market exits, and broader market trends), and no authoritative study documents those precise numbers as a direct causal effect. Therefore the precise numeric claim is not reliably established.

claim: "A majority of the men and women on this stage have previously and publicly embraced amnesty. I am the only candidate on this stage who has never supported amnesty."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it fails to identify which debate/stage and which individuals are meant; without that context it cannot be confirmed that a majority publicly embraced 'amnesty' or that the speaker alone never did. Public records show multiple candidates across recent debates have at various times supported policies described as amnesty (e.g., pathways to citizenship, DACA-related relief), so the absolute exclusivity asserted is unlikely. Because the statement is both specific and dependent on definitional and temporal details that are missing, it should be treated as false.

claim: Says Florida Gov. Rick Scott "just signed a bill that could make most of Florida’s beaches private."
rationale: This claim is misleading. While Governor Rick Scott signed legislation that expanded beachfront property owners’ rights and could make it harder for the public to use some dry-sand areas, he did not sign a law that converted most of Florida’s beaches into private property; the public trust doctrine and existing protections for wet-sand (seaward of the mean high water line) remain in place and legal outcomes are contested in courts.

claim: "We had 2 percent of the global market (for advanced batteries) when he (Obama) started. We now have 16 percent, headed to 40 percent by 2015."
rationale: The claim mixes different metrics and relies on planned capacity and announcements rather than verified market-share data. Independent fact-checkers and industry reports found the 2% baseline, the 16% current figure, and the 40% by 2015 projection to be misleading or unsupported by realized production or sales figures.

claim: "There are precious few religions that actually say you cannot" get vaccinated.
rationale: Most major world religions do not proscribe vaccination and many religious authorities explicitly endorse or permit vaccines. Only a small number of sects or specific religious movements (for example some Christian Science adherents or a few fringe groups) have doctrines or practices that discourage medical intervention, so explicit religious bans on vaccination are rare.

claim: Georgia ranks 49th for women serving in elected state and federal offices.
rationale: The claim gives no year or data source and is inconsistent with publicly available state-by-state trackers; rankings for women’s representation vary by year and by whether they count state legislatures, congressional delegations, or all elected offices. Reputable datasets (e.g., CAWP, NWLC) do not consistently list Georgia as 49th for combined state and federal elected women, so the assertion is unsupported as stated.

claim: "(GM and Chrysler) repaid their loans."
rationale: Both General Motors and Chrysler received large government rescue loans during the 2008–2010 auto bailout, but the U.S. government did not recover the full amounts advanced. While the companies repaid or restructured some obligations and the Treasury sold equity over time, overall recoveries were partial and resulted in net losses to taxpayers.

claim: If public employees don’t pay more for benefits starting April 1, 2011, "the equivalent" is 1,500 state employee layoffs by June 30, 2011 and 10,000 to 12,000 state and local government employee layoffs in the next two years.
rationale: I cannot verify the specific layoff numbers as a factual consequence tied to that exact date because the claim appears to be a partisan projection that depends on budget assumptions and methodology. Such specific figures (1,500 by June 30, 2011 and 10,000–12,000 over two years) were commonly asserted in political debates but were disputed and not independently confirmed as inevitable outcomes.

claim: Says Pete Gallego "went and lobbied after you fired him from Congress."
rationale: The claim asserts Pete Gallego 'went and lobbied after you fired him from Congress,' but Gallego was defeated in the 2014 election (not literally fired) and there is no clear, widely reported evidence that he immediately became a lobbyist for the person addressed. The statement conflates electoral defeat with being fired and alleges lobbying activity without specific, corroborated facts.

claim: "I unsealed my records" at Marquette University.
rationale: The claim is unverified because it provides no identifiable speaker, date, or documentary evidence and therefore cannot be confirmed. University records are protected by privacy rules and 'unsealing' typically requires legal or administrative action that would produce verifiable documentation; none is presented.

claim: "Under Republicans, recessions happen four times as frequently as under Democrats."
rationale: There is no robust empirical support for the categorical claim that recessions occur four times as often under Republican presidents. While some analyses find a higher rate of recessions beginning during Republican administrations in certain periods, the total number of recessions is small, results vary by time frame and definitions, and many recessions span or are driven by factors outside presidential party control.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Michael McCaul is "the sixth-richest person in Congress."
rationale: The statement lacks a date or source and congressional wealth rankings change year to year; Michael McCaul is a wealthy member of Congress but is not consistently identified as the "sixth-richest" across authoritative lists. Without a clear timeframe and citation, the specific ranking cannot be verified and is likely misleading.

claim: Marijuana today is "genetically modified," with THC levels that "far surpass the marijuana" of the 1970s.
rationale: It is true that average THC concentrations in seized and commercially sold cannabis have risen substantially since the 1970s, but calling modern marijuana broadly "genetically modified" is misleading. Most high‑THC varieties are the result of selective breeding and hybridization by growers, not widespread transgenic genetic engineering; lab GM cannabis exists but is not the norm.

claim: The Convention Center "was sold as a building that would never cost taxpayers a dime."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify which convention center, who made the claim, or provide supporting evidence. Promises that public projects “would never cost taxpayers a dime” are commonly made in promotional materials but frequently prove inaccurate in practice; without specific documentation (press releases, contracts, or contemporaneous reporting) the blanket quoted claim cannot be confirmed. Because the assertion is vague and absolute, the safest conclusion is that it cannot be treated as factual as stated.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "We need to repeal Daylight Savings Time as a primary measure to decrease the rate of climate change. Less hours of sun shine equal less heat hitting Earth’s surface."
rationale: There is no credible record of Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez saying that quote, and it appears to be a fabricated or misattributed statement. The content also misunderstands how daylight saving time works: changing clocks does not alter the amount of sunlight the Earth receives and thus cannot meaningfully reduce solar heating as claimed.

claim: Under the Arizona immigration law, police are required to check immigration status if someone's "lawn is overgrown" or if a dog is "barking too loudly."
rationale: Arizona's SB 1070 requires officers to attempt to determine immigration status during a lawful stop, detention, or arrest when they have reasonable suspicion the person is unlawfully present, but it does not specifically require checks for trivial local violations like an overgrown lawn or a barking dog. Whether a stop for such minor ordinance violations leads to an immigration check depends on whether the stop occurs and whether officers have reasonable suspicion, not on a statutory mandate naming those examples.

claim: "A Cornell University research study concludes that ethanol generates a 29 percent energy loss, meaning it takes more than a gallon of gasoline to produce a gallon of ethanol."
rationale: A widely cited Cornell-affiliated study by David Pimentel (co-authored with Tad Patzek) concluded that producing ethanol from corn results in about a 29% net energy loss — i.e., more fossil-fuel energy is used in production than is contained in the ethanol produced. The statement paraphrases that conclusion, though it simplifies energy inputs to a ‘‘gallon of gasoline’’ equivalence rather than reporting the study’s energy-accounting basis.

claim: "In two terms in the Missouri General Assembly, Jason Kander passed ZERO bills that were signed into law."
rationale: Official Missouri legislative records and contemporary fact-checking show Jason Kander had at least some bills he sponsored or co-sponsored signed into law during his two terms in the Missouri House, so the claim that he passed zero bills is incorrect. The exact count depends on whether one counts only sole-authored bills or also co-sponsorships/floor sponsorships, but he was not at zero.

claim: Says Barbara Buono "voted to raise her own pay 40 percent."
rationale: The claim is misleading: Barbara Buono did not simply 'vote to raise her own pay 40 percent.' That figure conflates different compensation changes and back-pay calculations and mischaracterizes her voting record on complex pay-related measures.

claim: Al Sharpton went to Ferguson, Mo., and is "declaring as a matter of fact that ... Michael Brown didn't use any deadly force or posed no deadly threat to the officer."
rationale: Al Sharpton traveled to Ferguson and repeatedly spoke at rallies and events there, publicly asserting that Michael Brown was unarmed and did not pose a deadly threat to Officer Wilson. News coverage from the time quotes Sharpton endorsing the 'hands up, don't shoot' narrative and criticizing the shooting as unjustified, which amounts to declaring Brown did not use deadly force or pose a deadly threat.

claim: Says the U.S. gives Israel "$3 billion annually" in aid and zero to Detroit.
rationale: The U.S. does provide roughly $3 billion per year in military assistance to Israel (commonly cited as about $3–3.3 billion annually under the 2016 MOU, plus additional missile-defense funding). However, it is false that the U.S. gives "zero" to Detroit: the federal government provides cities like Detroit with various federal funds and grants (HUD, FEMA, DOT, pandemic relief, community development block grants, etc.).

claim: "The average age of first marijuana use is 12."
rationale: Large, representative surveys and research report that the typical age of first marijuana use is in the mid-to-late teenage years (roughly 16–18), not 12. Age 12 may describe isolated early experimenters in some samples, but it is far below the population average reported in national studies.

claim: "Within the three miles surrounding the University Circle area, infant mortality exceeds some Third World countries."
rationale: Local public-health data and multiple news reports have documented very high infant mortality rates in neighborhoods within a roughly three-mile radius of Cleveland's University Circle, and those neighborhood-level rates have at times been higher than the infant mortality rates reported for some low-income (so-called "Third World") countries. The claim is supported when specific neighborhoods and time periods are compared to particular low-income countries' infant mortality statistics.

claim: "We understand that this heroin is primarily coming from Mexico, over the border."
rationale: U.S. law enforcement and drug control assessments in recent years indicate that the majority of heroin consumed in the United States is produced in Mexico and transported across the southern border by Mexican trafficking organizations. There are regional and temporal variations (and rising involvement of synthetic opioids like fentanyl), but the broad claim about heroin primarily coming from Mexico is supported by government reports.

claim: "Walmart rewards everyone with $75 coupon to celebrate its 125th Anniversary"
rationale: Walmart was founded in the 1960s (first store in 1962) and is not 125 years old, so no legitimate 125th-anniversary universal $75 coupon would be announced. Additionally, widely circulated claims that 'everyone gets a $75 coupon' are consistent with common online scams and there is no credible company announcement backing this.

claim: "The pace of missile development between (Kim Jong Il and Kim Jong Un) has increased the testing about twenty-fold."
rationale: It is true that missile testing accelerated under Kim Jong Un compared with Kim Jong Il, but the specific claim of an 'about twenty-fold' increase is not a well-documented, consistently supported figure. Published counts depend heavily on the chosen time windows, which types of launches are counted (ballistic, cruise, satellite, short-range), and how tests under Kim Jong Il are tallied; available public tallies show a substantial increase but not a reliably measured 20x multiplier.

claim: Says most of Austin’s biggest parks have recycling though as "many as 293 out of 300" Austin city "parks have no recycling, including almost every neighborhood park."
rationale: The claim mixes contradictory assertions and gives a very specific figure ("293 out of 300") for which there is no authoritative public evidence. While some of Austin’s large parks do offer recycling and many smaller neighborhood parks may lack bins, I am not aware of reliable city data or reporting that confirms nearly all (293/300) parks have no recycling; the precise number appears unsupported and misleading.

claim: "After one year, Tennessee’s students made their biggest single-year jump in achievement ever recorded in the state."
rationale: The statement is vague and unsupported as written: it does not specify the year, grades, or which assessment was used. Because Tennessee has changed tests and standards over time, single-year gains are not directly comparable across different assessments, and I find no specific, authoritative claim that any one year was definitively the largest "ever recorded" statewide without additional context.

claim: Says Rick Scott cut education by over a billion dollars, meaning thousands of teachers "lost their jobs" and "class sizes went up."
rationale: The claim mixes a partial truth with an unsupported causal leap. While Rick Scott’s early budgets included reductions in certain K–12 line items compared with the prior year, statewide education funding increased in later budgets and overall spending trends during his tenure do not support a simple, sustained "over a billion" permanent cut that directly caused thousands of statewide teacher layoffs and uniformly larger class sizes. Direct attribution of thousands of lost teacher jobs and systemwide class-size increases to Scott’s actions is not supported by consensus budget and employment data and ignores other factors (recession, local district decisions, and later state funding increases).

claim: "Both Cruz and Rubio are missing the vast majority of their votes."
rationale: The claim implies Cruz and Rubio each missed most of their votes; that is not supported by congressional voting records. Both senators have missed some roll-call votes at times, but neither has missed a ‘‘vast majority’’ of votes during their Senate tenures.

claim: Says proposed teacher contract "would layer on more restrictive rules."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify: it asserts that a proposed teacher contract "would layer on more restrictive rules" but gives no jurisdiction, contract text, or specific provisions. Without the actual contract language or an authoritative summary showing additional restrictions, the claim cannot be confirmed as true. Given the missing context, I cannot treat this as a factual assertion.

claim: "If we had been on 'Obamacare' and a bureaucrat was trying to tell me when I could get that CAT scan, that would have delayed my treatment."
rationale: The claim presents a speculative counterfactual that "Obamacare" would have caused a bureaucrat to delay a CAT scan and thus delayed treatment. The Affordable Care Act is a set of federal rules governing insurance markets and expansions of coverage, not a single centralized scheduler; prior-authorization delays can occur under many types of insurers (private, Medicare, Medicaid) but are not uniquely imposed by the ACA itself. There is no specific evidence that enrollment in ACA marketplace plans would have automatically produced the described bureaucratic delay in this individual case.

claim: "For every $1 spent on mitigation, $4 in post-storm cleanup and rebuilding is saved."
rationale: This statement is an oversimplification. Some government and academic reports have cited roughly $4 saved per $1 of mitigation in specific analyses, but estimates vary widely by hazard type, location, mitigation measure, and time horizon; more recent and comprehensive studies often report different averages (sometimes higher). A blanket claim that every $1 spent on mitigation saves $4 in post-storm cleanup and rebuilding is not universally supported.

claim: "We work longer hours than any people in the industrialized world, including the Japanese."
rationale: This statement is incorrect: the United States (presumably the 'we' here) does not work the longest hours of any industrialized country. OECD and international labor statistics show several countries (for example Mexico, South Korea, Turkey and others) with higher average annual hours than the U.S.; Japan’s average hours have also fallen and are not the global maximum. Therefore the blanket claim that "we work longer hours than any people in the industrialized world, including the Japanese" is false.

claim: "I've always known this is a real, this is a pandemic. I've felt it was a pandemic long before it was called a pandemic."
rationale: This is a report of the speaker’s internal belief and timing ("always known" and "long before it was called a pandemic"), which cannot be independently verified without contemporaneous records or public statements. Without documented evidence that the speaker expressed pandemic-level concern before official declarations, the claim is unsupported and thus treated as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: Says the California congressional district he represents "has a higher GDP than Russia."
rationale: Russia’s economy is measured in the trillions of dollars, while even the most economically productive U.S. congressional districts (including wealthy California tech districts) generate output measured in the low hundreds of billions. Therefore it is extremely unlikely a single California congressional district has a larger GDP than Russia.

claim: An episode of "The Simpsons" showed Donald Trump in a coffin.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that any official episode of The Simpsons showed Donald Trump in a coffin. While the show has referenced or depicted Trump (notably the 2000 episode "Bart to the Future" which mentions a Trump presidency) and many fan-made or edited images circulate online, no canonical episode contains a scene of Trump in a coffin.

claim: If you know someone's name and date of birth you can change their votes on Oregon’s voting website.
rationale: Oregon uses a vote-by-mail system and its online voter services do not allow someone to change another person's cast ballot simply by knowing their name and date of birth. Altering a vote would require intercepting or spoiling the physical ballot or successfully impersonating the voter through signature/ID checks and additional identity information required for online registration or replacement ballots.

claim: Says he "earned the highest possible credit ratings as state treasurer."
rationale: The statement is too vague and unverifiable as presented because it does not identify who “he” is, which state, which agencies issued the ratings, or the time period. Credit ratings for states are assigned by independent agencies (e.g., S&P, Moody’s, Fitch) and attributing them solely to a state treasurer requires specific evidence. Without those specifics or documentary proof that the named person’s actions directly produced the highest possible ratings, the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false.

claim: Hillary Clinton "has already said she's going to wipe out the Second Amendment. She doesn't believe in the First Amendment. And, she also believes in big government, which flies in the face of the 10th Amendment"
rationale: The statement conflates rhetoric and opinion with explicit admissions. Hillary Clinton has campaigned for gun-control measures and stricter laws but has not said she will ‘wipe out’ the Second Amendment; she has not publicly denied belief in the First Amendment; and describing her as favoring “big government” that violates the Tenth Amendment is a subjective political characterization rather than a factual claim about her stating opposition to the Tenth Amendment.

claim: "Hair stylists are required to undergo more government scrutiny than foreclosure consultants."
rationale: This is a sweeping, jurisdiction‑wide claim that cannot be supported. Regulatory regimes differ: cosmetologists/hair stylists typically face state licensing, training‑hour and sanitation requirements, while foreclosure consultants are often governed by separate consumer‑protection, registration, bonding and anti‑fraud rules in many states. Which occupation faces "more" scrutiny depends on the specific state and the metrics used.

claim: "A lot of people are talking about" the removal of a "very fair prosecutor" in Ukraine.
rationale: While it is true that the removal of Ukraine’s former prosecutor Viktor Shokin was widely discussed and that international actors (EU, IMF, some US officials) urged his ouster, characterizing him as a "very fair prosecutor" is contradicted by contemporaneous reporting and statements that described him as ineffective and accused of tolerating corruption. The combined claim (many people talking + he was "very fair") is therefore misleading.

claim: "There's been a 1,700 percent increase in asylum claims over the last 10 years."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as stated because it omits any country, region, baseline, or data source; internationally reported asylum statistics (UNHCR, Eurostat, national agencies) do not show a uniform 1,700% rise globally over the past decade. While very large percentage increases can occur for specific countries starting from a very small base, presenting a blanket 1,700% increase without context is misleading and unlikely.

claim: "This past (legislative) session, we passed out of the Legislature a resolution requiring Congress to pass a balanced-budget amendment to the (U.S.) Constitution."
rationale: A state legislature can pass a resolution urging or formally applying to Congress for a balanced-budget amendment, but it cannot legally require or compel Congress to pass a constitutional amendment. Under Article V, amendments must be proposed by two-thirds of both Houses of Congress or by a convention called for by two-thirds of state legislatures, so a single state resolution is not binding on Congress.

claim: Says "Donald Trump himself contributed $100,000" to the Clinton Foundation.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Donald J. Trump personally gave $100,000 to the Clinton Foundation. Public donor records and contemporary fact-checking reported no trace of a $100,000 personal donation by Trump; at most some donations to charities associated with Trump or donations routed through foundations have been misreported or conflated in political claims.

claim: "The only segment in the beer market that is growing is the craft beer segment."
rationale: This is false: while craft beer has grown in many markets historically, other segments such as hard seltzers/RTDs, certain premium mainstream brands, and non‑alcoholic beers have also experienced growth. Additionally, craft beer growth has flattened or declined in some regions, so it is incorrect to claim it is the only growing segment.

claim: "Seismic airgun blasting (used for energy exploration) is ... 16,000 times louder than" a conventional airhorn.
rationale: The statement presents a precise multiplicative factor without specifying measurement units, distance, medium, or whether it means sound pressure or intensity. Seismic airguns are extremely loud underwater (often quoted in hundreds of dB re 1 μPa at 1 m) and airhorns are loud in air (tens to low hundreds of dB re 20 μPa), but those scales and references differ and cannot be directly converted into a simple "times louder" number. No authoritative source supports the specific claim of "16,000 times louder" as a general fact; comparisons depend on medium, frequency, measurement reference, and distance.

claim: "Amazing fact: Senate has already voted on more amendments in 2015 than Reid allowed ALL YEAR last year."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and ambiguous: it does not define what counts as an 'amendment' or what 'allowed' means, and I find no reliable evidence that early 2015 amendment votes exceeded the entirety of 2014 under Senator Reid. Counts of amendment votes vary by definition (roll-call amendments, procedural votes, cloture on amendments), so the raw statement is misleading and likely false without clearer measures.

claim: Says Ted Cruz "said I was in favor in Libya. I never discussed that subject."
rationale: The quoted line is ambiguous and self-contradictory, and there is no clear, verifiable record that Ted Cruz ever uttered that exact phrase. Without a credible source, the statement appears to be a misquote or lacks context needed to confirm it. Because I cannot verify the quote as presented, I judge the claim false as stated.

claim: Says Ron Johnson justifies his support of trade agreements by saying the U.S. has the Trade Adjustment Assistance program for displaced workers, but then he "voted to eliminate it."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Senator Ron Johnson both cited the Trade Adjustment Assistance (TAA) program to justify support for trade agreements and then cast a vote that outright eliminated the TAA program. TAA has been periodically reauthorized and its funding adjusted, but congressional records do not show a vote that fully abolished the program tied directly to Johnson’s stated justification. At most, he has supported reforms or budget measures that reduced funding or altered program scope, not an explicit elimination vote.

claim: "We’ve got close to 7 million Americans who have access to health care for the first time because of Medicaid expansion."
rationale: Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act did extend coverage to millions of low‑income adults, but the commonly reported counts of expansion enrollees exceed 7 million (more often in the roughly 10–12 million range in later years). Without a clear time frame the claim understates the typical estimates of people gaining coverage through expansion.

claim: "We will have more people enter our country illegally than were born in this country in one year."
rationale: The claim is unspecified (no country or year) and implausible for typical countries: annual births generally number in the thousands to millions, while documented estimates of unauthorized entries are usually much lower. Without a specific country and clear definitions, the statement cannot be supported and is unlikely to be true in most cases.

claim: "A grant for $5,000 [from the Governor’s Workforce Board] went to teach an employee at a company that makes ornamental business card holders how to use Facebook and Twitter."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim as stated: there is no corroborating public record identifying a $5,000 Governor’s Workforce Board grant awarded solely to teach one employee at a company that makes ornamental business card holders how to use Facebook and Twitter. Governor’s workforce boards typically fund documented, broader training programs and the claim lacks basic identifying details, so it likely misstates or oversimplifies the grant purpose.

claim: "About 95 percent of America’s production of ethylene is produced on the Gulf Coast in Texas and Louisiana."
rationale: While a large majority of U.S. ethylene capacity is concentrated on the Gulf Coast (particularly Texas and Louisiana), credible industry data indicate the combined share is well below 95% of total U.S. ethylene production. The ~95% figure more accurately describes the share of new cracker capacity additions or projects in recent years rather than total historical production.

claim: Georgia’s unemployment rate has exceeded the national rate for 50 consecutive months.
rationale: I am not aware of reliable reports or Labor Department data showing Georgia’s unemployment rate exceeded the U.S. rate for a continuous 50-month span. State and national unemployment rates typically fluctuate month-to-month and long uninterrupted streaks of one state remaining above the national rate would be notable and widely reported. Without a specific timeframe and current BLS/state labor confirmation, the precise 50-month claim is not supported.

claim: "There have been zero reported instances of any child born alive after an abortion in Texas."
rationale: The absolute claim that there have been zero reported instances is unlikely to be true: medical literature and reporting show that infants born alive after attempted abortions are rare but documented occurrences in the United States, and Texas is not known to be uniquely exempt. Because definitions, reporting practices, and time frames vary, asserting a blanket zero is not supported.

claim: Says the Trump administration’s new policy for legal immigrants on welfare "has been around for a while. This is not a new thing that the president is trying to implement here, that the United States has been this way."
rationale: While the public‑charge ground for denying admission or green cards is a long‑standing part of U.S. immigration law, the Trump administration issued a 2019 rule that substantially broadened the definition to count many non‑cash benefits (like SNAP, Medicaid and housing subsidies) and tightened discretionary denials. That expansion represented a meaningful policy change rather than merely continuing prior practice unchanged.

claim: "With 320,000 net Ohio manufacturing jobs lost, (Sen. Rob) Portman calls NAFTA a ‘proven success’."
rationale: The claim bundles a specific numeric job-loss figure with a quoted characterization by Sen. Rob Portman that is not reliably supported together. Ohio manufacturing job counts vary by time period and data source, and the precise '320,000 net' loss is not a universally agreed figure; Portman has publicly defended NAFTA as beneficial but attributing the exact phrase 'proven success' in this context appears to be a paraphrase rather than a verifiable, documented quote tied to that specific statistic.

claim: "In Italy, they have thrown their money on the streets. A clear message to the whole world that money is not enough when health is in danger."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or widespread reporting that Italians collectively 'threw their money on the streets' as a public action; the claim appears to be a metaphor or viral misinformation. Reliable coverage of Italy’s public responses (e.g., balcony singing and applause during COVID-19) documents solidarity and protests but not mass disposal of currency.

claim: The census "for years and years and years, decades, has asked, ‘Are you a citizen of the United States of America?’"
rationale: The statement is misleading: the 100% decennial 'short-form' census has not consistently asked 'Are you a citizen...' for decades. Citizenship was collected on sample instruments (the long form historically and, since 2005, the American Community Survey), and the question's inclusion on the short-form decennial census has been intermittent and contested.

claim: "When I was speaker, we had four consecutive balanced budgets."
rationale: The claim lacks a named speaker, jurisdiction, and time period, so it cannot be verified as stated. Whether four consecutive balanced budgets occurred depends on which legislative speaker, which government (national, state/provincial), and the accounting definitions used. Without those specifics the statement is unverifiable and therefore treated as false.

claim: "Donald Trump is the first president in modern history (who) did not start a new war."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because several recent U.S. presidents did not initiate a new declared large-scale war. For example, Gerald Ford (1974–77) and Jimmy Carter (1977–81) did not start new major wars, and other presidents avoided opening wholly new theaters even if they ordered limited strikes or interventions. While Trump ordered strikes and raids, he did not launch a new full-scale conventional war, but he is not uniquely the first modern president to avoid starting a new war.

claim: "Remember that developers are forced to use the ‘195 land union’ contractors, so tap an extra $10 million into any construction project."
rationale: The claim presents a blanket assertion that developers are compelled to use a specific "195 land union" and therefore should add $10 million to projects; there is no general or widely known rule forcing developers to hire a named contractor or union universally. Procurement and labor rules vary by jurisdiction and project, so a universal requirement and fixed extra cost are unsupported. Without specific legal or contract evidence, the instruction to add $10 million is not factual.

claim: Says "we are overcharging students . . . to help pay for the health care law."
rationale: The statement as presented is vague and lacks verifiable context (who said it, when, and where). There is no general, documented policy that students are being systematically "overcharged" specifically to pay for the health care law; fee or insurance cost changes vary by institution and jurisdiction and cannot be generalized from this quote alone.

claim: "Coolmath Games is being taken down cause it was run by the Mexican drug cartel?"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Coolmath Games has been taken down due to being run by a Mexican drug cartel. The site is a commercial educational games service run by a legitimate company, and claims linking it to cartels appear to be internet rumors or misinformation.

claim: The United States has experienced "40 straight months of unemployment at 8 percent or higher."
rationale: This is incorrect. While the U.S. unemployment rate was above 8% during the Great Recession and peaked near 10% in 2009, it did not remain at or above 8% for 40 consecutive months according to monthly BLS U-3 data; the continuous period above 8% was substantially shorter.

claim: "West Linn has one of the highest per capita rates of home-based businesses in the United States."
rationale: There are no widely cited national data or reputable rankings that place West Linn among the U.S. cities with the highest per-capita rates of home-based businesses. The claim is unsupported in major data sources (e.g., Census business/entrepreneurship surveys) and provides no time frame or definition for verification.

claim: "Gov. Scott Walker (is) more than halfway to (his) 250,000 jobs goal."
rationale: The claim lacks a date and a clear definition of which jobs are counted (private‑sector vs. total), and available public reports from the Walker administration and independent data sources at common checkpoints did not unambiguously show he had achieved more than half (over 125,000) of the pledged 250,000 jobs. Because the statement is time‑dependent and not supported without specifying the period and job-definition, it cannot be confirmed as true.

claim: "Our jobless rate, our unemployment rate, is the lowest of all of the big cities in New Jersey."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific, time‑bound comparative fact but provides no city name, date, or data source. Without a defined city, a time period, and agreed list of “big cities,” the claim cannot be verified and therefore should be treated as false as stated. Such rankings fluctuate and require current labor statistics to support them.

claim: Says Jimmy Carter was the last "U.S. president to say flat out those (Israeli) settlements are illegal."
rationale: This is false. Jimmy Carter was not the last U.S. president to explicitly condemn Israeli settlements; later administrations, particularly under Barack Obama, publicly characterized settlement activity as illegitimate and inconsistent with international law and the U.S. allowed UN Security Council Resolution 2334 (2016) declaring settlements have no legal validity. The Trump administration later reversed aspects of that position, showing the label and policy have shifted over time.

claim: "After Texas defunded Planned Parenthood, both the unintended pregnancy and abortion rates dropped."
rationale: Empirical analyses of Texas’ decisions to exclude Planned Parenthood from state family-planning funds (2011–2013) found declines in publicly funded contraceptive services and increases in births for some populations, not a clear drop in unintended pregnancies. Abortion counts in Texas fell in some years but that change is partly attributable to clinic closures and broader national trends; the body of evidence does not support a causal finding that both unintended pregnancy and abortion rates dropped after the defunding.

claim: Twenty million Americans are "out of work."
rationale: The statement has no date or definition and is therefore misleading. Counts of Americans "out of work" vary over time and by definition (unemployed, not in labor force, or on temporary furlough); while roughly 20 million people were recorded as unemployed or not working in certain months of the COVID-19 downturn, the claim as presented without context cannot be treated as a factual, enduring statement.

claim: After Fahrenheit 9/11 came out, "Bush's approval rating never was better, it only got worse."
rationale: Fahrenheit 9/11 was released in June 2004 when Bush’s approval was roughly in the low-50s, but his approval ratings fluctuated afterward — he saw a modest post-election uptick around November 2004 and then later declines after events such as Hurricane Katrina and the Iraq war. Therefore it is incorrect to say his approval "never was better" after the film; ratings rose and fell over the subsequent years.

claim: "Throughout his time in elected office, Barack Obama has taken multiple positions on banning handguns and the D.C. handgun ban."
rationale: Over his public career Obama made differing public statements about handgun bans: in the late 1990s he expressed support for the D.C. handgun ban and for stricter restrictions on handguns, while later as a Senate candidate and as president he said he did not support an outright ban on handguns for law‑abiding citizens and emphasized other gun-control measures. Those shifts and nuances amount to multiple positions over time.

claim: If sea levels rise six feet due to climate change, Waterplace Park in Providence and Wickford village would be swamped
rationale: A 6-foot (≈1.8 m) sea-level rise would inundate low-lying waterfront areas in Rhode Island. Waterplace Park is at river/harbor elevation in downtown Providence and would be overtopped, and much of historic Wickford village sits at very low elevation along Narragansett Bay and would experience significant flooding.

claim: "We are now, for the first time ever, energy independent."
rationale: The claim as an absolute statement is false because it lacks context (who and by what metric) and is historically inaccurate. For example, the United States became a net energy exporter in recent years (around 2019) by some measures, but that is not the same as being entirely energy independent nor is it 'for the first time ever' in all forms of energy over history. Energy independence is a nuanced concept involving imports, exports, and different fuel types.

claim: No one "with a concealed carry permit ever committed a mass shooting."
rationale: The claim is false. There are documented instances reported in news and court records where individuals who held valid concealed-carry permits (or had recently held them) committed shootings that meet common definitions of a mass shooting. Whether a particular incident qualifies can depend on the definition used and the permit status at the time, but the absolute statement is contradicted by multiple reported cases.

claim: It "is estimated that as many as 300,000 auto workers may be out of a job before the end of the year."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it provides no source, timeframe, or jurisdiction. I am not aware of any authoritative, widely reported estimate that precisely 300,000 auto workers will be out of a job by year-end; media and industry accounts describe site- or company-specific layoffs and widely varying totals. Without a cited source or clear context, the statement cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says county parties representing more than half the state’s Republican voters approved resolutions "demanding changes" in Texas House leadership.
rationale: I cannot verify that county GOP organizations representing a majority of the state’s Republican voters formally approved resolutions demanding changes in Texas House leadership. Reporting on county resolutions has existed, but claims that the counties involved cumulatively represent over half of Texas Republican voters appear to be an extrapolation without clear, publicly verifiable tabulation of counties, their resolutions, and the precise voter totals used to weight them.

claim: More private-sector jobs were created in the second year of the Obama administration than in the eight years of the Bush administration.
rationale: Bureau of Labor Statistics payroll data and independent fact-checks show that the cumulative number of private-sector jobs added over George W. Bush’s full eight years exceeded the net private-sector job gains in President Obama’s second year. Therefore the claim that Obama’s second year created more private-sector jobs than Bush’s entire eight-year term is incorrect.

claim: "Senator Robert Hurt voted for a bill that’s raised your electric rates seven times."
rationale: There is no evidence that a specific bill voted on by Senator Robert Hurt directly caused seven discrete increases in a consumer's electric rates. Electricity prices change for many reasons (fuel costs, utility rate cases, regulations and market factors), and the claim provides no identifiable bill, timeframe, or jurisdiction linking Hurt's vote to seven separate rate hikes. As stated, the causal and numerical assertion is unsupported.

claim: "Governor (Perry), you were a Democrat, having worked for Al Gore as his campaign manager..."
rationale: The statement is incorrect: while Texas Governor Rick Perry began his career as a Democrat and switched to the Republican Party in 1989, there is no evidence he ever served as Al Gore’s campaign manager. Al Gore’s presidential campaigns were run by other staff and national campaign teams, and Perry’s political career was focused in Texas state offices.

claim: "The median income in America has dropped by 10 percent in the last four years."
rationale: Official U.S. income series do not show a uniform 10% decline in median income over the past four years; reported changes have been much smaller and vary by whether measures are nominal or inflation‑adjusted and whether they refer to households or individuals. Because the claim lacks a precise definition and timeframe, it is unsupported by available Census/BLS trends.

claim: Orrin Hatch co-sponsored a 1993 health care bill that had an individual mandate.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence in congressional sponsorship records that Senator Orrin Hatch co-sponsored a federal 1993 health-care bill containing an individual mandate. The most-cited individual-mandate laws and proposals occurred later (notably Massachusetts 2006 and the 2010 ACA), and searches of 1993 Senate bills do not show Hatch listed as a co-sponsor of a mandate provision.

claim: "Voting in the wrong precinct led to over 14,000 registered voters statewide to lose their vote in 2008."
rationale: The claim is not supported by verifiable, specific evidence and omits which state is meant. While some jurisdictions in 2008 experienced precinct and provisional-ballot problems, there is no well-documented, statewide finding that over 14,000 registered voters globally lost their votes specifically because they voted in the wrong precinct. Voters who cast ballots in the wrong precinct are typically given provisional ballots or other remedies, and verified counts/reports from states do not substantiate this broad figure.

claim: "About halfway through fiscal year 2009, Washington has run out of money."
rationale: The statement is vague and there is no evidence that either the federal government or the State of Washington literally 'ran out of money' about halfway through fiscal year 2009. Governments generally experience cash-flow shortfalls or budget deficits but continue operations through revenues, borrowing, use of reserves, or emergency measures; no widely reported, literal insolvency occurred mid‑FY2009.

claim: "Forty-seven percent of Americans pay no income tax."
rationale: The often-cited 47% figure referred to the share of households in a particular year who paid no federal individual income tax, not the share of all Americans who pay no taxes at all. Many in that group still pay payroll (Social Security/Medicare) taxes, state taxes, or other federal taxes, and the exact percentage varies by year and measurement unit (individuals vs. tax units/households).

claim: "1 in 4 Rhode Islanders under the age of 65 does not have health insurance."
rationale: Recent estimates from the Census American Community Survey and state-level reporting show Rhode Island’s uninsured rate for people under 65 has been well below 25% (generally in the single digits to low teens in recent years). Rhode Island expanded Medicaid under the ACA and has historically had lower-than-national uninsured rates, so the claim that 1 in 4 under-65 residents lack insurance is not supported by typical data sources.

claim: "59 percent of Americans today believe that Barack Obama is still a Muslim."
rationale: Multiple reputable polls over the past decade have shown only a minority of Americans believe Barack Obama is Muslim, with figures typically in the low-to-mid tens of percent overall. While higher percentages appear within specific partisan or demographic subgroups, no mainstream national poll has shown 59% of all Americans holding that belief.

claim: Photo shows Ice Cube and 50 Cent wearing Donald Trump hats.
rationale: There are no credible, verified reports or reputable news photos showing Ice Cube and 50 Cent together wearing Donald Trump hats; viral images of celebrities in political apparel are frequently edited or miscaptioned. Both artists have histories of public comments about politics, and purported photos of them in MAGA hats that have circulated online have not been substantiated by reliable sources.

claim: "You said you went to Delaware State but you forgot the name of your college."
rationale: I (as this assistant) do not have personal experiences or attend colleges, so I could not have said I went to Delaware State or forgotten a college name. The claim is also self-contradictory: stating one went to 'Delaware State' is naming a college, so claiming both that and forgetting the name is inconsistent.

claim: "Kim Martin Morrow the CEO of Netflix has just been charged with 15 charges for child pornography"
rationale: This claim is false. "Kim Martin Morrow" is not the CEO of Netflix, and there are no credible reports or public records that any Netflix CEO was just charged with 15 counts of child pornography. Such high-profile criminal charges would be widely reported by major news outlets and reflected in official court filings; known Netflix leaders in recent years are Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters.

claim: Common Core is "education through Washington D.C."
rationale: Common Core standards were developed and promoted by state-level organizations (the National Governors Association and the Council of Chief State School Officers) and individual states voluntarily adopted them. The federal government did not create or directly mandate Common Core, though it used incentives (e.g., Race to the Top grants and waiver policies) to encourage state adoption.

claim: Says "I never billed a single hour of my time to the City of Portland in the last 10 years -- so, no revolving door."
rationale: The claim is unverified and potentially misleading: without the speaker's identity and review of public payroll/contract billing records it cannot be confirmed that they billed zero hours to the City of Portland in the past decade. Even if true, not billing hours does not by itself prove there is no 'revolving door' (which can involve unpaid advisory roles, lobbying, employment, or other relationships).

claim: The "3 red stripes" in Joe Biden’s campaign logo refer to a Chinese socialist slogan.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the three red stripes in Joe Biden’s campaign logo refer to a Chinese socialist slogan. The stripes are a typographic device forming the middle bar of the letter 'E' and are widely interpreted as evoking the red stripes of the American flag and a sense of motion/energy, not any foreign political slogan.

claim: The impeachment inquiry hearings "going on behind closed doors over which Congressman Schiff is presiding—they are consistent with the rules" of the U.S. House of Representatives.
rationale: House committees have longstanding authority to conduct investigations and hold depositions in closed session, and the Constitution does not require a prior floor vote to begin an impeachment inquiry. While Republicans argued the informal process was improper, legal scholars and House practice support that committee-led closed-door depositions overseen by Representative Schiff were consistent with House investigatory rules; the House later adopted a resolution to formalize procedures.

claim: Says Dennis Miller said that if he didn’t see women protesting the Ghislaine Maxwell trial verdict "you're all frauds. This isn't justice for those women, this is a joke."
rationale: I find no reputable reporting, recording, or primary-source evidence attributing that quote to comedian/commentator Dennis Miller after the Ghislaine Maxwell verdict. The phrasing appears unverified and likely misattributed without a cited tweet, clip, or news item.

claim: "We know dangerous criminals can slip through immigration at airports just like ours. Yet Joe Donnelly stood right here with the radical left against all efforts to secure our most vulnerable entry points."
rationale: The claim mixes a plausible general point—that criminals have in some cases entered via airports—with a sweeping allegation that Joe Donnelly opposed “all efforts” to secure entry points and aligned with the “radical left.” Public records show Donnelly was a moderate Democrat with a mixed voting record on immigration and security, not someone who uniformly blocked security measures or consistently sided with an extremist faction. The statement thus overgeneralizes and lacks specific supporting evidence.

claim: "U.S. military at the White House arresting Congress."
rationale: There are no credible reports or evidence that U.S. military forces are at the White House arresting members of Congress; such an action would constitute an extraordinary and widely reported assault on constitutional order. The U.S. military operates under civilian control and domestic law, and arrests of legislators would normally involve lawful criminal processes and civilian law enforcement rather than unilateral military action.

claim: "Jim Justice is the first West Virginia governor to fight for pay raises for educators."
rationale: Jim Justice was a prominent governor who negotiated and supported teacher pay increases during the 2018–2019 strikes, but he was not the first West Virginia governor to fight for educator pay raises. Prior governors and administrations had proposed, advocated for, and enacted pay increases and education funding measures before Justice’s tenure.

claim: Says a video shows a "gay party in Italy few weeks before COVID-19."
rationale: Claims that a particular viral video shows a 'gay party in Italy a few weeks before COVID-19' are typically unsubstantiated and frequently misattributed; fact-checks of similar posts have found footage from other times or places or lacking metadata to confirm the alleged timing and location. Without verifiable source metadata, location confirmation, or corroborating reporting tying the clip to Italy and the claimed date, the assertion cannot be treated as true.

claim: "But for immigrants, we would have a contracting population..."
rationale: The statement is too sweeping without naming a country or timeframe. While immigration does prevent population decline in many high‑income countries, some countries would still have stable or growing populations for years because of natural increase and population momentum even with low fertility. Therefore the universal claim "But for immigrants, we would have a contracting population" is not reliably true as written.

claim: "CBO reports that delaying the Obamacare individual mandate will reduce the deficit by $35 billion over ten years."
rationale: There is no reputable CBO report that shows a delay of the ACA individual mandate would reduce the deficit by $35 billion over ten years. CBO analyses of ACA changes around that period showed much smaller and mixed budgetary effects from delays or enforcement changes, and the $35 billion figure appears to be a misstatement or confusion with other legislative cost estimates rather than a CBO finding.

claim: Says Tim Tebow wrote, "The government might be preparing us for a cashless society, but it was predicted by the Bible."
rationale: There is no credible primary source linking Tim Tebow to that exact wording; the line appears as a viral social-media quote that has been shared without attribution. Reliable fact-checking and searches of Tebow's known public posts do not corroborate that he wrote or said this statement.

claim: "Smartmatic and Dominion systems ... were built to do this very thing, for changing the results of elections."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Smartmatic or Dominion voting systems were intentionally built to change election results. Multiple independent audits, state certification processes, cybersecurity assessments, and court rulings (including defamation case outcomes) have found no proof that the systems were designed to or systematically altered vote counts. While software can have bugs or be misconfigured, investigations did not support the claim of purposeful design to manipulate elections.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "knows full well I voted for his amendment to increase military spending to $697 billion."
rationale: The claim presents a quoted statement but gives no source, date, speaker, or legislative context (which amendment or vote). Without verifiable attribution or a public record showing a specific amendment to raise military spending to $697 billion and a named lawmaker admitting they voted for it, the statement cannot be confirmed as factual. Given the lack of evidence, the claim should be treated as unverified and therefore not accepted as true.

claim: "There's no court session between now and the end of this election."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated and is likely false because it asserts a universal absence of any court sessions from now until an unspecified election ends. Courts at multiple levels regularly hold hearings and emergency sessions, and election-related litigation often proceeds up to and beyond election deadlines. Without a specific jurisdiction and timeframe the blanket statement cannot be supported.

claim: "More Texans have jobs today than ever before in the history of our state."
rationale: State and federal labor data show that Texas has reached record high employment levels in recent years; total numbers of employed Texans have generally risen with population growth and hit new peaks around 2022–2024. Therefore the statement that more Texans have jobs now than at any prior time is supported by available employment series.

claim: Says that singer Dolly Parton said, "Trump in one year is already better than 16 years of Bush, Obama put together."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Dolly Parton ever made that statement; major reliable coverage and fact-checking outlets do not attribute this quote to her. Parton has a long public record of avoiding partisan endorsements and has denied making sweeping political claims like this one, making the attribution implausible.

claim: "A portion of everything you pay A.A.R.P goes directly to the Democratic Party."
rationale: AARP is a nonprofit organization that describes itself as nonpartisan; membership dues fund services, advocacy, and operations and are not automatically sent to the Democratic Party. AARP does operate a separate PAC that collects voluntary contributions and may make political donations, but that is distinct from mandatory dues and is not an automatic transfer of a portion of everything members pay.

claim: "More than 20 million people are at risk of dying from starvation within 6 months in 4 nations."
rationale: This wording matches repeated public warnings from the United Nations and major aid agencies that over 20 million people in four conflict-affected countries (commonly Yemen, South Sudan, Somalia and northeastern Nigeria) were at risk of dying from starvation within months without immediate life-saving assistance. Those agencies have issued multiple notifications with similar figures and timeframes during acute crises.

claim: "In March 2020 the United States deployed 30,000 troops to Europe to ... free child-trafficked children and arrest deep state cabal members."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official Department of Defense reporting that the U.S. sent 30,000 troops to Europe in March 2020 to free trafficked children or arrest a so-called "deep state cabal." Public reporting from reputable media and DoD records show no such operation; troop movements at that time were routine rotations and pandemic-related adjustments. The claim echoes QAnon-style conspiracy narratives rather than documented military activity.

claim: Says more Austinites voted in the city’s 1973 election featuring a mayor’s race than in the city’s most recent mayoral election.
rationale: This claim is unlikely because Austin’s population and voter registration have grown substantially since 1973, and recent mayoral contests have generally produced larger raw vote totals. Without citing specific historic tallies, the default expectation is that a modern mayoral election in a much larger city would draw more voters than a 1973 contest.

claim: Says David Jolly’s former firm lobbied "for hundreds of millions (of dollars) for a dictator in Pakistan."
rationale: There is no reliable public evidence tying a firm where David Jolly formerly worked to lobbying efforts that secured “hundreds of millions” for a Pakistani dictator. Public reporting and lobbying disclosure records do not document a contract or campaign matching that description tied to Jolly’s former employer, so the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Mitt Romney "said it was 'tragic' to end the war in Iraq."
rationale: There is no clear record or reputable news reporting that Mitt Romney said it was "tragic" to end the war in Iraq. He frequently criticized Obama-era withdrawals and warned of negative consequences, and he used words like "tragic" in discussions of related security issues (e.g., Afghanistan), but the specific quoted claim appears to be a misattribution or paraphrase rather than a documented direct quote about ending the Iraq war.

claim: "We have more hospitals that are children’s hospitals than any other state in the union." 
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it does not identify which state 'we' refers to, and there is no universally cited fact that a particular state has more children's hospitals than all others. Counts of children's hospitals vary by source and by whether freestanding pediatric hospitals or pediatric units within general hospitals are counted, so the claim cannot be accepted without specific, current data.

claim: The U.S. spends "57 cents on the dollar on defense."
rationale: As stated, the claim implies 57 cents of every federal dollar overall goes to defense, which is incorrect — defense spending is only a minority of total federal outlays (roughly in the mid-teens percent). The ~57-cent figure is roughly correct only when limited to discretionary spending, where about 57% of discretionary dollars go to defense.

claim: Photos show "diesel generators" at the COP26 climate change conference.
rationale: Multiple independent fact-checks and organizer statements found that widely circulated photos purporting to show diesel generators powering COP26 were misattributed or taken elsewhere, and the conference reported using mains power and battery systems rather than on-site diesel generation for the event. While temporary power equipment was present for logistics, the specific viral images do not reliably show diesel generators operating at COP26 as claimed.

claim: "A law enforcement officer is more likely to commit a crime than a CWP (concealed weapons permit) holder."
rationale: This is an overly broad, cross-jurisdictional claim for which there is no consistent, generalizable evidence. Research in many U.S. jurisdictions finds concealed‑weapons permit holders are screened and tend to have lower arrest/conviction rates than the general population, while law‑enforcement criminality and misconduct occur but vary widely by jurisdiction and offense type; there is no robust data showing officers are overall more likely to commit crimes than CWP holders.

claim: Wall Street megabanks that received bailouts in 2009 now get taxpayer-funded advantages not available to community banks in Ohio.
rationale: Large Wall Street banks that received 2008–2009 rescue support continue to enjoy advantages tied to government backing and access to federal liquidity programs that community banks typically do not. Examples include implicit 'too‑big‑to‑fail' guarantees that lower their funding costs, eligibility for emergency Federal Reserve facilities and certain dealer programs, and historical access to taxpayer‑funded stabilizing actions during crises. Community banks in Ohio generally do not receive the same scale of implicit guarantees or selective program access.

claim: "Less mass shootings under Trump!"
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and unsupported: it gives no definition of 'mass shootings' or baseline period. Public databases and analyses use differing definitions and show that incident counts and fatalities did not consistently decrease during Trump's presidency and in some measures increased, so the blanket claim is not correct.

claim: Says Ted Cruz said: "While there may have been an age difference, Josh Duggar’s transgressions are far less an affront to God than what gays do to each other."
rationale: There is no reliable record or reputable news report quoting Ted Cruz saying that line; the attributed statement appears to be a fabricated or misattributed quote circulated online. While Cruz has spoken on social issues, no verbatim source supports this exact, highly specific comparison.

claim: Terry McAuliffe favors "taking the Pledge of Allegiance and the 4th of July out of the (school) curriculum."
rationale: There is no record of Terry McAuliffe calling for removing the Pledge of Allegiance or the Fourth of July from school curricula; multiple fact-checks during the 2021 Virginia governor campaign found claims to that effect were misleadingly framed or false. McAuliffe criticized efforts to have parents dictate specific curriculum content but did not propose eliminating patriotic elements like the Pledge or July 4 celebrations.

claim: "There has never been an alderman who has defeated an incumbent mayor in the history of this great city."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement but gives no city to check; across many municipalities historically, sitting aldermen or city council members have run for and defeated incumbent mayors, so a blanket never is implausible. Without a specific city and time period the claim cannot be substantiated and is likely false as stated.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Scott's approval ratings are up.
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify as presented — it gives no timeframe, poll, or source. Approval ratings change over time and can be up in some polls and down in others, so without a specific poll and date the claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Like every budget passed by the Senate since I have been lieutenant governor, Senate Bill 1 is within the spending limit set by the Texas Constitution."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim about every Senate budget since the speaker became lieutenant governor and about SB1 specifically; whether a Texas budget 'is within the spending limit' depends on technical accounting rules and official certifications and has been subject to dispute and differing interpretations. There is no uncontested public record that every Senate-passed budget in that span was certified as within the constitutional limit, and determinations (including for SB1) hinge on contested inclusions/exclusions of funds and comptroller or judicial rulings.

claim: "Pre-existing conditions are covered under my (health care) plan."
rationale: Whether pre-existing conditions are covered depends on the specific health plan and applicable law; it is not universally true. In the U.S., the Affordable Care Act prohibits insurers from denying coverage or charging higher premiums for pre-existing conditions in most individual and employer plans, but exceptions (e.g., short-term or certain limited-duration plans, some grandfathered plans, and policies in other jurisdictions) may still exclude them.

claim: Arnold Schwarzenegger slept on the ground in front of a bronze statue of himself because he had been turned away from a hotel.
rationale: There is no reliable biography or contemporary news account supporting this specific story, and statues honoring Schwarzenegger were erected long after he became famous, making the causal detail (turned away from a hotel leading him to sleep by his own bronze statue) implausible. The anecdote appears to be an unverified or conflated internet tale rather than a documented fact.
