Without original image metadata (EXIF), an independent timestamp, geolocation data, or corroborating sources, a photo caption claiming 'Myrtle Beach 30 minutes ago' cannot be reliably confirmed and could be reused, miscaptioned, or manipulated.

claim: "Unemployment insurance kept more than 620,000 children out of poverty in 2012."
rationale: Analyses of the 2012 Supplemental Poverty Measure (as reported by researchers and organizations such as the Census Bureau and CBPP) show that unemployment insurance benefits prevented over 600,000 children from falling below the poverty line in 2012. The cited figure of 'more than 620,000' matches published estimates that isolate the poverty-reducing effect of UI for that year.

claim: Photo shows Barack Obama and George Clooney in a compromising situation with a child.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that such a photograph exists of Barack Obama and George Clooney in a compromising situation with a child. Extreme allegations involving high-profile figures typically would be widely covered and verified by reputable news and fact-checking organizations; absent that, such images are usually misattributed or manipulated.

claim: "FDR was called a socialist and a communist."
rationale: Political opponents, conservative commentators, and some media repeatedly labeled Franklin D. Roosevelt a "socialist" or even a "communist" during the 1930s and 1940s as critiques of his New Deal policies. These labels were commonly used as political attacks rather than precise ideological descriptions.

claim: "The senior senator from Arizona (John McCain) said he couldn't support repealing 'don't ask, don't tell' because of the economy."
rationale: This is false. John McCain's publicly stated reasons for opposing repeal of "don't ask, don't tell" during the 2010–2011 debates centered on military readiness, unit cohesion, and the timing/process for changing policy, not on the state of the economy as the primary rationale.

claim: Says he was "not part of transferring" any priests accused of sexual abuse.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it does not identify who “he” is, when the transfers allegedly occurred, or provide supporting evidence. Without a named individual and documentary or investigative records, one cannot confirm the truth of the denial; many past investigations into clerical abuse have shown documented transfers by specific officials, so a generic denial is not provable. Given this ambiguity, the appropriate judgement is to treat the claim as unsubstantiated.

claim: Says the Obamas are connected to the Varsity Blues college admissions scandal.
rationale: There is no credible evidence linking Barack or Michelle Obama to the Varsity Blues college admissions scandal. Public DOJ indictments, plea agreements, and major news reports name the specific parents and intermediaries involved, and the Obamas are not among them. Rumors and social-media posts alleging such a connection have been repeatedly debunked by fact-checkers.

claim: "U.S. Department of Homeland Security has told banks -- in writing -- it may inspect safe deposit boxes without warrant and seize any gold, silver, guns or other valuables it finds inside those boxes!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Department of Homeland Security issued a written order telling banks they may inspect safe-deposit boxes without a warrant and seize valuables. Multiple independent fact-checkers and legal experts have debunked similar viral claims, and routine law-enforcement access to safe-deposit boxes generally requires a warrant, court order, or the customer's consent except in narrow exigent circumstances.

claim: "So far, out of 175 arrested in Kenosha, 102 were not from Kenosha. Rioting has become its own industry."
rationale: The specific numeric claim about '175 arrested in Kenosha, 102 not from Kenosha' is not supported by a consistent, verifiable public record — official counts from law enforcement and contemporary news reports gave varying totals and did not confirm that precise breakdown. The second clause, that 'rioting has become its own industry,' is a subjective characterization rather than an empirically verifiable fact and therefore cannot be labeled true or false in the same way.

claim: Says Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s "wealth has surged while in public office."
rationale: Public financial disclosure records for Sen. Jeanne Shaheen show routine fluctuations in assets consistent with market movements and investment income, but there is no clear, independently verified evidence of a dramatic or unusual "surge" in her wealth attributable to her time in office. Reporting on senators' finances has not singled out Shaheen as having an extraordinary increase beyond typical variation. The claim is vague about timeframe and magnitude, and cannot be substantiated as stated.
cited_knowledge: General knowledge of publicly filed congressional financial disclosures, media coverage of senators' net worth, and absence of widely reported extraordinary increases for Shaheen.
safety_notes: The claim is ambiguous about the period and what constitutes a "surge"; specific disclosure forms and exact year-to-year changes would be needed to verify or quantify any increase.

claim: Maj. Nidal Hasan, the man accused of the Fort Hood shootings, "was an ADVISOR to the Obama Administration."
rationale: Nidal Hasan was an Army major and psychiatrist stationed at Fort Hood and is the accused shooter in the 2009 Fort Hood attack. There is no evidence or official record that he served as an adviser to President Obama or held any White House/administration advisory post; media reporting and government records identify him only as a military officer.

claim: "Grandparents must pickup up all their grandchildren every weekend no matter what or they will be fined $5,000."
rationale: There is no general law that obligates all grandparents to pick up their grandchildren every weekend under threat of a $5,000 fine. Duties to care or transport children arise from specific custody, guardianship, or court orders or from private agreements, not from a universal statutory mandate applying to all grandparents.

claim: "Jim Renacci cheated on his income taxes" and is a "deadbeat citizen."
rationale: There is no public, verifiable evidence that Jim Renacci was convicted of cheating on his income taxes; allegations in political reporting have referenced tax disputes or liens tied to businesses at times, but those are not the same as proven criminal tax evasion. Calling him a "deadbeat citizen" is a subjective, pejorative claim that overstates and mischaracterizes the available public record.

claim: 40 percent of illegal immigrants "had a visa and then became illegal," mostly because "they changed jobs."
rationale: While U.S. research (DHS/Pew) has estimated that roughly 40% of unauthorized immigrants entered legally and overstayed a visa, the claim that this transition to illegality happened 'mostly because they changed jobs' is not supported. Most visa overstays are from expired visitor or student visas, not job changes; loss of status due to job changes affects a much smaller subset of work-visa holders.

claim: Says his barehanded catch posted on YouTube is real.
rationale: There is insufficient public evidence to verify the assertion that an unspecified person's YouTube video of a barehanded catch is genuine. Many online clips are edited, staged, or misleading, and without original unedited footage, corroborating witnesses, or independent verification the claim cannot be confirmed. Therefore the default position is to treat the unverified claim as false until validated.

claim: "African-Americans are more likely to be arrested by police and sentenced to longer prison terms for doing the same thing that whites do."
rationale: Multiple large-scale studies and government data have found that Black Americans are arrested at higher rates than white Americans for many offenses and, when convicted, receive longer prison sentences on average even after controlling for some legal factors. Research on drug enforcement, traffic stops, charging decisions, and sentencing outcomes consistently documents racial disparities that support this general claim.

claim: ISIS sends out "90,000 social (media) messages a day."
rationale: The specific claim of a steady 90,000 "social messages" per day by ISIS is not supported by robust evidence. Multiple media analyses and fact-checks found that reported volumes varied widely, were often misinterpreted or included duplicates/retweets and automated accounts, and no consistent, independently verified figure of 90,000/day exists.

claim: Says Bill Nelson "skipped 45 percent of the hearings on national security."
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that Bill Nelson skipped 45% of “hearings on national security.” The claim is imprecise about which hearings, what time period, and what metric was used, and public committee attendance records and mainstream fact-checkers do not support a nearly half absence rate. Without a clear definition and source, the 45% figure appears unsubstantiated.

claim: Congressman Robert Hurt has a plan to cut education by 40 percent.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Congressman Robert Hurt proposed a plan to cut education funding by 40%. Major legislative proposals and public statements associated with Hurt and widely reported budget plans did not call for a 40% reduction to education, and such a large, specific cut would have been notable in news and Congressional records. Without a specific source or context, the claim appears unsupported.

claim: "About 47 percent of able-bodied people in the state of Maine don’t work."
rationale: Labor statistics do not support that about 47% of able-bodied people in Maine "don’t work." Maine's labor force participation and employment-to-population measures show most working‑age adults are employed; a 47% nonworking rate would conflict with BLS-style participation data and is not a standard, verifiable statistic. Claims like this typically arise from misreading or miscounting categories (e.g., including retirees, students, disabled people, or using a narrowly defined subgroup).

claim: "Health care is the greatest contribution to spending increases in the state budget."
rationale: The claim is stated as a universal fact but gives no state or timeframe. While health care (especially Medicaid) is often a major driver of state budget growth, other factors—pension liabilities, K–12/higher education, debt service, or one-time shifts—can be the largest contributors in many states and years. Without specifying which state and period, the statement cannot be verified as generally true.

claim: "The violent crime rate has risen, and the homicide rate has risen by more than 20 percent in just two years, really after 30 years of decline in violent crime."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and mixes trends. In the U.S. there was a multi-decade decline in violent crime from the early 1990s into the mid-2010s and homicide counts did jump substantially around 2019–2020, but whether homicides rose “more than 20 percent in just two years” depends on the exact two-year window and data source. Because the claim lacks a defined location and timeframe and overstates a generalization, it is not reliably true as stated.

claim: "As of today, no one has the right to film or photograph Mr. Biden as he climbs the flight of stairs. New White House spokesman orders!!?"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the White House has issued a blanket order removing anyone’s right to photograph or film President Biden climbing stairs. In the U.S., press and public photography of public officials is generally protected by the First Amendment, though access can be limited by property ownership or temporary security restrictions. A spokesman cannot unilaterally erase constitutional or widely recognized press rights without specific lawful, narrowly tailored security measures.

claim: "Total deaths from COVID MUCH LOWER than reported."
rationale: Multiple independent analyses of excess mortality (WHO, IHME, and other research groups) show that total deaths attributable to the COVID-19 pandemic are generally equal to or higher than officially reported tallies, indicating undercounting in many places rather than widespread overcounting. Limited testing early in the pandemic, reporting delays, and differences in cause-of-death attribution explain why official counts often miss many pandemic-related deaths.

claim: There are "many unanswered and obvious questions" about the 2001 death of a staff member of Joe Scarborough.
rationale: The death of Joe Scarborough’s 28-year-old staffer, Lori Klausutis, was investigated and the medical examiner ruled it accidental — an undiagnosed cardiac arrhythmia that caused a fall and head injury. Official investigators found no evidence of foul play, and widely circulated conspiracy claims have been debunked. Therefore the claim that there are “many unanswered and obvious questions” is not supported by the available official findings.

claim: There are "360,000 (deaths) a year from swimming pools. But we don’t shut the country down for that."
rationale: The claimed figure (360,000 annual deaths from swimming pools) is implausible and not supported by major data sources. WHO estimates roughly 200–240 thousand global drowning deaths per year (all settings), and swimming-pool-specific fatalities are only a small fraction of that; national data (e.g., U.S. CDC) show pool drownings number in the low thousands at most.

claim: Says there’s no proven instance where hydraulic fracking has polluted groundwater.
rationale: Numerous peer-reviewed studies and regulatory investigations have documented groundwater contamination associated with shale gas operations, including methane migration and detection of fracking-related chemicals near wells. High-profile cases (e.g., Pavillion, WY; Dimock, PA) and studies such as Osborn et al. (2011) and EPA inquiries provide evidence contrary to the claim that no proven instances exist.

claim: "The job [of correctional officer] lowers your life expectancy . . . Metropolitan did a study in, I believe it was 1998, and the life expectancy was 58."
rationale: The claim as stated is not supported: while research shows correctional officers face elevated health risks and some studies report higher mortality rates, there is no well-documented 1998 'Metropolitan' study showing a general life expectancy of 58 for correctional officers. A nationwide occupational life expectancy that low is not supported by peer-reviewed literature or standard insurer life tables; the specific attribution and number appear to be a misquote or misunderstanding.

claim: "One percent of the American people make over 21 percent of all the income in America. That wasn’t the way before George Bush became president."
rationale: While data from sources like Piketty and Saez show the top 1% accounted for about or over 21% of U.S. income in the late 1990s and 2000s, that level had already been reached before George W. Bush took office (notably around 2000 under President Clinton). Thus the first numerical claim can be true for certain years, but the assertion that "that wasn't the way before George Bush" is incorrect.

claim: Says Wisconsin’s 2011-13 state budget contains "no fee increases"
rationale: Contemporary fact-checks and budget analyses found the 2011–13 Wisconsin budget included multiple fee increases (for example hunting/fishing licenses, various professional and service fees, and some state park and permit fees), so the blanket claim of “no fee increases” is incorrect. Supporters may have meant no broad new taxes, but fees were raised in several areas.

claim: Says Gerald Daugherty advocated lowering the penalty for crimes like strangulation in domestic violence cases because "they just ‘throw more people into the’" jail "‘system."
rationale: I am not aware of any credible source through mid-2024 showing Gerald Daugherty advocated lowering penalties for strangulation in domestic violence cases or used the quoted language about 'throw[ing] more people into the jail system.' Without a reliable attribution or supporting reporting, the claim appears unverified or misattributed and should be treated as false.

claim: "Since the president became the president, we have lost 3.3 million jobs in the private sector. But you know who's done OK and who's not complaining today? The public sector. We've gained 590,000 public sector jobs."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it fails to specify which president or exact time period; U.S. payroll employment totals (private vs. public) are reported monthly and vary greatly depending on start and end dates. Without a clear timeframe and source, the specific numbers (−3.3 million private, +590,000 public) cannot be confirmed and are likely inaccurate when applied ambiguously to different presidencies.

claim: "Trump’s daughter works at the White House. Her husband works at the White House. Rudy’s son works at the White House. Barr’s son-in-law works at the White House. Barr’s daughter works at Treasury. Trump’s sons do foreign business. Trump’s daughter is getting Chinese patents and Saudi grants."
rationale: The claim bundles several assertions: some are true (Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner served as White House advisors, and Andrew Giuliani worked in the Trump White House; Trump’s sons have had foreign business dealings). However other specific assertions are wrong or unverified — notably the statements about ‘Barr’s son‑in‑law’ and ‘Barr’s daughter’ working at the White House or Treasury are not supported by reliable public records, and the phrasing that Ivanka is “getting Chinese patents and Saudi grants” is misleading and lacks corroboration (she pursued trademarks abroad but the claim conflates different processes and funding sources). Because multiple elements are inaccurate or unproven, the overall bundled claim is false.

claim: Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp "mandates restaurants reopen"
rationale: In April 2020 Gov. Brian Kemp issued an executive order permitting restaurants to resume in-person service under social-distancing rules, but he did not compel businesses to reopen. Restaurants were free to remain closed and local authorities sometimes imposed different restrictions, so 'mandates restaurants reopen' is inaccurate.

claim: "I have no financial interests in Saudi Arabia."
rationale: There is no identifying information or supporting documentation with this standalone statement, so it cannot be independently verified. Absence of evidence is not proof of the claim, and financial interests can only be confirmed through disclosures, records, or other verifiable evidence.

claim: In "the past four or five" presidential elections, "people who poll high at the beginning are not the people who end up being the nominees."
rationale: The pattern is mixed rather than consistent: some early front‑runners in recent U.S. primary cycles did fail (e.g., Rudy Giuliani in 2008, Jeb Bush in 2016), but in other cycles early leaders did become the nominee (e.g., Mitt Romney in 2012, and Hillary Clinton was an early leader on the Democratic side in 2016). Therefore the blanket statement that in the past four or five elections early high pollers never became nominees is inaccurate.

claim: Says J. David Cox, "the boss" of the jail guards "who were supposed to keep" suspected sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein alive, is also "friends with Bill and Hillary Clinton."
rationale: The claim misstates roles and lacks evidence. J. David Cox is the president of the American Federation of Government Employees (a union representing some federal workers), not the direct "boss" of the jail guards at the Metropolitan Correctional Center, and there is no reliable public evidence that he said the guards' boss is "friends with Bill and Hillary Clinton" or that Cox himself has a documented personal friendship with the Clintons.

claim: "Muslims offended that their kids have to recite national anthem."
rationale: The claim is a sweeping generalization about all Muslims being offended; while some Muslim parents or communities in particular countries or cases have objected to children reciting a national anthem for religious or cultural reasons, it is not true that Muslims universally feel offended. Attitudes vary widely by country, community, and individual belief. Without context, the claim overgeneralizes and is inaccurate.

claim: "Corrupt political bosses. Money laundering. Fraud. It’s just another day at the office for Vin Gopal."
rationale: The claim accuses Vin Gopal of being routinely involved in corruption, money laundering, and fraud, but there are no widely reported criminal charges or convictions tying him to those crimes. Major news coverage and public court records (up to my knowledge cutoff) do not substantiate blanket allegations of criminal activity against him, so the statement is unsubstantiated and misleading.

claim: "All non-US citizens, illegal or not, will be provided with free health care services."
rationale: There is no federal policy that guarantees free healthcare to all non‑U.S. citizens regardless of immigration status. Eligibility for programs like Medicaid, marketplace subsidies, and other public benefits varies by immigration status and state; emergency care must be provided under EMTALA but that is limited to stabilizing treatment, not comprehensive free care.

claim: "We now consume at the federal level 25 percent of the gross domestic product. Historically we were at 20 percent. So we've taken 5 percent away from the private sector."
rationale: The claim mixes an imprecise accounting fact with a causal assertion. While federal spending as a share of GDP has varied and at times risen from around 20% toward the mid-20s depending on the year and definitions used, an increase in the government's share of GDP does not automatically mean a one-for-one 5 percentage-point transfer 'taken away' from the private sector. How spending is financed (taxes, borrowing, or money creation), timing, transfers versus consumption, and macroeconomic responses mean the relationship is more complex than the claim implies.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton and Tim Kaine "want to shut down shale, and shut down natural gas."
rationale: This overstates their positions. During the 2016 campaign Hillary Clinton called for tighter regulation of fracking, limits on new drilling on certain federal lands, and a transition to cleaner energy but did not advocate a nationwide shutdown of shale gas; Tim Kaine explicitly said he would not support a federal ban on fracking. Neither camp publicly proposed immediately “shutting down” shale or natural gas production outright.

claim: The "48, 49 percent" that supports President Barack Obama are "people who pay no income tax."
rationale: The claim conflates a rough percentage figure with tax status. The “48–49%” figure often cited in political debate refers to a broad share of the population cited in discussions (e.g., Romney’s “47%” remark about those who don’t pay federal income tax), but it is incorrect to say that the people who supported Obama are all those who pay no income tax — many Obama supporters do pay federal income tax, and many who pay no federal income tax still pay payroll and state/local taxes. The statement is an overgeneralization and factually inaccurate.

claim: "Half of all hospitalized seniors are suffering from malnutrition so severe that it either caused their illness or it prevents them from getting better."
rationale: The claim overstates and generalizes the evidence. While a substantial proportion of hospitalized older adults are malnourished or at risk (estimates vary roughly from about 20% to 50% depending on setting and criteria), saying half of all hospitalized seniors have malnutrition so severe it caused their illness or prevents recovery is an oversimplification and an unproven causal claim.

claim: Says "I've authored the first bipartisan tax reform bill in a quarter-century."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as written because it fails to identify who 'I' refers to, which legislative body or jurisdiction is meant, and what counts as 'tax reform' or 'bipartisan.' Without those specifics one cannot confirm a claim of being the "first" in 25 years, and historical records show multiple bipartisan tax measures at federal and state levels over recent decades, making the absolute claim unlikely.

claim: "We had 6,000 oil and gas spills in 2012" with "more oil and gas spreading in the United States than the entire Exxon Valdez spill."
rationale: While federal and state incident records show several thousand oil and gas releases in 2012 (commonly reported around 6,000–7,000 incidents), the combined reported volume for those incidents was only a few million gallons. The Exxon Valdez spilled on the order of 10–11 million gallons, so the claimed assertion that 2012 releases in the U.S. exceeded the Exxon Valdez total is misleading and not supported by the reported volumes.

claim: Says there is proof Democrats hired actors to plan violence in Charlottesville.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Democratic Party hired actors to plan the Charlottesville violence. Independent news investigations, law enforcement inquiries, and court records attribute planning and the violent actions to white supremacist organizers and fringe extremists, and the 'hired actors' narrative has been debunked.

claim: "Maxine Waters Is Getting Criminally Charged!"
rationale: There were no credible reports, indictments, or court filings charging Representative Maxine Waters with a crime as of mid-2024; statements that she "is getting criminally charged" appear to be political rhetoric or unverified claims rather than documented legal action. No official press release from the Department of Justice or major reputable news outlets announced criminal charges against her.

claim: Sherrod Brown "sent billions of our tax dollars to foreign countries."
rationale: The claim is misleading: a single U.S. senator cannot unilaterally "send" tax dollars abroad. Congress as a whole passes appropriations and the executive branch executes payments; while Sherrod Brown may have voted for bills that included foreign aid, there is no basis to say he personally sent billions of tax dollars.

claim: The daughter of a Donald Trump appointee posed as an El Paso shooting victim in a photo with the president.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a person in a photo with the president was the daughter of a Trump appointee posing as an El Paso shooting victim. The assertion circulated on social media but was not substantiated by reputable news organizations or independent fact-checkers, and public records or reporting confirming such a familial link were not produced.

claim: "Nobody’s invited us" to the Obama events in Atlanta.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it uses an ambiguous pronoun (“us”) and does not identify which Obama events in Atlanta or when. Political events vary—some are public rallies, some are ticketed or invitation-only—so a blanket statement that “nobody” was invited cannot be confirmed without a specific context or source. Given the lack of supporting evidence and the ambiguity, the claim is not reliable.

claim: Says revenues "are actually up after tax reform."
rationale: The statement is too general to be verified: whether revenues rose after a tax reform depends on which country, which reform, and the time period measured. Many tax cuts reduce government revenues at least initially, though in some cases growth or base-broadening provisions can later raise receipts — so the blanket claim without context is unsubstantiated.

claim: "In New York State, Democrats blocked a Bill expanding College Tuition for Gold Star families after approving aid for illegal immigrants."
rationale: The claim conflates and misstates events without clear supporting evidence. Up through mid‑2024 there is no well-documented record that New York State Democrats collectively blocked a specific bill to expand college tuition benefits for Gold Star families while or after approving a separate package of aid for undocumented/illegal immigrants; the statement appears to mix unrelated legislative debates and timing to create a misleading narrative.

claim: Says Republican Gov. Phil Scott "just voted to impeach President Trump."
rationale: This is false — a state governor does not vote in federal impeachment proceedings, and Phil Scott did not cast any congressional vote to impeach President Trump. While Scott publicly called for Trump's removal after January 6 and urged resignation or use of the 25th Amendment, that is not the same as voting to impeach in the House.

claim: "When I became mayor of Los Angeles, we had a 44 percent (high school) graduation rate. I said that was unacceptable. I challenged that notion. I said the mayor needs to be involved with our schools. We need to partner together. As I left, after a number of reforms, we grew our graduation rate from 44 percent to 72."
rationale: The precise 44% → 72% progression as stated is misleading. LAUSD graduation rates did improve during the period in question, but the 44% baseline and 72% endpoint depend on differing definitions and years; independent fact-checks and district data show gains but not a simple, single-step rise from 44 to 72 attributable solely to the mayor’s actions.

claim: "Taxpayers earning $1 million pay an effective tax rate that is about four times what taxpayers earning $100,000 pay."
rationale: While effective tax rates rise with income, taxpayers with $1 million in income typically face effective rates only about two to three times those of taxpayers earning around $100,000, not four times. IRS and tax‑policy analyses show $100k households often have effective federal tax rates in the low‑to‑mid teens percent, while $1M households commonly have effective rates in the mid‑to‑high twenties percent (varying by year and definitions).

claim: "$21T in Pentagon accounting errors. Medicare for All costs ~$32T. That means 66% of Medicare for All could have been funded already by the Pentagon."
rationale: The arithmetic (21/32 ≈ 66%) is correct, but the claim is misleading because the reported ~$21 trillion relates to bookkeeping adjustments and accounting entries in Pentagon audits, not $21 trillion of available cash that could be reallocated. Meanwhile the ~$32 trillion Medicare for All figure is a contested, aggregate cost estimate that depends on assumptions and potential offsets. You cannot treat DoD accounting adjustments as fungible funds to directly finance a health-care program.

claim: "Biden concedes 6 million votes."
rationale: There is no record of President Joe Biden publicly 'conceding 6 million votes' in any election. In the 2020 U.S. presidential election Biden was declared the winner and did not issue a concession; later public statements and certified results do not show him conceding by any margin of 6 million votes. The claim appears to be a misstatement or out-of-context assertion without supporting evidence.

claim: "A clear majority of Americans support removing the cost-sharing requirement for prescription contraceptive coverage."
rationale: Multiple national polls have consistently found a substantial majority of Americans favor removing out-of-pocket costs for prescription contraception. Surveys from organizations such as the Kaiser Family Foundation and Pew Research Center have regularly reported well over 50% (often in the 60–80% range) supporting no-cost contraceptive coverage, though levels vary by question wording and subgroup.

claim: Says Ted Cruz’s father "was with Lee Harvey Oswald" before the assassination of President John F. Kennedy.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rafael (Ted) Cruz’s father was with Lee Harvey Oswald before JFK’s assassination. Major fact-checkers and historical records found no corroboration, the Cruz family denied the claim, and the allegation appears to stem from unverified rumors and possible name confusion.

claim: "The number of uninsured people in Massachusetts is about the same as it was when the mandates were passed in 2006."
rationale: Massachusetts' 2006 health reform (the individual and employer mandates) produced a substantial decline in the uninsured population, and subsequent estimates show the number of uninsured remained well below pre-reform levels rather than returning to them. While the uninsured count has fluctuated somewhat in later years, it is not “about the same” as in 2006.

claim: The balanced-budget amendment once came within one vote of passing Congress but was defeated because of the no vote from a top Senate Republican, and Rick Santorum says he "stood up and called for him to resign his chairmanship."
rationale: The statement bundles several specific factual claims that are not supported by the historical record as stated. While balanced-budget amendment proposals had several close Senate votes in the 1990s, there is no clear, corroborated instance where the amendment was within a single vote of passage of Congress and was defeated solely by one 'top Senate Republican' no vote, nor is there verified contemporaneous reporting of Rick Santorum saying he 'stood up and called for him to resign his chairmanship.'

claim: Says the new coronavirus vaccines contain toxic ingredients and are more dangerous than getting COVID-19.
rationale: Extensive clinical trials and large-scale real-world safety monitoring show authorized COVID-19 vaccines do not contain unspecified 'toxic ingredients' at harmful levels and have a favorable safety profile. Serious adverse events are rare, and overall the vaccines substantially reduce the risks of hospitalization, death, and long COVID compared with remaining unvaccinated. While some vaccine types have been linked to very rare side effects, those risks are much smaller than the typical harms from COVID-19 infection for most age and risk groups.

claim: "Expanding Medicaid will worsen health care options for the most vulnerable among us in Texas."
rationale: Empirical research and state experiences with Medicaid expansion under the ACA show it generally reduces uninsured rates, increases access to primary and preventive care, lowers uncompensated care burdens, and in some studies improves health outcomes—effects that benefit vulnerable populations rather than worsen their options. While local provider shortages or implementation choices can create access challenges in specific areas, the overall evidence does not support the claim that expansion makes care worse for the most vulnerable in Texas.

claim: Rick Perry is "taking money away from hurricane victims" and diverting it to "remodel the Governor's Mansion."
rationale: There is no clear, documented evidence that Rick Perry personally took money away from hurricane victims and diverted it to remodel the Governor’s Mansion. While there were media reports and controversy about the use or proposed use of some state or federal disaster-recovery funds related to mansion repairs, the claim as a categorical assertion that he diverted victims' funds is misleading and not substantiated.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "was asked repeatedly to provide security in Benghazi on several occasions, including direct cables."
rationale: Multiple investigations (including the State Department Accountability Review Board and congressional inquiries) found that U.S. personnel in Benghazi made repeated requests for additional security in the months before the 2012 attack, and some of those requests were transmitted to Washington in formal cables and other communications. However, while the requests were directed to the State Department and its security bureaus (which Clinton led as Secretary), they were not always sent as personal, individual appeals directly addressed to Hillary Clinton herself.

claim: "There is currently no ability to vet these people," referring to Syrian refugees.
rationale: There are established procedures used to vet Syrian refugees, including UNHCR registration and biometric collection, national resettlement interviews, and security checks by host-country immigration, intelligence agencies and international databases. While vetting can be imperfect and complicated by lost or forged documents and porous borders, it is incorrect to say there is 'no ability' to vet these people.

claim: Rhode Island's state pension system "underperformed the median three out of the four years that Mr. [Frank] Caprio was in office."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as presented because it omits which “median” benchmark is intended and I find no clear public evidence showing Rhode Island’s pension returns were below the relevant median in three of the four years Caprio held office. Public reporting for that period shows mixed results, so the categorical claim that it underperformed the median three out of four years is unsubstantiated without a specified comparator and source.

claim: Says Texas U.S. Rep. John Culberson "was caught using campaign cash on collectibles, including Civil War memorabilia and fossils."
rationale: There is no clear public record that Rep. John Culberson was definitively 'caught' using campaign funds to purchase collectibles such as Civil War memorabilia and fossils. While some news reports and complaints at times flagged campaign expenditures and alleged questionable purchases, those accounts do not establish a proven finding or conviction that he used campaign cash for such collectibles.

claim: Says the New York bike path assault "was the ninth vehicle assault used by ISIS."
rationale: There is no authoritative count showing the New York bike path attack was the 'ninth' vehicle assault by ISIS. Numerous vehicle-ramming incidents before 2017 (e.g., Nice, Berlin, Jerusalem-related attacks, and many incidents in Iraq and Syria) were claimed by or linked to ISIS or its affiliates, and counts vary by definition. Because different sources include different incidents (inspirations, claims, VBIEDs, or simple vehicle-rammings), a definitive ordinal number like 'ninth' is not supported.

claim: "CDC announces that students may be kept from parents overnight as Ohio sets up COVID-19 FEMA camps."
rationale: There is no evidence the CDC announced that students may be kept from parents overnight as part of any program; CDC COVID-19 guidance included isolation and quarantine recommendations but did not order separations of students from parents or endorse 'FEMA camps.' Reports about Ohio setting up COVID-19 FEMA camps are unfounded and reflect a debunked conspiracy narrative rather than official public-health policy.

claim: After hiring a campaign manager in 2006, "I got this $100 and something fee ... for hazardous materials."
rationale: This statement is an unverified, context-free anecdote with no identifiable speaker, source, or corroborating records. I found no public documentation or reporting that confirms a 2006 hire of a campaign manager resulted in a '$100 and something' hazardous materials fee. Without independent evidence, the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: The Greenlight Pinellas transportation plan involves a "300% tax increase."
rationale: The Greenlight Pinellas proposal was not a 300% tax increase; it was a proposal to raise local transit funding via a modest local sales surtax increase (commonly described as a one‑cent/1% local sales tax increment in contemporary reporting) to pay for expanded transit. Claims of a '300% increase' were political exaggeration or misinterpretations of different baselines, not a literal tripling of an existing general tax rate.

claim: Says Target installed urinals in a women’s bathroom to "accommodate the ones who have giblets."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official Target statement that the company installed urinals in a women’s bathroom or said it was to “accommodate the ones who have giblets.” Reporting around Target has focused on gender-neutral or single-stall restrooms and transgender inclusion, not the installation of urinals in women’s restrooms, and the quoted line appears to be satirical or fabricated social-media content.

claim: Says he didn't call Dr. George Tiller a baby killer, as liberal groups charge, but was merely reporting what "some prolifers branded him."
rationale: The claim as presented is not verifiable because it omits who made the statement, when, and any primary source. Without a contemporaneous quote, transcript, or reliable reporting showing the person explicitly saying they were only "reporting what 'some prolifers branded him,'" the assertion cannot be confirmed and should be treated as unsubstantiated.

claim: Ilhan Omar called for "violence" against President Trump over Middle East dispute.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Ilhan Omar explicitly called for violence against President Trump over a Middle East dispute. Major fact-checkers and mainstream news outlets have found viral posts making this claim were misquotes, doctored, or taken out of context; her public statements criticized policy and warned against escalation rather than advocating violence.

claim: "The barber regulation here in Missouri is 10,000 words long….the book of Revelation is (also) 10,000 words long."
rationale: The statement that both the Missouri barber regulation and the book of Revelation are 10,000 words long is inaccurate. Word counts for Revelation vary by Bible translation (typically in the 9,000–12,000 word range) and do not consistently equal 10,000 words, and Missouri barber-related statutes or administrative rules vary in length by which document is meant and are not a standard 10,000 words. Claiming both are exactly 10,000 words is therefore misleading.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "We must block Trump from stopping the return of the heroic Alabama mother from ISIS. In many ways she is more of a hero then our veterans. Welcome home sister!"
rationale: There is no record in credible news outlets, AOC's verified social media accounts, or reputable fact-checkers of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez making this statement; it matches a pattern of fabricated or misattributed quotes that circulate on social media. The quote's tone and grammatical errors are inconsistent with her verified public communications.

claim: Says Gov. Evers "has refused to identify or discipline the staff member who secretly taped" a conversation with GOP leaders.
rationale: Available reporting through mid‑2024 does not show a clear, documented refusal by Gov. Tony Evers to identify or discipline a staffer who secretly recorded a conversation with GOP leaders. Evers’ office said it would review the matter and directed questions to legal counsel, and public coverage describes disputes and demands for names rather than a confirmed categorical refusal to identify or discipline.

claim: "The city of Portland has won more national Constitution contests than any city in America."
rationale: The claim is not supported by known records and is ambiguous about which contest and which Portland are meant. National-level Constitution competitions (e.g., We the People, Constitution Bee) publish winners by school, individual, or state, and there is no documented evidence that any Portland has won more such national contests than every other U.S. city. Given the lack of a standard, public tally attributing counts to a single city, the assertion is almost certainly incorrect.

claim: California’s marijuana legalization initiative, Prop. 64 "allows marijuana smoking ads in prime time, on programs with millions of children and teenage viewers."
rationale: Proposition 64 includes explicit limits on marijuana advertising: it prohibits ads that target minors and bars placing ads where a substantial portion of the audience is under legal age. That prevents a blanket allowance of marijuana smoking ads during prime-time programs with large child and teen audiences.

claim: "If the FAA is worried about what the 5G deployment will do to the planes, what do you think it will do to our bodies?"
rationale: The FAA's expressed concerns about 5G deployment have been about potential radio-frequency interference with aircraft instruments (notably radar altimeters) near specific C‑band frequencies, not evidence that 5G will harm human bodies. Scientific and regulatory bodies (WHO, FDA, FCC) find no conclusive evidence that 5G radiofrequency exposures at permitted limits cause adverse health effects.

claim: China recovered from COVID-19 "without a vaccine."
rationale: China did not recover from COVID-19 without vaccines. The country launched mass vaccination campaigns in 2020–2021 using domestically produced vaccines (e.g., Sinovac, Sinopharm) and achieved high vaccination coverage before and during later waves, even while also relying on strict nonpharmaceutical control measures.

claim: Says Adolf Hitler said, "The day mankind finds out what I was trying to defend this nation, Germany, from, then that’s the day World War III starts."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Adolf Hitler ever said or wrote this line. The phrasing and reference to 'World War III' are anachronistic for verified Hitler texts and speeches, and reputable historians and primary-source collections do not include this quote. It appears to be a modern misattribution circulated on unsourced quote compilations.

claim: "A new ruling by the EPA would force dairy farmers to comply with the Spill Prevention, Control and Countermeasure Program when dealing with spilt milk -- the same regulations oil and natural gas producers must follow."
rationale: There is no known EPA ruling that would broadly force dairy farmers to follow the SPCC for routine spilled milk. SPCC applies to discharges of oil and oil products to waters of the U.S. and has specific definitions, thresholds, and exemptions; milk is not typically treated the same as petroleum discharges and no sweeping new regulation targeting dairy spill response was adopted as described. The claim conflates the SPCC’s coverage of certain oils/animal fats with an across‑the‑board requirement for dairy farms.

claim: Congressional benefits include "free health care, outrageous retirement packages, 67 paid holidays, three weeks paid vacation, unlimited paid sick days."
rationale: The claim mixes some true elements with clear exaggerations. Members of Congress do have access to the Federal Employees Health Benefits program and government retirement plans, but insurance is not free (members pay premiums) and pensions follow statutory formulas and eligibility rules rather than being uniformly 'outrageous.' The specific counts — 67 paid holidays and 'unlimited' sick days — are false: the federal government recognizes about 10 federal holidays and sick/annual leave accrues under federal rules rather than being unlimited; 'three weeks paid vacation' is also a simplification that ignores accrual rules and congressional schedules.

claim: Says Ron Johnson voted to turn Medicare "into a voucher program."
rationale: There is no single roll-call vote by Ron Johnson that directly "turned Medicare into a voucher program." Johnson has publicly advocated converting Medicare to a premium‑support (voucher‑like) model and has voted for budget measures and proposals that would enable or promote such changes, but he did not cast a vote that itself enacted a conversion of Medicare into a voucher program.

claim: U.S. Senate candidate Michelle Nunn "earned as much as $300,000 running a nonprofit that had laid off 90 workers."
rationale: Michelle Nunn, as CEO of Points of Light, received compensation in the roughly $200–300K range reported on nonprofit tax filings while the organization underwent a reorganization that eliminated about 90 positions. Contemporary news reporting and the charity’s public filings documented both her pay and the staff reductions.

claim: "Wisconsin Republicans have not passed a single bill in 6 months."
rationale: The statement is incorrect — the Republican-controlled Wisconsin Legislature has passed and advanced multiple bills over recent months. Even when the governor vetoes measures, the legislature still routinely votes to pass bills in one or both chambers, so the claim that they have not passed a single bill in six months is implausible and inconsistent with normal legislative activity.

claim: "Cory Booker’s son charged with assault after attack on Santa."
rationale: There are no credible mainstream news reports or official records indicating that Senator Cory Booker’s child was charged with assault for attacking a person in a Santa costume. The story appears to have circulated on social media without verification and would be widely reported if true given Booker's public profile.

claim: Says in regard to providing "more tax cuts for the rich," Bill Pascrell said, "Republicans had great ideas. I liked some of their ideas."
rationale: There is no credible record of Rep. Bill Pascrell endorsing “more tax cuts for the rich” with the quoted praise of Republicans; he has a long record of opposing tax cuts that favor the wealthy. The phrasing appears inconsistent with his typical public statements and is likely a misattribution or taken out of context.

claim: "We’re seeing now 30 straight months of private-sector job growth, 4.6 million jobs created."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and not clearly supported by official monthly payroll data without a specified start date or data source. BLS nonfarm payroll series and private-sector employment reports must be cited to substantiate a 30‑month consecutive private‑sector growth streak totaling exactly 4.6 million jobs, and available public reporting does not unambiguously confirm that exact_combo. Because the claim lacks timeframe and source and does not match readily verifiable official summaries, it cannot be treated as factual as stated.

claim: Says "under our current sentencing laws, about 75 percent of all convicted felons in Oregon do not go to prison."
rationale: The claim is misleading and likely exaggerated. Oregon sentencing data and reporting distinguish felony convictions, admissions to state prison, and community/jail sentences; while a substantial share of felony convictions result in probation or local sentence, available state statistics do not support a stable figure that as many as 75% of convicted felons never serve any prison time. The true share varies by year, offense type, and definition used (convictions vs. admissions).

claim: Says Donald Trump said, 'Africans Are Lazy, Good At Sex, Theft.'
rationale: There is no credible transcript, primary source, or reputable news report documenting Donald Trump saying the exact phrase 'Africans are lazy, good at sex, theft.' The quote appears to be a fabricated or misattributed paraphrase; while Trump has been reported making racist remarks about certain countries, this specific wording is not verifiable.

claim: "Any Floridian who has ever requested an absentee ballot henceforth gets one automatically."
rationale: Florida does not automatically send mail ballots to every person who has ever requested one. Only voters who are on the state's permanent vote-by-mail (absentee) list or who submit a timely request for a given election will receive a ballot; a single past request does not universally guarantee lifetime automatic delivery regardless of current registration status. County practices and recent law changes can affect who gets mailed ballots, but the broad claim is incorrect.

claim: Says Rep. Betty Sutton supports allowing "welfare fund withdrawals from strip clubs, casinos and liquor stores."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or public record that Rep. Betty Sutton advocated allowing welfare withdrawals specifically at strip clubs, casinos, or liquor stores. SNAP/EBT rules already prohibit use of food benefits for alcohol and prepared hot foods, and while cash assistance can be withdrawn and spent legally anywhere, attributing a specific policy endorsement to Sutton is unsupported and appears to be a mischaracterization.

claim: "Inflation has gone up every month of the Biden presidency and just hit another 40-year high."
rationale: Consumer price inflation did not increase every month during President Biden’s term; after rising through 2021 and peaking in mid‑2022, CPI had months where it declined and year‑over‑year inflation fell thereafter. The major peak was around June 2022 (about 9.1% year‑over‑year), the highest since the early 1980s, but inflation has not 'gone up every month' nor has there been a recent new 40‑year high after that peak. The claim conflates different measures and timeframes and is therefore inaccurate.

claim: "The American economy is continuing its longest monthly streak of job growth in history, with 3.9 million jobs added since President Trump was elected."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate. Official BLS payroll data and independent fact-checkers show the cumulative job gain since the November 2016 election was larger than 3.9 million and claims about the "longest" monthly job-growth streak depend on how the streak is measured and which historical period is used, so the assertion as stated is misleading.

claim: "Due to ... tax cuts and lower (property) values, 2009 property taxes were almost $3 billion below 2007 property taxes."
rationale: The statement provides no jurisdiction or data source, so the specific numeric claim cannot be confirmed. While the 2008–2009 downturn did lower property values and in some places reduced property tax receipts, asserting a near-$3 billion drop from 2007 to 2009 without context is unverified and likely misleading.

claim: The United States Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit is "the most overturned court in the country."
rationale: The claim is presented as an absolute but is ambiguous and misleading. While the Ninth Circuit has historically had a high number of reversals in raw counts (partly because it is the largest circuit by caseload), it is not consistently the "most overturned" by reversal rate, and rankings change by timeframe and metric used.

claim: COVID spelled backward is "divoc" which means "possession of the evil spirit" in Hebrew.
rationale: Reversing “COVID” produces the string “divoc,” but that string is not a Hebrew word meaning possession by an evil spirit. The Hebrew term for a possessing spirit is דיבוק, transliterated as dybbuk/dibbuk (dibuk), which is neither spelled nor pronounced as “divoc.”

claim: Oregon Health Plan rations "covered procedures under certain circumstances"
rationale: Oregon’s Medicaid program (the Oregon Health Plan) uses a prioritized list of services, medical-necessity rules, and prior-authorization limits to determine which procedures are paid for, and it has curtailed or denied coverage for some procedures when budgets or clinical criteria require it. In practice this means covered procedures can be limited or withheld under certain circumstances, which is a form of rationing.

claim: "We haven't yet taken out a negative ad."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it omits who “we” refers to, the time period, and what counts as a “negative ad.” Verifying such a claim requires campaign ad-buy records, media monitoring, or independent tracking of political advertisements; absent those specifics it cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false.

claim: "Oregon school districts are directing 24 percent of their food budgets to purchase local foods. That’s the highest percentage in the country."
rationale: There is no clear, consistently reported national source that supports the precise claim that Oregon districts direct 24% of their food budgets to local foods and that this is the highest percentage nationwide. Oregon does have strong farm-to-school activity and above-average local procurement in some surveys, but reported percentages vary by year, data source, and the definition of 'local,' so the definitive 24%/"highest in the country" statement is unsupported.

claim: Compared to President Obama, "President Reagan rushed home from Santa Barbara vacation, from the Reagan ranch when the Korean jetliner was shot out of the air by the Russians."
rationale: President Reagan was at his Rancho del Cielo near Santa Barbara when Korean Air Lines Flight 007 was shot down by Soviet aircraft on September 1, 1983. He cut short his vacation, returned to Washington, and publicly condemned the Soviet action, so the statement that he 'rushed home' from the ranch is a fair summary of contemporaneous accounts.

claim: "90 percent of fires in Arizona are human-caused."
rationale: While a large majority of wildfires in Arizona are attributed to human activity, the exact share fluctuates by year and by data source and is not reliably a fixed 90%. Reporting typically shows a high human-caused proportion (often in the 70–90% range), so stating a definitive 90% as an absolute fact is misleading without a specific year or source.

claim: Says a photo shows an ambushed Los Angeles police officer and that the NFL intends to "honor and praise the organization" that stood outside of the hospital chanting, "We hope she dies."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the NFL announced plans to "honor and praise" an organization that stood outside a hospital chanting "We hope she dies," and the claim appears to conflate a miscaptioned photo with a fabricated NFL endorsement. Viral posts frequently repurpose protest photos out of context and falsely attribute endorsements to large organizations like the NFL; I found no reliable reporting supporting this specific allegation.

claim: "The health care price tag for childhood obesity in Georgia is $2.4 billion annually and rising."
rationale: I could not locate a clear, authoritative source that states Georgia (presumably the U.S. state) faces a $2.4 billion annual health-care bill specifically for childhood obesity. Published figures on obesity costs typically vary by source, year, and whether they cover adults vs. children or direct medical costs vs. broader economic impacts, so the claim appears unsupported or misleading without a cited study and timeframe.

claim: "39% of All California Students are illegals."
rationale: There is no evidence that 39% of California students are undocumented. Official enrollment and demographic research (state education data, Pew Research, Migration Policy Institute) indicate the share of undocumented students is much smaller—estimates typically put undocumented immigrants as a single-digit percentage of the overall population and undocumented K–12 students form a small fraction of total enrollment. The 39% figure appears to conflate other categories (such as students from immigrant families, English learners, or a particular ethnic group) with undocumented status.

claim: "In 1986, President Ronald Reagan" cut the business tax rate to 34 percent and "it worked -- our economy boomed, the middle class thrived and median family income increased."
rationale: The 1986 Tax Reform Act did lower the top corporate tax rate to about 34%, and the U.S. experienced an economic expansion in the late 1980s. However, claiming unequivocally that "it worked" in the sense that the middle class broadly "thrived" and median family income clearly increased is misleading: gains were modest and uneven, and income inequality rose, so the broad celebratory causal claim is not supported.

claim: Says Mike Enzi is "getting about 84 percent of his campaign funds from Washington-based PACs. That's more than any senator of either party."
rationale: The claim is implausible and lacks supporting context or a verifiable data source. An 84% share from Washington-based PACs is unusually high compared with typical senator fundraising mixes, and there is no corroborating evidence that Enzi received a larger share from such PACs than every other senator. Verifying this would require a specific time period and FEC or campaign finance analysis, which the claim does not provide.

claim: Athletes are collapsing with heart-related issues due to the COVID-19 vaccines
rationale: There is no evidence of a widespread phenomenon in which athletes are collapsing en masse because of COVID-19 vaccines. Surveillance data do show a small increased risk of myocarditis after mRNA vaccines in young males, but those events are rare and typically mild, and many athlete collapses have other causes or are linked to SARS-CoV-2 infection rather than vaccination.

claim: "Joe Biden just confirmed that he is running for president in 2020 and it has America applauding!"
rationale: Joe Biden did run for president in 2020, but he announced his 2020 candidacy on April 25, 2019 — so the phrasing that he 'just confirmed' it is misleading. The claim that 'it has America applauding' is an unqualified, subjective generalization not supported by evidence of a unanimous or universal reaction.

claim: "SpongeBob’s license address is Jeffrey Epstein’s private island!"
rationale: SpongeBob SquarePants is a fictional character whose license shows a fictional Bikini Bottom address (e.g., Conch Street), whereas Jeffrey Epstein owned a real private island (commonly called Little Saint James) in the U.S. Virgin Islands. There is no credible evidence that a canonical SpongeBob license lists Epstein’s island or that the fictional address corresponds to a real private island.

claim: Cover Florida "is available to any Floridian, offering basic coverage for about $150 a month, instead of the typical $600 a month."
rationale: There is no statewide universal "Cover Florida" plan that any Floridian can enroll in for a standard $150/month that replaces typical $600/month premiums. While some limited-benefit or short-term plans marketed under similar names can cost around $150, they have eligibility limits and substantially reduced benefits; marketplace (ACA) premiums vary by age, plan level, and subsidies and are not uniformly $600.

claim: The Obama administration has spent millions of taxpayer dollars for roadside signs to tout the economic stimulus.
rationale: The claim is misleading: the Recovery Act required recipients of stimulus funding to display project signage in many cases and the administration spent some money on public-awareness advertising, but there was not a coordinated, multi‑million dollar federal buy of roadside billboards to 'tout' the stimulus. Independent fact-checkers and oversight reports found only modest outreach and project signage costs (usually paid from project budgets), not a sweeping taxpayer-funded billboard campaign.

claim: "U.S. deaths since 1/22 (2020): COVID-19: 27, flu, 4,700; abortion: 118,000."
rationale: The quoted counts conflict with widely reported public-health data: U.S. COVID-19 deaths since January 2020 number in the hundreds of thousands to over a million, not 27. Typical U.S. influenza deaths are estimated in the thousands to tens of thousands per season (so 4,700 is not a representative aggregate claim), and annual induced abortions in the U.S. have been reported in the hundreds of thousands, making 118,000 since Jan 22, 2020 inconsistent with official estimates.

claim: "Cory Gardner is sponsoring a bill to ban all abortions right now."
rationale: Cory Gardner left the U.S. Senate in January 2021 and is not currently a member of Congress, so he cannot be sponsoring federal legislation 'right now.' There is no widely reported evidence that he is sponsoring a bill to ban all abortions; his past record was pro‑life but did not include sponsoring a complete nationwide ban while in office.

claim: "The yearly cost of religious tax exemptions: $71 billion. If the church paid taxes, everyone would only have to pay 3% taxes."
rationale: The $71 billion figure is a disputed and simplified estimate of lost revenue from various tax benefits for religious and other non‑profit organizations and is not a definitive, universally accepted number; different analyses produce widely varying totals depending on which exemptions are counted. Even if churches were taxed and $71 billion were recovered, that amount is small relative to total federal, state, and local tax receipts and would not plausibly allow a uniform reduction of everyone’s taxes to 3%—the claim conflates distinct budgets and ignores distributional and policy details.

claim: "I'm also the only lieutenant governor to not take a security detail."
rationale: The statement is unverified and implausible as a universal claim because security detail policies for lieutenant governors vary widely by jurisdiction and time. Without specifying which lieutenant governor, which state or country, and the relevant timeframe, it cannot be true that any one person is uniquely the only lieutenant governor to decline a security detail.

claim: Several times, Obama "has apologized for what he deems to be American arrogance, dismissiveness, and derision; for dictating solutions, for acting unilaterally ... ."
rationale: Obama did frequently acknowledge U.S. mistakes and used conciliatory, humble language (for example in his 2009 Cairo speech), but he also explicitly rejected an "apology tour" and did not repeatedly issue broad, formal apologies for "American arrogance." Characterizing his remarks as having "apologized several times" is misleading and overstates the record.

claim: "Illegal immigrants currently occupy 8 million jobs."
rationale: The claim is presented as a precise, current fact but is not supported by a single authoritative, up-to-date source. Estimates of unauthorized (often called "illegal") immigrant workers vary by year and definition and have typically been reported in a range (roughly mid-6 to low-8 million historically), so stating unequivocally that they "currently occupy 8 million jobs" is misleading without a specified country, date, and methodology.

claim: "We're experiencing a net outflow of illegal, undocumented workers from America back to Mexico."
rationale: Available data do not support a clear, sustained net outflow of undocumented workers from the United States back to Mexico. Research shows net migration from Mexico to the U.S. has been near zero in recent decades, the unauthorized population peaked around the mid-2000s and then stabilized or declined somewhat, and recent border encounters have been high but do not demonstrate a consistent net return flow to Mexico.

claim: "There's still about $400 billion or $500 billion of the stimulus plan that has not been spent. Why don't we stop it."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and likely incorrect: unspent balances depend on which specific stimulus package and what date is meant, and there is no single, verifiable $400–$500 billion ‘‘still unspent’’ across all stimulus programs at any one clear time. Different programs (e.g., CARES, PPP, ARPA) had varying amounts allocated, obligated, and remaining, so presenting a blanket $400–$500B figure without context is misleading.

claim: Says actor Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson wore a T-shirt stating: "We Stand for the flag, we kneel for the fallen."
rationale: I find no reliable contemporary reporting or verified image showing Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson wearing a T‑shirt with the exact phrase "We Stand for the flag, we kneel for the fallen." Images and posts with that text have circulated online but appear to be unverified or edited and not corroborated by trustworthy sources. Given the lack of confirmation, the specific claim is likely false or at least unproven.

claim: "For the month of February, Illinois has been the vaccination leader among the 10 most populous states in the country."
rationale: The claim lacks a specific year and metric (first doses, fully vaccinated, boosters, per-capita rate), and there is no consistent evidence that Illinois was the top performer among the ten most populous states for "the month of February." Vaccination rankings among the largest states have varied by month and metric, and available summary data through 2024 do not show Illinois consistently leading in February across standard measures.

claim: In 2021, "11,201 pounds of fentanyl were seized by Customs and Border Protection, which is enough to kill every American nearly seven times over."
rationale: While U.S. Customs and Border Protection did report seizing roughly 11,201 pounds of fentanyl/fentanyl-related substances in FY2021, the claim that this amount is "enough to kill every American nearly seven times over" relies on unrealistic assumptions (that the material is pure fentanyl and that a single fixed milligram dose applies uniformly). Purity, formulation, and bioavailability of seized material vary widely, and lethal-dose estimates for fentanyl are uncertain, so the extrapolation is misleading.

claim: "The majority of my contributions have been from private individuals" giving $125 on average, "not from PACs, not from groups."
rationale: This claim cannot be confirmed as stated because no specific campaign, time period, or supporting finance records are provided. "Majority of my contributions" is ambiguous (number of contributions vs. share of dollars) and the statement that they are "not from PACs, not from groups" can only be verified by checking official campaign finance filings. Without those records, the claim is unverified and thus treated as false for lack of evidence.

claim: "At least 450,000 ballots in the key states ... miraculously only have a mark for Joe Biden on them, and no other candidate."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific, large number without naming jurisdictions, dates, or providing verifiable evidence; publicly available post-election audits and vote tallies do not support an unexplained bloc of 'only Biden' ballots of that magnitude as proof of fraud. It is normal for many ballots to contain a vote for only one office (a valid single-choice vote), and isolated reports of unusual ballot markings have been investigated and attributed to ballot design, reporting artifacts, or normal voting behavior rather than mass illicit marking.

claim: Says that in Curry County, "if you make a 911 call you’re likely to wait for an hour for a response."
rationale: The claim is an unqualified blanket statement and there is no widely reported evidence that 911 calls in 'Curry County' are routinely met with hour‑long waits. Emergency response times vary by jurisdiction, call priority, and available resources; while remote rural areas can have longer delays, saying callers are 'likely' to wait an hour is an overgeneralization not supported by typical EMS/police/FD response data.

claim: The state contributed $80 million for the new Bucks arena, but new income tax revenue from basketball events alone "is estimated to be probably over $600 million over the life of the lease."
rationale: While some public reporting notes an $80 million state contribution toward the Bucks arena project, the specific claim that new income tax revenue from basketball events alone will 'probably' exceed $600 million over the life of the lease is not supported by independent, verifiable revenue projections. Independent analyses and reporting indicated that revenue estimates tied to the arena deal were highly uncertain, relied on broad economic assumptions, and that the Bucks' own or pro‑project studies produced much more optimistic figures than neutral reviews. Presenting the $600 million figure as a reliable estimate for income‑tax receipts from basketball events alone therefore overstates the documented evidence.

claim: "I personally am pro-choice. I always have been. And I made no qualms about that when I was elected governor."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as presented because it is a first-person statement with no identified speaker, election date, or jurisdiction. Whether someone 'always has been' pro-choice and 'made no qualms' when elected requires checking that individual's public statements, campaign records, and voting history; without that context it cannot be confirmed.

claim: "I was speaking out on pension reform almost 17 years ago."
rationale: This is a personal, time‑bound claim that cannot be verified from the statement alone because the speaker is unnamed and no date or supporting evidence is provided. Without corroborating records (dated speeches, articles, or other documentation) that the person spoke about pension reform roughly 17 years prior to the claim, the assertion cannot be confirmed and is treated as false.

claim: Ninety-seven percent of Americans do not receive subsidies for health care under the Affordable Care Act.
rationale: The claim is misleading. If one narrowly counts marketplace premium tax credits, roughly 10–15 million people receive them (about 3–5% of the U.S. population), so ~95–97% would not — but if you include Medicaid expansion and other ACA-related federal support, many more Americans receive government-subsidized health coverage, so the blanket 97% figure omits important context.

claim: Says that "all those who do not answer directly to the president, they've said (repealing Don't Ask, Don't Tell) is a terrible idea."
rationale: The claim asserts that every person who does not report directly to the president said repealing Don't Ask, Don't Tell was a terrible idea. That universal statement is false: during the DADT repeal debate opinions were mixed and many military leaders, lawmakers, and service members supported or accepted repeal and its implementation. The claim is an overbroad generalization inconsistent with the documented diversity of views at the time.

claim: "Every engine manufacturer in the United States is now in the state of Texas."
rationale: This claim is false. Major engine manufacturers and numerous smaller engine makers operate in many U.S. states, not solely Texas (for example Cummins in Indiana, Ford and GM engine plants in Michigan/Ohio, Pratt & Whitney in Connecticut, GE Aviation in Ohio/Massachusetts, Briggs & Stratton in Wisconsin, Honda engine facilities in Ohio).

claim: Terry McAuliffe "wants to raise your taxes $1,700 to pay for his infinite promises."
rationale: The claim mixes a specific dollar figure with a subjective phrase ('infinite promises') and presents it as a stated policy goal; there is no clear evidence McAuliffe proposed a uniform $1,700 tax hike per household as a single, explicit plan. Tax impacts depend on which taxes, which households, and the time period, and political ads commonly use selective estimates to create such claims. Without a precise policy and independent fiscal analysis showing a $1,700 average increase tied directly to McAuliffe, the statement is misleading.

claim: "Fauci admits Covid vax doesn't work"
rationale: This is false — Dr. Anthony Fauci did not admit that COVID vaccines 'don't work.' He has acknowledged that vaccine effectiveness against infection can wane over time and that breakthrough infections occur, especially with new variants, but he and public health data have consistently maintained that vaccines substantially reduce the risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death.

claim: "I've seen (life) from the factory floor when I was working the graveyard shift ...and I'd be ankle-deep in water at the Murray Ohio bicycle plant where I was running a machine that was so loud I couldn't hear myself yell if I wanted to."
rationale: This is a first‑person anecdote about specific past employment and working conditions at the Murray Ohio bicycle plant that cannot be confirmed from available independent sources. There are no verifiable employment records, contemporaneous reporting, or corroborating witness statements provided to substantiate the details (graveyard shift, ankle‑deep water, machine noise).

claim: Says President Donald Trump is selling coronavirus-themed commemorative coins through the White House Gift Shop.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the official White House Gift Shop was selling coronavirus-themed commemorative coins endorsed by President Trump. Fact-checkers and news reports found that social posts conflated privately produced 'challenge coins' or novelty items with official White House merchandise; the White House Gift Shop (a separate nonprofit) did not list such an item as an official Trump product.

claim: "Ted Cruz defended a Chinese company that stole an invention from an American inventor."
rationale: There is no well-documented, reliable evidence that Ted Cruz personally defended a Chinese company that stole an invention from an American inventor. Cruz worked as a private-practice lawyer and represented corporate clients earlier in his career, but public records and major fact-checks do not support the specific allegation as stated.

claim: Alex Sink was "the first official who said that BP should pay $25 million for an ad campaign to promote Florida tourism."
rationale: Alex Sink did publicly call for BP to fund a roughly $25 million advertising push to promote Florida tourism after the 2010 oil spill, but available reporting shows similar demands from other Florida officials and tourism leaders around the same time, so it is not verifiable that she was the very first official to make that call.

claim: "The bill also provides full federal funding for abortions…"
rationale: The claim is unspecified and therefore cannot be verified as stated. As a general matter, federal funding for most abortions has been restricted for decades by the Hyde Amendment and related policies, so an unqualified claim that "the bill also provides full federal funding for abortions" is false unless a particular bill that explicitly authorizes full federal funding is identified.

claim: Says Joe Cunningham voted for $5 million in taxpayer funds to go into his and other politicians’ campaigns to pay for personal expenses and TV ads.
rationale: There is no evidence that Rep. Joe Cunningham voted to direct $5 million of taxpayer funds into politicians’ campaigns for personal expenses and TV ads. Federal law does not authorize straightforward taxpayer transfers to candidates for personal use, and no congressional measure allocating such a $5 million slush fund is recorded. The claim appears to mischaracterize or invent a vote that did not occur.

claim: "Jeff Greene can buy anything" ...  he owns two mansions.
rationale: Owning two mansions does not mean someone can literally 'buy anything.' Jeff Greene is a wealthy real-estate investor who can afford many high-value purchases, but individual wealth is finite and constrained by legal, market, and practical limits.

claim: "Simply being in this country without documentation is not a crime"
rationale: The claim is an overbroad generalization. Whether mere presence without documentation is a crime depends on the country's laws: many countries (and specific acts like illegal entry or reentry after removal) are criminal offenses, while in others — including many cases in the U.S. — unauthorized presence is treated as a civil immigration violation rather than a standalone criminal offense.

claim: Says according to the FBI, more people are killed each year with hammers and clubs than rifles.
rationale: FBI Uniform Crime Report summaries show that the category 'blunt objects' (which includes hammers and clubs) typically accounts for more homicides annually than the 'rifle' category. Rifles make up a small portion of firearm homicides while blunt-object homicides have been higher in many recent years.
