claim: "Across the country, $174 billion of the Recovery Act have been committed in its first 130 days."
rationale: Public reporting on the Recovery Act shows several different milestone figures and dates, but there is no clear, well-documented record that exactly $174 billion was "committed" within the first 130 days after enactment. Officials reported varying totals (and often distinguished "committed/obligated" from "spent/outlay") over spring and summer 2009, so the specific claim as phrased is not reliably supported.

claim: Says the American Civil Liberties Union opposes H.R. 1 on grounds that "it threatens our freedom of speech."
rationale: The ACLU did not broadly oppose H.R.1 as threatening freedom of speech; instead it has generally supported the For the People Act as pro-democracy and has called for improvements on specific provisions (for example around privacy or disclosure) rather than rejecting the entire bill on free-speech grounds. While other organizations have argued H.R.1 or similar reforms could chill speech, that characterization does not match ACLU's public positions.

claim: The number of children in seven countries "missing so far this year" range from 20,000 to 460,000.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it gives no source, no date, and does not name the seven countries; reputable agencies (UNICEF, national police, IOM) publish country-by-country figures and would specify definitions and timeframes. Without that context the quoted range (20,000 to 460,000) appears to mix incompatible statistics or misattribute figures and cannot be confirmed as true.

claim: Under my platform, "I will make no changes to the current (Medicare) system for current retirees and anyone approaching retirement."
rationale: This is a forward-looking political pledge that cannot be independently verified as an objective fact and is legally and practically unlikely to be absolutely guaranteed. Medicare policy is set largely by Congress and subject to future legislative or regulatory changes, and terms like "anyone approaching retirement" are vague. Therefore the claim that no changes will ever be made is not reliably supportable.

claim: Says Edward Snowden "could have gotten all of the protections of being a whistleblower."
rationale: While Snowden could have reported concerns through internal inspector general or congressional channels that provide some whistleblower protections, those frameworks do not authorize public disclosure of classified material and do not shield a person from criminal prosecution for large unauthorized leaks. Because Snowden made mass public disclosures of classified information and was a contractor in the intelligence community, he would not have received ‘‘all’’ whistleblower protections and faced criminal charges.

claim: Chinese workers made "90,000 banners" for Trump’s 2020 re-election campaign and the president chose to hire "Chinese workers instead of American workers"
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that exactly “90,000 banners” for Trump’s 2020 campaign were made by Chinese workers or that the president personally chose to hire Chinese workers instead of Americans. While some campaign signs and merchandise are routinely manufactured overseas (including in China), the precise number cited is unsupported and procurement decisions are typically made by campaign vendors, not by the president directly.

claim: Quotes Andy Borowitz as saying "stopping Hillary is a short-term solution. The long-term solution — and it will be more difficult — is fixing the educational system that has created so many people ignorant enough to vote for Hillary."
rationale: There is no evidence in Andy Borowitz’s verified columns, social media, or reputable news fact-checks that he authored that hostile, bluntly partisan quotation. Borowitz is a satirist whose work is published in specific outlets (e.g., The New Yorker), and this line does not appear in his known corpus and instead circulates as an unattributed or fabricated social-media image. Given the absence of credible sourcing and the frequent misattribution of provocative quotes online, the claim is almost certainly false.

claim: A CNN chyron said, "Antifa has just taken responsibility for storming Capital Hill."
rationale: There is no evidence that CNN ever ran a chyron reading "Antifa has just taken responsibility for storming Capital Hill." Independent fact-checkers and CNN itself have identified the widely circulated image as a doctored/altered screenshot that was shared online during the Capitol riot reporting. Contemporary broadcasts and archives of CNN’s coverage do not show that wording.

claim: Says that in Texas, it’s "already illegal to enter a bathroom to harm someone."
rationale: Texas criminal statutes already prohibit assault, sexual assault, indecent exposure, and criminal trespass, so entering a bathroom with the intent to harm or committing harm there would be illegal under existing law. There is no need for a separate statute to forbid harming someone in a restroom because general criminal laws cover those acts.

claim: The United States is "the only developed country in the world that has not cut its corporate tax rate."
rationale: This claim is false because the United States substantially cut its federal corporate tax rate in 2017 (Tax Cuts and Jobs Act), lowering it from 35% to 21%. Moreover, many other developed countries have also reduced corporate tax rates over recent decades, so the U.S. is not uniquely resistant to such cuts.

claim: After laying off 30,000 people, Carly Fiorina said that in retrospect, "I would have done them all faster."
rationale: There is no credible record of Carly Fiorina saying the quoted line. Fact-checkers examined campaign-era claims and contemporaneous reporting: while Fiorina oversaw roughly 30,000 job cuts at HP, the specific phrasing "I would have done them all faster" is a misquote and cannot be substantiated by reliable sources.

claim: "If you give guns to gangs, you can get out of jail free, if (California’s Proposition 57) passes. If you do a drive-by shooting, you can get out of jail free, if Proposition 57 passes. If you discharge guns on a school yard, you can get out of jail free."
rationale: California Proposition 57 did not create blanket 'get out of jail free' protections for violent acts. It expanded parole review and earned credits for people convicted of nonviolent felonies and changed juvenile transfer rules, but explicitly excluded violent felonies; actions like supplying guns to gangs, drive-by shootings, or discharging firearms on school grounds would generally be treated as violent or serious offenses and remain ineligible for automatic early release under Prop 57.

claim: "The Border Patrol has 20,000 agents – more than twice as many as there were in 2004."
rationale: While U.S. Border Patrol staffing is roughly 20,000 in recent years, that figure is not more than twice the 2004 level. Historical CBP/Border Patrol counts in the mid-2000s were on the order of about 10–12 thousand agents, so 20,000 is roughly double or somewhat less than double rather than 'more than twice.'

claim: The federal debt is more than $14 trillion, "almost equal to the size of our entire economy," and "every child born today inherits a $45,000 share of the national debt before they take their first breath."
rationale: The claim mixes a roughly-accurate headline with misleading implications. Around the early 2010s the gross federal debt did exceed $14 trillion and was close to U.S. GDP, so the first two phrases can be contextually true; however the ‘‘$45,000 per child’’ figure is a simplistic per-capita division of total debt that ignores which debt measure is used and does not mean each newborn legally inherits that amount. The statement omits important context (time, whether gross debt or debt held by the public, and how the per-child number is calculated), making the overall claim misleading.

claim: "Since 1904, the Ohio victor has won the presidency 25 out of 27 times "
rationale: The statement is misleading. Ohio is a strong historical bellwether, but it has sided with the losing presidential candidate in multiple elections (notably 1944, 1960 and 1976, and again in 2020), so a flat claim of '25 out of 27 since 1904' is not reliably correct without a specific end year and appears inaccurate.

claim: The U.S. ranks 37th in the world for health care.
rationale: The statement is misleading as written: the U.S. was ranked 37th by the WHO in its 2000 World Health Report, but that is a single, two-decades-old assessment and many other rankings (and more recent analyses) place the U.S. differently. Without specifying the source and year, claiming a blanket global rank of 37th is inaccurate.

claim: "They were going to build the wall a while ago, not so long ago, like in '06. And they couldn't get environmental impact statements."
rationale: The statement is misleading. Congress passed the Secure Fence Act in 2006 authorizing large-scale border fencing, so plans did exist then; environmental reviews were not categorically unobtainable — moreover, the REAL ID Act of 2005 gave the Secretary of Homeland Security authority to waive environmental and other laws to expedite border barriers, and waivers and legal disputes (not a blanket inability to get EISs) explain delays.

claim: "We were promised (the stimulus) would provide 'green jobs' for Americans, but 80% of the $2 billion they spent on alternative energy went to purchase wind turbines built in China!"
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that 80% of a $2 billion stimulus pot for alternative energy was spent on wind turbines built in China. Federal stimulus programs (ARRA) included multiple energy investments and Buy American provisions, and reporting at the time noted some foreign-made components but not a verification of that specific 80% figure. The claim appears to be an unsubstantiated exaggeration or a mischaracterization of more complex procurement and sourcing data.

claim: A photo shows a recent White House event was actually filmed at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a recent White House event photo was filmed at Tyler Perry Studios. Official White House events are normally held and photographed on White House grounds, and similar viral claims have been debunked by fact-checkers who found misattribution or differences in architecture and context.

claim: Says Sen. Kay Hagan "has missed half of the (Senate Armed Services) Committee's hearings in 2014."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Sen. Kay Hagan missed half of Senate Armed Services Committee hearings in 2014; publicly available attendance records and contemporaneous fact-checks found the claim misleading or inaccurate. Committee calendars include many hearings and meetings, and Hagan’s absences were far fewer than half when properly counted and when excused absences and subcommittee distinctions are considered.

claim: Says "there’s 400,000" anchor babies born in the United States a year, which are "individuals coming to our country and having their children so their children can be U.S. citizens."
rationale: The statement is misleading: recent empirical estimates of births to unauthorized or noncitizen mothers are generally lower than a flat 400,000 figure in recent years, and the claim implies most are short-term arrivals who travel to give birth. Available research (Pew/DHS analyses) finds many births to noncitizen mothers are to women already living in the U.S., and having a U.S.-born child does not confer immediate legal status on the parents (a citizen child can only sponsor a parent when age 21).

claim: "Belarus declares war on Poland."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or major international reporting that Belarus has formally declared war on Poland; a declaration of war would be a widely reported, formal diplomatic or legislative act. While Belarus–Poland relations have been tense at times, no such declaration has occurred.

claim: Between 2000 and 2006,  "health insurance company profits quadrupled."
rationale: The claim is underspecified and not reliably supported as stated. While some U.S. health insurers saw large profit increases in the early 2000s, industry-wide profit figures depend on the metric (net income, operating profit, after-tax profit) and available aggregate data do not clearly show a uniform quadrupling between 2000 and 2006.

claim: Says Tucker Carlson said, "What if these bodies of tortured, dead civilians were staged? What if they’re fake? What if the Ukrainian military killed them & then blamed Russia? I’m not saying any of this is true, I’m just asking the questions. Why can’t we ask these questions?"
rationale: Tucker Carlson did publicly raise the hypothetical that images of tortured, dead civilians (in coverage of the Bucha/Ukraine killings) might have been staged, asking variations of “what if” and prefacing them with “I’m not saying this is true, I’m just asking the questions.” Major news outlets and recordings/transcripts of his show documented him posing those scenarios on air.

claim: Hacked emails "revealed that Hillary Clinton & pals are involved in sex trafficking children."
rationale: The claim is a baseless conspiracy born from misreadings of the 2016 hacked Podesta/Wikileaks emails; extensive reporting, law-enforcement checks, and fact-checkers found no credible evidence that Hillary Clinton or her associates were involved in child sex trafficking. The emails do not contain verifiable proof of such crimes and the allegation has been widely debunked.

claim: In Europe, "church attendance rates (are) in the single digits" because churches are supported by taxes.
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes: church attendance in Europe varies widely—some countries (e.g., Czech Republic, Sweden) have very low weekly attendance, but others (e.g., Poland, parts of Italy and Ireland) have much higher rates well above single digits. The stated causal link is unsupported: state or parish funding (including church taxes in some countries) is neither universal across Europe nor a demonstrated primary cause of low attendance, which social scientists attribute mainly to secularization, cultural change, and historical factors.

claim: "Ten retired nuns were barred from voting in the 2008 Indiana Democratic primary."
rationale: There is no credible contemporary reporting or documented evidence that specifically ten retired nuns were barred from voting in the 2008 Indiana Democratic primary. Major coverage of the 2008 Indiana primary noted voter challenges and administrative errors in some precincts, but I am not aware of any verified incident matching this precise claim.

claim: "According to the most recent report, Wisconsin’s high school graduation rates are also up again -- to third best in the country."
rationale: I cannot confirm the claim as stated. Publicly available federal and state graduation-rate reports (e.g., NCES/EDFacts cohort rates) show Wisconsin has a relatively high graduation rate but rankings fluctuate by year and source, and recent national rankings typically place other states (such as Iowa, New Jersey, or Nebraska) ahead of Wisconsin rather than Wisconsin being clearly third. Without a specific, dated report naming Wisconsin third, the assertion is unsupported.

claim: Image shows Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky "has joined the front lines with his troops."
rationale: There is insufficient evidence to confirm that the unnamed image actually shows President Zelensky 'joining the front lines.' While Zelensky has periodically visited troops and front-line areas, public reporting and his security posture indicate these are controlled visits rather than him joining combat, and images are frequently miscaptioned or lack provenance.

claim: Says in the last 20 years, the French have not "stood by" the United States on foreign policy.
rationale: The claim is overly categorical and false: although France opposed the 2003 Iraq invasion, over the past 20 years France has repeatedly cooperated with the United States on major foreign-policy actions. Examples include NATO operations in Afghanistan after 2001, leading the 2011 Libya intervention with U.S./UK support, coordinated counter‑terrorism and intelligence work after the 2015 Paris attacks, and aligned sanctions and limited military actions related to Syria and Russia. France has therefore both stood with and disagreed with the U.S. depending on the issue.

claim: Says Steve Chabot "voted to strip insurance protections for pre-existing conditions."
rationale: Steve Chabot voted for Republican bills (notably the 2017 American Health Care Act and related repeal measures) that would have weakened Affordable Care Act protections by allowing states to obtain waivers and change rules that could permit higher premiums or limits for people with pre-existing conditions. Those votes were widely described as removing or rolling back federal protections for pre-existing conditions.

claim: "Babysitter on crystal meth eats 3-month-old baby."
rationale: There are no credible, corroborated reports from reputable news organizations or authorities confirming that a babysitter on crystal meth ate a 3-month-old baby. Allegations of cannibalism are extremely rare and would receive widespread, verifiable coverage; similar sensational claims frequently originate as rumors or unverified social-media posts.

claim: "We have over 300,000,000 weapons, firearms in this country. That’s almost as big as the population."
rationale: Multiple reputable estimates place civilian-held firearms in the United States well above 300 million (many estimates in the 300–400+ million range). The U.S. population is roughly 330 million, so saying there are over 300 million firearms and that this is nearly as large as the population is accurate in broad terms.

claim: Says Vicks VapoRub caused a child’s death.
rationale: The claim as stated is unverified and too general: while Vicks VapoRub contains camphor and camphor ingestion or misuse has been linked to poisoning and, in rare cases, death, causation requires specific medical investigation. There is no blanket, independently verified evidence that ordinary topical use of Vicks VapoRub directly causes a child's death without additional factors (ingestion, overdose, underlying condition).

claim: "Business spirit is the highest it's ever been, according to polls."
rationale: The claim is too vague and unsupported: it does not specify which country, timeframe, or which polls. Business sentiment and confidence metrics (PMI, national business confidence surveys, Ifo, NFIB, etc.) vary by country and period and are not universally at all-time highs. Without specific poll names and dates, the statement cannot be verified and is therefore not reliable.

claim: Mt. Hood Community College is No. 1 on average and top faculty pay and benefits.
rationale: The claim gives no source, timeframe, or geographic scope and there is no well-known national or state ranking that lists Mt. Hood Community College as the #1 institution for average or top faculty pay and benefits. Public salary datasets (IPEDS and state community college reports) and common higher-education pay comparisons do not identify MHCC as the top-ranked pay/benefits provider for faculty.

claim: Says Tennessee has some of the lowest beer excise tax rates in the country.
rationale: I cannot confirm that Tennessee is clearly among the very lowest in the country. State beer excise taxes vary widely and while Tennessee's rate has been relatively low to moderate historically, several states have equal or lower rates, so the claim that Tennessee has "some of the lowest" is not robust without up-to-date comparative data.

claim: Only 56 coronavirus deaths a day was enough to collapse the world economy, even though thousands of people die daily from tuberculosis, hepatitis B, and other diseases.
rationale: The claim is misleading. Economic shutdowns and global recession during COVID-19 were driven by the virus’s high transmissibility, potential to overwhelm health systems, and government mitigation measures to prevent exponential spread—not simply a low daily death count like '56'. Moreover, many other diseases (e.g., tuberculosis and viral hepatitis) do cause thousands of deaths daily, but they do not typically trigger the same acute, systemic policy responses because they are endemic, have different transmission dynamics, and lack the same short-term surge risk.

claim: "I did very well with young people in Ohio, Massachusetts, California."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it gives no speaker, time period, metric, or supporting data. Whether someone 'did very well with young people' in those states depends on specific polls, vote shares, or events; without evidence the claim cannot be confirmed and should be treated as unsupported.

claim: "Schools that are consistently implementing COVID-19 mitigation strategies remain among the safest places for our students."
rationale: Multiple public-health analyses and CDC guidance indicate that K–12 schools using layered COVID-19 mitigation (masking, improved ventilation, vaccination, testing, cohorting) have had low levels of in-school transmission and fewer outbreaks, making them comparatively safe environments for students. The claim is supported insofar as these strategies are properly and consistently applied.

claim: Says Proposition 205 "blocks market entry" for new marijuana dispensaries.
rationale: The measure commonly called Proposition 205 (Arizona, 2016) did not literally ban new dispensaries; it gave priority or automatic transition rights to existing medical marijuana businesses and allowed local governments to cap or regulate outlets. Opponents argued that those provisions would make market entry harder for new firms, but the initiative did not explicitly 'block' new dispensaries statewide.

claim: There is a provision in the economic stimulus plan that means that "students cannot meet together in their dorms, if that dorm has been repaired with this federal money, and have a prayer group or a Bible study."
rationale: There is no known provision in major U.S. economic stimulus legislation that bars students from privately meeting for prayer or Bible study in dormitories that received federal repair funds. Federal grant rules may restrict using funds for explicitly religious worship spaces or direct religious activities, but they do not prohibit private, resident-led religious gatherings in student housing. Constitutional protections for private religious exercise further prevent blanket bans on such meetings.

claim: The Democratic health care bill in the House would "create 53 new government bureaucracies."
rationale: Independent fact-checks and reading of the House health-care bill show critics inflated the count by treating many programs, advisory boards, and state-run exchanges as separate "new bureaucracies." The bill did create some new offices and regulatory structures and encouraged state exchanges, but it did not establish 53 new federal bureaucratic agencies as the claim asserts.

claim: "Last year, we borrowed $1.4 trillion -- or 41 cents of every dollar we spent. Over half of this debt is held by foreign investors."
rationale: The claim is incorrect or misleading on both counts. U.S. federal deficits in recent years have not equaled 41 cents of every dollar of federal spending (that ratio would imply an implausibly low total spending), and foreign investors hold substantially less than half of U.S. marketable Treasury debt (roughly around one-quarter to one-third in recent years, not over 50%).

claim: A recent Gallup poll found that 72 percent of Americans and 56 percent of Democrats "say the biggest threat to our nation's security is big government."
rationale: I find no evidence of a recent Gallup poll reporting exactly 72% of Americans and 56% of Democrats saying the biggest threat to U.S. security is "big government." Gallup has asked about perceived national threats in various years, but published results and partisan breakdowns do not match these precise figures and Democrats are generally far less likely than that to name "big government" as the top threat. The claim appears to misstate or misattribute poll numbers.

claim: Says West Virginia is "down to around 50 percent of the adult workers who are actually working now because of addiction or conviction."
rationale: Available labor-force statistics do not support the sweeping claim that West Virginia is 'down to around 50 percent of the adult workers who are actually working' because of addiction or conviction. While West Virginia has a below‑average employment‑to‑population ratio and serious problems with opioid addiction and higher incarceration rates, no credible data show that addiction or convictions are the proximate cause for half of all adults not working. The claim conflates a rough employment metric with an unsupported causal attribution.

claim: "This rule could prevent children under 18 from using such tools as a power screwdriver, a milking machine or something as simple as a wheelbarrow on the family farm . . . "
rationale: The claim is too broad and unlikely as stated: most child‑labor rules include specific exemptions for family farms and allow ordinary chores. Restrictions that bar use of power tools typically apply to employed youth in hazardous occupations, not to common farm tasks like pushing a wheelbarrow or routine milking by family members. Without naming the jurisdiction and specific rule the assertion cannot be verified as universally true.

claim: Graduation rates in Buffalo’s school district, which were "around 48 percent are now up to 64 percent" since Say Yes Buffalo launched.
rationale: While Buffalo Public Schools’ graduation rates have risen since Say Yes Buffalo began and some reports cite increases from roughly the high-40s to the mid-60s, the specific claim as stated is misleading. Official rates depend on the cohort definition and reporting year, and multiple factors (data methodology changes, other reforms, and changing student populations) affect the numbers, so attributing a clean jump “since Say Yes launched” oversimplifies and is not strictly accurate.

claim: Elderly people were "beat up by a BLM hate group" for being white.
rationale: There is no credible, corroborated evidence that an organized 'BLM hate group' systematically beat up elderly people for being white; viral claims of this kind have repeatedly been debunked or shown to be misattributions. The Black Lives Matter movement is decentralized and focused on police violence, and reliable reporting does not support the broad allegation as stated.

claim: In 1988, in response to Iran’s attack on the U.S.S. Samuel Roberts, President Ronald Reagan "destroyed half of Iran’s Navy."
rationale: The U.S. response to the April 1988 mining incident was Operation Praying Mantis, in which U.S. forces sank and damaged several Iranian warships and struck oil platforms, but they did not destroy half of Iran’s navy. Iran lost some ships (notably the frigate Sahand) and suffered damage, yet the Iranian naval forces remained largely intact and operational afterwards. The claim is an exaggeration of the actual losses.

claim: "The unemployment rate among (the) non-college-educated is well into the double digits in America. It's 4 percent or 5 percent for people who have college degrees."
rationale: Bureau of Labor Statistics data show that people without a college degree generally have higher unemployment than college graduates but their unemployment rate is typically in the mid-single digits, not "well into the double digits." College-educated workers commonly have unemployment around 2–5% in normal periods; only during the 2020 COVID shock did many non-college groups briefly exceed 10%.

claim: Says Amazon has removed "an educational game about Gettysburg."
rationale: I am not aware of any widely reported incident or reliable evidence that Amazon removed an "educational game about Gettysburg." Major removals by Amazon that attract public attention are usually documented by multiple news outlets, and no such coverage is known for this specific claim. While Amazon does occasionally remove individual listings for policy reasons, there is no corroborating information to support this particular assertion.

claim: "In this country, we have a 25 percent dropout rate."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not specify which country, which education level or age cohort, the year, or the data source. Dropout rates differ widely between countries, over time, and by definition (e.g., secondary school vs. tertiary vs. overall youth). Without those specifics the flat assertion of a 25% rate cannot be treated as fact.

claim: "Donald Trump to issue an executive order to ban Facebook across U.S."
rationale: There is no evidence that Donald Trump has issued or formally announced an executive order to ban Facebook across the United States. A president generally lacks clear constitutional authority to unilaterally ban a domestic company nationwide without legislative or judicial action, and past threats to restrict social platforms were not implemented as blanket bans.

claim: "NASA will pay you $18,000 to stay in bed and smoke weed for 70 straight days."
rationale: This claim conflates two different things and is false. NASA does run long bed‑rest clinical studies that have paid participants amounts in the low tens of thousands for multi‑week stays, but NASA does not pay people to smoke marijuana; federal law and NASA policy would preclude sponsoring recreational cannabis use and there is no credible evidence of a program paying people to both stay in bed for 70 days and smoke weed.

claim: Photo shows Time magazine cover with Barack Obama that says "Treason."
rationale: The image is a doctored/hoax cover that circulated online; Time magazine has no record of publishing a cover of Barack Obama with the single-word headline "Treason." Multiple independent fact-checkers and Time's archive have debunked that particular cover as fabricated.

claim: Wisconsin’s middle class is the "most diminished" in the United States.
rationale: There is no authoritative, consistent national analysis that identifies Wisconsin as having the single most diminished middle class; reputable studies (e.g., state-by-state analyses of the share of middle-income households) show other states—such as New Mexico, Louisiana, and West Virginia—experiencing larger declines depending on definition and timeframe. Rankings vary by metric and period, so the superlative claim is not supported as a general factual statement.

claim: "On the pace that we're on with job creation in the last four months ... we will have created more jobs in this year than in the entire Bush Presidency."
rationale: The claim compares an extrapolation from a four-month run rate to the cumulative eight-year total under President Bush, which is misleading and unlikely to be true. Historical U.S. employment changes across a full presidential term amount to millions of jobs, and a brief four-month pace would have to be extraordinarily large and sustained to exceed the total job change over an entire Bush presidency.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "was for immigration reform and a pathway to citizenship before he was against it."
rationale: Marco Rubio supported the 2013 bipartisan 'Gang of Eight' immigration bill that included a multi-step path to legal status and eventual citizenship, and later, during his 2015–2016 presidential campaign, publicly renounced that position and opposed a pathway to citizenship. His sponsorship and later statements document a clear change from earlier support to later opposition.

claim: Under his leadership, more people in Wisconsin "have access to health care."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it does not identify which male leader, what time period, or how 'access to health care' is being measured (insurance coverage, provider availability, Medicaid expansion, etc.). Without those specifics, I cannot confirm a net increase attributable to a particular leader's actions versus other factors. Therefore the statement as a standalone factual claim cannot be supported.

claim: Says Joe Biden’s website shows that he supports the Green New Deal, despite denials in debate.
rationale: Biden did deny backing the Green New Deal in debates, and his campaign website later described supporting many of the Green New Deal’s goals (a clean-energy transition and emissions targets). However the site did not explicitly adopt the Green New Deal resolution as written; fact-checkers noted the campaign said Biden supported the objectives or framework rather than the specific bill. The claim as stated — that the website shows he supports the Green New Deal despite denials — is misleading.

claim: Says Joe Biden "helps build Afghanistan’s pipeline."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Joe Biden materially “helped build” a pipeline in Afghanistan. While regional pipeline ideas (e.g., the proposed Turkmenistan–Afghanistan–Pakistan–India/TAPI project) have been discussed and the U.S. has offered diplomatic support at times, no completed Afghanistan pipeline project was built under Biden’s direct oversight or with him as a primary builder.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton's "been very clear where she stands on trade."
rationale: The claim is subjective and depends on timeframe; Hillary Clinton's trade positions have shifted over decades (for example she supported NAFTA in the 1990s but later opposed the TPP in 2016), so many observers describe her record as evolving rather than uniformly "very clear." Without a specified time or specific trade policy, the blanket statement that she has "been very clear" is misleading.

claim: Planned Parenthood has "now (been) found to also illegally sell baby parts."
rationale: Multiple state and federal investigations following the 2015 video sting did not find evidence that Planned Parenthood illegally sold fetal tissue. Independent fact-checkers and official probes concluded that while clinics might receive reimbursement for tissue handling costs and some recordkeeping was questioned, there was no proof of criminal illegal sale as alleged in the claim.

claim: Wisconsin has "the number one health care system in the country. Everyone in poverty now has health care"
rationale: The claim is unsupported: there is no consensus or authoritative ranking that consistently lists Wisconsin as having the single best health-care system in the country, and measurable indicators (access, outcomes, coverage) are mixed across states. Likewise, not every person in poverty in Wisconsin has health care — low-income residents can remain uninsured or underinsured due to eligibility rules, enrollment gaps, and coverage limitations.

claim: "Trump bailed out Wall Street, but not Main Street."
rationale: The claim is an oversimplification. Under Trump in 2020 the administration and Congress enacted the CARES Act and the Paycheck Protection Program which provided substantial direct support to small businesses and workers ("Main Street"), while the Treasury and the Federal Reserve also implemented large market and corporate credit facilities that supported financial markets ("Wall Street"). Critics argue the balance favored larger firms, but it is not accurate to say only Wall Street was bailed out and Main Street received no relief.

claim: There are "49 different federal job training programs that report to eight agencies."
rationale: This specific numeric claim is not reliably true without context—counts of federal job training programs and the agencies that oversee them have varied across reports and over time, and different analyses use different inclusion criteria. Commonly cited counts in official reviews have ranged (for example, mid‑40s programs under differing numbers of departments/agencies), so the precise phrase '49... that report to eight agencies' cannot be confirmed as a stable fact.

claim: Says Cal Cunningham "got a $40,000 tax incentive to update his butler’s pantry."
rationale: Fact-checks determined the claim is misleading: Cunningham was not personally given a $40,000 tax incentive to remodel a private butler’s pantry. The tax credits referenced were tied to a larger renovation project and historic/rehabilitation incentives and were attributed to a property/project arrangement, not a direct personal payment for a private pantry.

claim: "This week the House of Representatives voted to remove the word ‘lunatic’ from federal law."
rationale: I have no verified record at my June 2024 knowledge cutoff that the U.S. House of Representatives enacted a vote this week to remove the word 'lunatic' from federal law. While lawmakers have periodically introduced bills to modernize archaic terms in statutes, there was no widely reported House floor passage in the referenced timeframe.

claim: "Public sentiment in favor of collective bargaining and in favor of the unions has actually gone up as these governors, I think, have overreached and gone too far and tried to destroy the labor movement."
rationale: The claim is a broad, causal assertion without a specified time, place, or data source. While some high-profile state fights (for example Wisconsin in 2011) produced short-term spikes in sympathy for unions in some polls, there is no consistent, nationwide evidence that public support for collective bargaining and unions has uniformly increased as a direct result of governors 'overreaching.' The statement therefore overgeneralizes and is not verifiable as stated.

claim: "The KKK officially endorses Trump 2020."
rationale: There is no single, centralized organization called "the KKK" that issued a unified, official endorsement of Trump in 2020. While individual Ku Klux Klan factions, local chapters, and white supremacist figures publicly praised or supported Trump, reporting and monitoring groups did not document a single national KKK endorsement.

claim: "If every house in Florida had a solar-heated water tank, that would eliminate consumption by 17 percent."
rationale: Residential water heating typically represents roughly 17–18% of household energy use in U.S. homes; replacing conventional water heaters with solar-heated tanks could largely eliminate that portion of residential energy consumption. In practice the exact reduction would vary because of backup heaters, system performance, and behavioral factors, but the 17% figure aligns with standard energy breakdowns.

claim: Says Hunter Biden "died of a crack overdose."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hunter Biden died of a crack overdose; major news organizations, public records, and his public appearances indicate he is alive. The claim appears to be a false rumor or misreporting circulating on social media rather than a verified fact.

claim: "Vern Buchanan. His old business was caught illegally funneling over $60,000 in campaign donations to Buchanan to influence his election."
rationale: There is no verified official finding that Vern Buchanan's former business was 'caught' illegally funneling over $60,000 to his campaign. Reporting has noted investigations and allegations about contributions tied to dealerships and associates, but Buchanan was not criminally charged and authorities did not publicly substantiate an illegal $60,000 funneling scheme.

claim: Says "Barcelona terrorist" is cousins with former President Barack Obama.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that any attacker in the Barcelona attacks was a cousin of Barack Obama. Independent fact-checkers and official reports identified the assailants as Moroccan or of North African origin or local residents and found no familial link to Obama, whose extended family is largely Kenyan.

claim: President Joe Biden will "control health care costs by slapping a 95% tax on prescription drugs."
rationale: There is no evidence that President Biden has proposed or will impose a 95% tax on prescription drugs. His administration and recent legislation (e.g., the Inflation Reduction Act) include measures like Medicare drug price negotiation and rebates for price increases above inflation, but not a 95% tax on drugs.

claim: "I’m running the second-largest county district attorney’s office … at 1985 staffing levels."
rationale: This claim is not verifiable as stated because it lacks a named county, timeframe, and a clear definition of 'staffing levels' (budgeted positions vs. current employees). Determining whether a given county DA office is the second-largest and whether staffing equals 1985 levels requires consulting specific historical staffing records and current payroll/budget data, which are not provided. Without those specifics the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: The typical anglerfish is seven feet long.
rationale: That statement is incorrect for a typical anglerfish. Most anglerfish species (especially deep‑sea forms) are quite small — often only a few inches to a couple of feet, with males much smaller — while only some related benthic species (like monkfish/goosefish) grow larger; seven feet is far above the common size for most anglerfish species.

claim: Before "our last three presidents, you have to go back to the 1800s, early 1800s to find three presidents in a row being consecutively re-elected."
rationale: Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, and Barack Obama each won re-election, forming three consecutive two-term presidents. The previous time three successive presidents each won re-election was Thomas Jefferson, James Madison, and James Monroe in the early 1800s; no other three-in-a-row of presidents winning consecutive terms occurred between those periods.

claim: "Since 2004, more than 2,000 suspected terrorists have legally purchased weapons in the United States."
rationale: There is no reliable, publicly available government evidence showing that over 2,000 people identified as "suspected terrorists" have legally purchased firearms in the U.S. since 2004. Fact-checkers have found that the frequently cited figures stem from misread or extrapolated data and from inconsistent definitions of who counts as a "suspected terrorist," and official background-check systems do not corroborate that precise total.

claim: Says Pope Francis "was arrested Saturday in connection with an 80-count indictment of charges including possession of child pornography, human trafficking, incest, possession of drug paraphernalia and felony fraud."
rationale: No credible news organizations or official Vatican communications have reported that Pope Francis was arrested on any charges, and an arrest of the pope would be a globally major, well-documented event. The claim appears to be a fabricated social-media rumor conflating or inventing allegations; there is no evidence supporting an 80-count indictment or such charges against him.

claim: "People are starting to enter ERs with fungal lung infections from wearing masks!!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or public-health data showing a surge of ER visits for fungal lung infections caused by wearing masks. Fungal lung infections are typically seen in people with weakened immune systems or with specific environmental exposures, and major health authorities (CDC/WHO) have not reported masks as a cause. While improperly cleaned or very damp masks can be unhygienic and cause skin irritation or bacterial growth, they have not been shown to cause fungal pneumonia in the general population.

claim: "There hasn't really been a lot of net growth in the federal workforce when you compare it to say, 1990."
rationale: By common measures the U.S. federal civilian workforce has been roughly flat since 1990, with total on‑roll civilian employee counts generally in the ~2.0–2.3 million range, so there has not been large net growth. Whether the claim is true can depend on which pools are counted (civilian vs. military, Postal Service, contractors) and the exact endpoints chosen.

claim: The "moon has more than 250 million citizens."
rationale: There are no permanent human residents or recognized citizens on the Moon; only a few dozen astronauts have visited (e.g., Apollo missions) and no population remotely near 250 million exists. International space law and current records show no sovereign or populated lunar colonies that would create citizens.

claim: "Malia Obama just got arrested buying cocaine"
rationale: There are no credible news reports, official police statements, or public records indicating Malia Obama was arrested for buying cocaine. High-profile arrests of public figures are widely reported by multiple trusted outlets, and this claim appears to be a viral rumor without substantiation.

claim: "Biden resigned, Pelosi was detained."
rationale: There are no credible reports or official records that President Joe Biden resigned or that former Speaker Nancy Pelosi was detained. Such high‑profile events would have been widely and continuously reported by major national and international news outlets and reflected in government records, but they did not occur through at least mid‑2024. The claim appears to be misinformation or conflation with other stories.

claim: "There are no tax increases in this debt limit bill. Period."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim about an unspecified "debt limit bill," which makes it unverifiable as written. Historically, debt-limit or deficit-relief packages sometimes include tax or revenue-related provisions (changes to credits, fees, enforcement, or sunsets) that can affect revenue even if they do not raise headline tax rates, so the blanket "Period" is misleading without examining the specific bill text and scoring.

claim: Says 1 in 5 Texans did not have health insurance coverage before the pandemic, and now "nearly 1 in 3 Texans under the age of 65 don’t have access to health care insurance."
rationale: The first part is roughly accurate: before the COVID-19 pandemic Texas’s uninsured rate was about one in five residents. The second part is misleading and likely false — recent data do not show that nearly one in three Texans under 65 lack health insurance; overall uninsured rates in Texas for the nonelderly have been in the high‑teens to low‑twenties percent range, not ~33%.

claim: The Baucus health care bill would require taxes on medical devices such as X-ray machines, female condoms, HIV tests and surgical needles.
rationale: The claim misstates how proposed taxes would work. Baucus-related drafts and the later 2010 law referenced an excise-style levy on medical device industry sales (applied to manufacturers/sellers), not a direct consumer tax on items like X-ray machines, female condoms, HIV tests or surgical needles; political ads that listed such consumer items were misleading.

claim: "Heidi Cruz, Ted’s wife, is managing director of Goldman Sachs. They oversee the Texas utilities."
rationale: While Heidi Cruz has worked as a managing director at Goldman Sachs in the past, the claim that she or Goldman Sachs "oversee the Texas utilities" is incorrect. Oversight and regulation of Texas utilities are handled by the Texas Public Utility Commission and local utility boards and regulators, not by Heidi Cruz or her husband Ted Cruz.

claim: Data show that more white people than Black people are shot and killed by police.
rationale: In absolute counts reported by major U.S. police-shooting databases (e.g., Washington Post, Mapping Police Violence) more white people have been recorded as shot and killed by police than Black people, reflecting the larger white population. However, Black people are killed at a higher rate per capita, so the statement is true only for raw totals, not for risk-adjusted comparisons.

claim: A government analysis shows under a proposed transportation tax, "metro Atlanta will create or support an additional 200,000 new jobs, including jobs that are maintained year over year."
rationale: I could not find a verifiable government analysis showing that a proposed transportation tax would produce or sustain an additional 200,000 net new jobs in metro Atlanta as ongoing year-over-year employment. Official regional and state studies typically report much smaller long‑term employment impacts and often separate temporary construction jobs from permanent positions, so the 200,000 figure appears to conflates different job categories or overstates sustained job creation.

claim: Says President Barack Obama released a statement on the "death of brother Robin Williams before ... a statement on brother Michael Brown."
rationale: President Obama publicly released condolences on the death of Robin Williams (Aug 11, 2014) before he offered a public presidential comment specifically about the killing of Michael Brown, which drew public remarks from the President several days later and prompted criticism for the perceived delay. Media coverage at the time noted the sequence and criticism that Obama addressed the celebrity death prior to making a personal statement about Brown.

claim: President Joe Biden cut "$30 billion to Black colleges and universities."
rationale: There is no record that President Biden enacted a $30 billion cut to Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs). The Biden administration has generally proposed or supported increased funding for HBCUs and related programs, and the specific $30 billion figure does not correspond to any known Biden policy action or signed legislation cutting HBCU funding.

claim: John Boozman supports "privatizing Social Security"
rationale: There is no clear, consistent public record showing Senator John Boozman has endorsed outright privatizing Social Security. While he has generally supported conservative proposals to reform Social Security and Republican ideas about private accounts have circulated, the specific claim that he supports 'privatizing Social Security' as an explicit policy position is not clearly documented.

claim: "People were hopeless. Sixty percent of the population, 70 percent of the population wanted to live somewhere else. . . . By the time I left, 70 percent wanted to stay."
rationale: The statement asserts precise percentages about public opinion (60–70% wanting to leave, later 70% wanting to stay) but gives no country, timeframe, speaker, or source. Without identifiable, contemporaneous polling data or documentation showing that exact swing in majority sentiment, the claim is not verifiable and should not be treated as factual.

claim: Says "about 100,000 kids in this country leave their home state and go to another state to be educated. Out of that 100,000 young people, 30,000 of them are from New Jersey, by far the largest amount."
rationale: The numeric claim is inconsistent with national education enrollment data: far more than 100,000 U.S. students attend school out-of-state (college enrollment figures show hundreds of thousands to millions moving between states), so the 100,000 total is too low. Likewise, it is implausible that New Jersey alone supplies 30,000 of those and is “by far the largest” source given larger states (e.g., California, Texas) produce many more out-migrating students in absolute terms.

claim: "Newgard owed more than $13,000 for unpaid taxes on his $1 million Milwaukie apartment complex."
rationale: I cannot verify this specific assertion from available knowledge: the statement names a person 'Newgard' and a precise tax amount and property valuation, but I have no corroborating public records or reputable news reports in my training data that confirm those figures. Claims about individual property tax debts require checking local county tax assessor records or reliable reporting to be confirmed. Without that evidence, the claim should not be treated as established fact.

claim: "I'm probably one of the four or five best-known Americans in the world."
rationale: The statement is a subjective, self-assessed claim about global fame that cannot be objectively verified as stated. Whether someone ranks among the 'four or five best-known Americans' depends on specific metrics, time, and population sampled; no evidence is provided to support such a precise global ranking.

claim: "The national unemployment rate has been above 8 percent for a record 36 months."
rationale: The statement is false as written: it provides no country or timeframe and there is no clear evidence that any major nation's headline unemployment rate has remained above 8% continuously for a record 36 months in recent data. For example, U.S. monthly unemployment did exceed 8% for periods around the Great Recession but did not produce a widely reported continuous 36-month record above 8%; other countries' histories vary and would require specification.

claim: Says more Republicans than Democrats voted for the Wall Street bailouts.
rationale: Key congressional votes on the 2008 bailout (the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act/TARP) were carried largely by Democrats while many Republicans opposed them; the final House and Senate tallies show more Democratic yes votes than Republican yes votes. Thus the statement that more Republicans than Democrats voted for the Wall Street bailouts is incorrect.

claim: "One of the first nurses to receive the vaccine in AL is now dead."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or authoritative reporting that one of the first nurses vaccinated in “AL” (commonly Alabama) has died as a consequence of receiving the vaccine. Major news outlets and public health authorities did not confirm such a death, and similar claims circulated as misinformation and were debunked or found unsubstantiated.

claim: "Wisconsin lost more jobs over the past 12 months than any other state."
rationale: The claim gives no specific 12-month period and thus cannot be verified as stated. State-level job gains and losses are reported monthly and fluctuate; without a defined date range one cannot determine that Wisconsin lost more jobs than every other state. To establish the claim would require checking Bureau of Labor Statistics monthly state employment change data for the exact 12‑month window.

claim: California has seen a "56 percent decline in the gun murder rate" since the 1990s.
rationale: The precise claim is not reliably supported because percentage changes in California’s firearm homicide rate depend strongly on the chosen baseline year in the 1990s and the end year and data source. While firearm homicides fell substantially from the mid-1990s to the mid-2010s, different official series (CDC, FBI, California DOJ) produce different percentage declines and recent increases around 2020–2021 reduce the cumulative drop, so an unqualified '56 percent decline since the 1990s' is misleading.

claim: "Kyle Rittenhouse files $400 million suit against CNN!"
rationale: There are no credible news reports or court records indicating Kyle Rittenhouse has filed a $400 million lawsuit against CNN. While Rittenhouse and his lawyers have threatened or pursued various legal actions in the past, a $400 million filing specifically against CNN has not been substantiated by mainstream reporting or public court dockets.

claim: "Marco Rubio made it clear: Not only does he think Donald Trump is a con man, he went on to say he doesn't trust Donald Trump with the nuclear codes."
rationale: I am not aware of any verifiable instance in which Marco Rubio both labeled Donald Trump a 'con man' and explicitly said he 'doesn't trust Donald Trump with the nuclear codes.' Rubio did sharply criticize Trump at times during the 2016 campaign, but the specific quotation about not trusting him with nuclear codes is more commonly attributed to other Republican figures and appears not to be documented as Rubio's remark.

claim: "Teenage births cost Texas taxpayers $1.1 billion in health care, foster care and lost tax revenue in 2010 alone."
rationale: This figure comes from a 2011 state-level analysis (published by organizations focused on preventing teen pregnancy) that estimated public costs attributable to births to teens in Texas in 2010 at about $1.1 billion, including Medicaid/health care costs, foster care, and reduced tax revenue. The claim matches that published estimate, though it reflects the report’s specific methodology and attribution rules rather than a single universally agreed accounting of all economic effects.

claim: Says as GOP was picking a convention city, "I recommended Ohio."
rationale: The claim is underspecified (no speaker, date, or which GOP convention) and I find no clear, verifiable record of a public figure saying simply "I recommended Ohio" in connection with the Republican Party selecting a convention city. Without an identifiable source or context this statement cannot be confirmed as factual. Because the assertion is ambiguous and unverified, it is treated as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: Says the logo of a porn website appeared during a CNN broadcast.
rationale: The claim is vague and provides no specific date, program, screenshot, or corroborating evidence; major broadcast errors like a porn-site logo on CNN would likely have been widely reported and documented. In absence of verifiable details or independent confirmation, the claim cannot be treated as true.

claim: The snow is government-generated or fake.
rationale: Snow is normally a natural form of precipitation formed when atmospheric water vapor freezes; governments do not generate widespread 'fake' snow. While cloud seeding exists as a limited weather-modification technique and ski areas produce artificial snow locally, these are localized and do not support a broad claim that snow in general is government-made or fake.

claim: Marco Rubio's "income skyrocketed while his power increased."
rationale: The claim is vague and not supported by clear public evidence: while Marco Rubio’s reported income and assets have changed over time (for example from salary, investments, and occasional book or speaking revenue), there is no clear, well-documented record that his income “skyrocketed” in direct parallel with an objectively measured rise in political power. ‘‘Skyrocketed’’ and ‘‘power increased’’ are subjective and without a defined timeframe or metric the statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: "There is already a mosque four blocks away."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific nearby mosque but gives no location or time, so it cannot be verified as presented. Such proximity claims are location-dependent and may be true in some places and false in others, but without local evidence (address, map, or witness) the claim is unsupported.

claim: Photo shows R. Kelly being released from prison in 2021.
rationale: There are no credible reports or court records showing R. Kelly was released from prison in 2021; he remained in custody on federal charges around that time and was later convicted and incarcerated. Photos claiming to show a 2021 release have been miscaptioned or are of other times/people.

claim: Says Marco Rubio endorsed Obamacare for his own family.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Marco Rubio publicly ‘endorsed Obamacare for his own family.’ Rubio has been a long‑time vocal opponent of the Affordable Care Act and campaigned on repealing it; claims that he personally signed his family up for ACA marketplace coverage are unsupported and likely stem from mischaracterizations of his family's insurance arrangements.

claim: Microsoft and Bill Gates created a 1999 video game called "Omikron."
rationale: The 1999 game Omikron: The Nomad Soul was developed by Quantic Dream and directed by David Cage and published by Eidos Interactive; Microsoft and Bill Gates were not the creators. Bill Gates/Microsoft are not credited with creating or developing the title.

claim: Kelly Loeffler has a "long history of donating to abortion-on-demand Democrats."
rationale: Public campaign contribution records and reporting show Kelly Loeffler and her husband have made bipartisan donations over time, but there is not clear evidence of a long-standing pattern specifically giving to Democrats defined as supporting 'abortion-on-demand.' Characterizing her as having a long history of donating to such Democrats overstates and misframes the donation record.

claim: Says Marco Rubio tweeted a verse from the New Testament to shame "his own constituents for flocking to Trump rally."
rationale: I am not aware of any credible reporting or primary-source evidence that Marco Rubio tweeted a New Testament verse specifically to shame his own constituents for attending a Trump rally. While Rubio has occasionally posted Bible verses on social media, there is no well-documented instance tying such a verse to an effort to shame constituents for flocking to a Trump event.

claim: "We've got to find 2 billion gallons (of water per day) between now and 2025."
rationale: The statement is unverified and lacks necessary context (who 'we' refers to, which geographic area, and what metric this target represents). No authoritative, widely accepted projection or policy mandate states a universal requirement to 'find 2 billion gallons per day by 2025.' Water demand and supply targets vary by region and agency, so the blanket claim is not supported as stated.

claim: "There is a 34 percent increase in violent crime in the state of California. … And that’s just within the last year."
rationale: Publicly available statewide crime statistics from the California Department of Justice and FBI Uniform Crime Reporting do not show a 34% increase in overall violent crime in a single year; year-to-year changes in California have been much smaller and vary by category and locality. Claims of a 34% jump typically cherry-pick a particular city, specific crime category, or an atypical short timeframe rather than statewide violent crime over a full year.

claim: "Speaker Rubio supported gun restrictions that included background checks and waiting periods."
rationale: There is no clear record of a 'Speaker Rubio' who publicly supported gun restrictions including background checks and waiting periods. Marco Rubio (the well-known politician) has not been Speaker of the House and his public record shows opposition to broad federal background-check mandates and other major gun-control measures, though he has at times offered limited proposals after mass shootings. The claim conflates titles and overstates support.

claim: "Since 2007 David Jolly has given almost $30,000 to keep Democrats in Congress!"
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim that David Jolly has given almost $30,000 'to keep Democrats in Congress' since 2007. Public contribution records (FEC and watchdog databases) are the authoritative sources for such totals and would be needed to substantiate the precise amount; without checking those, the claim is unverified and likely misleading in wording.

claim: "Puerto Rico mayor facing fraud charges over $3M in federal disaster relief"
rationale: I cannot confirm this specific claim as stated: it lacks a named mayor, date, or source and I find no clear corroboration in widely reported DOJ or news releases. While U.S. authorities have prosecuted some Puerto Rico officials for misuse of federal disaster relief in past years, this exact allegation about a mayor facing fraud charges over $3M is unverified.

claim: " ... following World War II war crime trials were convened. The Japanese were tried and convicted and hung for war crimes committed against American POWs. Among those charges for which they were convicted was waterboarding."
rationale: It is true that many Japanese servicemen were tried and some executed after World War II for atrocities against Allied POWs, but I find no reliable evidence that “waterboarding” as that specific interrogation technique was a named charge that led to convictions and hangings. The postwar indictments more commonly charged killings, beatings, starvation, forced labor, and medical experiments rather than the modern legal label “waterboarding.”

claim: Says there’s an 800 number you can call to track the status of your stimulus check.
rationale: There is no single official 800-number that the IRS provided for tracking stimulus payments; the IRS used the online "Get My Payment" tool and provided limited phone support for specific groups. Many circulated phone-number claims were scams or misunderstandings about general IRS/SSA contact numbers, not a dedicated stimulus-tracking hotline.

claim: Says that according to a report, "the tech sector now drives more than one-quarter of Austin’s economy."
rationale: The tech sector is a major driver of Austin’s economy, but the exact share depends on the metric (jobs, GDP, payroll) and the time period, and I cannot confirm a specific, reputable report that unequivocally states it now drives more than 25% of Austin’s economy. Available public summaries typically describe tech as a large single-sector contributor often cited near—but not consistently above—one quarter, so the claim as stated is not reliably verifiable without the named report.

claim: "Trump revokes Barack Obama’s security clearance."
rationale: There is no record that President Trump formally revoked a security clearance belonging to Barack Obama. Former presidents do not typically hold a standing security clearance as private citizens, and news fact-checks and statements indicate Obama did not have an active clearance to be revoked.

claim: Says 13 Texas universities "have announced or implemented a $10,000 degree."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that as many as 13 Texas universities have announced or implemented a $10,000 bachelor's degree; only a handful of institutions nationwide (and a smaller number in Texas) have promoted low‑cost degree pilots, and the figure 13 appears to conflate different programs, institutions, and definitions. Public reporting and university announcements identify a few Texas examples but not a broad set of 13 schools offering a true $10,000 degree program.

claim: "Nonpartisan experts have consistently ranked Claire one of the most independent senators — right in the middle."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported as stated: it does not identify which 'Claire' is meant, which nonpartisan experts, what metric of 'independence' was used, or the timeframe. Without a specific senator and consistent, cited rankings, the assertion that experts 'consistently ranked Claire one of the most independent — right in the middle' cannot be verified and is self-contradictory (being 'one of the most independent' is not the same as being 'right in the middle').

claim: "‘MAGA bomber’ identified as former CNN employee who donated to heavily to Hillary Clinton."
rationale: The individual widely labeled the “MAGA bomber” in the 2018 mail-bomb spree was Cesar Sayoc, a Florida man and avid Trump supporter, not a former CNN employee. Public records and reporting about Sayoc show he donated to Republican candidates (including Donald Trump) and displayed pro-Trump imagery; there is no evidence he was a CNN employee or a heavy donor to Hillary Clinton.

claim: Says five studies show his tax plan can cut rates and still bring the same revenue without raising taxes on the middle class.
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated because it does not identify who 'his' is or which five studies are being referenced, and broad surveys of tax‑cut proposals and independent analyses typically do not find that cuts fully pay for themselves without offsetting measures. Whether a tax plan can cut rates and keep revenue constant depends heavily on specific assumptions and modeling choices; blanket statements that five studies prove this are therefore misleading.

claim: Says President Dwight Eisenhower "moved 1.5 million illegal immigrants out of this country."
rationale: President Dwight D. Eisenhower's administration did carry out mass removals of Mexican nationals (notably Operation Wetback in 1954), but credible historical estimates do not support the specific figure of 1.5 million removals attributed to him. Most scholarly and official counts put removals/returns in the hundreds of thousands to around one million range, so the 1.5 million number is an overstatement.

claim: Wisconsin was embroiled in a "constitutional crisis" brought on by the Democratic senators fleeing the state for Illinois to block Gov. Scott Walker's budget-repair bill.
rationale: In early 2011 fourteen Wisconsin Democratic state senators left the state for Illinois to deny a quorum and block Gov. Scott Walker’s budget-repair/bill on collective bargaining; that action precipitated a high-profile legislative standoff and was widely described by media, commentators, and some legal observers as a constitutional or legislative crisis. The flight to Illinois directly triggered the quorum impasse and subsequent legal and political confrontations.

claim: "Japan says goodbye Moderna, hello ivermectin."
rationale: There is no evidence that Japan has abandoned Moderna vaccines nationwide or officially adopted ivermectin as a replacement. Japan’s health authorities continue to rely on approved COVID-19 vaccines (including mRNA vaccines) and have not approved ivermectin as standard COVID-19 therapy; occasional temporary suspensions of specific vaccine lots or isolated advocacy for ivermectin do not equate to a national policy change.

claim: Says "city leadership is threatening to lay off police and emergency services personnel to balance the budget."
rationale: The statement provides no specific city, officials, timing, or source and therefore cannot be independently verified. While municipal leaders occasionally propose layoffs of police or emergency personnel to address budget shortfalls, this particular blanket claim is unsubstantiated without evidence.

claim: Republican election challengers were unfairly barred from observing absentee ballot processing and counting in Detroit.
rationale: Reporting and legal reviews from the 2020 Detroit ballot-counting period show Republican challengers were generally present but required to stay at prescribed distances (and behind barriers) for health and security reasons; some individuals were temporarily removed for disruptive behavior. Courts and multiple fact-checks found no evidence of a blanket, unfair prohibition on Republican observation of absentee processing.

claim: Opposition to having a fully elected Chicago Board of Education is in the "super minority."
rationale: The claim asserts a precise political composition (opposition being in a 'super minority') but provides no data and there is no widely reported, consistent evidence showing opposition to an elected Chicago Board of Education is overwhelmingly small. Opinion and voting on this issue have varied by poll, constituency (voters, City Council, parents, teachers), and over time, so the blanket statement is unverified and unlikely to be accurate as stated.

claim: Says Mitt Romney flip-flopped on gun control.
rationale: Romney’s public stance on gun policy has shifted over time: earlier he aligned more with pro-gun positions and received NRA support, while in later years he endorsed measures such as expanded background checks and publicly criticized the NRA. Media outlets and opponents have characterized those changes as a flip‑flop on gun control.

claim: "More people, almost twice as many, pay the penalty or take the waiver than signed up for (Obamacare)."
rationale: Annual ACA marketplace enrollment has been on the order of millions (often 8–12+ million in major open enrollment years), whereas the number of people who actually paid the individual mandate penalty or claimed exemptions is smaller and not nearly double enrollments. Public CMS/IRS data and reporting on enrollments versus penalty/exemption filers do not support the claim that almost twice as many people paid penalties or took waivers than signed up.

claim: In Texas, "sexting is a felony sex offense for teenagers — that can mean up to 10 years in prison."
rationale: The claim is overly broad. While explicit images of minors can be prosecuted under Texas child‑pornography laws as felonies (with long prison ranges in some cases), Texas has enacted statutory exceptions and diversion options so that consensual teen‑to‑teen sexting is often handled as a lesser offense (or via noncriminal alternatives) rather than an automatic felony sex‑offense carrying a 10‑year sentence. Actual charging and penalties depend on the ages involved, distribution, coercion, and other facts.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton’s approval rating went from 70 percent to 52 percent in 18 months.
rationale: The claim gives a specific 70%→52% change over 18 months but does not cite a poll or dates, and there is no widely accepted single polling series that documents that exact shift for Hillary Clinton. Poll results for Clinton varied by pollster, question wording (approval vs. favorability), and timeframe, so the precise claim as stated cannot be verified.

claim: "Yale study: Vaccinated people more likely to be infected than those without the jab."
rationale: There is no credible, widely accepted Yale study concluding generally that vaccinated people are more likely to be infected than unvaccinated people. Most peer‑reviewed studies, including work by researchers at major universities, show COVID vaccines reduce the risk of infection (particularly before waning or variant immune escape), and claims to the contrary have typically misinterpreted limited or biased analyses. Reports that appear to show higher infection rates among the vaccinated usually reflect specific timeframes, variants, waning immunity, differences in prior infection, testing behavior, or other confounders rather than a general vaccine harm finding.

claim: "Whether you like to admit it or not, half our general revenue goes to education."
rationale: The claim is not generally true. Public budgets vary by jurisdiction and level of government, but education rarely consumes half of a government's general revenue; for example, in many U.S. state budgets education is a leading item but typically represents roughly 20–40% of general fund spending, and at the federal level education is a much smaller share. Without specifying which government, year, or definitions, the blanket statement that 'half our general revenue goes to education' cannot be supported.

claim: Says Tom Barrett "voted to ban 15 different kinds of guns, even a lot of common deer rifles."
rationale: The claim blends inaccuracy and misleading framing. While Tom Barrett has supported assault-weapons restrictions in the past, those laws targeted specific semi‑automatic, military‑style firearms (the 1994 federal ban listed around 19 named models and/or categories) and focused on cosmetic/features, not banning “a lot of common deer rifles” such as typical bolt‑action hunting rifles. The specific figure “15 different kinds” is not an accurate characterization of the law’s scope.

claim: "794 law enforcement officers have fallen in the line of duty since B.H. Obama took office, with no special recognition from the White House."
rationale: The precise count of line-of-duty law-enforcement deaths depends on the source and date, and the widely used Officer Down Memorial Page (ODMP) shows different cumulative totals than the quoted 794 for the span of Barack H. Obama’s presidency. Furthermore, the White House regularly issued proclamations, statements, and hosted or participated in memorial events (such as National Peace Officers Memorial Day) recognizing fallen officers during Obama’s tenure, so the claim that there was “no special recognition” is inaccurate. Because the claim mixes a specific numeric assertion with a categorical claim about recognition, it does not hold up.

claim: President Barack Obama "is the first president to keep a dog-trainer on retainer for $102,000 a year at taxpayer expense."
rationale: The claim is false. The frequently-cited $102,000 figure referred to a federal employee’s salary whose duties included caring for the Obamas’ dog, not a standalone private “retainer” paid solely to a dog trainer, and previous administrations have also had taxpayer-funded staff or handlers who care for presidential pets. Thus Obama was not uniquely the first president to have publicly funded pet care.

claim: "Expanding Medicaid, which if we had done at the beginning of the Abbott administration, would have brought in $100 billion to this state's economy."
rationale: The claim gives a precise $100 billion figure for an unspecified period and definition of “brought in,” but there is no widely accepted analysis that exactly supports that number for the state if expansion had started with Governor Abbott’s term. While Medicaid expansion does draw federal matching dollars and typically produces measurable economic gains, estimates for any single state vary greatly depending on the timeframe, whether one counts federal reimbursements, total economic output, or cumulative health-care spending. Because the claim is specific and lacks clear sourcing or timeframe, it cannot be verified as stated.

claim: The debt limit deal "allows President Obama to borrow unlimited amounts of money."
rationale: Debt-limit legislation either raises or temporarily suspends the statutory borrowing cap set by Congress; it does not give the president unilateral authority to borrow unlimited sums indefinitely. Any increase or suspension is constrained by the terms of the specific deal (amounts or dates) and Congress remains the body that authorizes federal borrowing.

claim: "During my administration, funding for education has increased by over $930 million."
rationale: The claim provides no identifying context (which administration, jurisdiction, baseline period, or which education funding categories are counted), so it cannot be independently verified as stated. Confirming an increase of a specific dollar amount requires comparing official budget or audited expenditure records over defined years; without that information the claim is unprovable.

claim: "Twitter reaches only 15 percent of the population."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and false as a blanket claim: globally Twitter/X has far fewer than 15% of the world’s population as users (hundreds of millions vs ~8 billion people, ~5–6%), while in some countries (for example U.S. adults) survey-measured usage is around 20–25%. Reach varies substantially by country, age group, definition (monthly active users vs unique reach) and time, so a single 15% figure is misleading.

claim: "$3 billion over the next five years will be taken out of our public schools and be put into vouchers."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as presented because it claims a specific $3 billion transfer without identifying which government, law, or enacted budget would make that shift. Budgetary reallocations are enacted via specific legislation or appropriations and vary by jurisdiction; absent a cited bill or official budget showing that exact amount redirected to vouchers over five years, the claim cannot be verified and is therefore false as a general assertion.

claim: "60 percent of all Americans do not want to see Planned Parenthood defunded."
rationale: Polling on whether Americans want Planned Parenthood defunded varies by pollster, question wording, and timing; there is no single definitive nationwide figure that 60% oppose defunding. Some polls have shown a majority opposing defunding at certain times, but results differ and the claim presents a precise percentage without a source or timeframe.
