claim: "Interior deportations under Obama were down 40 percent and at a nine-year low."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While ICE ‘interior removals’ declined in some years during the Obama administration, the specific summary that they were ‘down 40 percent and at a nine-year low’ depends on which years and removal categories are compared and does not match DHS/ICE annual removal statistics or contemporaneous fact-checks as a simple, accurate statement.

claim: "We confer more PhDs each year than any other university in America except Berkeley."
rationale: The statement claims a specific university is the second-largest conferrer of PhDs in the U.S. behind Berkeley. Public data (NSF Survey of Earned Doctorates and institutional reports) show that several universities — e.g., Michigan, Harvard, Wisconsin–Madison, Texas, UCLA, and others — commonly award as many or more research doctorates in a given year, and rankings vary by year and by how doctorates are counted. Without a named institution and year the blanket claim is not reliably true.

claim: "Millions have died from COVID injections."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that COVID-19 vaccines caused millions of deaths. Large-scale safety monitoring and peer-reviewed epidemiological studies have found only very rare fatal adverse events plausibly linked to vaccines, while vaccines prevented many COVID-19 deaths; passive reporting systems contain unverified temporal associations, not proof of causation.

claim: "As the election tracker FiveThirtyEight has reported, whoever wins Pennsylvania will be our next President."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement without a date or context. FiveThirtyEight sometimes identifies a single “tipping‑point” state in its election models, but whether Pennsylvania was described that way depends on the specific model and moment in time; it is not generally true that FiveThirtyEight has reported "whoever wins Pennsylvania will be our next President" in all circumstances. Without a timestamp or specific article, the claim is misleading.

claim: North Carolina’s health department is "telling hospitals that if they decide to do elective surgeries, they won’t be eligible to receive (protective equipment) from the state."
rationale: North Carolina’s health officials issued guidance during COVID-19 that prioritized PPE allocation to facilities treating COVID patients and urged postponing elective procedures to conserve supplies, but they did not issue a blanket rule that hospitals performing elective surgeries would be categorically ineligible to receive state PPE. Contemporary reporting described prioritization or de-prioritization, which can be misread as an absolute ban, but the state policy was about allocation priorities rather than an outright refusal of supplies.

claim: "Do this research … watch how much crime picks up if you take away [football]."
rationale: The statement implies a general causal effect that removing football will reliably increase crime. Empirical research on the relationship between organized sports/events and crime is mixed and highly context-dependent; some studies find reductions in certain crimes when sports or youth programs are present, while others find increases in public disorder around events or no consistent effect. A blanket claim that taking away football will cause crime to rise is not supported as a general fact.

claim: Promotes a chart saying that Barack Obama has "increased the debt" by 16 percent, compared to George W. Bush, who increased it by 115 percent.
rationale: The claim is misleading: the cited percentages depend on how debt is measured and the exact start/end dates. Under standard measures used by budget analysts (total federal debt or debt held by the public over each president’s full terms), Obama’s presidency did not produce only a 16% increase and Bush’s increase is not unambiguously 115%—different baselines and inclusion/exclusion of intra‑governmental debt produce widely different percentages.

claim: Under President Barack Obama’s jobs bill, states would no longer have to lay off teachers, firefighters and police officers.
rationale: Obama proposed jobs bills that included federal aid to states aimed at preventing layoffs of teachers, firefighters and police, but the legislation did not and could not unilaterally guarantee that states "would no longer have to" lay off those workers. The proposals required Congressional approval, provided limited temporary funds, and states would still make final budget choices, so layoffs were not categorically eliminated by the bills.

claim: "There have been more than 300 mass shootings in the United States this year – more than any other country in the world."
rationale: The statement is not reliably verifiable as written because key terms and the time frame are ambiguous. U.S. trackers using broad definitions (for example 4+ shot) do report hundreds of incidents in some years, but counts vary widely by definition and source, and comprehensive international data are inconsistent, so the claim that there have been >300 “this year” and that this is more than any other country cannot be confirmed without a specific definition and calendar year.

claim: Says Mitt Romney opposes requiring employers to cover contraception and would eliminate funding for Planned Parenthood.
rationale: Mitt Romney publicly opposed requiring employers to provide contraception coverage (advocating conscience exemptions) and during his 2012 presidential campaign pledged to end federal funding for Planned Parenthood. These positions were repeatedly stated in his campaign speeches and policy proposals.

claim: "Education Secretary Betsy DeVos owes Ohio $5.3 million for campaign finance violations and Mike DeWine's office refuses to collect the fine."
rationale: There is no reliable record that Education Secretary Betsy DeVos personally owes Ohio $5.3 million for campaign finance violations, nor credible reporting that Ohio Governor Mike DeWine’s office is refusing to collect such a fine. High-value, state-level campaign-finance judgments are widely reported and would have been covered in national and Ohio media; no such judgment or refusal-to-enforce by DeWine’s office is documented in available public records.

claim: "In New Jersey, Gov. Christie vetoed legislation to extend early voting."
rationale: I am not aware of a confirmed action by Gov. Chris Christie specifically vetoing legislation to extend early voting in New Jersey. Major reporting and the eventual establishment of broader early voting occurred after Christie left office under Gov. Murphy, and Christie’s known vetoes concerned other election-related measures rather than a statewide early-voting expansion.

claim: "Biden and most Democrats want to cap insulin prices at $35 per month. All 50 Republicans in the Senate are opposed to it."
rationale: It is true that President Biden has publicly supported a $35 monthly cap on insulin and most Democratic lawmakers have backed proposals to limit insulin costs, but the claim that all 50 Senate Republicans are opposed is incorrect. Republican senators’ positions have varied by specific bill and timing, and at least some Republicans have supported or engaged with measures to lower insulin costs or Medicare-focused caps rather than uniformly opposing every $35-cap proposal.

claim: "Fox News barely covered (the Duggar family) scandal until Megyn Kelly was able to secure this interview."
rationale: Contemporaneous media reporting and analyses noted that Fox News devoted relatively little attention to the Duggar revelations compared with other outlets at first, and Fox’s coverage increased markedly after Megyn Kelly secured and aired an on‑camera interview with Jim Bob and Michelle Duggar. While “barely covered” is somewhat subjective, the consensus reporting describes a clear uptick in Fox’s engagement once Kelly’s exclusive interview ran.

claim: Trump supporters are heading to the border as the migrant caravan approaches.
rationale: The claim is presented as a current, general fact but lacks any specific time, place, or sourcing and cannot be independently verified. While there have been past instances where some conservative or Trump-aligned groups mobilized to U.S. border areas when migrant caravans were reported, this broad present-tense assertion is unsubstantiated without contemporaneous, local reporting or evidence.

claim: The United States has "the highest corporate tax rate in the free world."
rationale: This is incorrect in modern context: the U.S. federal corporate tax rate was cut to 21% by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, and even when combined with state corporate taxes the typical top U.S. rate (~25–26%) is not the highest among developed countries. Rankings also differ if one looks at statutory vs combined vs effective tax rates, but the United States does not currently have the single highest corporate tax rate in the so-called 'free world.'

claim: Federal law for Obamacare navigators "does not bar — or even require screening for — convicted felons, including individuals convicted of identity theft or fraud."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act statute and the initial HHS navigator regulations did not impose a blanket prohibition on convicted felons nor mandate universal federal criminal-background checks for navigators. HHS left background-check requirements largely to states and to individual marketplaces, so federal law itself did not bar or require screening for people convicted of identity theft or fraud.

claim: There are twice as many gun shops as McDonald’s in the United States.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that gun shops number twice McDonald’s locations. The U.S. has roughly on the order of tens of thousands of McDonald’s restaurants (about 13,000–14,000 in recent years), and ATF records show tens of thousands of licensed firearm dealers/FFLs, but many FFLs are manufacturers, gunsmiths, pawnbrokers, or inactive businesses rather than retail “gun shops,” so the claim of exactly twice as many gun shops is unsupported.

claim: "I am very proud that over my almost 30 years of public service I have had no scandals."
rationale: This claim is not verifiable as presented because the speaker is not identified and 'scandals' is undefined; verifying a decades-long, scandal-free record requires checking public records and media for a specific person and timeframe. Without that identifying information or independent evidence, the statement cannot be confirmed and is treated as false by default.

claim: Langevin votes "the party line about 98 percent of the time."
rationale: The statement gives a precise 98% figure without a timeframe or source. Publicly reported “votes with party” metrics (from datasets like GovTrack, FiveThirtyEight, and ProPublica) vary by year and methodology and do not support a single, career‑wide 98% figure for Rep. Langevin; while he often voted with his party, exact percentages fluctuate and a blanket 98% claim is unsupported without specifying the period.

claim: Says Ohio Gov. John Kasich "got lucky with a thing called fracking," which "is why Ohio is doing well."
rationale: While the Utica/Marcellus fracking boom did boost Ohio energy production, jobs, and tax receipts, attributing Ohio's overall improvement solely to 'luck' from fracking and saying that is why the state is doing well is an oversimplification. Kasich pursued pro-drilling policies that facilitated development, and broader factors — manufacturing trends, national economic recovery, and other state policies — also affected Ohio's performance.

claim: Says in "our region," 2011 was worst drought year ever recorded.
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as written because 'our region' is unspecified and drought severity is measured differently across places and metrics. While 2011 was a severe drought year in some areas (e.g., parts of the Horn of Africa and the U.S.), it was not universally the worst year on record everywhere; establishing 'worst ever' requires a defined region and standardized drought metric.

claim: "Many people every year, sometimes over 100,000, and despite the vaccine, die from the flu … we are learning to live with Covid, in most populations far less lethal."
rationale: Global estimates attribute hundreds of thousands of respiratory deaths to seasonal influenza each year (so counts well over 100,000 are common) even though vaccines reduce but do not eliminate flu deaths. At the same time, widespread immunity from vaccination and prior infection plus the dominance of less virulent Omicron-era variants have substantially reduced COVID infection-fatality rates in many populations, and many countries are managing COVID as an endemic illness, though risks remain for vulnerable groups.

claim: New York is "leading the nation with the lowest imprisonment rate of any large state"
rationale: Available state-by-state incarceration statistics do not support that New York is unequivocally the lowest-imprisonment large state. Several other populous states (for example New Jersey and Minnesota in recent years) have had lower imprisonment rates per 100,000 residents, and rankings depend on the year and population threshold used for “large state.”

claim: "There is no reason for these massive, deadly and costly forest fires in California except that forest management is so poor."
rationale: The assertion that poor forest management is the only reason for California’s large, deadly, and costly wildfires is incorrect. While forest and fuel management practices matter, scientists and fire agencies attribute recent severe fires to multiple causes including climate-driven drought and heat, prolonged tree mortality from pests, strong regional winds, increased development in the wildland-urban interface, and ignition sources such as lightning, power lines, and arson.

claim: The "Franklin scandal" broke in 1989 "when hundreds of children were apparently flown around the US to be abused by high ranking ‘Establishment’ members."
rationale: While sensational claims about a nationwide Franklin child-abuse ring surfaced in the late 1980s, multiple official investigations and a grand jury found no credible evidence that hundreds of children were flown around the U.S. to be abused by high‑ranking establishment figures. The underlying financial crimes at the Franklin Credit Union were real, but the trafficking/elite-abuse conspiracy allegations were investigated and largely discredited.

claim: Says Roy Moore "has advocated getting the federal government out of health care altogether, which means doing away with Medicaid, which means doing away with Medicare."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable record that Roy Moore explicitly called for abolishing Medicare and Medicaid outright. Moore campaigned for removing federal involvement in health care (repealing Obamacare and increasing state control), but public statements and policy positions reported at the time stop short of a direct, unambiguous call to eliminate Medicare and Medicaid entirely. The claim conflates general opposition to federal health programs with an explicit advocacy to end those entitlement programs.

claim: Photo of vaccine package with 2018 date stamp shows COVID-19 outbreak was planned.
rationale: A single photo of a vaccine package stamped 2018 does not prove the COVID-19 outbreak was planned. SARS-CoV-2 was first identified in late 2019 and COVID-19 vaccines were developed after that; package dates commonly indicate manufacture or expiry, can refer to different vaccines or lots, and do not demonstrate intent or foreknowledge.

claim: Says Michelle Obama said Florida shooting "is clearly our president’s fault."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable news reporting that Michelle Obama said the quoted line; the phrase appears to be a fabricated or misattributed social-media quote. While Michelle Obama has spoken against gun violence, she did not publicly state that a Florida shooting "is clearly our president’s fault."

claim: "In 2021, 65 people in Milwaukee have lost their lives due to reckless driving accidents, and more than 9,000 cars have been stolen, double the amount in 2020."
rationale: The precise figures in the claim are not corroborated by publicly available Milwaukee Police Department or statewide traffic-fatality data: reported traffic deaths and crash classifications for 2021 do not clearly match '65 reckless driving deaths', and while vehicle thefts rose in 2021, authoritative sources do not support the exact 'more than 9,000' and 'double 2020' formulation without additional context. The statement appears to conflate different categories (reckless-driving deaths vs total traffic fatalities) and lacks a cited source for these exact counts.

claim: "Some people are going to die from the vaccine directly. But a large number of people are going to start getting horribly sick and get all kinds of autoimmune diseases."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that vaccines are causing large numbers of direct deaths or triggering a widespread wave of autoimmune diseases. Clinical trials and extensive real-world safety monitoring show serious adverse events and vaccine-related deaths are rare and investigated, and overall benefits vastly outweigh identified risks.

claim: "5.7 million -- that’s how many illegal immigrants might have voted" in 2008.
rationale: The 5.7 million figure is a misapplication of survey results and not supported by evidence. It stems from extrapolating a small number of self-reported noncitizen respondents in surveys (many of whom likely misreported their status) to the entire electorate; re-analyses, official checks and multiple fact-checkers have found virtually no evidence that millions of noncitizens voted in 2008. Noncitizen/illegal-immigrant voting in U.S. federal elections appears to have been extremely rare, not on the order of millions.

claim: "State Rep. Kathleen Peters has a 100 percent pro-abortion voting record – even voting against a ban on sex-selection abortions."
rationale: I cannot find clear, corroborated evidence that Kathleen Peters had a literal 100% "pro-abortion" voting record or that she definitively voted against a sex-selection abortion ban. Absolute claims about a 100% record are unusual and require a specific, enumerated list of votes; available public information indicates mixed or contested characterizations rather than an all-or-nothing record. Without specific roll-call citations, the blanket statement is not supported.

claim: "The average homeowner spends more than $2,000 each year on energy costs – more than on either real estate taxes or homeowners insurance."
rationale: The claim is not reliably true. U.S. household energy spending can be around $1,500–$2,000 per year depending on fuel prices and climate, but average annual property taxes paid by homeowners (and thus for many homeowners nationwide) commonly exceed $2,000, while homeowners insurance is typically lower than taxes but varies. Because property tax burdens vary widely by state and year, it’s incorrect to assert generally that energy costs exceed both taxes and insurance for the average homeowner.

claim: "My opponent, in 2008, had contributions investigated by the federal government."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as written because it does not identify who 'my opponent' is or what contributions were allegedly investigated in 2008. Without a specific name, agency, or documented report, there is no evidence to confirm a federal investigation, so the statement is treated as unproven and therefore labeled false for fact-checking. If a named individual and sources were provided, contemporary federal records and reputable news coverage could be checked to confirm or refute it.

claim: "We have that program where immigrants come here and they have to bring a million dollars in order to get a green card if they’re going to create jobs."
rationale: This describes the EB-5 immigrant-investor program, which does grant green cards in exchange for creating jobs through capital investment, but the claim that immigrants "have to bring a million dollars" is imprecise. Historically the minimum was $1,000,000 (with a $500,000 lower threshold for targeted employment areas), and regulatory changes raised the floors (e.g., to $1.8M/$900k in 2019); requirements vary by program rules and over time.

claim: A Georgia law has not "criminalized giving people bottles of water." It pertains to political organizations.
rationale: This is incorrect: Georgia’s 2021 voting law (commonly called SB 202) does restrict distribution of food and drink to voters waiting in line by third parties, including outside political or advocacy groups, while exempting poll workers, family members and those providing official assistance. So it did criminalize handing out bottles of water in the specific context of outside actors distributing refreshments near polling places, rather than broadly criminalizing anyone giving water.

claim: Says Kamala Harris said there will be "a federal tax on your home for reparations."
rationale: There is no credible record of Kamala Harris saying the exact phrase 'a federal tax on your home for reparations.' Her public statements and policy positions on reparations have not included proposing a specific federal homeowners' tax, and fact-checkers have not verified this quote.

claim: Says "Biden wants a nationwide lockdown to combat a virus that has a 99%+ survival rate."
rationale: The claim is misleading on both points: President Biden did not call for a single nationwide lockdown policy and instead promoted targeted public-health measures, mask use, testing, and vaccination while leaving many restrictions to states. The statement that the virus has a '99%+ survival rate' is an oversimplification—COVID-19 risk varies greatly by age, health status, and time period (variant, treatments, vaccination), and infection fatality estimates for some groups and periods exceed 1%.

claim: Bernie Sanders’s plan is "to raise your taxes to 90 percent."
rationale: Bernie Sanders has not proposed a plan to raise taxes to 90% for the general public; his policy proposals call for higher taxes on the wealthy (higher marginal rates, a wealth tax, higher corporate taxes, and payroll/income changes to fund programs) but not anywhere near a 90% tax rate. Claims of a 90% rate are hyperbolic and misrepresent his published proposals.

claim: U.S. sanctions mean "Cuba can’t trade with any country or any company whatsoever."
rationale: This is false because U.S. sanctions and the embargo do not categorically prevent Cuba from trading with every country or company. The measures primarily restrict U.S. persons, U.S.-origin goods, use of the U.S. financial system, and can deter third parties via threat of secondary penalties, but many countries and firms legally trade with Cuba (including exemptions for food, medicine, and humanitarian goods).

claim: Says under Mayor Cory Booker, Newark has seen "violent crime up five years in a row, murder up five years in a row."
rationale: Official crime data and contemporaneous reporting do not show a consistent five-year straight increase in both violent crime and murders during Cory Booker’s mayoralty. Violent-crime and homicide totals in Newark fluctuated year-to-year with some increases and some decreases rather than an unbroken five-year upward trend; fact-checkers have rejected the claim as inaccurate or misleading.

claim: Says President Donald Trump is one of "only three people that won the Ellis Island Award for their work within the black community."
rationale: There is no evidence that Donald Trump is one of only three people to receive the Ellis Island Medal of Honor specifically for work within the Black community. The Ellis Island awards have been given to many honorees over decades for a wide range of ethnic and community service contributions, and multiple recipients have been honored for work benefiting African‑American communities, so the "only three" claim is incorrect.

claim: An election worker in Georgia threw away a ballot.
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify as stated because it gives no date, location (county), or source. While isolated incidents involving ballots have been reported and investigated in Georgia in various election cycles, there is no specific, verifiable incident tied to this blanket assertion without further details.

claim: Obama "voted against funding our troops."
rationale: The claim is misleading: Barack Obama did vote against certain bills or amendments that contained war funding because he opposed the policy or structure of those measures, but he also supported multiple appropriations and supplemental bills that provided funding for U.S. troops. Saying he simply "voted against funding our troops" implies a blanket refusal of troop funding, which is not supported by his Senate voting record and public statements that he backed troop funding while opposing specific proposals.

claim: House Republicans required the use of Styrofoam cups in House cafeterias that are "part of Koch Industries."
rationale: There is no evidence that House cafeterias were "required" to use Styrofoam cups or that the cafeterias are part of Koch Industries. House cafeterias are operated by congressional administrative offices, not owned by a private conglomerate, and no credible reports show a Republican mandate linking cafeteria cups to Koch.

claim: Wisconsin’s economy has "tanked" under Gov. Scott Walker and "so far in 2015 over 6,685 people have been laid off, already more than in all of 2014."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Broad economic indicators for Wisconsin during Scott Walker’s tenure through 2015 generally showed net job gains and a declining unemployment rate rather than an economy that "tanked," and the specific assertion that "over 6,685 people have been laid off so far in 2015, already more than in all of 2014" is not corroborated by statewide labor data or official layoff records and appears to overstate or misattribute layoff counts.

claim: Says Nancy Pelosi said, "Building a wall will violate the rights of millions of illegals." ​
rationale: There is no reliable record of Nancy Pelosi uttering that exact sentence. While Pelosi has repeatedly criticized construction of a border wall on policy and humanitarian grounds, the precise quoted wording about "violat[ing] the rights of millions of illegals" does not appear in credible transcripts or news reports and likely misattributes or paraphrases her views.

claim: Says Scott Walker rejected legislation to make college loan payments tax deductible and the result was "to raise taxes on students."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Vetoing or rejecting a bill to allow a new tax deduction would prevent that deduction from taking effect but does not itself 'raise taxes' above the existing law — it leaves tax policy unchanged rather than increasing rates. Without a specific bill, jurisdiction, and timing, the causal claim that Walker's action 'raised taxes on students' is unsupported.

claim: Cher "is moving to Canada because of President Trump."
rationale: Cher did make public, often jocular comments about moving to Canada in reaction to Donald Trump's election, but there is no credible evidence she actually relocated to Canada because of him. Media coverage and her own posts frame the remarks as expressions of displeasure or hyperbole rather than a confirmed move.

claim: Says over 90 percent of Travis County’s eligible residents have registered to vote.
rationale: There is no evidence that Travis County overall has more than 90% of eligible residents registered; county-level registration rates in U.S. jurisdictions are typically below 90%, and available historical data for Travis County shows registration rates lower than that threshold. Without a specific date or definition of “eligible” (citizen voting-age population vs total adult population), the claim is unlikely to be accurate for the entire county.

claim: Says a CNN headline said, "In And Out is the fast food of white supremacists."
rationale: There is no evidence that CNN published a headline reading "In And Out is the fast food of white supremacists." This phrasing appears to be a misattribution or social-media meme; while CNN has reported on controversies involving the chain, it did not run a headline with that explicit wording.

claim: Bing Energy said it decided to move to Florida because of Gov. Rick Scott’s "plan to eliminate the corporate tax."
rationale: I am not aware of any verifiable public statement or reputable news report in which Bing Energy explicitly said it moved to Florida because of Gov. Rick Scott’s ‘plan to eliminate the corporate tax.’ While Scott has advocated eliminating or reducing the corporate income tax and firms sometimes cite tax climate when relocating, this specific attribution to Bing Energy appears unverified or misattributed.

claim: Bill White "is discriminating. He's taking jobs from African Americans and giving them to his friends."
rationale: This is an unverified allegation about an individual's hiring practices. There is no widely reported or corroborated evidence (such as official investigations, court findings, or credible reporting) establishing that Bill White systematically removed jobs from African Americans to give them to friends, and the claim appears to be a politically charged accusation that requires supporting documentation.

claim: Says Joe Biden has a medical device implanted in his skull so he can hear someone give him answers to questions.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Biden has a medical device implanted in his skull that lets someone feed him answers; mainstream fact-checkers and medical experts have debunked this rumor. Such an implant would be medically and logistically extraordinary and would likely be documented or reported by his medical team and independent journalists, which it has not been.

claim: "Our economy created over 6.5 million new jobs just last year, more jobs in one year than ever before in the history of the United States of America."
rationale: Official BLS data for the most recent full year show total nonfarm payroll employment rose by roughly 6.3–6.5 million, not clearly "over 6.5 million," and whether it is the largest single-year gain depends on the employment series used and the exact 12‑month window. Historical comparisons show other years have had comparable or larger gains depending on whether one uses the payroll (establishment) series or the household survey and on the chosen year span, so the blanket claim is inaccurate without specifying the measure and period.

claim: A president must "obtain Congress' consent before formally accepting the Nobel Prize."
rationale: Although the Constitution's foreign emoluments clause bars officers from accepting presents or emoluments from foreign states without Congress' consent, in practice and common legal interpretation international prizes like the Nobel have been accepted by U.S. presidents (for example Theodore Roosevelt, Woodrow Wilson and Barack Obama) without seeking formal congressional approval. The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded by a Norwegian committee and is generally not treated as a prohibited foreign office or title that would trigger required congressional consent.

claim: "We’ve got an average of 5,600 soldiers committing suicide. That’s about 20 a day."
rationale: The arithmetic is incorrect and the terminology is ambiguous. 5,600 deaths per year equates to about 15 per day, not 20, and U.S. official data distinguish active-duty service member suicides (roughly 500–600/year) from veteran suicides (around 6,000/year), so the claim mixes categories and misstates the daily rate.

claim: Says President Barack Obama promised he would cut the deficit in half, but instead will at least double it.
rationale: During the 2008 campaign President Obama pledged to cut the federal deficit roughly in half by the end of his first term. After the 2008 financial crisis the annual deficit surged above $1 trillion in 2009–2012 (well over double the pre-crisis FY2008 deficit), so the deficit did increase to at least twice the earlier level during his presidency.

claim: In the U.S. agreement with the Cuban government, "no commitment was made to allowing the establishment of political parties or to even begin the semblance of a transition to a democracy."
rationale: The 2014–2015 U.S.-Cuba normalization agreements and joint statements restored diplomatic relations and addressed travel, consular and economic issues but did not secure a Cuban commitment to permit opposition political parties or to begin a transition to multiparty democracy. U.S. officials voiced hopes for human rights improvements, but the formal agreements did not include binding requirements for political pluralism or democratic transition.

claim: "We do not have an overcrowding problem. As a matter of fact, Rhode Island has one of the lowest incarceration rates in the country."
rationale: The claim bundles two assertions that are not uniformly true. While Rhode Island's incarceration rate has often been below the national average and in the lower half of states in recent years, whether it is “one of the lowest” depends on the year and metric used; furthermore, reports and corrections data have documented capacity and crowding issues at Rhode Island facilities at various times, so the categorical statement that there is no overcrowding problem is not reliably supported without more context.

claim: U.S. military involvement in Libya "allowed thousands of surface-to-air missiles to fall into the hands of radical Islamists."
rationale: While the 2011 NATO/US-assisted intervention and the collapse of the Libyan state led to widespread looting and proliferation of weapons, independent assessments do not support the claim that "thousands" of surface-to-air missiles fell into the hands of radical Islamists. Official and expert estimates after 2011 warned of hundreds (not multiple thousands) of MANPADS and other air-defense items being unaccounted for, and dispersal resulted from state collapse and looting by many actors, not solely U.S. military action.

claim: Says U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement "will be at every polling station" on Nov. 3, 2020.
rationale: There is no evidence that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement planned to be physically present 'at every polling station' on Nov 3, 2020. ICE and other federal officials denied any plan to station agents at polling places, and independent fact-checkers rejected the claim.

claim: "The reality is when you look at the Biden plan, it reads an awful lot like what President Trump and I and our task force have been doing every step of the way."
rationale: The claim asserts Biden’s plan “reads an awful lot like” Trump’s task-force approach at every step, but public policy documents and reporting show clear differences in priorities and mechanisms (e.g., federal coordination, mask guidance, testing strategy and mandates, and economic relief frameworks). While there is overlap on some goals like vaccine development and reopening phases, Biden’s proposals emphasized a stronger federal role, mask requirements, and expanded testing/contact-tracing compared with the Trump task force’s documented actions, so the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: "Only a few months ago the FBI arrested three Broward County Commissioners for accepting millions of dollars in trade for illegal favors."
rationale: There are no credible, widely reported accounts that the FBI recently arrested three Broward County Commissioners for accepting millions in exchange for illegal favors. Major arrests of multiple county commissioners would have received substantial local and national coverage; while individual Broward officials have faced legal troubles at times, this specific claim is not supported by verified news.

claim: "In the 2000 Florida election, at least 1,100 eligible voters were wrongly dropped from voting rolls in an attempt to purge a list of felons. Many of those who were dropped showed up to vote and were told they could not."
rationale: The broad claim that Florida ran a flawed felon-purge in 2000 and that eligible voters were wrongly flagged is supported by post-election investigations, but the specific assertion that 'at least 1,100' eligible voters were wrongly dropped and many then showed up and were told they could not vote is not well supported by a single authoritative count. Different investigations and news reports produced varying estimates (often in the thousands) and the precise numbers of wrongly removed voters and those turned away at polls remain disputed. Therefore the specific numeric claim as stated is misleading.

claim: Says Adam Putnam "was for amnesty."
rationale: The claim is misleading: Adam Putnam has not publicly advocated a blanket 'amnesty' for undocumented immigrants. He has in the past supported tougher enforcement and has spoken of limited, conditional measures (such as pathways tied to enforcement or earning legal status for certain groups), but he explicitly rejected broad, unconditional amnesty during his campaigns.

claim: A poll conducted in Egypt revealed that 80 percent of Egyptians oppose receiving foreign aid from the United States.
rationale: I am not aware of any reputable, widely reported poll showing that 80% of Egyptians oppose receiving U.S. foreign aid; public opinion in Egypt about the United States and its assistance has varied by year and by question wording, and no authoritative source corroborates that exact figure. The claim appears to be an unsupported or misreported statistic without a cited poll or date.

claim: "So that 2005 energy bill was a big step backwards on the path to clean, renewable energy. That's why I voted against it."
rationale: The statement combines a subjective policy judgment (“a big step backwards”) and a claim about motive for a vote. Whether the 2005 energy bill was a ‘‘big step backwards’’ is a contested, value-laden assessment and cannot be established as an objective fact; likewise the claim about the voter’s motive is unverifiable here without a direct contemporaneous statement or record. Absent specific evidence tying the speaker’s stated reason to the vote, the combined claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: About "1 percent of all the gun sellers are responsible for more than half of the guns that are used in crimes."
rationale: Analyses of ATF trace data and academic/advocacy studies have repeatedly found that a very small fraction of licensed gun dealers (roughly 1%) account for a majority of guns later traced to crimes. The claim is a commonly cited summary of those findings, though exact percentages vary by year and dataset.

claim: "Women in Oregon are paid 79 cents for every dollar paid to men. If the wage gap was eliminated, a working woman in Oregon would have enough money for 2,877 gallons of gas, 72 more weeks of food for her family or nearly 12 more months of rent."
rationale: The statement mixes a broadly cited summary statistic (women earning about $0.79 per dollar compared with men is commonly reported for the U.S. in certain years and when using median annual earnings for full‑time workers) with a set of precise purchasing-power calculations that depend on unstated assumptions. The specific figures for gallons of gas, weeks of food, and months of rent require a particular year, price levels, definition of “working woman” (full‑time/median), household size, and methodology; without those assumptions the numeric claims cannot be verified and are misleading. Therefore the overall claim presented as a fact is not reliably supported as stated.

claim: Says U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson "voted to cut $700m from Medicare."
rationale: The statement is misleading. There is no clear roll-call where Sen. Ron Johnson voted to cut exactly $700 million from Medicare; fact-checkers have noted that critics sometimes conflate or misstate votes on budget resolutions or proposals that projected roughly $700 billion in Medicare reductions over a decade, not a $700 million one-time cut.

claim: "There have been 30 published polls in this election cycle and Harry Reid's been trailing in every single one."
rationale: The claim asserts a precise count (30 published polls) and that Harry Reid trailed in every one, but no timeframe or sources are provided and such unanimity across dozens of polls is extremely unlikely. Polls vary by sponsor, timing, and methodology, so without a specific election cycle and list of polls this statement cannot be verified and should be treated as false.

claim: The number of pregnant women who have miscarried increased by "366% in just six weeks" as a result of their receiving a COVID-19 vaccine.
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed studies and CDC analyses found no evidence that COVID-19 vaccination increases the risk of miscarriage, and claims of a 366% rise rely on misinterpreted passive-reporting counts rather than controlled epidemiologic data. Passive surveillance systems (like VAERS) record unverified reports and can show spikes from increased reporting or rollout timing, which do not establish causation.

claim: "Mexico’s Next President Calls for An Invasion Of The US"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that any incoming Mexican president has publicly called for invading the United States; such a statement would have triggered immediate, widespread international reporting and diplomatic responses. Official records, mainstream media coverage, and statements from Mexican presidential campaigns emphasize diplomacy and domestic issues rather than military aggression toward the U.S.

claim: "In eighth grade math, we’ve fallen to ninth place."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify—it omits which country 'we' refers to, which assessment (e.g., TIMSS or PISA), and which year. International math rankings for eighth-grade students vary by assessment and year, so a blanket claim that 'we've fallen to ninth place' is unsubstantiated without those specifics.

claim: "Certainly we're going to be the most restrictive state in the land … in terms of who can get medical marijuana, how it will be prescribed and how it will be achieved in terms of moving it into the marketplace."
rationale: This is an unverified, forward-looking comparative claim presented without context (which state, what timeframe or enacted laws). US states’ medical marijuana eligibility, prescribing rules, and market rules vary widely and change over time, so asserting with certainty that one state 'will be the most restrictive in the land' cannot be confirmed from available evidence. Without specific, time-bound policy comparisons or enacted statutes proving that status, the claim is unsupported.

claim: "Over 65% of the country believes that (the) 2020 election was fraudulent. That number was around 35% a year ago."
rationale: National polling from major survey organizations has generally found that roughly 30–40% of all Americans say the 2020 election was fraudulent or not legitimate, while much larger shares of Republicans (often in the 60–70% range) hold that belief. The claim appears to conflate the Republican subgroup with the entire country and misstates the overall change from ~35% to over 65%.

claim: Billie Eilish's younger sister has an OnlyFans account.
rationale: Billie Eilish is publicly known to have one sibling, her older brother Finneas O'Connell; she does not have a publicly documented younger sister. There are no credible reports or evidence that a younger sister of Billie Eilish exists or maintains an OnlyFans account, so the claim is false.

claim: If you work 40 hours a week at the proposed minimum wage of $10.10 an hour, "you get out of poverty."
rationale: Earning $10.10/hour for 40 hours a week is about $21,000 per year, which may exceed the federal poverty line for a single person but is insufficient for many households with children or in high-cost areas; many full-time minimum-wage workers remain in or near poverty. The statement as written is an absolute claim and is therefore false because outcomes depend on household size, location, taxes, and benefits.

claim: "I have cut taxes 63 times, including a 2006 property tax reduction that ranks as the largest in state history."
rationale: The claim is specific but lacks attribution to a named official and a named state, and I cannot verify a universally recognized record of '63 tax cuts' or a 2006 property tax reduction described as the largest in any state's history. Such round numbers and superlatives are common in political exaggeration and typically require state-specific legislative records or independent auditing to confirm. Without corroborating evidence tied to a specific jurisdiction and official record, the claim cannot be treated as factual.

claim: "A black woman in New York City is 12 times more likely to die in childbirth than a white woman."
rationale: There are substantial and well‑documented racial disparities in maternal mortality in New York City, but the exact multiplier depends strongly on the years, definitions (maternal death vs pregnancy‑related death) and small sample fluctuations; a blanket claim that a Black woman is 12 times more likely to die than a white woman is not reliably true across standard datasets. Some short time periods or narrowly defined metrics have produced very large ratios, but typical multi‑year analyses show smaller, though still large, disparities.

claim: Obamacare is a "massive, massive income redistribution" with "$250 billion a year in Medicaid expansion (and) in the subsidy structure that's basically being paid for by people on Medicare, through Medicare cuts, and a lot of tax increases."
rationale: The claim mixes some accurate components of the ACA (it expanded Medicaid and included Medicare payment reductions and new taxes) with misleading and exaggerated numbers and attributions. Independent budget analyses do not support a $250 billion per year Medicaid expansion figure, and while the law included Medicare payment cuts to providers and targeted tax increases, those measures and the general federal revenues — not direct transfers from typical Medicare beneficiaries — primarily financed the law. Labeling the ACA a ‘‘massive income redistribution’’ paid for as described overstates and simplifies how the law was funded.

claim: The "president of Drag Queen Story Hour" was "arrested, charged with child pornography."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that the national or widely recognized "president of Drag Queen Story Hour" was arrested and charged with child pornography. Independent fact-checkers and mainstream news outlets have not corroborated the viral social-media claims, which appear to conflate or misidentify individuals or incidents.

claim: Says Texas high school "graduation rates are at an all-time high—the third-highest in the nation—which represents a significant turnaround from just a few short years ago."
rationale: The claim is misleading: while Texas has seen rising graduation rates and recent record highs by its own reporting, it has not consistently ranked third-highest among all states in national adjusted-cohort graduation rate rankings. National data and state-by-state comparisons typically show several states (e.g., Iowa, New Jersey, Massachusetts and others) with higher rates than Texas in recent years, and the claim lacks a clear year or metric to substantiate the specific "third-highest" assertion.

claim: "If there were not derivatives, there would be no bank loans at all today."
rationale: Derivatives are risk-management and transfer instruments that facilitate hedging and large-scale or cross-currency lending, but they are not a prerequisite for lending. Banks have issued loans for centuries before modern derivatives markets existed, and many loans today are made without any derivatives hedging.

claim: Says Measure 3-386 will cost a fortune for elections while Measure 3-388 will cost less.
rationale: The claim compares costs for 'Measure 3-386' and 'Measure 3-388' but provides no jurisdiction or source and I have no verified records tying those exact measure numbers to specific fiscal analyses. Without an official fiscal impact statement or authoritative budget estimate for the named measures, the assertion that one "will cost a fortune" and the other "will cost less" cannot be substantiated.

claim: "I’ve never supported legislation that invades people’s choices about contraception."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because the speaker is not identified and there is no timeframe or definition of what counts as "invading" contraceptive choice. Verifying such a universal statement requires checking a specific person’s complete voting, sponsorship, and public record; absent that, the claim cannot be established as true and is therefore treated as false.

claim: "We are currently using only around 20% of our testing capacity."
rationale: The claim is unverified because it does not specify who 'we' refers to, what type of testing is meant, or the timeframe. Testing capacity utilization varies widely by jurisdiction and date, and without a cited official dataset showing ~20% usage the statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: The Affordable Care Act "will likely go down as the biggest tax increase in history."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act included several targeted tax increases (e.g., Medicare payroll surtax on high earners, net investment income tax, excise taxes and other levies), but these were modest relative to major historical U.S. tax increases. Large revenue expansions during World War I, World War II and other periods increased tax receipts by far larger amounts or shares of GDP, so the ACA is not plausibly the largest tax increase in U.S. history.

claim: "Making public colleges and universities tuition-free, that exists in countries all over the world, used to exist in the United States."
rationale: While many countries today offer tuition‑free public higher education, the United States did not have a sustained, nationwide tuition‑free system for public colleges and universities. Some U.S. states and individual institutions historically charged little or no tuition for in‑state students or offered broad waivers at various times, but there was no universal national policy making public higher education tuition‑free.

claim: "Beginning in the early 1990s, we built barriers in 4 sectors at our southern border. Since each was built, those sectors have seen massive drops in apprehensions of people crossing the border illegally," including 90 percent to 95 percent decreases in the Tucson, Yuma, San Diego and El Paso sectors. ​
rationale: It is true that barrier construction and stepped-up enforcement began in the early 1990s (e.g., Operation Gatekeeper in San Diego and Hold the Line in El Paso) and several sectors later saw large drops in Border Patrol apprehensions. But the blanket assertion that Tucson, Yuma, San Diego and El Paso all experienced 90–95% decreases is inaccurate: only some sectors (notably San Diego and El Paso) saw declines of that magnitude, while declines in Tucson and Yuma were smaller or occurred at different times. The statement also over-attributes the declines to barriers alone, ignoring other factors (enforcement posture, migrant flows, economic conditions).

claim: "I'm not taking any corporate PAC money."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it lacks an identified speaker, timeframe, and jurisdiction; whether it is true depends on that candidate’s campaign finance records. Many campaigns either accept donations from corporate-connected PACs or benefit from corporate-funded independent groups, and confirming the assertion requires checking FEC or state filings. Without that evidence the default judgement is that the blanket statement cannot be verified as true.

claim: "We in Indiana have . . . the highest credit rating in the nation."
rationale: The claim implies Indiana uniquely holds the nation’s single highest credit rating. Major rating agencies (S&P, Moody’s, Fitch) often assign top-tier ratings to multiple states; while Indiana has had strong/high ratings at times, it has not been uniquely the highest across agencies and years. Without a specific agency and date this statement is misleading.

claim: Says a deer became "riddled with tumors from eating plants sprayed with Monsanto’s Roundup."
rationale: There is no credible, documented evidence that a specific deer was proven to be "riddled with tumors" as a result of eating plants sprayed with Monsanto’s Roundup. Reports making this claim are anecdotal or based on viral images without veterinary necropsy, histopathology, or toxicology linking glyphosate exposure to those tumors. Scientific literature and wildlife pathology do not support a confirmed causal link between Roundup exposure and tumor formation in deer.

claim: "About 80 percent of (the manufacturing and agriculture) tax credit goes to claimants who are making $1 million or more."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported as written: it does not specify which jurisdiction, which specific tax credit, or the time period. While some business tax benefits are concentrated among higher‑income firms or large claimants, there is no general, well‑supported finding that 'about 80 percent' of manufacturing and agriculture tax credits go to claimants making $1 million or more across all programs. Without a clearly identified program and empirical source, the blanket 80% figure cannot be verified and is likely incorrect.

claim: "At his father's bank, Alexi made tens of millions in risky loans to convicted mobsters. Then, the bank collapsed."
rationale: This mixes fact and exaggeration. Alexi Giannoulias ran his family's Broadway Bank and the bank failed in 2010, and the institution made some controversial loans (including to people later convicted of unrelated crimes), but independent reporting and regulators did not substantiate that he personally made "tens of millions" in risky loans specifically to convicted mobsters—that phrasing overstates and conflates borrowers and criminal labels.

claim: "Death penalty opponents like Roy Cooper and Josh Stein have imposed a de-facto moratorium on capital punishment."
rationale: This overstates the situation. While individual officials who oppose capital punishment can slow or limit executions by declining to pursue death sentences or issuing reprieves, there is no clear evidence that Roy Cooper and Josh Stein have formally imposed a statewide, legally binding moratorium; North Carolina still retains the death penalty in statute and prosecutions can seek it. Periods with few or no executions have also resulted from court rulings, procedural problems, and prosecutorial choices rather than a unilateral statewide moratorium.

claim: Says Sandra Bullock said to Hillary Clinton, "If you don’t like our president you can leave and never come back again."
rationale: There is no evidence from reputable news outlets, transcripts, or fact-checkers that Sandra Bullock addressed Hillary Clinton with that phrase; the line appears to have circulated as an unverified social-media claim. Bullock's public statements and coverage do not support this attribution, so the quote is almost certainly misattributed or fabricated.

claim: During the lead-up to the American Revolutionary War, "some guy in Boston got his head blown off because he tried to secretly raise the tax on tea."
rationale: There is no historical record of a person in Boston having "his head blown off" for trying to secretly raise the tax on tea. The Tea Act (1773) was passed by Parliament (it actually lowered certain duties and granted the East India Company a monopoly), and colonial responses were protests, tarring-and-feathering, and the Boston Tea Party; the Boston Massacre involved British soldiers firing on colonists but was unrelated to someone raising tea taxes. The claim appears to conflate or invent events.

claim: Protest vandalism in Richmond "all started two weeks ago when Mayor Stoney’s police gassed - tear gassed - a peaceful crowd of protesters, moms and children, at 7:30 p.m. sharp."
rationale: The claim bundles precise, verifiable details (exact 7:30 p.m. timing, that police under Mayor Stoney tear-gassed a peaceful crowd of ‘moms and children’, and that all subsequent vandalism “started” at that moment) that are not fully supported by available reporting. Contemporary coverage of Richmond protests shows police used crowd-control tactics on some nights and accounts of who was present, timing, and whether vandalism began then are contested, so the definite causal statement is unverified.

claim: A 13-year-old girl "is now in critical care in the hospital here in Halifax because her heart stopped right after she had a vaccine."
rationale: There is no independently verifiable public record or hospital/public-health statement confirming that a 13-year-old in Halifax went into critical care because her heart stopped immediately after a vaccine. Temporal proximity alone does not establish causation, and such serious incidents would normally be publicly confirmed and investigated before being reported as vaccine-caused.

claim: Kyle Rittenhouse was an "armed person" crossing state lines when he came to Kenosha protests in 2020.
rationale: Kyle Rittenhouse, an Antioch, Illinois resident, drove to Kenosha, Wisconsin on August 25, 2020 and was carrying a semiautomatic rifle. Court testimony, video evidence, and contemporaneous news reporting established that he crossed from Illinois into Wisconsin while armed.

claim: As Florida secretary of state, Kurt Browning "allowed 1,800 illegal voters to register in Florida."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Browning personally "allowed 1,800 illegal voters" to register. The 1,800 figure stems from preliminary DMV flag lists and reporting errors; voter registration is carried out by local supervisors and subsequent state reviews found far fewer confirmed noncitizen or ineligible registrations, with many flagged records being duplicates or data errors.

claim: Says President Barack Obama's parents were communists.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that either of Barack Obama’s parents were members of a Communist Party. Biographical records show his father was a Kenyan economist and government employee with anti-colonial views at times, and his mother was an anthropologist and development specialist; neither is documented as a communist.

claim: Says New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg says "we can only have three bullets" and "the NRA wants firearms with nukes on them."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Michael Bloomberg said those exact lines; the statements are extreme and appear fabricated or satirical rather than verbatim quotes. Major news outlets and transcripts of Bloomberg’s public remarks do not record him claiming 'we can only have three bullets' or that 'the NRA wants firearms with nukes on them.'

claim: Says Hillary Clinton’s energy agenda "will cost the U.S. economy over $5 trillion"
rationale: There is no authoritative, widely accepted analysis establishing that Hillary Clinton’s energy agenda would unambiguously 'cost the U.S. economy over $5 trillion.' Estimates of policy costs vary greatly by which specific measures, time horizon, discounting, and included benefits are counted, and the $5 trillion figure is tied to partisan or worst-case studies rather than a consensus estimate.

claim: "In Cobb County, every meeting opened with a prayer. The ACLU objected. Sued ... [Sam] Olens took on the ACLU and won!"
rationale: The claim overstates and misattributes a simple outcome. While the ACLU and others have challenged legislative prayers and there were local disputes over prayers at Cobb County meetings, the definitive legal shift came from broader court decisions (not a single Cobb County courtroom triumph credited solely to Sam Olens). Olens was a Cobb County official and later Georgia Attorney General, but portraying the dispute as ‘Olens took on the ACLU and won’ is misleading.

claim: The CDC delivers groceries and cleaning products "twice while you’re in quarantine."
rationale: The CDC is primarily a public health agency that issues guidance and coordinates disease control, not a provider of routine grocery or cleaning-product deliveries to people in quarantine. While local health departments, community organizations, or emergency response agencies may arrange deliveries, there is no general CDC program that delivers groceries 'twice while you’re in quarantine.'

claim: Says President Obama has cracked down "on employers who are attracting undocumented immigrants and hiring them more than any previous president."
rationale: The Obama administration did increase and publicize employer-focused immigration enforcement (prosecutions, audits, and administrative sanctions) and emphasized penalizing employers who hire undocumented workers. However, the claim that he cracked down on employers “more than any previous president” is a broad comparative assertion that is not clearly supported by comprehensive, comparable metrics across administrations and time periods. Historical enforcement levels vary by metric (criminal prosecutions, civil fines, raids) and era, so the absolute comparative statement is unsupported.

claim: The impeachment process against Donald Trump "provides fewer due process protections and fewer protections for minority rights than what we have seen in previous impeachment efforts."
rationale: The claim is vague and context-dependent: impeachment procedures are set by the Constitution and by the House and Senate rules in each case, and those procedures have varied across impeachments. Some observers argued that aspects of the Trump impeachments were more expedited or limited relative to certain prior cases, while others argued they were within normal historical practice; there is no clear, objective standard showing they universally provided fewer due-process or minority-protection safeguards than all previous impeachments.

claim: "[N]early one in three primary care doctors are forced to limit the number of Medicare patients they see."
rationale: Multiple national physician surveys and reports in recent years have found that roughly one-third of primary care doctors say they limit or stop taking Medicare patients, citing low reimbursement and administrative burden as reasons. The phrasing "nearly one in three" matches the approximate proportion reported in these surveys.

claim: "Not a single person in the crowd on January 6 was found to be carrying a firearm. Not one."
rationale: Post‑event investigations and arrests showed that firearms and other weapons were recovered from some people connected to the January 6 events and from vehicles used by attendees, and the Department of Justice brought weapons-related charges against several participants. Therefore the categorical claim that not a single person was found carrying a firearm is incorrect.

claim: "More than 9,000 Rhode Island voters used the Moderate Party master lever mechanism and they didn't have a single Moderate on their ballot."
rationale: I find no corroborating evidence that more than 9,000 Rhode Island voters used a Moderate Party “master lever” while no Moderate candidates appeared on their ballots. Official ballot design and election tallies published by state election officials record party-line votes and candidate slates; such a large anomalous count would be documented and reported, but there is no widely reported or verifiable record of this specific occurrence. Without a specific election date or official precinct tallies this claim is unsubstantiated and implausible given how party-line voting and ballot listings are administered.

claim: In 2008, "only 54 percent of Latinos in Texas were registered to vote and only 35 percent actually turned out."
rationale: I could not corroborate the precise 54% registration and 35% turnout figures as stated for Texas Latinos in 2008; available sources show higher Hispanic registration and turnout among eligible/citizen voters in 2008 nationally and the claim likely mixes metrics or populations. The statement appears to conflate 'Latinos' (which may include noncitizens) with 'eligible/citizen' voters or misstates whether the turnout figure is of registered voters or of the total Latino population.

claim: Photo shows "the aftermath of the ‘CHOP’ Zone’ in Seattle, WA. July 2020."
rationale: I cannot verify the claim because no photo or metadata was provided; verification requires inspecting the image, its metadata, or independent reporting. The Capitol Hill Organized Protest (CHOP) enclave in Seattle existed primarily in June 2020 and was cleared at the end of June, so a photo labeled as the 'aftermath' in July 2020 is unlikely without supporting provenance. Because the claim lacks evidence and timing is inconsistent with well-documented events, I judge it false absent corroboration.

claim: Republicans "created a trillion dollar prescription drug entitlement program without paying for it."
rationale: The Republican-led 2003 Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act created Medicare Part D, a large federal prescription drug benefit. Analyses by the Congressional Budget Office and others projected long-term costs that exceed a trillion dollars on common multi-decade horizons, and the law did not establish dedicated offsets sufficient to fully pay for those added federal outlays, increasing net federal spending.

claim: Says Donald Trump "doesn't make a thing in America."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that Donald Trump “doesn't make a thing in America,” which is incorrect. The Trump Organization is U.S.-based and operates many U.S. businesses (real estate, hotels, golf courses) that produce services and economic activity in America, even though some Trump-branded manufactured goods have been produced overseas. The blanket phrasing ignores these domestic operations and therefore is false.

claim: Gas prices during the Obama-Biden administration were $5.49 a gallon.
rationale: The Obama-Biden administration (2009–2017) did not see U.S. national average gasoline prices of $5.49 per gallon; historical national average data from that period never reached that level. While some local stations or certain California/regional markets occasionally showed pump prices above $5 for short periods, the claim as stated (without specifying location or date) is misleading and inaccurate for the national average.

claim: "When the national debt reaches $15 trillion, it means that U.S. debt-to-GDP ratio will reach 99.7 percent of our debt and this is $47,900 for every living American."
rationale: The claim presents two precise ratios without specifying a year or whether it refers to gross debt or debt held by the public. Whether $15 trillion equals ~99.7% of GDP depends entirely on the GDP figure used (GDP near $15T would imply a ~100% ratio, but GDP and debt levels fluctuate), and the per‑person figure (~$47,900) depends on the population baseline used. Because the statement gives firm percentages and a per‑capita number as if fixed, but they vary by year and definition, the claim is not reliably true as stated.

claim: Says he "raised graduation rates to nearly 90 percent."
rationale: The statement provides no named individual, timeframe, jurisdiction, or data source, so it is unsubstantiated as presented. Graduation-rate figures are highly context-dependent (different cohorts, definitions, and reporting changes), and without specifics the claim cannot be verified.

claim: "Disneyland estates have been used for MK-ULTRA mind control, human trafficking, occult rituals, and parading sexual deviants."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Disneyland properties were used for MK‑ULTRA experiments, human trafficking, occult rituals, or organized sexual parades. MK‑ULTRA was a mid‑20th century CIA program with declassified records that do not implicate Disneyland, and major journalism and law‑enforcement investigations have not substantiated such claims. These allegations appear to be unsubstantiated conspiracy theories rather than fact.

claim: "Of the 18 stadiums built from 2004 to 2013, 47 percent of the total cost came from public sources."
rationale: I cannot verify this precise 47% figure and available analyses of stadium financing for that period use different samples and definitions and report varying public shares. The claim likely mixes different kinds of public costs (direct construction subsidies, infrastructure, debt, tax breaks) without specifying methodology, making the specific percentage unsupported as stated.

claim: California has instituted a "bacon ban."
rationale: California has not enacted a statewide ban on bacon; pork products are legal to produce, sell, and consume statewide. Reports of a 'bacon ban' usually stem from confusion with animal welfare laws (such as Proposition 12), local institutional food policies, proposed legislation, or satire, none of which amount to a statewide prohibition on bacon.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "collaborated with Marxist regimes in the Soviet Union, Nicaragua and Cuba."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Bernie Sanders "collaborated" with Marxist regimes in the Soviet Union, Nicaragua, or Cuba. While Sanders made occasional visits to or expressed criticisms of U.S. policy toward those countries and met with officials (for example visiting Nicaragua and Cuba at different times), public records and reporting show no formal cooperation or operational collaboration with those governments. His long career as an independent/democratic socialist includes criticism of authoritarianism rather than documented collaboration.

claim: Says "some people in the Great State of North Carolina have been sent TWO BALLOTS. RIGGED ELECTION in waiting!"
rationale: The claim is presented without time, source, or evidence and reads like a broad assertion of coordinated fraud. While isolated cases of voters receiving duplicate mail ballots have occurred due to administrative errors, that alone is not proof of a “rigged” election and state election officials and safeguards (signature matching, duplicate-detection, provisional ballots) prevent simple double-vote fraud. Without corroborating official data showing widespread double-mailing and successful double voting, the blanket claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "As Ohio treasurer, Josh Mandel loaned your money to Chinese business interests, and Mandel opposed a bill holding Communist China accountable when they cheated and stole American jobs."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate-seeming but misleading elements with unsupported assertions. As Ohio Treasurer Mandel oversaw state investments and critics noted some exposure to Chinese companies through pooled or market investments, but there is no clear evidence he directly ‘loaned’ Ohio residents’ money to Chinese businesses in the literal sense implied. The allegation that he opposed a specific bill “holding Communist China accountable” is vague and unsupported — as state treasurer he did not vote on federal legislation, and no clear record ties him to opposing a named accountability bill in the way the claim asserts.

claim: Work requirements "have been proven to help impoverished families move from dependency to self-sufficiency."
rationale: Empirical research on work requirements is mixed: some programs produce modest short-term increases in employment, but they have not been consistently proven to move impoverished families into sustained self-sufficiency and can produce harms (e.g., benefit loss, increased hardship). Effects vary greatly by program design, available supports, and local labor markets, so the blanket claim that work requirements have been proven to achieve self-sufficiency is unsupported.

claim: "Greg Abbott said it would be a ‘waste’ to expand pre-k to all Texas children."
rationale: Multiple news reports and Abbott’s public statements record him opposing universal pre-K expansion in Texas and using language that it would be a "waste" (of taxpayer dollars/resources) to expand pre-K to all children. He advocated targeted programs instead of a universal expansion.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Paul Ryan promised to "end health care for our seniors."
rationale: Paul Ryan did not literally promise to "end health care for our seniors." He authored and promoted plans to restructure Medicare (e.g., premium-support/voucher-style approaches and spending reductions) that critics said would effectively end traditional Medicare as an entitlement, but his stated proposals focused on transforming funding and delivery rather than an explicit pledge to cut off seniors' health care entirely. The claim misstates the nature and wording of his proposals.

claim: On Donald Trump’s plan to cut federal funding to sanctuary cities, "because of a decision by the Supreme Court, no president's in a position to cut off funding across the board. It has to be very specific to the matter at hand."
rationale: Supreme Court precedent and separation-of-powers principles prevent a president from unilaterally rescinding or broadly redirecting funds that Congress has appropriated; the executive generally needs statutory authority or narrowly tailored legal grounds to withhold money. Courts have required specificity and congressional authorization when the executive conditions or cancels funding, so a blanket across-the-board cutoff is legally vulnerable.

claim: A Virginia principal "expelled two kids for wearing a crucifix around their necks  saying, ‘there is no place for religion at school.’"
rationale: I cannot find credible, verifiable evidence that a Virginia principal legitimately expelled two students for wearing crucifix necklaces and said, ‘there is no place for religion at school.’ Public schools in the U.S. are generally prohibited from punishing passive religious expression in that way, and a disciplinary action this extreme would have produced widely reported documentation and legal challenges.

claim: "Tony Evers is cutting child support."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Governor Tony Evers has enacted a policy that reduces court-ordered child support payments. Individual child support obligations are set and modified by courts, and while a governor can propose budget changes affecting program administration, that is not the same as 'cutting child support' payments themselves.

claim: "Moderna patent uncovers horror nanocensor contained in bioweapon."
rationale: The claim is a vague, sensational assertion not supported by evidence. Moderna’s publicly available patents cover mRNA constructs and delivery technologies (e.g., lipid nanoparticles) for vaccines and therapeutics; they do not describe a covert “horror nanocensor” or a bioweapon. Independent experts and patent reviewers do not identify weapons or secret surveillance devices in these filings.

claim: "When they say Mexico can't pay for the wall, I say of course they can. We have a trade deficit with Mexico that's unbelievably big. ... It's billions and billions of dollars -- far more than what we're talking about for the wall."
rationale: The United States has run a sizable bilateral trade deficit with Mexico in recent years, measured in the tens of billions of dollars annually. Many public estimates for constructing the proposed border wall were in the low tens of billions; the Mexico trade deficit has exceeded those commonly quoted wall cost figures, so the claim that the deficit is "billions and billions" and larger than many wall estimates is accurate. The inference that the deficit means Mexico can or will pay is political, but the numerical comparison is factually supported.

claim: Says "for the first time ever," Texas lawmakers are not funding student population growth.
rationale: The absolute claim that this is "for the first time ever" is unlikely to be true. Texas lawmakers have a long history of adjusting school funding and in prior budget cycles there have been shortfalls or changes in how enrollment growth was funded, so not funding growth would not be unprecedented.

claim: "I have asked the Division of Emergency Management to report directly to me."
rationale: There is no supporting context, date, jurisdiction, or publicly verifiable evidence provided to confirm this administrative action. Changes to agency reporting lines are typically documented via official orders, memos, or press statements; without such corroboration the claim cannot be verified and should be treated as unproven.

claim: Says the United States has the "highest corporate tax rate in the world."
rationale: This is false. The U.S. federal corporate tax rate was cut from 35% to 21% by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, and even after adding state-level taxes the typical combined U.S. rate is in the mid‑20s percent — not the highest in the world. Several countries have higher statutory or combined corporate tax burdens than the United States.

claim: "As your Lieutenant Governor…I cut your taxes."
rationale: The claim is presented without identifying which lieutenant governor or jurisdiction and is therefore unverifiable as a general statement. In most U.S. states and similar systems, lieutenant governors do not have unilateral authority to cut taxes—tax changes require legislative action and typically the governor's approval—so the blanket statement is misleading. It could be true in a specific, documented circumstance (for example if the individual served as acting governor or was instrumental in passing tax legislation), but as stated it cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Our economy is so much stronger than when (Barack Obama and Joe Biden) took office. Nearly 15 million new private-sector jobs."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and the cited figure is inconsistent with official labor statistics. When Barack Obama and Joe Biden took office (January 2009) and through the end of Obama’s presidency, private‑sector payrolls rose by roughly 11–12 million jobs, not “nearly 15 million.” Because the statement gives no clear timeframe and overstates the commonly reported BLS totals, it is not supported.

claim: John McCain's health care plan "leaves you on your own to pay McCain’s health insurance tax."
rationale: McCain’s 2008 health care proposals did not create a new ‘‘health insurance tax’’ or an individual mandate penalty; they focused on tax credits/subsidies, allowing purchases across state lines, and market-based reforms. Saying his plan ‘‘leaves you on your own to pay McCain’s health insurance tax’’ misstates those proposals — critics argued subsidies were insufficient, but the plan did not impose a specific new tax on individuals to buy insurance.

claim: "Snitker has been virtually ignored by the major media."
rationale: The statement is subjective and broadly inaccurate: Brian Snitker (Atlanta Braves manager) has been covered extensively by major national and local media, particularly during the team's playoff runs and the 2021 World Series, including profiles, interviews, and game coverage. Saying he was "virtually ignored" conflicts with the observable volume of coverage in major sports and news outlets.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s book "The Art of the Deal" advises: "Never admit defeat. You win. If you don’t win, claim they cheated."
rationale: The exact wording is not a documented quotation from The Art of the Deal. While the book contains boastful negotiation advice and combative themes, this specific line appears to be a later paraphrase or summary of Trump's behavior rather than a verbatim passage in the published text.

claim: "Over the last 40 years, real wage growth has been flatlined because of the policies of the Federal Reserve ... It was all driven by the Federal Reserve."
rationale: While Federal Reserve monetary policy (through inflation and interest rates) can influence real wages, attributing four decades of flat real wage growth entirely to the Fed is incorrect. Empirical evidence points to multiple major factors—globalization/offshoring, technological change and automation, declining unionization and bargaining power, changes in labor market institutions and fiscal policy—that jointly explain wage stagnation.

claim: "California Democrat Maxine Waters charged on 3 counts."
rationale: There are no credible reports or official filings up to mid‑2024 indicating that U.S. Representative Maxine Waters has been criminally charged on three counts. She has been the subject of political criticism and calls for censure at times, but no indictment or formal charges against her have been reported by major news outlets or prosecutors.

claim: "Black Lives Matter, who are attacking law enforcement officers" -- Barack Obama "had them to the White House."
rationale: This is misleading. While President Obama and White House officials did meet with some activists and family members affected by police violence during his presidency, there is no evidence he invited or hosted an organization whose stated purpose is to 'attack law enforcement,' and Black Lives Matter as a movement does not officially advocate attacking officers. The claim conflates attendance at meetings with endorsement and wrongly characterizes the movement.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. John Carter "hasn’t held a town hall in five years."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Rep. John Carter completely avoided town halls for a continuous five-year period; members of Congress commonly hold constituent meetings, office hours, or virtual town halls (especially during the COVID-19 era) and such events would likely have been reported locally. Without a specific five-year window or definition of “town hall” (in-person vs. virtual), the blanket statement is unsupported.

claim: The omicron variant’s name is evidence the coronavirus pandemic is a hoax.
rationale: The name 'Omicron' is a label assigned by the WHO using the Greek alphabet to avoid geographic stigmatization and does not indicate fabrication. The Omicron variant corresponds to a genetically distinct SARS-CoV-2 lineage identified by viral genomic sequencing and linked to real increases in cases reported by multiple countries.

claim: "Woodrow Wilson borrowed $30 billion to fund World War I in 1917. That money has not been paid back. And we are still paying interest on it."
rationale: The U.S. did borrow roughly $20–30 billion to finance World War I using Liberty Bonds and taxes, but those bonds were issued with maturities and were redeemed or refunded over ensuing decades. The federal government is not still paying interest on original 1917 WWI bonds; any current interest payments are on later or refinanced federal debt, not unpaid 1917 borrowings.
